en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
Janamejaya said:
09,001.001 When Karṇa had thus been struck down in battle by Savyasācin, O twice-born one, what indeed did the few remaining Kurus do? And seeing his army being driven away, King Suyodhana—

What did the Kaurava do when the time had come for action by the Pāṇḍavas? I wish to hear this; tell me that, O best of the twice-born, for I am not satiated by hearing the great deeds of my ancestors.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O King, when Karṇa had been slain, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son Suyodhana was deeply submerged in an ocean of grief and became hopeless on all sides.
Lamenting again and again, "Alas Karna! Alas Karna!", he proceeded with great difficulty toward his own camp along with the kings who had survived the slaughter;
even though he was being consoled with arguments established by the scriptures.
The kings found no protection, remembering the slaughter of the Sūta’s son;
considering fate to be powerful and that which was destined to be, the king made his resolve for battle and went forth once more to fight.
Having duly appointed Śalya as the commander-in-chief and placing the King of Madra at the forefront, that bull among kings set out for battle;
the monarch marched forth for the fray together with the remaining kings who had survived the slaughter.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, a most tumultuous battle took place between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, resembling the war between the gods and the asuras.
Then, O great king, Śalya, having caused a carnage in the combat—
At midday, he was struck down by Dharmarāja in the midst of the Pāṇḍu army.
Thereupon King Duryodhana, his kinsmen having been slain,
fled from the field of battle and entered a formidable lake out of fear of his enemies.
Then,
in the afternoon of that day, having surrounded Suyodhana who was stationed there with great chariot-warriors,
Bhīmasena, by means of a stratagem, challenged him from the lake and struck him down.
When that great archer had been slain, three chariot-warriors remained among those who had survived the slaughter— Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa— as did Suyodhana along with his followers.
O king of kings, having entered the sleeping camp at night, those warriors led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, filled with fury, slaughtered the Pāñcāla soldiers.
Then, at the time of forenoon, Saṃjaya returned from the camp.
Dejected and overwhelmed by misery and grief, he entered the city.
Having quickly entered the city with his arms raised in distress,
he then, trembling, entered the king’s residence.
And that tiger among men wept, distressed, crying out, "O King!
"Alas! We are truly agitated by the death of this great-souled one. Alas! Time is indeed all-powerful, and its course is supreme."
"In this matter, destiny is powerful, while human effort is useless;
for there, all the kings, whose strength was equal to that of Śakra, were slain.
And as soon as he saw Pura, O King, all the people [saw] Saṃjaya."
O best of kings, overwhelmed by great affliction on all sides and deeply agitated,
he wept aloud, crying out, "Alas, O King!
O tiger among men, that entire city, including the children, was likewise filled with lamentation on every side.
Hearing the great cry of distress after the king had been slain,
he saw three bulls among men running there,
as if deprived of their senses, like madmen, and intensely tormented by grief.
Upon seeing the men, he spoke immediately, overcome with extreme sorrow. Thus, the charioteer, agitated, entered the royal palace and beheld the lord, the best of kings, whose wisdom was his eye.
And having seen the sinless one seated, surrounded on all sides by his daughters-in-law, O best of the Bharatas, as well as by Gāndhārī, Vidura,
and other friends, kinsmen, and well-wishers, [he approached].
O Janamejaya, as he was meditating on that very matter concerning the death of Karṇa,
the Sūta, weeping with a mind not at all joyful, spoke these words to the king in a voice choked with tears.
He spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the best of the Bharatas and lord of men:
"O tiger among men, O bull of the Bharata race, I am Sañjaya; salutations to you!
Śalya, the lord of the Madras, has been slain, as have Śakuni and the son of Subala."
O tiger among men, Ulūka, the son of Kaitava, who possesses firm prowess,
has been slain; all the Saṃśaptakas have been killed, along with the Kambojas and the Śakas,
and the Mlecchas, the mountaineers, and the Yavanas have been struck down.
O great king, those from the east were slain, and all those from the south;
O lord of men, all those from the north and the west were likewise killed;
O king, kings and princes were slaughtered on every side.
O King, Duryodhana has been slain by the Pāṇḍava just as he had foretold;
with his thighs broken, O Great King, he lies covered in dust.
Bhīma has shattered the two thighs of your son, Duryodhana.
He lies fallen upon the ground, covered with dust;
O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna has been slain, as well as the unconquered Śikhaṇḍin,
Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, and likewise the Prabhadrakas, O King.
The Pāñcālas, those tigers among men, and the Cedis have been slaughtered;
all your sons have been killed, O Bhārata, as have the sons of Draupadī. The heroic and mighty Vṛṣasena, the son of Karṇa, has also been slain.
O tiger among men, all the men have been slain and the elephants struck down;
the chariot-warriors and horses have also been killed in battle. O Lord, only a small remnant of your camp remains.
When the heroic Pāṇḍavas encountered one another,
the world, deluded by Time, was reduced for the most part to a remnant of women;
only seven remained from the side of the Pāṇḍavas, and likewise three from the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Those five brothers, as well as Vāsudeva, Sātyaki,
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the son of Droṇa, the best among victors—
these, O great king, O best of monarchs, are also your chariot-warriors.
O lord of men, of all the assembled akṣauhiṇīs, O great king, these are the survivors; all others have met their end. Indeed, O bull of the Bharatas, the entire world has been struck down by Time.
"O Bhārata, having placed Duryodhana at the forefront of this enmity,"—
having heard these cruel words, O Great King, Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the lord of men, fell to the ground, deprived of his life-force.
When he had fallen to the ground, O great king, the highly illustrious Vidura also fell down, emaciated by the king’s calamity;
and so too did Gāndhārī, O best of kings, and all the Kuru women.
Hearing those cruel words, they suddenly fell to the ground; at that moment,
the entire circle of kings lay unconscious upon the earth,
like a great narrative filled with lamentation depicted upon a canvas.
Then, with great difficulty, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth,
who was emaciated by the calamity of his sons, slowly regained his breath. Having regained consciousness, that king trembled, deeply afflicted by sorrow.
Having gazed in all directions, he spoke these words to the Kṣattṛ:
"O learned Kṣattṛ, O man of great wisdom, you are the refuge for me, O bull of the Bharatas,
for I am utterly helpless and entirely deprived of my sons."
Having spoken thus, he then fell down once more, unconscious.
Seeing him fallen in that manner, whatever kinsmen were there sprinkled him with cold water and fanned him with fans as well.
After a long time, that lord of the earth,
the protector of the world, having recovered his breath, reflected in silence, O lord of the people, emaciated by the calamity of his son and sighing like a snake confined in a jar.
Seeing the king so afflicted, Sañjaya wept there,
as did all the women and the illustrious Gāndhārī.
Then, after a long time had passed, he spoke these words to Vidura:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that tiger among men, being repeatedly bewildered, said:
"Let all the women depart, as well as the illustrious Gāndhārī, and likewise all these friends; my mind is failing me utterly."
O bull of the Bharatas, having been addressed thus, the Kṣattṛ, trembling again and again, slowly dismissed those women. Then all those women departed, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then all his friends, seeing the king afflicted, [approached him]. Thereupon, O scorcher of enemies, when the lord of men had regained consciousness,
he was overwhelmed with anxiety, wondering, "Who will now be my refuge?"
Beholding the king weeping and deeply distressed, Saṃjaya, dejected,
stood with palms joined in reverence as the lord of men sighed again and again;
then Vidura, having sent away the kinsmen and the women, entered once more.
While the king was grieving, Vidura repeatedly consoled him who was mourning again and again with sweet words.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the women had been dismissed, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, having fallen into a sorrow more grievous than sorrow itself, lamented;
sighing as if with smoke and wringing his hands again and again.
Having reflected, O Great King, he then spoke these words, hearing which a profound compassion arose even among his friends:
"Alas! What great misery it is that I [must face] the Pāṇḍavas in battle!"
"O Sūta, I hear from you indeed that they are safe and unharmed;
surely my heart is very firm, made of the essence of a diamond,
since it does not shatter into a thousand pieces upon hearing that my sons have been slain."
O Sañjaya, having reflected upon their words and their childhood play,
my heart is now rent asunder with grief upon hearing that my sons have been slain today; for because of my blindness, I had no sight of their forms.

O sinless one, I have always maintained a joy born of affection for my sons; hearing that they had passed beyond childhood, were established in youth, and likewise reached middle age, I was filled with such delight.

Hearing today that they have been slain, their sovereignty taken away and their vitality stripped, I find no peace anywhere, overwhelmed as I am by the mental anguish for my sons. Come, come, O son, O Indra among kings, now that I am left without a protector!
"O mighty-armed one, deprived of you, what destiny indeed shall I follow? Having been the refuge, O great king, of my kinsmen and friends alike,
where indeed are you going, O hero, leaving me behind— blind and aged as I am?"
O King, that compassion of yours, that affection, and that great honor—
how was he, who was undefeated in battles, slain by the sons of Pṛthā? O dear one, how could you, having enjoyed the company of assembled rulers of the earth, [meet such an end]?
Slain upon the ground like an ordinary, base king,
who now will address me when I have risen at dawn, saying "Father,
Father," and constantly, "Great King," and repeatedly, "Lord of the World"?
Embracing me around the neck with eyes moistened by affection, he said, "O Kauravya, instruct me. Speak those excellent words to me.
Indeed, my dear son, have I not heard your voice before?
This earth is far more mine than it is Pārtha’s.
Bhagadatta, Kṛpa, Śalya, the prince of Avanti, Jayadratha,
Bhūriśravas, Somadatta, and the great king Bāhlika— [all these are on my side].
Aśvatthāman, Bhoja, and the mighty Māgadha;
Bṛhadbala, the lord of Kāśī, and Śakuni the son of Subala;
and many thousands of Mlecchas, along with the Śakas and Yavanas.
Sudakṣiṇa the Kāmboja, as well as the lord of the Trigartas; Bhīṣma the grandfather, and likewise Bhāradvāja and Gautama; Śrutāyus, Acyutāyus, and the heroic Śatāyus.
Then Jalasandha, Arshyaśṛṅgin, the Rākṣasa Alāyudha,
the mighty-armed Alambusa, and the great car-warrior Subāhu—
these and many other kings, O best of monarchs.
"O Lord, all these men have exerted themselves for my sake, even at the cost of their lives in battle. Standing in the midst of them, surrounded by my brothers,
I shall fight the Pārthas and the Pañcālas in every way."
O tiger among kings, even a single one among these— the Cedis, the sons of Draupadī in battle,
Sātyaki, Kuntibhoja, and the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca—
is capable of resisting you, O Great King.

How much more so these heroes, who are united and have long harbored enmity toward the Pāṇḍavas? Or rather, all of them together with the followers of the Pāṇḍava— [will they not overwhelm me] when I am enraged and rushing against the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle?
O Indra among kings, they will fight together and slay them in battle;
but Karna alone, along with me, shall destroy the Pāṇḍavas.
Then the heroic kings will remain under my command.
"And he who is their leader, the mighty Vāsudeva—
he does not arm himself, O King," such were the words he spoke to me.
O Sūta, as he was speaking thus many times in my presence, I heard it.
For by reason, I perceive the Pāṇḍavas as already slain in battle; yet,
while my sons stand in their midst and exert themselves in the fray, they are being struck down— what else can this be but fate?
Where Bhīṣma, the powerful lord of the world, was slain after encountering Śikhaṇḍin—
like a lion attacking a jackal—
and where the Brahmin Droṇa, who had reached the further shore of all weapons and missiles, [fell].
Slain by the Pāṇḍavas in battle, what else can this be but destiny?
And Karṇa, the knower of divine weapons and possessed of great strength, has been slain in battle;
as have Bhūriśravas and Somadatta in the encounter.
And Bāhlīka, O great king—what else can this be but fate? For Bhagadatta, who was skilled in elephant warfare, has been slain;
and Jayadratha has been killed—what else can this be but fate?

Where Sudakṣiṇa was slain, as well as Jalasaṃdha the Kaurava, Śrutāyus, and Acyutāyus— what else can this be but fate? Likewise, the mighty Pāṇḍya, who had reached the further shore of all weapons and missiles.
Slain by the Pāṇḍavas in battle, what else can this be but destiny?
For there Bṛhadbala was killed, as well as the mighty Māgadha and the valiant Ugrāyudha, who was a peerless standard for all archers.
He was a hundred years old and full of prowess; what else could this be but fate?
For there the king of Avanti was slain, as well as the lord of Trigarta and many Saṃśaptakas; what else could this be but fate?
Śakuni Saubala,
the mighty-armed Trigarta, and the Śaṃśaptakas of great strength—
those heroes and great archers who have renounced their lives for my sake— are there.
They were slain by Bhīmasena; what else can this be but destiny?
Likewise, O King, Alambuṣa, the Rākṣasa Alāyudha, and the son of Ṛśyaśṛṅga have been killed; what else can this be but destiny?

Where the Nārāyaṇas were slain, as well as the cowherds who were fierce in battle and many thousands of Mlecchas— what else can this be but fate? Where Śakuni Saubala and the mighty son of Kitava [were also killed].
That hero has been slain along with his army; what else can this be but the work of destiny?
These and many others—masters of weapons, intoxicated by battle, kings and princes, heroes with arms like iron clubs—[have likewise fallen].
Where so many have been slain, what else can it be but fate? Where heroes, great archers, skilled in weapons and fierce in battle;
where high-souled heroes who have reached the further shore of all scriptures and missiles [have perished].
"O Sūta, many have been slain, O Sañjaya, who possessed prowess equal to that of Mahendra; Kṣatriyas gathered from various lands have all been killed in battle— what else can this be but destiny?"
My sons have been slain, as have my grandsons of great strength;
Duryodhana has been killed, as well as the son of that high-souled one, along with his friends and brothers— what else can this be but the work of destiny?
In this terrible battle with Pārtha, what else can it be but destiny?
A man surely arises endowed with destiny;
and that man who is joined with good fortune shall attain auspiciousness.
"O Sañjaya, I am bereft of my own fortune and even of my sons here;
how shall I exist today, old as I am and fallen under the power of my enemies?
O Lord, I consider nothing else to be better than dwelling in the forest."
Therefore, O Sañjaya, now that my kinsmen have perished and I am left without kin, I shall go to the forest;
for there is nothing better for me than taking refuge in the woods,
having reached this state of being like a bird with clipped wings.
Where Duryodhana has been slain, and Śalya struck down in battle, and Duḥśāsana slaughtered, and the mighty Vikarṇa as well—
how indeed shall I hear the loud cry of Bhīmasena?
Tormented by grief and sorrow, I shall not hear the harsh words of him who, in battle, single-handedly slew my hundred sons, as he speaks repeatedly of Duryodhana’s slaughter.
Thus, that king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, tormented by grief for his kinsmen,
repeatedly fainting and overwhelmed by the mental anguish caused by his sons,
lamented for a very long time.
Sighing long and hot breaths and reflecting upon his defeat,
the king, O bull of the Bharatas, tormented by great sorrow,
again questioned the charioteer Sañjaya, the son of Gavalgaṇa, for the truth of the matter.

Having heard that Bhīṣma and Droṇa were slain, and that the Sūta’s son, the general and leader, had been struck down— what did my men do when they heard likewise of Śalya, the great archer, the powerful lord of the Madras?
Whichever commander my men appoint in battle,
the Pāṇḍavas slay him in no long time.
Bhīṣma has been slain at the head of the battle by Kirīṭin while you were looking on.
In this very manner was Droṇa slain while everyone was looking on;
in this very manner was Karṇa, the powerful son of a charioteer,
slain by Kirīṭin while all you kings were watching.
Long ago, indeed, I was told by the high-souled Vidura:
"Through the transgression of Duryodhana, this progeny shall perish.
Some fools do not see correctly, while others likewise see clearly.
This very thing has now come to pass for me, a fool,
exactly as those words spoken by the righteous and far-sighted Vidura to me have turned out; the speech of that speaker of truth has been fulfilled.
"O son of Gavalgaṇa, tell me again what was the fruit of that misconduct which I previously committed with a mind afflicted by fate. And who,
indeed, stood at the head of the armies once Karṇa had been struck down?"
Which chariot-warrior advanced against Arjuna and Vāsudeva? Who protected the right wheel of the King of Madra in the battle, and who stood at the rear of that hero as he desired to fight?
And how was the mighty Madra king slain by the Pāṇḍavas in battle while you were all assembled there, or how was my son slain, O Sañjaya?
Tell me everything exactly as it happened regarding this great destruction of the Bharatas.
Just as my son Duryodhana was slain in battle,
and just as all the Pāñcālas were killed along with their followers,
as well as Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the five sons of Draupadī.
Just as the Pāṇḍavas were liberated, so too were both the Sātvatas in battle;
and Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the son of Bhāradvāja—
whatever manner and of whatever kind the battle has now transpired.
"I wish to hear everything, for you are skilled, O Sañjaya.
Sañjaya said:
"Listen attentively, O King, to how that great destruction occurred."
When the Sūtaputra had been slain by the high-souled Pāṇḍava, and the armies of both the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas had encountered one another,
they fled and were repeatedly rallied.
When Karṇa was slain, O King, in that terrible battle where the best of elephants among men were being destroyed, Pārtha let out a lion’s roar;
at that moment, a great fear entered your sons.
When Karṇa was slain, not a single one of your warriors possessed the resolve to rally the ranks or to display prowess;
they were like merchants stranded on a shattered ship in the bottomless deep.
O King, when the island was destroyed by the Diademed One (Kiritin) and the Suta’s son was slain, those who desired the further shore in the shoreless sea became terrified and wounded by arrows;
like deer tormented by a lion, they were without a protector and sought one.
Like bulls with broken horns or serpents with shattered fangs,
we returned in the evening utterly defeated by Savyasācin;
our foremost heroes slain, we were scattered and mangled by his sharpened arrows.
O King, when the Sūta’s son had been slain, your sons fled in fear; all of them were deprived of their weapons and armor, bewildered, and seeking refuge in every direction,
striking one another as they looked about, tormented by terror.
"Surely Bibhatsu is attacking me alone, and Vṛkodara is attacking me alone!"— thinking thus, O Bhārata, they fell down and grew faint;
some great car-warriors abandoned their horses, others their elephants, and others their chariots.
Having mounted swift-footed horses, the infantrymen fled out of fear;
chariots were shattered by elephants, horsemen by great car-warriors,
and throngs of foot-soldiers were violently struck down by swarms of fleeing cavalry.
Just as a caravan abandoned in the forest becomes beset by wild beasts and robbers, so did your army become when the Sūtaputra had been slain. Likewise,
the elephants were deprived of their riders, and others had their trunks severed.
Afflicted by fear, they indeed beheld the entire world as being filled with Pārtha;
seeing them all fleeing, tormented by the fear of Bhīmasena, Duryodhana then cried out "Alas! and spoke thus to his charioteer.
Pārtha will not bypass me as I stand here with bow in hand;
urge the horses forward quickly against me as I fight from the rear.
For Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, shall indeed encounter me as I fight in battle.
Just as the great ocean cannot overstep its shore, he would not be able to overcome me today. Having slain Arjuna along with Govinda, the proud Vṛkodara,
and the remaining enemies, I shall attain freedom from my debt to Karṇa.
Having heard those words of the Kuru king, which were worthy of a hero and a noble man,
the charioteer slowly urged on the horses covered in golden trappings. But the foot soldiers, O sire, were deprived of their elephants, horses, and chariots.
Twenty-five thousand [soldiers] fled as if slowly;
Bhīmasena, enraged, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
surrounded them with a fourfold army and struck them with arrows.
They all fought back against Bhīmasena and the son of Pṛṣata;
others there called out the names of Pārtha and Pārṣata.
Bhīma grew enraged in the battle at being opposed by them in the fray.

Quickly descending from his chariot, he fought with mace in hand. Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, who was observant of dharma, did not fight those men standing on the ground while remaining in his chariot; instead, he relied solely on the strength of his own arms.
Grasping a massive mace encased in gold,
he struck down all your men like Death himself with staff in hand;
for the foot soldiers were enraged, having renounced both their lives and their kin.
They rushed at Bhīma in battle like moths toward a blazing fire.
Having encountered Bhīmasena, those furious warriors, intoxicated by the pride of combat,
perished suddenly upon seeing him, like hosts of living beings meeting Death himself.
Like a hawk, Bhīma moved about with his sword and mace;
he struck down twenty-five thousand of your men.
Having slaughtered that army of men, Bhīma, whose prowess is truth, stood firm.
Placing Dhṛṣṭadyumna at their head, the mighty one stood once more;
the heroic Dhanañjaya advanced against the division of chariots,
as did the two sons of Mādrī and the powerful Sātyaki against Śakuni.
Joyfully charging with speed, they struck down Duryodhana’s army;
having slain his numerous horsemen with sharp arrows,
they pursued him swiftly, and there a battle ensued.
Then, O King, Dhanañjaya plunged into the division of chariots,
brandishing the bow Gāṇḍīva, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
having seen the chariot with white horses approaching with Kṛṣṇa as its charioteer.
Your warriors also fled in fear from Arjuna, the combatant;
deprived of their chariots and horses, and enveloped by arrows,
twenty-five thousand foot-soldiers rushed toward Pārtha.
Having slain that army of men, the great car-warrior of the Pañcālas—
glorious, a wielder of the great bow, and a crusher of the hosts of enemies— appeared before long with Bhīmasena at his head.
Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the highly illustrious son of the Pāñcāla king,
whose horses were the color of pigeons and whose excellent banner bore the emblem of a Kovidāra tree,
your men fled from the field of battle out of fear.
O noble one, having pursued the King of Gāndhāra, who was swift with his weapons,
the two illustrious sons of Mādrī, along with Sātyaki, Cekitāna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the sons of Draupadī, soon came into view.
Having slaughtered your vast army, they then blew their conchs. Seeing all your men fleeing with their backs turned,
they rushed forward, striking them down like bulls after defeating other bulls.
O King, seeing that remnant of your son’s army standing firm, the powerful Savyasācin, the Pāṇḍava, became enraged; then, O King,
he suddenly overwhelmed him with arrows.
Then, as dust rose up, nothing at all could be seen;
when the world was turned to darkness and the surface of the earth became like a shroud,
O Great King, all your men fled in fear in every direction.
O lord of the people, as his armies were being broken, the Kuru king rushed toward both the enemy and his own men from all sides. Then Duryodhana challenged all the Pāṇḍavas.
O best of the Bharatas, like Bali against the gods in ancient times,
they rushed together toward him as he roared,
discharging various weapons in their fury and reviling him again and again.
Duryodhana, too, remained unperturbed and struck down those enemies with his arrows.
There we beheld the extraordinary prowess of your son,
in that all the Pāṇḍavas were unable to overcome him.
When Kṛtabuddhi had not gone very far, having resolved to flee,
Duryodhana beheld his own army severely wounded. Then, O king of kings, your son Kṛtabuddhi halted [the troops].
As if gladdening those warriors, he spoke these words:
"I do not see any place on earth or among the mountains where the Pāṇḍavas would not slay you once you have gone there; what is the use of your flight?"
Their strength is indeed very small, and both the Kṛṣṇas are severely wounded.
If we all remain here, our victory will be certain; but if you depart and are scattered, the Pāṇḍavas will strike at you as you are separated and guilty of transgression.
Having pursued them, they shall slay us; in battle, death is better for us.
For one who fights according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, death in combat is pleasant;
having died, he does not know suffering and enjoys infinity after passing away.
"Let all the Kṣatriyas who have assembled here listen:
you shall now fall under the power of the enraged Bhīmasena, your enemy.
You ought not to abandon the dharma practiced by your ancestors."
Indeed, there is no sin more grievous for a Kṣatriya than flight;
for there is no path to heaven better than the duty of battle, O Kauravas. A warrior instantly attains those worlds that others acquire only after a very long time.
Having honored those words of the king, those great car-warriors,
the Kṣatriyas, once again turned back toward the Pāṇḍavas,
unable to endure defeat and resolved upon valorous exertion.
Then once again a most terrible battle commenced between your men and the enemy, resembling the war between the gods and the asuras;
[the combatants fought] against the Pāṇḍavas, who were led by Yudhiṣṭhira with their entire army.
O great king, your son Duryodhana pursued him;
for while your son had turned his face away, his mind overwhelmed by grief,
and while the horses, elephants, and chariots had been struck down.
O Bhārata, when the armies were deeply agitated upon seeing the prowess of Pārtha,
and while the troops were brooding in grief,
they heard the supreme roar of their forces being crushed.
O noble one, having seen the disfigured corpses of the lords of men in battle,
the fallen chariot-seats and the chariots of the high-souled warriors,
and having beheld the elephants and foot soldiers slaughtered in the fray;

The battlefield was exceedingly terrible, resembling the playground of Rudra. O King, Kṛpa— who was endowed with age and virtue— was filled with compassion for the hundreds of thousands of kings who had met their end and fallen into obscurity.
Approaching King Duryodhana there, that radiant one, skilled in speech, spoke these words out of the power of his wrath:
"O Duryodhana, O Kaurava, listen to this which I shall say to you."
"Having heard this, O great king, do as you please, O sinless one. O Indra among kings, there is indeed no path superior to the duty of war,
relying upon which Kṣatriyas fight, O bull among Kṣatriyas."
Son, brother, father, sister’s son, maternal uncle, as well as kinsmen and relatives—these indeed must be fought by one who lives the life of a Kṣatriya.
To slay them is the highest duty; likewise, to flee is unrighteousness.
Seeking a livelihood, they have indeed entered upon a terrible way of life.
In this regard, I shall speak to you a few words that are truly beneficial,
now that Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the great car-warrior Karṇa have been slain.

O sinless one, now that Jayadratha has been slain, as have your brothers and your son Lakṣmaṇa, what remains for us to wait upon? It was upon them that we placed our burden and set our minds on the kingdom.
Having cast off their bodies, those heroes have gone to the destination of the knowers of Brahman;
but we, deprived here of those virtuous great car-warriors,
shall live a wretched life after having caused so many kings to fall.
Moreover, while all were still living, the invincible Bibhatsu—
the mighty-armed one with Kṛṣṇa as his eye— was unassailable even by the gods; he possessed the luster of Indra’s bow and the thunderbolt, and stood tall like the banner of Indra.
Upon encountering the monkey-bannered standard, that great army trembled;
yet our hearts rejoice at the lion-roar of Bhīma, the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, and the thundering twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Moving like a great flash of lightning, it stole away the brilliance of the eyes;
the Gāṇḍīva bow appeared like a whirling firebrand,
that great bow variegated with gold being shaken to and fro.
In all directions, he was seen like lightning amidst thick clouds;
and the horses yoked to his chariot— white, endowed with great speed, and possessing a luster like that of the moon or the *kāśa* flower— seemed as if they were drinking up the very sky.
Carried along by Kṛṣṇa like a cloud driven by the wind,
Arjuna— with his limbs adorned with gold— swept through the battle against your army,
O King; for Arjuna is the foremost among those skilled in weapons.
Like a fire that has arisen, he consumed the dense thicket of the Śiśira army;
as he plunged into the ranks with a splendor equal to that of Mahendra,
we beheld Dhanañjaya like a four-tusked elephant.
We beheld Dhananjaya agitating your army and terrifying the kings, like an elephant in a lotus pond; likewise,
we saw the son of Pāṇḍu striking terror into the warriors with the roar of his bow.

Once more we beheld them like a lion amidst herds of deer; those two great archers of all the world, the bulls among all bowmen, the two Kṛṣṇas, shone resplendently in the midst of the people with their armor fastened on.
O Bhārata, today marks the seventeenth day of this most terrible battle, as men are being slain on all sides in combat;
your armies have been scattered in every direction, like by the wind.
The masses of autumn clouds were scattered on all sides;
O great king, Savyasācin caused your army to tremble like a ship tossed about by a gale in the great ocean.
Where indeed was your son of the Sūtas, and where was Droṇa with his followers?
Where was I, where were you yourself, and where was the son of Hṛdika? And where was your brother Duḥśāsana, together with his brothers?
Seeing Jayadratha come within the range of his arrows, he disregarded all your kinsmen—
his brothers, allies, and maternal uncles— and,
displaying his prowess, overran them all while they looked on, trampling them beneath his feet.
"Jayadratha has been slain, O King; what indeed remains for us to wait upon?
What man is there here who will conquer the son of Pāṇḍu?
And what man exists today who will defeat Dhanañjaya?"
The various divine weapons of that high-souled one,
and the roar of the Gāṇḍīva, indeed rob us of our prowess;
this army, its leader slain, is like a night deprived of the moon.

And the woman who loves her husband is like a river whose beloved has died; she becomes as distressed as a dried-up river whose trees have been broken by elephants and whose waters have run dry— just so is an army without Karṇa.
When his army has lost its leader, the mighty-armed Śvetavāhana will roam at will like a blazing fire in a forest thicket. And the impetuosity of both Sātyaki and Bhīmasena—
O lord of the people, he who spoke those words in the midst of the assembly— Bhīma— has accomplished all of it, and he will do even more. He could shatter all the mountains and dry up the oceans.

With Karṇa standing at the head, the army protected by the Pāṇḍavas was then difficult to assail; it was guarded and shielded by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow. As for those wicked deeds you have committed against the virtuous—[for those, you shall now reap the fruit].
"The fruit of those very deeds you committed without cause has now come upon you.

For the sake of your own interests, O bull of the Bharatas, you have with great effort brought the entire world under your control; yet now, my son, both that world and yourself are placed in jeopardy."
"Protect yourself, O Duryodhana; the self is the vessel for everything. For when the vessel is broken, my dear, whatever was contained within it scatters in all directions.
One who is declining, as well as one who is equal, should indeed seek peace."

Warfare with one who is growing in power— this is the policy of Bṛhaspati. Since we are inferior to the sons of Pāṇḍu in our own strength and capability, O Lord, I consider it appropriate for you to make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
For he who does not know what is beneficial, and who disregards that which is beneficial, is swiftly deprived of his kingdom and does not find what is good. Indeed,
if we were to obtain the kingdom by bowing down to the king, [it would be well].

"O King, it would be better for you to attain prosperity than to go to ruin through folly. At the word of the son of Vicitravīrya and by the counsel of Govinda, Yudhiṣṭhira, who is compassionate by nature, will install you in the kingdom."
Ajātaśatru, the descendant of Kuru, who is devoted to serving his elders and is righteous,
will not disregard the word of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
and his brothers will likewise follow his word— of this there is no doubt.
For whatever Hṛṣīkeśa might say to the unconquered king,
to Arjuna, and to Bhīmasena, they would undoubtedly do it all;
Kṛṣṇa will certainly not disregard the word of the Kaurava.
I believe that neither Dhṛtarāṣṭra nor Kṛṣṇa would find fault with this, O Pāṇḍava;
I consider it appropriate for you not to engage in hostilities with the sons of Pṛthā.
I do not say this to you out of weakness, nor for the sake of protecting my own life.
"O King, I tell you what is beneficial; you shall remember it when your life has departed.
Having lamented these words, the aged Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat, sighed long and hot, and both grieved and fainted.
Saṃjaya said:
O lord of the people, having been thus addressed by the illustrious Gautama,
the king sighed long and hot, and remained silent.
Then, having meditated for a moment, the high-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
that scorcher of foes, spoke these words to Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat:
"I have indeed been made to hear everything that ought to be said by a well-wishing friend."
Everything has been accomplished by you as you fought, sacrificing your very life;
the world has watched you as you plunged into the ranks and battled with the great car-warriors, the Pāṇḍavas of exceeding splendor.
"O friend, all that you have told me— which was indeed spoken by you as something that ought to be said—
does not please me at all, like medicine to one who is about to die,
however excellent and beneficial those words may be, joined as they are with logic and reason."
"O mighty-armed one, though it is being said thus, O foremost of Brahmins, it does not please me.
How could he, who was deprived of his kingdom by us, place his trust in us? Moreover, the king, possessing great wealth, was defeated by us at a game of dice."

How then shall he place further faith in my words? For Kṛṣṇa, who is devoted to the welfare of Pārtha, arrived as an envoy and was thus deceived; Hṛṣīkeśa was mocked, and that act was contrary to righteousness.
O Brahmin, how indeed will he take my words to heart?
For Kṛṣṇa cannot endure that which Draupadī lamented while gathered in the midst of the assembly, nor can he endure the seizure of the kingdom in such a manner.
"O Lord, those two dark ones who were once joined together as one soul— I hear today that very thing which was heard long ago;
and having heard that his sister's son has been slain, Keśava sleeps in sorrow."
We have committed an offense against him; how could he forgive it for my sake? Arjuna finds no peace due to the destruction of Abhimanyu;
how then will he make an effort for my benefit when entreated?
The middle Pāṇḍava, the fierce Bhīmasena of great strength, has made a terrible vow; he would rather break than bend. He will slay me, even if I were protected by the hand of Rudra himself.
Both of them had their swords girded and both were clad in armor;
those two heroes, who had conceived enmity toward me, were like the twin Yamas and equal to Yama himself.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin likewise had conceived enmity toward me.
"O best of the twice-born, how could those two possibly exert themselves for my benefit,
when Kṛṣṇā— clad in a single garment and in her courses—
was tormented by Duḥśāsana in the midst of the assembly while all the world looked on?"
Even today, the Pāṇḍavas remember her thus, stripped of her garments and miserable;
Kṛṣṇa, intent on my destruction, speaks this very thing every single day:
"While those sons of Pṛthā still live, and while that Keśava lives."
"I shall surely meet my destruction along with my younger brothers through my own sin alone;
those subduers of foes cannot be turned back from battle.
And when Draupadī Kṛṣṇā is distressed for the sake of my destruction,"
Kṛṣṇā performed fierce austerities for the sake of accomplishing her husbands' purpose;
she slept perpetually on the bare ground until the end of the enmity.
Having cast aside pride and arrogance, [she did so] along with Vāsudeva’s sister.
"Having become like a servant to Kṛṣṇā, he always performs service for her;
thus, everything is so highly agitated that it cannot be extinguished by any means.
How can I make peace with him now, given the destruction of Abhimanyu?"
How indeed could I, having enjoyed this earth girt by the oceans through the favor of the Pāṇḍavas, now enjoy such a small kingdom,
shining like the sun above all other kings?
"How shall I follow behind Yudhiṣṭhira like a slave?
Having myself enjoyed pleasures and bestowed abundant gifts, how shall I lead a wretched life, subsisting on a miserable livelihood along with the wretched?"

"I do not find fault with the affectionate and beneficial words spoken by you; however, I do not consider peace to be appropriate at this time in any way. O scorcher of foes, I perceive that a well-executed course of action lies in fair combat."
"This is not the time for cowardice; it is precisely the time for us to fight.
I have performed many sacrifices, bestowed sacrificial fees upon the Brahmins, acquired the Vedas through traditional study, and stood upon the heads of my enemies."
"My servants have been well-supported, dear friend, and the distressed people have been uplifted.
O best of the twice-born, I cannot now speak such words to the Pāṇḍavas;
foreign kingdoms have been conquered and my own kingdom has been protected."

I have enjoyed various pleasures and cultivated the three aims of life; I have discharged my debt to both my ancestors and the duty of the warrior class. Yet, there is no permanent happiness here in this world—whence then could there be sovereignty, and whence fame?
In this world, fame must be established, and that is achieved through battle and no other way.
Even for a kṣatriya, death at home is despised;
it is a very great unrighteousness to die upon one's bed in the house.
The man who casts off his body in the forest or in battle, having performed great sacrifices, attains greatness. But he who is afflicted by suffering, lamenting piteously, and overwhelmed by old age—
That man does not die in the midst of weeping kinsmen; rather,
having abandoned various enjoyments and attained the supreme goal,
I shall now go to the same world as the virtuous through a noble battle.
For all those who are heroic, of noble conduct, never retreating in battles, wise, true to their word, performers of sacrifices,
and who have attained the ritual bath of weapons— surely their dwelling is in the third heaven.
Indeed, the radiant hosts of *apsarases* surely gaze with joy upon the warriors who have cast off their bodies in battle; the hosts of *apsarases* surely wait upon them in heaven with delight.
Surely the ancestors behold them now, honored in the assembly of Śakra,
rejoicing in Triviṣṭapa, surrounded by Apsarases,
having followed the path traveled by the immortals and by heroes who never retreat.
May we also ascend the path traversed by them—
the aged grandfather, as well as the wise preceptor,
Jayadratha, Karṇa, and Duḥśāsana.
Duryodhana, though fallen in battle, sports in heaven together with them;
yet these heroic lords of men, who strove for my sake,
lie upon the earth, their limbs smeared with blood and mangled by arrows.
Those heroes, experts in the supreme weapons and performers of sacrifices as prescribed, having duly renounced their lives, are established in the abodes of Indra.
By them this path has been fashioned; indeed, it would otherwise be difficult to traverse.
Remembering the service rendered by those heroes who were slain for my sake— those who have departed from here with great speed toward the good destination—
and discharging that debt, I set my mind not on the kingdom.
If I were to spare my life after having caused my friends, brothers, and grandfathers to fall, the world would surely condemn me. And what kind of kingdom would it be for me, deprived of my kinsmen?
Having prostrated before the Pāṇḍava along with my friends and well-wishers,
and having brought about such a defeat for this world through fair combat, I shall then attain heaven; it cannot be otherwise.
When Duryodhana had spoken thus, all honored those words; having heard that speech of your son, who was endowed with courage, the kṣatriyas addressed the king, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!"

Not grieving over their defeat and setting their minds on valor, they all became resolute in battle, their spirits uplifted. Then, having encouraged their mounts, they all rejoiced in the prospect of war.
Having traveled less than two yojanas, the Kauravas halted on a sacred,
auspicious plateau of the Himalayas, in the sky-like expanse of the Vidruma region. Reaching the Aruṇā Sarasvatī, they drank its water and bathed therein.
Then your sons, having regained their resolve, rallied once more; and having steadied themselves through mutual encouragement,
O King, all those kṣatriyas, impelled by time, turned back to the fight.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O great king, all the warriors, rejoicing in battle, assembled there upon the Himalayan plateau.
Śalya, Citrasena, and the great car-warrior Śakuni;
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata;
Suṣeṇa, Ariṣṭasena, and the heroic Dhṛtasena.
Then King Jayatsena and those other kings, having spent the night there,
were terrified in battle by those who appeared victorious now that the hero Karṇa had been slain;
those sons of yours found no peace anywhere except on the Himavat mountain.
Having exerted themselves in battle, O King, and having duly honored the monarch there in the presence of the army, they spoke together:
"Having appointed a leader of the host, you ought now to fight the enemies."
"By whom we, being protected, may conquer our enemies in battle.
Then Duryodhana, standing upon his chariot, [addressed] that best of excellent car-warriors,
who was knowledgeable in all divisions of warfare and equal to Death itself in combat.

He possessed beautiful limbs, a concealed head, and a neck like a conch shell; he was pleasant of speech, with a face like a blooming lotus and a countenance like a tiger’s, yet possessed the majesty of Mount Meru.
He resembled the bull of Śiva in his shoulders, eyes, gait, and voice.
With well-nourished, muscular, and long arms, and a broad, solid chest;
equal to the younger brother of Aruṇa (Garuda) and the Wind-god in speed and strength;
like the splendor of the Sun, and equal to Uśanas in intellect.
In his three qualities of splendor, beauty, and majesty, he was like the moon;
his joints were well-knit, resembling a mass of golden stones.
His thighs, hips, shanks, feet, fingers, and nails were perfectly formed and beautiful.
Having repeatedly recalled his virtues, [the Creator] fashioned him with great effort—
one endowed with every auspicious mark, skillful, an ocean of sacred learning,
a conqueror of enemies by his own prowess, and invincible against foes through force.
He whose application, withdrawal, and atonement are auspicious,
and whose merits are known through his ritual practice and deployment,
and who knows the science of archery with its ten branches and four divisions according to reality— [he is the one].
Having diligently propitiated Tryambaka with fierce vows and great austerities, that man of great asceticism mastered the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and the Purāṇas as the fifth;
he was born of a woman not born from a womb by Droṇa, who himself was not born from a womb.
Approaching him— who was of incomparable deeds, peerless in form upon this earth,
a master of all sciences, an ocean of virtues, and beyond reproach—
your son addressed Aśvatthāman.
"Placing whom at our head shall we together defeat the Pāṇḍavas in battle?
Today, the son of the preceptor is the supreme refuge for us all.
Therefore, by your command, who shall be my commander-in-chief?"
The son of Droṇa said:
"Let Śalya, who is endowed with all virtues— lineage, heroism, splendor, fame, and prosperity— be our commander-in-chief."
"Having abandoned his own nephews, this grateful one has come to us;
Mahābāhu Mahāsena is like another Mahāsena himself.
O best of kings, having made him our general, [rule] as king."

"Victory can be achieved by us, just as the gods [conquered] the unconquerable Skanda. When the son of Droṇa had spoken thus, all the lords of men stood surrounding Śalya and raised shouts of victory.
They set their minds on battle and attained a state of supreme intensity.
Then Duryodhana, standing upon the ground, addressed Śalya— who was seated in his chariot and equal to Rāma and Bhīṣma in combat— with palms joined in reverence.
O you who are affectionate toward your friends, that time has now arrived for friends,
wherein wise men examine whether a person is a friend or an enemy. May you, O hero, be our leader at the head of the army.
"When you have gone to the battle, the Pāṇḍavas will become dull-witted,
along with their ministers and the Pañcālas, and they will be devoid of effort.
Having heard these words of Duryodhana, Śalya, the lord of Madra, then [replied].
The knower of dharma spoke these words to the king in the presence of the kings.
Śalya said:
"O King, O ruler of the Kurus, whatever you think of me, that I shall do."
"For my sake, everything—my very life, my kingdom, and my wealth—is for your pleasure.
Duryodhana said:
"O incomparable maternal uncle, I choose you for the command of the army."
O best among warriors, protect us as Skanda protected the gods in battle!
O Indra among kings, be consecrated like the son of Agni for the gods!
O hero, slay the enemies in combat as Mahendra slew the Dānavas!
Saṃjaya said:
O King, having heard these words of the king, the powerful ruler of the Madras then spoke these words to Duryodhana.
"O mighty-armed Duryodhana, best among those skilled in speech, listen!
As for these two Kṛṣṇas whom you consider to be the foremost of chariot-warriors standing upon their chariots—
neither of them is my equal in the strength of arms in any way whatsoever."
If the entire earth, including the gods, asuras, and humans,
were to rise up against me, I would fight them at the front of the battle in my wrath— how much more so the Pāṇḍavas?
And I shall conquer the sons of Pṛthā and the assembled Somakas in battle.

"I shall be your army commander, of this there is no doubt; and I shall arrange such a battle formation that the enemies shall not cross it. I tell you this truth, O Duryodhana, there is no uncertainty."

Thus addressed, O lord of the people, the king, appearing joyful, then immediately consecrated the lord of the Madras in the midst of the army according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures, O best of the Bharatas.
When he had been consecrated, a great lion-roar then arose;
and musical instruments were sounded among your troops, O Bhārata.
And then the warriors and the Madra great-chariot fighters were filled with joy.
And they praised King Śalya, who graces the battlefield:
"Be victorious, O King! Live long! Slay the assembled enemies!
Having obtained the strength of your arms, the mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [have been restored]."
May they rule over the entire earth, having slain their enemies;
for you are indeed capable of conquering in battle even the gods, asuras, and humans—
how much more so the Somakas and Sṛñjayas here, who are subject to the laws of mortality?
Thus being praised, the powerful hero, the lord of the Madras,
then attained a joy that is difficult for those of undisciplined souls to obtain.
Śalya said:
"O king of kings, this very day in battle I shall slay all the Pāñcālas along with the Pāṇḍavas; either I shall go to heaven slain, or I shall go to heaven having slain them.
Today let the worlds behold me moving about fearlessly."
Today all the sons of Pāṇḍu, Vāsudeva along with Sātyaki, the Pañcālas and the Cedis, all the sons of Draupadī,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and all the Prabhadrakas [are here].
"Let them behold my prowess, the great strength of my bow,
my lightness of hand, the power of my weapons, and the strength of my arms in battle; today let the sons of Pṛthā, along with the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, witness these."
Whatever strength I possess in my arms, and whatever perfection I have in weapons—
let the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, having seen my prowess today,
exert themselves in various actions, intent upon a counter-attack.
"Today, O Lord, I shall put the armies of the Pāṇḍavas to flight on all sides;
surpassing Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and the Sūtaputra in battle,
I shall move about the field of combat fighting for your sake, O Kaurava."
Saṃjaya said:
O giver of honor, O Bhārata, when Śalya had been consecrated among your troops at that time, they did not consider the calamity of Karṇa to be anything at all.
The soldiers there became joyful and high-spirited;
they considered the sons of Pṛthā as already slain, having fallen under the power of the King of Madra.
O bull of the Bharatas, your army attained great exultation.
That night she slept happily and felt as if her mind were at ease.
Hearing that roar of your army, King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi while all the kṣatriyas listened.
O Mādhava, Śalya, the king of the Madras, has been appointed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as the commander-in-chief of all the armies, a great archer honored by everyone.
Having heard this as it truly is, O Mādhava, do what is appropriate.
"You are the leader and the protector; ordain what must be done next.
Vāsudeva spoke thus to that lord of men, O great king:
"O Bhārata, I know Ārtāyani according to the truth."
He is energetic, possessed of great majesty, and especially high-souled; he is skilled, a versatile warrior, and endowed with lightness of hand—
just as Bhīṣma is, so too is Droṇa, and just as Karṇa is in battle.
"In my opinion, the King of Madra is either equal to him or even superior.
When Kṛṣṇa had spoken thus, Dharmarāja, the lord of the people and conqueror of enemy cities, set his mind upon battle.
The sky there was filled with the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, and likewise of tabors from both those armies;
O Bhārata, even as he reflected while fighting in that battle, he remained thus.
"O lord of men, O Bhārata, I do not find any warrior of equal form to Śikhaṇḍin, Arjuna, Bhīma, the Sātvata,
or Dhṛṣṭadyumna in terms of strength in battle."
O great king, the King of Madra, possessing the prowess of a lion or an elephant,
will roam about fearlessly at the proper time like the enraged God of Death among living beings;
today, I see no one who can oppose him in battle.
O tiger among men, whose prowess is equal to that of a tiger, were it not for you,
there would be no other man in this entire world, including the realm of the gods,
who could slay the King of Madra when he is enraged in battle, O descendant of Kuru.
Day after day he fights and agitates your army;
therefore, slay Śalya in battle, just as Maghavan slew Śambara.
That hero has been highly honored by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, yet he stands far behind [in merit].
"Indeed, victory will surely be yours alone once the Lord of Madra has been slain in battle;
for when he is killed, that great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons is as good as destroyed.
Having heard these words of mine just now, O Great King—
Advance against the mighty King of Madra in battle, O Pārtha!
Slay him, O mighty-armed one, just as Vāsava slew Namuci. Indeed, you must not show any compassion here on the grounds that "he is my maternal uncle."
Placing the duty of a Kṣatriya before you, slay the lord of the Madra people!
Having crossed the ocean of Bhīṣma and Droṇa, which arose from the abyss of Karṇa,
do not sink along with your followers upon reaching Śalya, who is but a puddle in a cow’s hoofprint.
Whatever power you possess from asceticism and whatever kṣatriya strength you have, O lord of men, and that for which you are called "the Eye of Dharma" in the world—
display all of that in battle and slay this great car-warrior.
Having spoken these words, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
departed for his camp in the evening, being honored by the Pāṇḍavas. When Keśava had thus departed, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira—
Having dismissed all his brothers, as well as the Pāñcālas and the Somakas,
he slept that night like an elephant freed from its arrows.
And all those great archers— the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas likewise— [remained there].
He spoke to all your men regarding the death of Karṇa; delighted by the slaughter of Karṇa, they then slept through that night,
[seeing] the great archer, the great car-warrior, as one whose fever had departed and who had reached the further shore.
At night, O sire, the army of the Pāṇḍavas became exceedingly joyful,
having achieved victory upon the death of the Sūta’s son;
and at the time of dawn, the delighted warriors, mounted on their excellent chariots, prepared for battle.
Saṃjaya said:
When the night had passed, King Duryodhana then spoke to all your men: "Let the great chariot-warriors arm themselves!"
Having understood the king’s intention, that army equipped itself;
they quickly yoked the chariots, while others ran about in all directions. The elephants were adorned and the infantry put on their armor.
Others, by the thousands, prepared horses equipped with saddles and rugs;
and a sound of musical instruments arose, O lord of the people,
for the purpose of awakening the warriors and the advancing armies.
Then, O Bhārata, all the remaining forces of the army were seen fully armored, having made death their only means of turning back;
those great car-warriors, having appointed Śalya, the King of Madra, as their commander-in-chief.
Having divided the entire force and stationed it within the ranks,
all your soldiers then assembled together with your son—
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, the son of Droṇa, Śalya, and the son of Subala.
And the other remaining kings then made an agreement:
"We must not fight the Pāṇḍavas one-on-one under any circumstances;
for whoever should fight the Pāṇḍavas alone, or whoever should abandon one who is fighting, [shall be punished]."
He would be burdened with the five great sins along with their minor offenses.
Now, the son of the preceptor, the son of Droṇa, could not fight the enemies alone;
we must fight together, protecting one another.
Having thus made this agreement, all those great chariot-warriors there,
placing the King of Madra at their head, swiftly rushed against the enemy.
Likewise, O King, the Pāṇḍavas, having arrayed their army in that great battle, [advanced].
Desiring to fight, they advanced from all sides against all the Kauravas.
O best of the Bharatas, that army had a sound like the agitated ocean;
it took on the appearance of a surging sea, with its chariots and elephants tossed about.
Dh�r̥tarāṣṭra said:
"I have indeed heard of the fall of Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and the son of Rādhā;
tell me further of the fall of Śalya and then of my own son."
O Sañjaya, how was Śalya slain in battle by Dharmarāja? And how was my son Duryodhana, that mighty-armed one who was skilled in mace-fighting, struck down in combat by Bhīma?
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, becoming steadfast, listen as I describe to you the battle— the destruction of human bodies and the slaughter of chariots, elephants, and horses."
"Listen attentively, O King, to the destruction of elephants, horses, and men;
I shall describe to you the terrible battle of all your warriors.
At that time, O King, your sons possessed a powerful hope."
"O noble one, once Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been slain and the Sūta’s son has been struck down,
Śalya will slay all the Pārthas in battle.
Keeping that hope in your heart and taking heart, O Bhārata," [he said].
Relying upon the great car-warrior, the King of Madra, in that battle,
your son then considered himself to have found a protector;
yet when Karṇa was slain, the sons of Pṛthā let out a lion’s roar.
Then, O King, a great fear entered the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
But then the powerful king of Madra, having comforted them,
O great king, drew up his army in the prosperous Sarvatobhadra formation.
The powerful King of Madra advanced against the sons of Pṛthā in battle,
brandishing his variegated bow, which was capable of bearing great weight and possessed of exceeding speed.
That great car-warrior, mounted upon his excellent chariot yoked with horses from the Sindhu region, went forth.
O great king, Sītā, standing upon his chariot, graced the vehicle;
O great king, having stationed himself at the front of the battle array,
that hero, the crusher of enemies, was protected by that chariot while clad in armor.
O great king, that hero stood dispelling the fear of your sons.
At the time of the advance, the King of Madra, clad in armor,
became the head of the battle array, accompanied by the Madrakas and the invincible sons of Karṇa.
On the left was Kṛtavarman, surrounded by the Trigartas;
on the right flank was Gautama, together with the Śakas and Yavanas;
and Aśvatthāman was at the rear, surrounded by the Kambojas.
Duryodhana stood in the center, protected by the bulls among the Kurus;
the son of Subala was surrounded by a vast force of cavalry,
and the great car-warrior, the son of Kitava, advanced with his entire army.

And the Pāṇḍavas, those great archers and subduers of enemies, having arrayed their army and divided themselves into three bodies, O great king, rushed against your troops. Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki— these were the leaders.
They swiftly rushed against Śalya’s army in the battle.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounded by his own division,
rushed toward Śalya himself, desiring to slay him, O bull of the Bharatas.
Arjuna, the slayer of enemy hosts, rushed with speed against the great archer Hārdikya and the throngs of Saṃśaptakas; meanwhile,
Bhīmasena and the great car-warriors of the Somakas advanced against Gautama.
O Indra among kings, they rushed forward in battle, desiring to slay their enemies.
Then the two sons of Mādrī, those great car-warriors, together with their respective armies, confronted Śakuni and Ulūka in the fray.
In that very same way, tens of thousands of your warriors, enraged and with various weapons in their hands, rushed at the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When the great archer Bhīṣma had been slain, and Droṇa and Karṇa, that great car-warrior,
when the Kurus were few in number and the Pāṇḍavas were still engaged in battle,
O Sañjaya, while the sons of Pṛthā were highly incensed and exerting their prowess—
"What strength remained, O King, among my men and those of the enemy?
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, listen to how we and our enemies stood arrayed for battle."
Now learn from me, O bull of the Bharatas, what force remained in that battle:
eleven thousand chariots,
ten thousand elephants, and seven hundred more.
O bull of the Bharata race, your force consisted of two full hundred thousand horses,
as well as thirty million infantrymen;
furthermore, there were six thousand chariots and six thousand elephants.
O Bhārata, ten thousand horses and ten million foot soldiers—
this was the remaining force of the Pāṇḍavas in the battle;
though small in number, it was here powerfully protected.
O bull of the Bharatas, these very [forces] assembled for battle;
there arose terrible banners, destroyers of men, amidst the weapons and missiles.
Hundreds of horses, reeling in confusion, rained down fiercely upon the eyes.

Having thus divided our forces, O Indra among kings, and remaining firm in the counsel of the King of Madra, we advanced against the Pāṇḍavas, greedy for victory and filled with wrath. In the same way, the heroic Pāṇḍavas, appearing victorious in battle, [advanced].
The tigers among men and the illustrious Pāñcālas have arrived;
thus, O Lord, these tigers among men, desiring to slay one another, have arrived with a flood of troops at the time of the morning twilight.
Then there commenced a battle of terrible form and fearsome aspect between your men and the enemy as they struck one another down.
Saṃjaya said:

Then, O king of kings, there commenced a terrible battle between the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas, increasing the fear [of all] and resembling the conflict between the gods and the asuras. Men, chariots, throngs of elephants, and horsemen by the thousands [engaged in combat].
The powerful and valiant steeds met one another,
and the great roar of the charging elephants of fearsome form was heard like the thundering of clouds in the sky during the rainy season.

Struck by the *nāgas*, some chariot-warriors fell along with their chariots; other heroes fled in battle, being put to flight by those intoxicated with rut. There, skilled chariot-warriors [attacked] the throngs of horses and the foot-guards.
O Bhārata, they dispatched them to the other world with arrows;
O King, the trained cavalrymen, surrounding the great car-warriors as they moved about the battlefield, struck them down with spears, javelins, and double-edged swords.
Some archers, having warded off the great chariot-warriors, approached a single man and sent him to the abode of Yama;
and other great chariot-warriors, surrounding elephants and the best of chariots, [did the same].
As he rushed forward with raised weapons, they struck him with a great roar;
likewise, O Great King, the elephants, surrounding him on all sides, slew the enraged chariot-warrior as he scattered many arrows.
In that battle, elephant after elephant rushed at one another, and chariot-warrior against chariot-warrior;
they struck each other down here and there with spears, javelins, and iron arrows. Chariots, elephants, and horses trampled the foot soldiers beneath them.
In the midst of the battle, they were seen creating great turmoil;
and horses, adorned with chowries,
galloped about like swans on the plateau of the Himalayas as if drinking up the earth.
O lord of the people, the earth, variegated by the hooves of those horses, shone like a woman marked by the scratches of fingernails;
it resounded with the sound of the horses' hooves and the clatter of the chariot rims.
O Bhārata, with the clamor of the foot soldiers, the trumpeting of the elephants,
the sound of musical instruments, and the blare of conchs,
the earth resounded as if with the roar of thunderclaps.
Due to the twanging of bows, the flashing of swords,
and the luster of armor, nothing could be discerned at all. Many severed arms, resembling the trunks of lordly elephants, lay scattered about.
They writhed and twisted, exerting a terrible force;
O Great King, the sound of their heads falling upon the surface of the earth was heard like the crashing of palm fruits falling from their stalks.
The earth shone with fallen heads drenched in blood,
O Bhārata, like lotuses resembling refined gold at the proper season;
those heads, though their eyes were rolled back and they were deprived of life, were yet deeply marked by wounds.
O great king, it shone like a land covered with white lotuses;
O lord of kings, the earth gleamed with those fallen arms— smeared with sandalwood paste and adorned with costly bracelets— resembling the banners of Śakra.
That battlefield was covered with the severed thighs of kings, resembling the trunks of elephants,
and was strewn with hundreds of headless torsos, adorned with umbrellas and chowries.
That army-forest shone like a forest covered in blossoms;
there, O great king, the warriors wandering about fearlessly appeared with their limbs smeared with blood, like *kiṃśuka* trees in full flower.
Mātaṅgas were also seen there in the battle, afflicted by arrows and *tomaras*,
falling here and there like shattered clouds,
O great king, as that elephant division was being slaughtered by those high-souled warriors.
All the directions were rent asunder like clouds driven by the wind;
those elephants, resembling massive clouds, fell upon the earth on all sides,
appearing like mountains shattered by thunderbolts at the end of an eon.
Heaps as large as mountains were seen here and there on the surface of the earth, consisting of horses fallen together with their riders;
indeed, a river flowing toward the other world arose upon the field of battle.
With blood for its water, chariots for its whirlpools, banners for its trees, and bones for its pebbles;
with arms for its crocodiles, bows for its currents, elephants for its mountains, and horses for its stones; with fat and marrow for its mud, parasols for its swans, and maces for its rafts.
Covered with armor and turbans, with banners as its beautiful trees, frequented by chariots and rows of wheels, and filled with triple-poled poles and shafts,
it generates joy for the brave and increases the fear of the timid.
A fierce river, crowded with Kurus and Sṛñjayas,
began to flow; those heroes, whose arms were like iron clubs, crossed that most terrifying river— which was carrying them toward the world of the ancestors— by means of their mounts as boats.
O lord of the people, while that lawless battle was thus proceeding—

terrible, involving the destruction of the fourfold army, and resembling the ancient conflict between the gods and the asuras— others there, O scorcher of foes, cried out to their kinsmen in various places.
While others, afflicted by fear, did not turn back despite their kinsmen crying out,
as that terrifying and lawless battle proceeded,
Arjuna and Bhīmasena confounded the enemies.
O lord of men, that great army of yours, being slaughtered,
became utterly bewildered here and there like a woman under the influence of intoxication;
and having thus confounded that host, Bhīmasena and Dhanañjaya—
There, the two born of water (the conchs) were blown and they uttered a lion’s roar;
upon hearing that great sound, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin,
placing Dharmarāja at their head, rushed toward the King of Madra.
There, O lord of the people, we beheld a marvel of terrible form:
how those heroes, having encountered Śalya, fought him in their respective divisions;
and how the two sons of Mādrī, impetuous, skilled in weapons, and fierce in battle, [fought].
Eager for victory and filled with haste, they both advanced against your army. Then, O bull of the Bharatas, your force turned back,
driven in many directions by the arrows of the Pāṇḍavas who appeared radiant in their triumph.
O great king, while your sons looked on, that army, being slaughtered and driven away by those firm bowmen, fled in all directions;
a great cry of "Alas! arose among your warriors, O Bhārata.
"Stay! Stay! was the cry raised by those high-souled Kṣatriyas as they fled from one another in battle, each desiring victory. Yet, though being pursued, your soldiers were broken by the Pāṇḍavas.
Having abandoned their beloved sons, brothers, grandfathers, maternal uncles, nephews, as well as kinsmen and relatives in battle,
the warriors, urging on their horses and elephants, fled in every direction.
"O bull of the Bharatas, your men exerted themselves to protect their own lives.
Saṃjaya said:
"Seeing that army thus broken, the powerful King of Madra..."
He said to his charioteer: "Urge on the horses of great speed quickly!
There stands King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, shining with a white umbrella held over him."
"Bring me there quickly; behold my strength, O charioteer!
For the sons of Pṛthā are not capable of standing before me today in battle.
Having been addressed thus, the charioteer of the King of Madra then proceeded.
Where King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and true to his promise, was present,
there Śalya alone held back the great army of the Pāṇḍavas as it suddenly rushed forward in battle, just as the shore holds back the surging ocean.
O noble one, when the flood of the Pāṇḍava army encountered Śalya in battle,
it came to a standstill, like the current of the ocean against a mountain. And seeing the King of Madra stationed for battle in the encounter, they halted.
The Kurus turned back, making death their only means of retreat. O King, when they had returned with their forces arrayed in divisions according to their parts,
there commenced a most terrible battle in which blood was the water.

Nakula, fierce in battle, encountered Citrasena; and Citrasena, O great king, likewise assailed the son of Pāṇḍu like a protector. Having come together with one another, those two wielders of variegated bows—
Like two clouds risen up, raining upon the south and the north,
those two drenched each other with the waters of their autumnal arrows in battle;
I could perceive no difference there between the Pāṇḍava and his opponent.
Both were skilled in weapons, powerful, and experts in the maneuvers of chariots;
they were intent on slaying one another and devoted to seeking each other's weaknesses.
Then Citrasena, with a sharp, yellowed broad-headed arrow, [struck].
O great king, he severed Nakula’s bow at the handle; then,
remaining unperturbed, he struck the bowless Nakula in the forehead with three gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone.
With sharp arrows, he dispatched his horses to death;
likewise, with three arrows each, he struck down both his standard and his charioteer.
With those three arrows released from the enemy's arm, now fixed in his forehead, [he shone].
O King, Nakula shone like a three-peaked mountain;
with his bow broken and deprived of his chariot, that hero took up a sword and a shield and descended from the chariot like a lion from a mountain peak.

As he charged on foot, Nakula released a shower of arrows; Nakula, swift in his prowess, indeed warded it off with his shield. Reaching Citrasena’s chariot, that warrior of varied combat, who had conquered all fatigue, [stood firm].
While the entire army looked on,
the mighty-armed Pāṇḍava severed Citrasena’s head— adorned with earrings and a crown, with a beautiful nose and long, lovely eyes— from his body and cast it away.
He, possessing a splendor equal to the sun, fell from the seat of his chariot.
Seeing Citrasena there thus slaughtered, all the great car-warriors and all the soldiers of the Pāṇḍava army beheld Citrasena slain.
"O great king, Citrasena was slain in battle by Nakula. They raised shouts of 'Excellent! and let out abundant lion-roars.
Seeing their brother slaughtered, the two sons of Karṇa, both great chariot-warriors,"
Suṣeṇa and Satyasena, discharging sharpened arrows,
then rushed swiftly toward the Pāṇḍava, the best of chariot-warriors,
O King, like two tigers seeking to kill an elephant in a great forest.
Those two fierce warriors both rushed toward that great car-warrior,
discharging volleys of arrows perfectly, like two clouds pouring down rain.
Pierced on all sides by those arrows, the son of Pāṇḍu seemed as if filled with joy.
Then Nakula, the best of the Bharatas and the crusher of enemy forces,
taking up another bow and mounting his chariot,
stood upon the battlefield, that hero appearing like the Destroyer himself in a state of rage.
O King, O lord of the people, those two brothers then began with straight-jointed arrows to shatter his chariot into pieces. Thereupon,
Nakula, laughing, struck four [of them] in the battle with four [shafts].
With sharp, whetted arrows, he struck the horses of Satyasena.
Then, O king of kings, having fixed a gold-feathered iron shaft sharpened on stone,
the Pāṇḍava cut through the bow of Satyasena.
Then, mounting another chariot and taking up another bow,
Satyasena and Suṣeṇa rushed toward the Pāṇḍava. The powerful son of Mādrī pierced those two, who remained unperturbed.
O Great King, with two arrows each at the forefront of the battle,
the great car-warrior Suṣeṇa, becoming enraged, laughed aloud and severed the Pāṇḍava’s great bow in that combat using a razor-headed shaft.
Then Nakula, overcome with rage, took up another bow;
having pierced Suṣeṇa with five arrows, he cut down his standard with one.
And, O noble one, he [severed] Satyasena’s bow and his hand-guard.
He cut it down swiftly in the battle, and then the people raised a loud shout.
Then, taking up another bow that was capable of checking speed and enduring great strain,
he completely covered the son of Pāṇḍu on all sides with arrows.
Having warded off those arrows, Nakula, the slayer of enemy heroes, pierced both Satyasena and Suṣeṇa with two shafts each. Then, raising a spear, he hurled it at Satyasena.
Those two pierced him individually with straight-flying arrows,
O king of kings, and they also struck his charioteer with sharp shafts. Satyasena, moreover, [struck] Nakula’s chariot-pole as well as his bow.
The powerful and skillful warrior severed them separately with two arrows.
Standing upon his chariot, that great car-warrior (atiratha) seized a chariot-spear (rathaśakti)—
one with a golden shaft, an unblunted tip, polished with oil, and perfectly clean.
O Lord, as if licking a highly venomous Naga maiden,
he raised her up and hurled her at Satyasena in the encounter;
O King, she pierced his heart in that battle into a hundred pieces.
He fell from his chariot to the ground, deprived of life and with his senses fainting. Seeing his brother slain, Suṣeṇa, overwhelmed with rage,
quickly showered arrows upon the son of Pāṇḍu who stood on foot.
Having severed the four horses with four arrows and the standard with five,
and having slain the charioteer with three, the son of Karṇa let out a roar. Seeing Nakula deprived of his chariot, the mighty son of Draupadī—
Sutasoma rushed forward in battle, desiring to rescue his father;
then Nakula, the best of the Bharatas, having mounted Sutasoma’s chariot, shone like a lion standing upon a mountain.
Taking up another bow, he engaged Suṣeṇa in combat. Those two great car-warriors, having assailed one another with showers of arrows, exerted themselves to slay each other.
Then Suṣeṇa, filled with rage, struck the Pāṇḍava with three arrows,
and Sutasoma with twenty in the arms and chest.
Thereupon, O great king, Nakula, the slayer of enemy heroes, became enraged.
The heroic one covered all directions with his arrows.
Then, seizing a sharp-pointed, well-sharpened crescent-headed shaft,
he hurled it with great force at the son of Karṇa in the battle.
O best of kings, with that [weapon], he severed his head from his body while all the troops looked on; it was like a marvel. O King, having been slain by the high-souled Nakula, he fell down.
Like a great tree growing on a riverbank broken by the force of a current,
O bull of the Bharatas, your army fled in fear upon seeing the slaughter of Karṇa’s son and the prowess of Nakula.
But that army, O great king, was protected in battle by the powerful Madra king, the heroic commander-in-chief and subduer of foes. That army, O king, fled in terror toward the ten directions.
O great king, having arrayed his army, Vibhīṣaṇa stood firm,
letting out a mighty lion’s roar and a terrible sound from his bow;
O King, your troops in battle were thus protected by that wielder of the strong bow.
Free from distress, they advanced against their enemies from all sides;
surrounding the great archer, the King of Madra, on every side,
O King, that vast army stood ready for battle in every direction.
Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
placing Yudhiṣṭhira— the subduer of foes who restrains himself with modesty— at their head,
surrounded him in battle and let out lion-like roars.
They produced the fierce sounds of whizzing arrows and various kinds of war-cries;
likewise, all your men, having quickly surrounded the lord of Madra,
became highly enraged and once again set their hearts on battle.
Then the battle commenced, increasing the fear of the timid,
between your men and the enemy, making death the only means of retreat,
O Lord of the People, just like the ancient battle between the gods and the asuras.
O King, that [battle] of those who were fearless thus increased the population of Yama’s realm.
Then, O King, having slain the Saṃśaptakas in battle, the son of Pāṇḍu, whose banner bears the ape, rushed against that Kaurava army.
In the same way, the remaining Pāṇḍavas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
rushed toward that army, discharging sharp arrows.
As they were overwhelmed by the Pāṇḍavas, a state of utter confusion arose among them.
The armies could no longer distinguish the cardinal directions nor the intermediate points,
being overwhelmed by the sharp arrows discharged by the Pāṇḍavas;
their foremost heroes were slain, they were shattered, and they were being scattered in every direction.
O Kauravya, the army was being slaughtered by the sons of Pāṇḍu, those great car-warriors;
and likewise, O King, the Pāṇḍava host was being struck down on all sides in battle by your sons with arrows by the hundreds and thousands.
Those two armies, being severely tormented as they slaughtered one another,
became utterly agitated like two rivers during the rainy season;
then, a sharp and great fear entered your warriors.
And while the great battle between the Pāṇḍavas was thus proceeding, O Indra among kings,
Sañjaya said:
"While that army was thrown into confusion and they were slaughtering one another..."
While the warriors were fleeing and the elephants were trumpeting,
and while the foot soldiers were groaning and moaning in that great battle,
