O Great King, the horses then scattered in many directions.
When a terrible destruction had arisen, a dissolution of all embodied beings,
amidst a shower of various weapons and the entanglement of chariots and elephants— that which gladdens those intoxicated by battle and increases the fear of the timid—
While the warriors were plunging forward, each desiring the slaughter of the other,
in that most terrible contest for life which was like a deadly game of dice—
a battle of horrific form that swelled the kingdom of Yama—
The Pāṇḍavas shattered your army with sharpened arrows,
and likewise your warriors struck down the soldiers of the Pāṇḍavas; while that battle, which brought terror to the timid, was thus proceeding.
When the forenoon had arrived and the sun was rising,
O King, the enemies— having found their mark and being protected by that high-souled one—
fought your army, making death their only means of retreat.

O Kaurava, the army collapsed before the powerful Pāṇḍavas— who were arrogant, skilled in their aim, and formidable strikers— like a doe distressed by fire. Seeing that army sinking like a weak cow in the mud, [he...]
Then Śalya, desiring to rescue him, advanced toward the Pāṇḍava host.
But the King of Madra, filled with rage and seizing an excellent bow,
rushed in battle against the attacking Pāṇḍavas.
O great king, the Pāṇḍavas, appearing victorious in battle,
encountered the King of Madra and pierced him with sharpened arrows;
likewise, your warriors assailed Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, while Dharmarāja looked on, the mighty king of the Madras afflicted that army with hundreds of sharp arrows.
Thereupon, O King, portents of many forms appeared in great numbers.
The earth, along with its mountains, shook while emitting a great sound;
meteors with blazing tips, falling from the sky after striking the solar disc, shattered on all sides as they struck the ground, accompanied by staffs and tridents.
O lord of the people, O king, deer, buffaloes,
and birds repeatedly kept the army to their left; at that time,
the son of Bhṛgu and the son of the Earth were joined by the son of the Moon.
At the very end, before all the kings, a flame appeared at the tips of the weapons of the sons of Pāṇḍu, raining down as it struck their eyes;
and crows and owls swarmed violently upon their banners.
Then that battle became exceedingly fierce among those moving in groups;
likewise, O lord of men, all the divisions having come together,
the Kauravas, O King, advanced against the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
But Śalya, with a shower of arrows like the thousand-eyed Indra pouring down rain,
being undaunted in spirit, rained upon Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī,
and also upon Bhīmasena with stone-sharpened arrows feathered in gold.
The mighty warrior pierced all the sons of Draupadī, as well as the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the descendant of Śini (Sātyaki), and Śikhaṇḍin—
each one with ten arrows.
Then he released a shower of arrows, like Maghavan at the end of the summer heat.
Thereupon, O King, the Prabhadrakas and the Somakas by the thousands were seen fallen and being struck down by Śalya’s shafts.
Like swarms of bees or flights of locusts,
like lightning flashes from the clouds, Śalya’s arrows fell. Afflicted elephants, horses, foot soldiers, and chariot-warriors likewise fell.
By Śalya’s arrows, [the warriors] fell, wandered about, and likewise cried out;
the Lord of Madra, as if possessed by wrath and prowess,
covered his enemies in battle like Death himself unleashed by Time.
Roaring like a thundercloud, the immensely powerful lord of the Madras let out a great cry.
O great king, that army of the Pāṇḍavas, being struck by Śalya and tormented by his arrows, fled in all directions.
He rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, whose enemy is unborn;
then, having delivered her in that battle, the light-handed warrior afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira with a great shower of sharp arrows.
Enraged in battle, he showered arrows upon Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma. As he charged forward with his infantry and horses, King Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with wrath,
checked him with sharp shafts, just as one restrains a rutting elephant with goads.
Śalya released a terrible arrow at him, resembling a venomous serpent;
it pierced the high-souled one and fell to the earth with great force.
Then Vṛkodara, filled with rage, struck Śalya with seven arrows.
Sahadeva [struck him] with five arrows, and Nakula with ten;
and the sons of Draupadī showered arrows upon the heroic son of Ārta-yani, the slayer of enemies and highly fortunate one, just as clouds rain upon a mountain.
Then, seeing Śalya being struck from all sides by the Pārthas,
Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa, filled with rage, rushed forward;
as did Ulūka, Patatri, and Śakuni, the son of Subala.
Smiling gently, the great chariot-warrior Aśvatthāman,
along with all your sons, protected Śalya in the battle.
Kṛtavarman, having pierced Bhīmasena with three stone-tipped arrows, [remained there].
With a great shower of arrows, Kṛpa, assuming a furious form, checked Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
enraged, he afflicted him with showers of shafts. Śakuni assailed the sons of Draupadī, and the son of Droṇa advanced against the twins.

Duryodhana, possessed of fierce energy and great strength, advanced against Keśava and Arjuna— the two best of warriors in combat— and struck them with arrows. In this manner, there were hundreds of duels between your men and the enemy.
O lord of the people, there were various sights of terrible form here and there;
in that battle, the Bhoja king slew Bhīma’s deer-colored horses. With his horses slain, that son of Pāṇḍu descended from the seat of his chariot.
Like Time itself raising its staff, the King of Madra, mace in hand, fought in the presence of Sahadeva; he slew Sahadeva’s horses,
whereupon Sahadeva struck Shalya’s son with a sword.
The preceptor Gautama, remaining unperturbed himself, fought against the unperturbed Dhṛṣṭadyumna with great effort against one who was even more diligent;
likewise, he struck each of the heroic sons of Draupadī with ten arrows.
Not excessively enraged and as if smiling, the preceptor’s son pierced him as he was attempting to mount the middle of his chariot with his horses harnessed;
and once again in that battle, he slew Bhīmasena’s horses.
Having quickly descended from his chariot, his horses slain, that son of Pāṇḍu,
possessed of great strength, raised his mace like Kāla raising his staff in anger and crushed the horses and the chariot of Kṛtavarman.
Kṛtavarman, however, leaping down from that chariot, retreated;
and Śalya too, O King, filled with rage, slaughtering the Somakas and Pāṇḍavas,
once again afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira with sharp arrows in battle.
Then the valiant Bhīma, enraged in battle and biting his lips,
resolved upon his destruction and took up his mace,
which resembled the staff of Yama and was raised like the Night of Doom.
It was capable of ending the lives of elephants, horses, and men;
encircled with bands of gold like a blazing torch, it was made of iron, as fierce as a venomous female serpent, and as hard as a diamond.
Like a desired woman smeared with sandalwood and aloe paste,
yet like the tongue of Yama stained with fat, marrow,
and blood; like the thunderbolt of Indra, resounding with the sharp ring of bells.
Resembling a venomous serpent freed from its skin, yet smeared with the ichor of elephants;
terrifying to enemy armies and gladdening one's own troops;
renowned throughout the world of men for its power to shatter mountain peaks.
By means of which, O son of Kuntī, the mighty one challenged the enraged lord of Alakā— the friend of Maheśvara— in the palace of Kailāsa;
and by which he [confronted] many proud masters of illusion in the abode of the Giver of Wealth.
Enraged for the sake of the *mandāra* flower, the mighty one struck down the *guhyakas*,
even as he was being restrained by many, intent on doing what was pleasing to Draupadī.
[He seized] that [bow], which possessed a multitude of diamond-jewels, was eight-sided, and had the weight of a thunderbolt.
Raising his mace, the mighty-armed one, skilled in combat, rushed at Śalya in battle;
with that weapon of terrible roar,
he crushed Śalya’s four horses of great speed.
Then the heroic Śalya, enraged in battle, roared as he plunged a *tomara* into Bhīmasena’s broad chest; having pierced his armor, it passed right through.
But Vṛkodara, remaining unperturbed, pulled that very *tomara* out.
He hurled it at Bhīmasena, and [Bhīma] bled profusely;
then Bhīma, filled with rage,
seized that very same weapon and pierced the heart of the Madra king’s charioteer.

With his armor shattered and vomiting blood, his mind terrified and dejected, he fell facing forward; meanwhile, the King of Madra withdrew. Seeing that his counter-strike had been successfully executed, Śalya was struck with amazement.
Leaning upon his mace, the steadfast-souled one gazed at his adversary.
Then the sons of Pṛthā, with joyful minds, honored Bhīmasena;
and the Siddhas, standing in the sky and filled with delight, spoke as follows:
"In a previous birth, this Bali was seen by us as Prahlāda. Having witnessed that terrible deed in battle performed by him of untiring action,
and having seen that feat of Śalya, all the Siddhas paid him homage."
09,011.001 Saṃjaya said: 09,011.001a Seeing his charioteer fallen, O King, Śalya took up a mace made entirely of iron and stood with speed, immovable like a mountain.
He was like the blazing fire of time, like Death with noose in hand;
he was like Mount Kailāsa with its peak, like Indra with his thunderbolt;
he was like Haryakṣa with his trident, or like an elephant in rut in the forest.
Grasping his great mace, Bhīma rushed forward with speed, like a wheel-bearer toward a chariot with its wheel, or like a general toward one armed with a spear.
Without any agitation, he [pierced] the King of Madra while all the archers looked on. Then there arose the blaring of conchs and thousands of musical instruments,
along with lion-roars that increased the joy of the heroes.
Beholding those two great elephant-warriors from all sides, the warriors on your side as well as those of the enemy cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
Indeed, there was no one other than the Lord of Madra or Rāma, the joy of the Yadus, [who could withstand them].

No one else in battle, save for Vṛkodara, is capable of withstanding the force of Bhīmasena in combat; likewise, no warrior other than he can endure the force of the mace of the high-souled lord of Madra.
Roaring like two bulls, those two—
the King of Madra and Vṛkodara— moved in circles with maces in hand,
leaping about in the paths of circular maneuvers and the various techniques of wielding the mace.
The battle between those two lions among men was indistinguishable;
Shalya’s mace, adorned with bright bands of refined gold, became a source of increasing terror,
appearing as if enveloped in flames of fire.
As the high-souled Bhīma moved along his paths within the circles,
his mace shone like lightning amidst the clouds;
the mace of Bhīma struck the mace of the King of Madra as they clashed.
O King, it seemed as if it were blazing and emitted flames of fire;
thus struck by Bhīma’s mace,
Śalya’s mace released a shower of glowing coals, which was like a marvel.
Like two great elephants with their tusks, or two mighty bulls with their horns,
they then struck one another with the ends of their maces as if with goads. With their limbs struck by the maces, the two of them were drenched in blood in an instant.
Struck on the left and right with the mace by the King of Madra, the mighty-armed Bhimasena remained as immovable as a mountain, appearing even more beautiful than two blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
O King, though struck repeatedly by the force of Bhīma’s mace,
Śalya did not waver, like a mountain struck by an elephant;
and the sound of those two lions among men was heard in all directions.
The crashing sound of their falling maces was like the roar of two thunderbolts.
Then, turning back with their maces raised high, those two of great prowess once more took their positions in the center of the path and moved in circles.
Then, having approached within eight steps, a collision occurred between those two of superhuman deeds as they raised their iron clubs;
seeking one another, they then moved in circular maneuvers.
Then those two skillful warriors displayed their specialized maneuvers;
raising their terrible maces like two peaked mountains,
they struck one another as mountains do during an earthquake.
Struck violently by each other’s force and by their maces, those two heroes fell simultaneously like two Indra-poles;
at that moment, the warriors of both armies raised a cry of "Alas! (hāhākāra).

Both of them, severely struck in their vital organs, were utterly overwhelmed. Then Kṛpa, having placed Śalya— the bull among the Madras— upon his chariot with his mace, quickly bore him away from the field of battle.
But because he was reeling like one intoxicated, Bhīmasena, mace in hand, rose up again after a moment and challenged the King of Madra.
Then your brave warriors, equipped with various weapons, [rushed forward].
With the sound of various musical instruments, they fought against Pāṇḍu’s army;
then, O great king, raising their arms and weapons with a loud roar,
those warriors led by Duryodhana charged forward.
Beholding that army, those sons of Pāṇḍu then advanced with lion-like roars, desiring the slaughter of Duryodhana. As they were rushing forward swiftly, O bull of the Bharatas, your son—
With a *prāsa* dart, he pierced Chekitāna deeply in the heart;
struck by your son, he fell upon the floor of his chariot,
drenched in a flood of blood and entering into a vast darkness.
Seeing Chekitāna slain, the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas rained down showers of arrows incessantly and in succession. The Pāṇḍavas, appearing victorious, [assailed] the ranks of your troops.
O great king, they moved about in all directions, a sight to behold;
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the mighty Saubala,
with the King of Madra at their head, fought against Dharmarāja.
O great king, Duryodhana fought against Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the slayer of Bhāradvāja, who possessed immense heroism and prowess;
O king, three thousand chariots were urged on by your son.
Placing the son of Droṇa at their head, they fought for victory;
resolved upon victory and having utterly cast away their lives,
your men, O King, entered [the enemy ranks] like swans into a great lake.
Then a terrible battle took place between those who sought to slay one another— a conflict characterized by mutual slaughter, yet increasing their mutual passion.
O King, as that battle proceeded, it brought about the destruction of the foremost among heroes.
A terrible dust of the earth, stirred up by the wind, rose up;
yet, by hearing the names and reciting the names of the Pāṇḍavas,
we recognized one another among those who were fighting fearlessly.
O tiger among men, that dust was laid by the blood;
and when that dust was settled, the quarters of the sky became clear.
While the battle proceeded in such a manner—terrible in form and fearsome—
Among your men and those of the enemy, there was not a single one who turned his back;
intent upon the world of Brahmā and seeking victory in battle,
those men displayed their prowess through fair combat, desiring heaven.
Then the warriors, resolved upon their duty to their master and with their minds fixed on heaven, fought for the sake of liberating him from the debt of his sustenance;
those great chariot-fighters discharged weapons of various forms.
Roaring at one another and striking each other, the words "Kill! Pierce! Seize! Strike! Cut them down!
were heard from both your army and theirs.
Then, O great king, Śalya, desiring to slay that great car-warrior, pierced Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, with sharpened arrows.
In response, O great king, Pārtha [Yudhiṣṭhira] indeed loosed fourteen iron shafts at him.
Aiming at his vital spots, the highly illustrious one, who was skilled in the knowledge of such points, struck the Pāṇḍava with arrows as if laughing, desiring to kill him in battle;
enraged, he pierced him with many heron-feathered shafts.

Then once more, O Great King, while the entire army looked on, he struck Yudhiṣṭhira with a straight-knotted arrow. The highly illustrious Dharmarāja, filled with rage, [then struck] the King of Madra.
The great car-warrior pierced him with sharp arrows feathered with the plumes of herons and peacocks;
he struck Candrasena with seventy arrows, his charioteer with nine,
and Drumasena with sixty-four.
When the wheel-protector had been slain by the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
O King, Śalya then struck twenty-five Cedis,
as well as Sātyaki with twenty-five arrows and Bhīmasena with five.
Mādrī’s two sons pierced him in battle with a hundred sharpened arrows.
As he was thus maneuvering in the combat, O best of kings,
Pārtha dispatched sharp arrows resembling venomous serpents.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), struck down from his chariot the standard-top of that [enemy] as he stood at the front in battle; indeed,
the banner of that high-souled one was severed by the son of Pāṇḍu.
We beheld it falling like a mountain peak struck down;
seeing the banner fallen and the Pāṇḍava standing firm,
the King of Madra became enraged and released a shower of arrows.
Śalya, of immeasurable soul and a bull among kṣatriyas, rained down a shower of arrows upon that kṣatriya like a rain-bearing cloud—
upon Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī.
Piercing each one with five arrows, he afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira. Then, O great king, we beheld a web of arrows spread across the chest of the Pāṇḍava, like a mass of clouds risen in the sky.
Enraged in battle, the great car-warrior Śalya covered the cardinal and intermediate directions with straight-knotted arrows. Then King Yudhiṣṭhira was afflicted by that net of shafts.
He became deprived of his prowess, like Jambha before the slayer of Vṛtra.
Saṃjaya said:
O noble one, when Dharmarāja was thus afflicted by the King of Madra,
Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
having surrounded Śalya with their chariots, oppressed him in the battle.
Seeing that single great car-warrior being oppressed by many, [the enemy forces were struck with wonder].
A great cry of "Excellent! arose, and the Siddhas were filled with joy;
even the assembled sages exclaimed, "It is a marvel!
Bhīmasena, in that battle, [encountered] Śalya, who was like a thorn in prowess.
Having pierced him with one arrow, he pierced him again with seven;
and Sātyaki, desiring to protect the son of Dharma,
overwhelmed the Lord of Madra with a hundred arrows and then let out a lion’s roar.
Nakula pierced him with five arrows and Sahadeva with seven;
having struck him thus, he then quickly pierced him again with seven.
That hero, though exerting himself in battle, was afflicted by those great car-warriors.
O noble one, having drawn his terrible bow— which was capable of checking the enemy's momentum and achieving great feats— Śalya pierced Sātyaki with twenty-five arrows,
Bhīmasena with seventy-three, and Nakula with seven.
Then, having severed the bow along with the arrow of the archer Sahadeva with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) in that battle, he pierced him with twenty-one arrows.
Sahadeva, however, [pierced] his maternal uncle of great splendor in the encounter.
Having strung another bow, he struck him with five arrows that were like venomous serpents and blazing like fire;
and in that battle, he struck his charioteer with a straight-knotted shaft.
Highly incensed, he pierced him again with three arrows;
Bhīmasena struck him with seventy-three, Sātyaki with nine arrows,
and Dharmarāja likewise struck Śalya in his body with sixty.
With five arrows each,
all those heroes struck him in his limbs;
then, O great king, Śalya was pierced by those great car-warriors.
Blood flowed from his limbs like red chalk from a mountain.
And he, O King, swiftly pierced all those great archers with five arrows each; that was truly marvelous.
Then, O noble one, with another broad-headed arrow, that great car-warrior cut the strung bow of Dharmaputra in the encounter. Thereupon, the great car-warrior Dharmaputra took up another bow.
He covered Śalya, along with his horses, charioteer, standard, and chariot, with arrows. Being thus shrouded in battle by the shafts of the Son of Dharma,
he then pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with ten sharpened arrows.
In this manner, hundreds of duels took place between your men and the enemy.
Then Sātyaki, enraged that the son of Dharma had been afflicted by arrows,
checked the heroic lord of the Madras with a flood of shafts.
With a razor-sharp arrow, he cut off Sātyaki’s great bow; then,
O Great King, the enraged Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth, struck those warriors headed by Bhīmasena with three arrows each.
He hurled a gold-staffed, highly precious *tomara* spear;
then Bhīmasena [discharged] an iron shaft (*nārāca*) like a flaming serpent,
Nakula a javelin (*śakti*) in the battle, and Sahadeva a beautiful mace (*gadā*).
The King of Dharma, desiring to strike Śalya with a *śataghnī* weapon in the battle, [discharged it]. Their weapons fell upon him in the fray with many arrows;
indeed, he swiftly [cut down] those five weapons as they were being released from their arms and were falling toward him.

In that battle, the King of Madra warded off [the attack] with a multitude of weapons; O King, he severed each one individually in the encounter. Śalya, with broad-headed arrows (*bhalla*), cut down the lance hurled by Sātyaki.
Moreover, the powerful and skillful warrior cut in two the gold-adorned arrow discharged by Bhīma in that battle; he likewise [cut] the terrifying,
gold-shafted *śakti* hurled by Nakula.
And with a shower of arrows, he warded off the mace hurled by Sahadeva;
and with two shafts, O Bhārata, he cut down that *śataghnī* weapon of the king while the sons of Pāṇḍu looked on, and he let out a lion’s roar.
But Śaineya could not endure that victory of the enemy in battle; then Satyaki,
overwhelmed with rage, took up another bow and pierced the lord of Madra with two arrows and his charioteer with three.
Then, O great king, Śalya, becoming violently enraged, pierced all of them with ten arrows each, like great elephants being struck with goads.
Those great car-warriors, though being resisted in battle by the King of Madra, [remained firm].
The destroyers of enemies were unable to stand before him.
Then King Duryodhana, seeing the prowess of Śalya,
considered the Pāṇḍavas, as well as the Pañcālas and the Sṛñjayas, already slain.
O Great King, O bull among men, such was the prowess of the King of Madra in battle that it became unbearable for human beings. Then, O King, the mighty-armed and majestic Bhīmasena—
Having mentally renounced his life-breaths, he fought the lord of the Madras;
then Nakula, Sahadeva, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
having surrounded Śalya on all sides, covered him with arrows.
Surrounded by four great archers, the mighty chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas,
the powerful King of Madra fought them.
O King, in that great battle, the son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira] struck him with a razor-sharp arrow.
O King, he swiftly slew the wheel-protector of the Madra king.
When that brave wheel-protector, the great car-warrior, had been slain,
the exceedingly powerful Madra king covered the soldiers with arrows.
Then, O King, seeing those soldiers completely covered,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, reflected in the midst of the battle:
"How indeed may those great words of Mādhava not prove false?"
For the king, when enraged in battle, would surely destroy my army; yet neither I, nor my brothers, nor the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
nor the Pañcālas and the Sṛñjayas, are capable of defeating the lord of Madra.
"If our highly illustrious maternal uncle should slay us today, how will Govinda’s word be made true? What is this?
Then, O elder brother of Pāṇḍu, the Pāṇḍavas, together with their chariots, elephants, and horses—
They assailed Madreśvara from all sides, afflicting him;
but he, O King, dispersed in battle that rising shower of weapons— abounding with a multitude of various arms— just as the wind scatters great clouds.

Then we beheld that shower of gold-feathered arrows discharged by Śalya, coursing through the sky like a swarm of locusts. Those arrows were sent forth by the King of Madra at the forefront of the battle.
O lord of men, the sky became as if without any gaps due to the gold-adorned arrows released from the bow of the King of Madra, appearing like swarms of locusts falling down.
Neither among the Pāṇḍavas nor among ourselves could anyone be seen there,
for a great and terrifying darkness of arrows had been created by the mighty King of Madra through his lightness of hand with showers of shafts.
Seeing the ocean-like army of the Pāṇḍavas thus being agitated,
the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas were struck with supreme wonder.
But he, O noble one, having oppressed those who were striving from all sides with his arrows—
Having covered Dharmarāja, they roared repeatedly like lions.
Those great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, being thus shrouded by him in battle,
were unable at that time to advance against that great car-warrior in combat.
But the chariot-warriors, led by Dharmarāja and headed by Bhīmasena,
did not abandon the heroic Śalya, who graces the field of battle, in that encounter.
Saṃjaya said:
Arjuna, pierced in battle by the son of Droṇa with many iron shafts, as well as by his followers— the heroic great-chariot warriors of the Trigartas—
pierced the son of Droṇa in the encounter with exactly three stone-tipped arrows.
Likewise, Dhananjaya struck the other great archers with two arrows each;
moreover, the mighty-armed one overwhelmed them further with showers of shafts. O bull of the Bharatas, your warriors were then bristling with arrows.
Though being struck by sharp arrows in the battle, they did not abandon Pārtha;
those great car-warriors, led by the son of Droṇa, surrounded Arjuna with a multitude of chariots and fought him in the fray.
Surrounding him with joy, they shone as they fought;
O King, the arrows adorned with gold that were discharged by them quickly filled the interior of Arjuna’s chariot.
Likewise, O Lord, seeing those two great archers, the bulls among all bowmen— the two Kṛṣṇas— exultant and intoxicated with battle, their limbs pierced by arrows,
[the chariot’s] pole, wheels, shafts, and traces were shattered.
Then the yoke and the undercarriage became as arrows;
O King, such a thing had never been seen before, nor had it ever been heard of by us,
as that which your men wrought against Pārtha there.
That chariot shone on all sides with sharp arrows furnished with variegated feathers,
like a celestial mansion blazing with hundreds of meteors upon the earth.
Then, O great king, Arjuna [struck] with straight-jointed arrows.

He overwhelmed that army as a cloud covers a mountain with rain. Being struck in battle by arrows marked with the name of Pārtha, they, beholding him in such a state, thought the entire world had become Pārtha.
Then the fire of Pārtha, with the wondrous arrows for its flames and the great sound of the bow for its wind, swiftly consumed your army as its fuel; likewise,
it scorched wheels and yokes falling upon the surface of the earth.
Along with quivers, banners, and standards together with chariots;
and also from all sides, poles, yokes, and bamboo shafts;
and likewise arms and heads, together with parasols and fans.
There, O Bhārata, as Pārtha became enraged, the earth became impassable due to the shafts, the undercarriages, the triple-pole yokes,
the axles, the traces, and the goads on all sides.
O Great King, there were heads falling down, adorned with earrings and turbans; arms and shoulders fell on every side,
as did all the royal parasols falling everywhere.
O Bhārata, heaps of umbrellas along with fans and crowns were seen upon the paths of Pārtha’s chariot.
Then, O lord of the people, on the path of the enraged Pārtha’s chariot—
O best of the Bharatas, the earth became impassable, mired in flesh and blood, like the playground of Rudra;
it was a source of terror for the timid and an increaser of joy for the brave.
Having slain two thousand chariots equipped with protective fenders in battle, O scorcher of foes, Pārtha blazed like a smokeless fire; indeed,
just as the Lord Agni consumes the world of moving and unmoving beings.
O King, the great car-warrior Pārtha was seen to be like a smokeless fire;
but the son of Droṇa, beholding the prowess of the Pāṇḍava in battle,
checked the Pāṇḍava with his chariot adorned with many banners.
Then those two tigers among men, both possessing white horses and being the foremost of archers,
swiftly encountered one another, each desiring to slay the other.
O great king, there was a most terrible shower of arrows between them.
Like the rain from clouds at the end of the summer heat, O bull of the Bharatas,
those two, vying with one another, hacked at each other in battle with straight-jointed arrows,
like two bulls with their horns.

O great king, the battle between those two continued for a long time as if it were equal; there, a truly terrible and great clash of weapons took place. Then [Duryodhana struck] Arjuna with twelve gold-feathered, well-sharpened arrows.
O Bhārata, the son of Droṇa pierced Vāsudeva with ten arrows;
then, laughing, Bībhatsu drew his bow Gāṇḍīva,
having shown respect for the preceptor’s son for a moment in that great battle.
Then, having rendered the son of the preceptor breathless, the high-minded Arjuna, the best among victors, loosed his arrows in battle;
with four arrows, he struck the horses as well.
The great car-warrior Savyasācin deprived him of his horses, charioteer, and chariot;
then, with gentle words first, he pierced him with three arrows. Standing on that chariot whose horses had been slain, the son of Droṇa took up an iron [mace].
Like the staff of Yama, terrible and terrifying to the enemy host,
he hurled a mace resembling an iron club at the son of Pāṇḍu.
As it came rushing suddenly, adorned with bands of gold—
The heroic Pārtha, the destroyer of enemies, cut it into seven pieces.
Seeing his club shattered, the son of Droṇa became exceedingly enraged and seized a terrible iron mace that resembled the peak of a great mountain.
And the son of Droṇa, skilled in battle, hurled it at the son of Pṛthā.
Seeing that iron club approaching like the enraged God of Death,
Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava, swiftly struck it down with five excellent arrows.

Cut down by Pārtha’s arrows in that great battle, it fell to the earth, O Bhārata, rending the hearts of the lords of the earth with its sound. Then the Pāṇḍava pierced the son of Droṇa with three other arrows.
Deeply pierced by the mighty Pārtha, that exceedingly powerful son of Droṇa was not at all bewildered; instead, he remained steadfast in his own manliness.
Then, O King, Sudharmā [pierced] the great car-warrior, the son of Bharadvāja.
He covered him with volleys of arrows while all the kṣatriyas looked on.
Then Suratha, that great car-warrior of the Pañcālas,
also rushed toward the son of Droṇa in battle on his chariot, which thundered like a cloud.
Drawing his excellent bow, which was firm and capable of bearing every strain,
he covered him with arrows resembling blazing venomous serpents.
Then, toward the enraged Suratha, that great car-warrior who was charging forward—
In that battle, the son of Droṇa became enraged like a serpent struck by a staff;
knitting his brows into three furrows and licking the corners of his mouth,
he glared at Suratha in fury and rubbed his bowstring.
He released a sharp iron arrow, possessing a brilliance equal to the staff of Yama;
having pierced his heart, it entered with extreme velocity,
like the thunderbolt of Śakra hurled down after rending the surface of the earth.
Then, having been struck by that iron shaft, he fell to the ground like the great peak of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt. When that hero had been slain, the powerful son of Droṇa—
That best of chariot-warriors swiftly ascended that very chariot. Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa, prepared for battle and intoxicated with the pride of war,
surrounded by the Saṃśaptakas, engaged Arjuna in combat.

There, at midday when the sun had reached its zenith, there was a great battle between Arjuna and his enemies, increasing the population of Yama’s kingdom. We beheld a marvel upon witnessing their prowess.
When Arjuna alone simultaneously engaged those heroes in combat,
there was a great clash between him and his enemies,
just as in former times there was a great conflict between Śatakratu and the vast army of the Daityas.
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, Duryodhana and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
engaged in a truly great battle, thick with arrows and spears.
O great king, from those two there issued thousands of streams of arrows,
like torrents of water from clouds on all sides during the rainy season.
Then the king, having pierced the son of Pṛṣata with five iron arrows—
The fierce-arrowed one pierced the slayer of Droṇa again with seven shafts;
meanwhile, the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna, firm in his prowess,
afflicted Duryodhana in battle with seventy arrows.
O bull of the Bharatas, seeing the king thus afflicted, his uterine brothers,
together with a vast army, surrounded the son of Pṛṣata.
He was completely hemmed in on all sides by those heroic great car-warriors.
O King, displaying his lightness of hand, he moved through the battle;
Śikhaṇḍin, joined by the Prabhadrakas, fought those two archers, Kṛtavarman and the great car-warrior Gautama.
There too, O lord of the people, there was a most great and terrible battle among those who were staking their very lives in that game of dice where life was the wager. Shalya,
meanwhile, discharged showers of arrows in every direction.
O king of kings, he oppressed the Pāṇḍavas— Sātyaki and Vṛkodara—
as well as both the twins, who possess prowess equal to Yama, fighting them with his valor and strength in battle.
In that great battle, among the Pāṇḍavas who were pierced by Śalya’s arrows,
none of those great car-warriors could find a protector.
Then, while Dharmarāja was being tormented, the heroic Nakula [intervened].
The son of Mādrī rushed with speed toward his maternal uncle;
having covered Śalya in battle, Nakula, the slayer of enemy heroes,
pierced him in the center of the chest with ten arrows while smiling.
With arrows made entirely of iron,
polished by smiths, gold-feathered, whetted on stone, and launched from the mechanism of his bow,
Śalya was thus afflicted by his high-souled sister’s son.
He afflicted Nakula with straight-jointed feathered arrows.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Sātyaki,
and Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, rushed against the king of Madra.
As they rushed forward swiftly, filling the quarters and intermediate directions with the roar of their chariots and making the earth tremble,
the commander-in-chief, the conqueror of enemies, received them in battle.
Having pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with three arrows, Bhīmasena with seven,
Sātyaki with a hundred in the battle, and Sahadeva with three shafts,
he then [struck] the bow and arrow of the high-souled Nakula.
Then, O noble one, Madreśvara cut that [bow] with a razor-edged arrow;
that bow of Śalya, severed by his shafts, fell to pieces.
Thereupon, the great car-warrior, the son of Mādrī, took up another bow.
He quickly covered the chariot of the King of Madra with feathered arrows.
But Yudhiṣṭhira and Sahadeva, O Sire,
each pierced the lord of the Madras in the chest with ten arrows.
Then Bhīmasena with sixty arrows and Sātyaki with nine,
having rushed at the King of Madra, struck him with heron-feathered shafts.
Thereupon the King of Madra, enraged, struck Sātyaki with nine arrows.
He pierced him again with seventy straight-knotted arrows;
then, O noble one, he cut off his bow, along with the arrow fixed upon it, at the grip,
and dispatched his four horses to death in that battle.
Having deprived Sātyaki of his chariot, the mighty King of Madra struck him from all sides with a hundred arrows; meanwhile,
the two sons of Mādrī and the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena were filled with fury.
And he pierced Yudhiṣṭhira, O Kauravya, with ten arrows.
There we beheld the wonderful prowess of the King of Madra,
in that the Pārthas, though united, could not prevail over him in battle.
Then, mounting another chariot, the mighty Sātyaki, whose prowess is truth,
seeing the Pāṇḍavas oppressed and fallen under the power of the King of Madra,
rushed with speed toward the lord of the Madras.

As his chariot was rushing toward him, Śalya, the ornament of the assembly, advanced against it with his own chariot, like one rutting elephant against another. That collision was tumultuous and wonderful to behold.
Between the heroic Sātyaki and the lord of the Madras,
there occurred a battle such as was formerly fought between Śambara and the king of the immortals.
Beholding the King of the Madras stationed in the fray, Sātyaki [advanced].
He pierced him with ten arrows and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
But the King of Madra, having been severely wounded by that high-souled one, pierced Satyaki in return with sharp, variegated-feathered shafts.

Then the sons of Pṛthā, those great archers, rushed swiftly on their chariots toward the king who had been assailed by the Sātvata, desiring to slay their maternal uncle. Thereupon, there occurred a tumultuous slaughter, with blood for its water.
O great king, as those heroes fought like roaring lions, there occurred between them a mutual clash in that battle,
like the clamor of hungry lions seeking prey.
The earth became strewn with floods of thousands of their arrows,
and the sky suddenly turned into a mass of shafts;
a darkness of arrows was created there in every direction in many ways.
Like the shadow of a cloud, it appeared due to the arrows released by those great-souled ones.
There, O King, with the released arrows—
resembling sloughed-off serpents and shining with golden shafts— the quarters of the sky likewise blazed forth.
There, Śalya, the destroyer of enemies, performed a supreme marvel,
in that he alone, a hero in battle, fought against many.
[He did so] with arrows released from the arms of the King of Madra, fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks.
The earth was strewn with those terrible, falling arrows.
There, O King, we beheld Śalya’s chariot as it moved through that great battle, just as in former times we saw the chariot of Śakra during the destruction of the Asuras.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O Lord, your troops, with the King of Madra at their head,
once again rushed against the sons of Pṛthā with great speed in the battle.
All your men, though hard-pressed, rushed forward fierce in battle;
and in an instant, by virtue of their great numbers, they threw the Pārthas into total confusion.
Being slaughtered by the Kurus, those Pāṇḍavas could not hold their ground.
Though being restrained by Bhīma while Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha looked on,
Dhanañjaya then, filled with rage, overwhelmed Kṛpa along with his followers and Kṛtavarman as well with a torrent of arrows.
Sahadeva, however, held back Śakuni along with his army;
Nakula, standing at the side, watched the King of Madra;
and the sons of Draupadī mostly held back the kings.
And Śikhaṇḍin, the prince of the Pañcālas, held back the son of Droṇa;
Bhīmasena, mace in hand, held back the king;
and Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, held back Śalya along with his army.
Then a close-quarters battle broke out here and there between your men and the enemy, none of whom would retreat from the fray. There,
we beheld the exceedingly great feat of Śalya in that combat.
When that single warrior fought against all the armies of the Pāṇḍavas,
Śalya was then seen near Yudhiṣṭhira like the planet Saturn in the vicinity of the moon in battle.
Having afflicted the king with arrows resembling venomous serpents,
he rushed again toward Bhīma and overwhelmed him with showers of shafts. Seeing his agility as well as his mastery of weapons, [Bhīma was amazed].
Both your troops and those of the enemy honored [Shalya] as they fought.
But the Pāṇḍavas, being tormented by Śalya and severely wounded,
fled from the battlefield, even though Yudhiṣṭhira was crying out to them.
While his armies were being slaughtered by the King of Madra, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu and King of Dharma, fell under the sway of indignation; then,
summoning his prowess, he began to afflict the King of Madra.
"Whether it be victory or death," the great car-warrior, having made up his mind,
challenged all his brothers and Kṛṣṇa Mādhava, saying:
"Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and whatever other rulers of the earth there may be..."
For the sake of the Kauravas, you have displayed your prowess and met your end in battle;
according to your respective shares and according to your zeal, you have all performed deeds of manliness.
Only this one portion remains for me: the great car-warrior Śalya.
Therefore, today I hope to conquer the lord of the Madrakas in battle.
I shall declare to you all that which is in my mind regarding this matter.
These two heroic sons of Mādravatī are the protectors of my chariot wheels.
"Unconquerable even by Vāsava himself in battle and esteemed as heroes,
let these two, honoring the duty of the Kṣatriya, fight against their maternal uncle in combat for my sake— they who are worthy of honor and true to their promise."
"What is the use of this further lamentation, or indeed anything at all that is useless?
Either Śalya shall slay me in battle, or I shall slay him; may it be well with you. O heroes of the world, understand these words as the truth."
"O kings, today I shall fight with my maternal uncle according to the duty of a Kṣatriya,
having myself resolved upon either victory or its opposite. For him, I have superior weapons and all necessary implements."
"Let the chariot-yokers yoke [the chariot] quickly in battle according to the scriptures.
Let the descendant of Śini guard the right wheel and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the left.
Let Pārtha Dhananjaya be my protector from the rear today."
"Let Bhīma, the best among wielders of weapons, be my vanguard today;
thus I shall become superior to Śalya in the great battle.
Having been addressed thus, all those who desired the king's welfare acted accordingly.
Then, O King, there was once again great joy among the troops—
especially among the Pāñcālas, the Somakas, and the Matsyas—
as he fulfilled that vow of Dharmarāja in battle.
Having then made that vow, the king marched against the Lord of Madra. Then the Pāñcālas sounded conchs, kettledrums, and hundreds of drums, and they let out lion-like roars.
Then those swift bulls of the Kuru race, filled with great joy, rushed impetuously toward the King of Madra with a roar born of exultation,
accompanied by the clanging of elephant bells and the blare of conchs.
Making the earth resound with the great noise of musical instruments,
your son and the heroic King of Madra received them,
just as the two mountains of Sunrise and Sunset receive the many great clouds.
But Śalya, who delighted in battle, rained a shower of arrows upon the subduer of foes, Dharmarāja, just as Maghavan rains down a torrential downpour.
In the same manner, the Kuru king also took up his beautiful bow.

Displaying various instructions received from Droṇa, the high-minded one discharged diverse arrows, demonstrating his manual dexterity; he rained down showers of shafts with skill, swiftness, and great precision.
And no one could find any opening as he moved about in battle;
both of them mangled each other with various arrows,
like two powerful tigers vying for meat in a fight.
But Bhīma, having encountered your son who is skilled in battle,
the Pāñcālya, Sātyaki, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
received the heroes led by Śakuni from all sides.

Then, O King, due to your evil counsel, there occurred once again a tumultuous battle between your men and the enemies, as both sides sought victory. Duryodhana, however, [struck] Bhīma with a straight-knotted arrow.
Having aimed it in the battle, he cut down the gold-adorned banner,
which was beautiful to behold with its great network of tinkling bells;
the resplendent lion-standard of Bhīmasena fell down, no longer roaring.

Then again, the lord of men cut his variegated bow, which resembled the trunk of a king elephant, with a sharp-edged razor-headed arrow. With his bow severed, that radiant warrior [struck] your son with a chariot-spear.

Exerting his prowess, he pierced him in the chest and entered the interior of his chariot. When the other had fallen into a swoon, Vṛkodara once again struck off the head of the charioteer from his body with a razor-sharp arrow.

O Bhārata, O King, with their driver slain, his horses fled in all directions carrying the chariot, and a cry of "Alas! then arose. Then the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, rushed toward him for the sake of protection.
Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, desiring to rescue your son,
found themselves amidst that tumultuous army; terrified, his followers were scattered,
while the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, having drawn his bow, struck them down with arrows.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with indignation, rushed toward the Lord of Madra,
personally urging on his ivory-colored horses that were as swift as thought.
There, we beheld a marvel in Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
Having previously been mild and self-controlled, he who had then become fierce—
the son of Kuntī, with eyes wide open and trembling with wrath—
cut down warriors by the hundreds of thousands with his sharpened arrows.
Whichever army that eldest son of Pāṇḍu encountered,
O King, he struck down with his arrows, just as the thunderbolt strikes down mountains;
he felled many chariot-warriors along with their horses, drivers, banners, and chariots.
Alone and powerful, he sported like the wind among the clouds;
in battle, he crushed horses with their riders and foot soldiers by the thousands, just as the enraged Rudra destroys the sacrificial animals.
Having made the battlefield empty by means of showers of arrows on all sides,
he rushed toward the Lord of Madra and cried out, "Stay, Śalya!
Witnessing those deeds of that warrior of terrible exploits in battle—
All your men were terrified, but Śalya advanced against him.
Then, both of them, highly enraged, blew their conch shells and,
having challenged one another, they encountered each other while hurling insults.
Śalya, however, covered Yudhiṣṭhira with a shower of arrows,
and the son of Kuntī likewise covered the King of Madra with showers of arrows;
at that time, O King, they both appeared in the battle [covered] by heron-feathered shafts.
With blood gushing forth, the two heroes, the King of Madra and Yudhiṣṭhira,
shone like flowering *śalmali* and *kiṃśuka* trees in the forest;
they both gleamed like blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees in the springtime.
Seeing those two high-souled ones blazing with energy, both intoxicated by battle for their very lives,
all the troops could not determine the victory of either; yet they thought,
"Having slain the lord of the Madras, Pārtha shall today enjoy the earth."
"Either Śalya, having slain the Pāṇḍava, shall give the earth to Duryodhana"—
such was not the resolve of the warriors there, O Bhārata; rather,
everything became favorable to Dharmarāja as he fought.
Then Śalya quickly released a hundred arrows at Yudhiṣṭhira and cut his bow with a sharp-pointed shaft. Taking up another bow, he [Yudhiṣṭhira] struck Śalya with three hundred arrows.
He pierced his bow and cut it asunder with a razor-headed arrow;
then, with straight-knotted shafts, he struck down his four horses, and finally,
with two sharp-pointed arrows, he slew both the outriders and the charioteer.
Then, with a blazing,
yellow, and sharpened broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he struck down the standard of his opponent as he stood before him.
Thereupon, O subduer of enemies, that army of Duryodhana was utterly broken.
Then the son of Droṇa rushed toward the lord of the Madras who had been treated in that manner;
having placed him upon his own chariot, he fled in haste.
After they had traveled for but a moment, Yudhiṣṭhira let out a roar in battle.
Having stopped there, the lord of the Madras then mounted another chariot—
one that was bright, prepared according to rule, thundering like a great cloud,
equipped with ready weapons and implements, and hair-raising for his enemies.
[It was] with beautiful fenders, beautiful wheels and axles, obedient horses, and an excellent charioteer.
Sañjaya said:
Then, taking up another bow that was more powerful and swifter, [he stood ready].
Having pierced Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of the Madras roared like a lion. Then, that bull among Kṣatriyas of immeasurable soul, like a rain-bearing cloud, showered the Kṣatriyas with a rain of arrows.
Having pierced Sātyaki with ten arrows, Bhīmasena with three,
and having pierced Sahadeva with three, he afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira;
[and likewise] those various other great archers, along with their horses, chariots, and elephants.

That best of chariot-warriors afflicted them with his arrows as one might strike elephants with firebrands; he struck down the elephants along with their riders, the horses along with their riders, and the chariots together with their charioteers.
He likewise severed arms still grasping weapons and standards;
he covered the earth with warriors as if it were a sacrificial altar strewn with *kuśa* grass.
Thus he struck down the enemy forces like Death, the Ender himself.
The Pāṇḍus, Pāñcālas, and Somakas, being violently enraged, surrounded him;
as did Bhīmasena, the grandson of Śini, and the two sons of Mādrī— those foremost of men.
Having encountered the king of terrible strength,
they then challenged one another and surrounded him.
Then those heroes in the battle [assailed] the lord of men.
Having reached Madreśvara, the best among warriors,
those heroes among men hemmed him in on the battlefield and struck him with feathered arrows of fierce velocity.
Protected by Bhīmasena, the King,
as well as by the two sons of Mādrī and by Mādhava,
[struck] the lord of Madra with feathered arrows of fierce velocity.
Then, in the midst of the fray, the son of Dharma struck down the multitudes of chariots belonging to your men upon seeing the lord of Madra afflicted by arrows.
The preeminent warriors surrounded him from all sides on every account, with the consent of Duryodhana;
then, in that battle, the lord of the Madra people quickly—
He pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with seven arrows,
and in that tumultuous encounter, O King, the high-souled Pārtha likewise struck him with nine shafts.
Then, in that battle, those two great chariot-warriors covered each other with arrows that were polished with oil and drawn back as far as the ear.
Then the lord of Madra and Yudhiṣṭhira,
both great car-warriors, quickly watched for each other's opening in the battle.
Those two best of kings, possessed of great strength and unassailable by enemies, pierced each other deeply with arrows;
the sound of their bowstrings and palms was immense.
The sound of those two great-souled heroes, the Madra king and the Pāṇḍava, as they rained down volleys of arrows upon one another, was like the roar of Indra’s thunderbolt.
Those two, resembling tiger cubs, roamed through the great forests like two hungry beasts of prey,
both appearing like excellent horned elephants.
Then those two, their pride born of battle, struck out;
thereafter, the high-souled lord of the Madras forcibly assailed Yudhiṣṭhira of terrible strength.
He pierced the hero in the heart with great force using an arrow possessing a radiance equal to the sun and fire;
then Yudhiṣṭhira, having been deeply pierced, [fell].
O King, with that well-aimed arrow,
he was then pierced by the son of Vidhi-dharma,
who possessed great strength and the prowess of Indra.
The high-souled bull of the Kurus slew the lord of the Madras and attained great joy;
then, after what seemed like a mere moment, that lord of kings—
Regaining consciousness, his eyes bloodshot with rage, he—
whose power was equal to that of the thousand-eyed Indra— swiftly struck Pārtha with a hundred arrows.
Then the high-souled son of Dharma, acting with haste,
being enraged, pierced Śalya’s chest and his golden armor with nine arrows.
He struck him with six other arrows;
then the lord of Madra, greatly delighted,
drew his bow and released more shafts.
With two razor-sharp arrows, he likewise cut the bow of the king, that bull among the Kurus; thereupon,
the latter took up another new one in the battle.
The high-souled king, having pierced Śalya all over with sharpened arrows from his most formidable bow,
was like Mahendra striking Namuci with his sharp-pointed shafts.
Then Śalya, with nine arrows,
having sliced through the bright golden armor of both Bhīma and King Yudhiṣṭhira in that battle;
The high-souled one tore apart his two arms;
then, with another razor-headed arrow blazing with the brilliance of the sun, he shattered the king's bow.
And Kṛpa slew his charioteer with six arrows, and he fell down facing him;
and the lord of Madra [also struck] Yudhiṣṭhira in battle.
With four arrows he struck down the horses;
having slain the horses, the high-souled one caused a slaughter of the warriors of King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
The king, out of dejection, [spoke] to that one who alone had performed a wondrous deed, difficult for others to endure, which was like a thorn [piercing him].
Mṛdaṅgaketu reflected:
"How can these words of the younger brother of Indra become fruitless today through the power of destiny?"
"Kill him," for he spoke thus in that battle;
the word of the Lord of the World cannot be otherwise.
When the king had acted accordingly, Bhīmasena—
Then the high-souled one, having swiftly severed the bow of the lord of Madra with a swift arrow,
pierced the king deeply with two more.
Then, with another [arrow],
he severed the head of the driver from the middle of his armored body,
and he quickly struck down the four horses.
Thus Bhīmasena, the foremost of all wielders of the bow, being violently enraged,
[assailed] him who was moving alone with extreme speed in battle.
Bhīma scattered [him] with a hundred arrows,
and Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī, did likewise.
Seeing Śalya bewildered by those shafts, [he struck him again].
With sharp,
fiercely blazing, stone-tipped arrows, Bhīma cut through his armor.
His armor having been cut away by Bhīmasena,
that high-souled lord of the Madras took up a sword and a shield adorned with a thousand stars and [leaped] from his chariot.
Having leaped forward, he charged at the son of Kuntī;
then, having severed Nakula’s chariot-pole,
that man of terrible strength rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
And as that king was springing forward,
like the enraged God of Death himself rushing toward them,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the sons of Draupadī, and Śikhaṇḍin [rushed against him].
And the grandson of Śini suddenly surrounded him;
then the high-souled Bhīma cut down his incomparable shield with ten feathered arrows.
And with broad-headed arrows, he cut the sword from Bhīma’s grip while roaring joyfully in the midst of your army;
seeing that feat of Bhīma, they were filled with delight.
Those preeminent hosts of charioteers among the Pāṇḍavas let out a great roar with wide smiles and blew their conchs,
which were as white as the moon.
Then, by that terrifying sound, your army became distressed and dispirited;
overcome by sweat, their limbs were drenched in blood.
Rendered unconscious and despondent,
the King of Madra was suddenly overwhelmed by those foremost Pāṇḍava warriors led by Bhīma.
He rushed with speed toward Yudhiṣṭhira,
like a lion springing for the sake of a deer;
that King of Dharma [beheld] him whose horses and charioteer had been slain.
Seeing the lord of the Madras blazing with the brilliance of a fire kindled by wrath, he quickly rushed toward that enemy with all his might.
Quickly reflecting upon Govinda’s words,
that King of Dharma, whose horses and charioteer had been slain, set his mind upon the destruction of Śalya.
Standing on his chariot, he longed for the *śakti* weapon alone,
having heard of that deed of Śalya and knowing that only the portion remaining for the high-souled one was left.

Having remembered this, the self-controlled Dharmarāja, intent on destroying the thorn in his mind, acted as instructed by the younger brother of Indra; he [took up] a staff adorned with jewels and gold.
He seized a spear shining like gold,
suddenly opened his blazing eyes,
and with a mind full of wrath, he gazed at the lord of the Madras.
O god among men, although he was gazed upon by the king—
himself pure of soul and cleansed of all taint— he did not turn to ashes, O King of Madra.
O King, that appeared wonderful to me;
then [he took] a spear with a beautiful and fierce shaft,
blazing with jewels and corals and set aflame.
The high-souled and preeminent hero of the Kurus hurled that blazing weapon with great force and power at the lord of the Madras.
All the assembled Kurus beheld it falling suddenly with sparks,
like a great meteor at the end of an eon.
Like the Night of Doom with noose in hand,
like the fierce-formed nurse of Yama, she was infallible and resembled the staff of Brahmā.
The King of Dharma, exerting himself in battle,
released [the weapon] that had been diligently honored by the sons of Pāṇḍu with perfumes, foremost garlands, seats, drinks, and food.
Resembling the fire of universal destruction, blazing like a fierce *kṛtyā* spell of the Atharva-Aṅgirases,
she had been specially fashioned for the sake of the Lord.
Created by Tvaṣṭṛ to consume the bodies of enemies, she was capable of forcibly slaying all beings, including those dwelling on earth, in the intermediate space, and in the waters.
Adorned with bells, banners, jewels,
and diamonds, variegated with lapis lazuli and possessing a shaft of refined gold, it was fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ with great effort and according to the prescribed rules.
Having empowered with terrible mantras that unerring weapon— which brings an end to those who hate the Brahmins and has been mounted with forceful effort— he [discharged it].
He then discharged it along the supreme path for the slaughter of the lord of Madra,
roaring aloud, "You are slain!"
Like Rudra at the end of the aeon,
the King of Dharma, as if dancing in his wrath, extended his very firm arm with its excellent hand, like an arrow that brings an end to the end-maker.
At the time of Madra’s destruction, the son of Dharma stood before him like the one who uprooted the three cities, with a shimmering halo of light radiating from his mass of rays.
At that time, he assumed the form of Maheśvara,
with his long arms curled at the elbows, wandering at twilight, and possessing a slender, rounded waist.
With a broad chest like the Lord Hara,
the elder brother of Arjuna became difficult to behold;
he [then] [warded off] that spear which had been hurled with all his might.
Shalya roared in response to Yudhishthira’s irresistible prowess,
as fire roars at a stream of clarified butter properly poured into it.
Having pierced his vital organs,
that brilliant [arrow] likewise entered his broad chest and armor, plunging into the earth like water unimpeded.
Burning the king’s vast fame with the flowing pus born of his wounds, which issued forth from his nose, eyes, ears, and mouth;
His body was drenched in blood,
like a great mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt;
stretching out his arms, he fell from the chariot to the earth.
His armor shattered by the joy of the Kurus,
that high-souled one, who resembled the mount of great Indra,
was like the peak of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Stretching out his arms and facing the King of Dharma, the King of Madra,
stretching out his arms and facing him, very swiftly approached the presence of the King of Dharma.
Then he fell upon the earth like a lofty banner of Indra;
with all his limbs thus shattered and drenched in blood,
that bull among men was as if welcomed by the earth out of affection.
Like a lover pressed against the breast of his beloved,
having long enjoyed the earth as a lord enjoys a dear and lovely mistress,
he lay there as if fast asleep, embracing her with all his limbs.
Slain in a righteous battle by the son of Dharma, whose very soul is dharma,
he was like a well-sacrificed fire that has been properly extinguished at the altar;
his heart pierced by a spear, his weapons and banner cast away.
Even though the Lord of Madra was completely pacified, Fortune did not abandon him at all.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, taking up a bow with the splendor of Indra’s rainbow,
scattered his enemies in battle like the king of birds dispersing serpents.
Destroying the bodies and lives of his enemies in an instant with sharp broad-headed arrows,
he then overwhelmed your soldiers with a flood of Pārtha’s shafts;
their eyes closed in pain, they struck one another violently as they were tormented.
With their armor cast off, their bodies stripped of weapons and life,
when Śalya had thus fallen, the youthful younger brother of the King of Madra—
a chariot-warrior equal to his brother in every virtue— rushed against the Pāṇḍava.

And that best of men, fierce in battle, acting with haste and desiring to avenge his slain brother, pierced him with many iron shafts. Dharmarāja, as if in great haste, pierced him in return with six swift arrows.
With two razor-sharp arrows, he cut through his bow and his standard as well.
Then, with a blazing, very firm,
and keen broad-headed shaft (bhalla), he struck off the head of the one standing before him.
With a straight-knotted, broad-headed arrow, he severed the head;
that head, adorned with earrings, was seen falling from the chariot like a dweller of heaven falling after his merit has been exhausted.
Seeing his body fallen from the chariot with its head severed and its limbs drenched in blood, the army broke; for that younger brother of the Madra king, clad in variegated armor, had been slain.
Uttering cries of "Alas! Alas!", the Kurus fled in all directions;
seeing the younger brother of Śalya slain, your warriors, having abandoned all hope for life, were utterly terrified by the fear of the Pāṇḍavas and were heavily covered in dust.
O bull of the Bharatas, as those Kauravas were thus being broken and terrified,
that army of your son fled in every direction out of fear;
then Sātyaki, the grandson of Śini, advanced against them, scattering his arrows.
As that great archer, irresistible and difficult to approach, was advancing,
O King, the son of Hṛdika quickly received him fearlessly.
Those two high-souled, unconquered scions of the Vṛṣṇi race then encountered one another.
Hārdikya and Sātyaki, like two lions fierce with rut,
covered each other with arrows of pure luster;
they were equal in splendor to the sun, like the rays of the maker of day.
We beheld in the sky the arrows discharged by the strength of the arms of those two lions of the Vṛṣṇis, moving swiftly like insects;
having pierced Sātyaki with ten shafts and his horses with three.
With a single straight-knotted arrow, the son of Hṛdika cut his bow asunder.
Casting aside that severed, excellent bow, the bull among the Śinis swiftly took up another weapon of even greater power.
Taking up that most excellent bow, he, the best among all archers,
pierced Hārdikya in the center of the chest with ten arrows;
then, having cut through the chariot’s yoke and pole with well-aimed broad-headed shafts.
He swiftly slew his horses and both his flank-drivers. O Lord, seeing the son of Hṛdika deprived of his chariot, the valiant Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat,
quickly took him up onto his own chariot and carried him away.
O King, when the King of Madra had been slain and Kṛtavarman rendered carless,
the entire army of Duryodhana once again turned its back in retreat. Enveloped by the dust raised by the troops, the enemy could not perceive anything.
At that time, the army was mostly slain and turned its back in retreat.
Then, after a moment, O bull among men, they saw the dust raised from the earth being settled by various flows of blood.
O lord of the people, seeing various surging floods of blood,
Duryodhana, beholding his own army broken nearby,
then alone withstood all the Pārthas as they rushed forward with speed.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas with their chariots, as well as Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata and the invincible Ānarta, he covered them with sharp arrows;
the enemies did not advance against him, just as mortals do not approach death when it has arrived.
Then Hārdikya, mounting another chariot, also turned back; grasping his formidable bow, he rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira. Thereupon, King Yudhiṣṭhira, that great car-warrior, acted with haste.

With four feathered arrows, he struck down the horses of Kṛtavarman, and he also pierced Gautama with six well-sharpened broad-headed shafts. Then Aśvatthāman [beheld] him whose horses had been slain by the king and who was rendered carless.
The son of Hṛdika bore Yudhiṣṭhira away from him on his own chariot.
Then the son of Śaradvat pierced Yudhiṣṭhira in return with eight arrows,
and he struck his horses with eight sharp, stone-tipped shafts.
"O Great King, it was thus that this remnant of battle proceeded,
O Bhārata, due to the evil counsel of you and your son, O King.
When that foremost of great archers had been slain..."
In the midst of the battle,
the sons of Pṛthā, having assembled and seeing Śalya slain by that bull among the Kurus, were exceedingly joyful and blew their conchs.
And they praised Yudhiṣṭhira in battle, just as the gods of old praised Indra upon the slaying of Vṛtra;
and they made the sounds of various kinds of musical instruments.
Making the earth resound on all sides,
Sañjaya said:
"O King, when Śalya had been slain, the followers of the Madra king [advanced]."
Seven hundred heroic chariot-warriors went forth from that great army.
Duryodhana, however, having mounted an elephant resembling a mountain,
was shaded by a parasol and fanned with yak-tail whisks.
"Do not go! Do not go!"—thus he restrained the Madras. Though those heroes were repeatedly forbidden by Duryodhana, they entered the army of the Pāṇḍavas, desiring to slay Yudhiṣṭhira.
O great king, those heroes, having resolved upon battle,
fought with the Pāṇḍavas while producing a great sound from their bows;
they heard that Śalya had been slain and that the son of Dharma was being afflicted.

Then the great car-warrior Pārtha, skilled in pleasing the King of Madra and accompanied by the great chariot-fighters of the Madrakas, arrived there, brandishing his bow Gāṇḍīva and filling all directions with the roar of his chariot.
Then Arjuna, Bhīma, the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī, Sātyaki— that tiger among men— and all the sons of Draupadī,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the Pañcālas together with the Somakas [advanced].
Desiring to seize Yudhiṣṭhira, they surrounded him on all sides. Surrounded on all sides by the Pāṇḍavas, those bulls among men agitated that army like sea-monsters agitating the ocean.
O King, like the great river Gaṅgā being agitated by a headwind,
the army of the Pāṇḍavas was once again thrown into turmoil.
Then those great car-warriors, reckless of their own lives, plunged into the vast host.
Like great winds shaking trees, your men caused them to tremble;
many there cried out, "Where is King Yudhiṣṭhira?
Where are those heroic brothers of his? None of them are to be seen here."
The highly heroic Pāñcālas, the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the grandson of Śini (Sātyaki), and all the sons of Draupadī—
these great car-warriors, the sons of Draupadī, [encountered] those speaking heroes.
Yuyudhana struck down the followers of the King of Madra;
some were seen in the battle with their wheels crushed, others with their great banners severed— all your men slain by the enemies.

O King, O Bhārata, seeing the Pāṇḍavas in battle, the warriors rushed forward from all sides with great speed despite being restrained by your son. But Duryodhana, seeking to pacify them, tried to hold back those heroes.
And no great car-warrior there could withstand his command.
Then, O Great King, Śakuni, the son of the king of Gāndhāra and skilled in speech, addressed these words to Duryodhana:
"Why is our army being slaughtered while we Madrakas look on?
This is not fitting while you stand here in battle, O Bhārata.
It was this agreement that was made: 'We must fight together.'"
"09,017.020c Then why, O King, do you tolerate those who are striking down others?
09,017.021 Duryodhana said:
09,017.021a Though previously restrained by me, these men did not heed my words."
"For all these have been slain and have fled toward the Pāṇḍava army.
Śakuni said:
"Though being restrained..."

"O hero, previously I did not heed your words; for those who are indignant do not carry out their master's command in battle. Enough of this anger toward them, for this is not the time for indifference."
"O King, let us all go there together, with our horses, chariots,
and elephants, to protect those great archers who follow the King of Madra;
let us guard one another with great effort."
Having thus reflected, they all proceeded to where the soldiers were.
Sañjaya said:
Thus addressed, the king, surrounded by a great force, [set out].
He advanced, making the earth tremble with his lion-like roar:
"Slay! Pierce! Seize! Strike!
Cut them down!"—such was the tumultuous clamor from your army, O Bhārata.
But the Pāṇḍavas, seeing the followers of the King of Madra in battle while your sons looked on, advanced without agitation against them in a body,
taking up their positions in the center of the array.

Within a moment, O lord of the people, those heroic followers of the King of Madra were seen slain in hand-to-hand combat on the battlefield. Then, as we advanced, those swift warriors whose enemies had been killed [rejoined us].
The enemies, gathered together, joyfully raised a tumultuous shout of "kilakila.
Then, headless trunks were seen rising up on all sides,
and a great meteor fell through the center of the solar disc.
The earth was covered with broken chariots, shattered yokes and axles, slain great car-warriors, and fallen horses;
with steeds galloping like the wind, their harnesses still attached to them.
O great king, the warriors there on the field of battle were seen [in various states]:
some horses dragged chariots with broken wheels in the fray;
others, taking up half-chariots, wandered in all ten directions.
And here and there, O best of men, horses were seen entangled in their harnesses,
and chariot-warriors were seen falling like Siddhas dropped from the sky at the exhaustion of their merits.
When the heroes and the followers of the King of Madra had been slain,
and seeing us rushing toward them, the great car-warriors of the Pārthas,
those strikers greedy for victory, advanced with speed.
Having produced the sounds of whizzing arrows mingled with the blasts of conchs,
those strikers, having found their mark once more, shook their bows and uttered lion-like roars toward us.
Then, beholding that great army of the King of Madra destroyed,
and seeing the heroic King of Madra himself struck down in battle,
the entire force of Duryodhana once again turned its back in flight.
O great king, being slaughtered by the Pāṇḍavas who appeared victorious,
he then fled in all directions, bewildered and terrified by those firm bowmen.
Saṃjaya said:
When the invincible Madra king, that great car-warrior, was struck down in battle,
your men and your sons for the most part turned their backs,
like merchants whose ship has been wrecked in the fathomless ocean where no raft exists.
O great king, when the heroic and high-souled King of Madra was slain, those who were without shore sought a shore; terrified and mangled by arrows,
they were like leaderless deer tormented by a lion, seeking a protector.

Like bulls with broken horns or elephants with shattered tusks, we retreated at midday, utterly defeated by the son of Dharma. O King, neither could our ranks be rallied, nor was there any prowess left in us.
O Bhārata, lord of the people, when Śalya had been slain, and Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the Sūtaputra had also been killed, what thought occurred to any of your warriors,
and what grief and fear arose among your soldiers?

That fear and that grief of ours returned once again; for when the great car-warrior Śalya was slain, we were hopeless of victory. O King, when Śalya was killed, the highly illustrious king was also without hope.
With their foremost heroes slain, shattered, and mangled by sharp arrows,
O King, when the King of Madra was killed, your warriors fled in fear;
some on horses, others on elephants, and others on chariots, O great car-warriors.
Mounting [their mounts], the swift-footed infantry fled in fear;
and two thousand striking elephants, resembling mountains,
fled away once Śalya was slain, urged on by hooks and toes.
O best of the Bharatas, your troops fled in all directions from the battle;
as they ran, they were seen gasping for breath, afflicted by arrows.
Seeing them broken, fleeing, their enthusiasm destroyed, and defeated—
The Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas, desiring victory, rushed forward;
and a great clamor of whizzing arrows, a massive lion-roar,
and the fierce sound of the heroes' conchs arose.
Seeing the Kuru army fleeing in terror,
the Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, spoke to one another:
"Today King Yudhiṣṭhira, whose resolve is truth, has conquered his enemies."

Today Duryodhana has been deprived of his blazing royal splendor. Today, by good fortune, Draupadī—who had never looked upon anyone else as her husband—has found her bed upon the earth. Let it be proclaimed that the vow she made has been fulfilled.
Having heard today that his son has been slain, let Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
fall senseless to the ground and incur the fruit of his sin.
Today let him recognize the son of Kuntī as the most capable of all archers.
Today the evil-minded evildoer will reproach himself,
remembering the true and beneficial words spoken by Vidura.
From this day forward, serving as their servant, he shall attend upon the sons of Pṛthā.
Let the king understand today the suffering that has been experienced by the sons of Pāṇḍu as a result of their past deeds;
let that lord of the earth recognize today the greatness of Kṛṣṇa.
Today in battle, let the king hear the terrible roar of Arjuna’s bow;
today the king shall hear of the horrific slaughter of his sons by Bhīma,
and the full power of all weapons as well as the strength of his arms in combat.
Today he shall know the terrible strength of the high-souled Bhīma,
once Duryodhana has been slain in battle— just as Maya was by Śakra—
by that which Bhīmasena performed at the time of Duḥśāsana’s slaughter.
There is no other agent in this world besides that Bhīma of great strength;
let them now witness the prowess of the eldest Pāṇḍava,
having heard that the King of Madra— so difficult even for the gods to withstand— has been slain.
Today in battle, he will recognize the two sons of Mādrī as possessed of great strength,
once the heroic son of Subala has been slain and all the Gāndhāras have been destroyed.
How could victory not belong to those who have Dhanañjaya as their warrior?
Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
the five sons of Draupadī, the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
the great archer Śikhaṇḍin, and King Yudhiṣṭhira himself.

For those worlds whose protector is Kṛṣṇa Janārdana, how could they not be victorious, since Dharma is their refuge? Victory belongs to them, victory belongs to them; whence could there be defeat for them?
Those for whom Hari, the Lord of the Senses and Sovereign of all worlds, is their protector— Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and the King of Madra,
as well as other heroic kings by the hundreds and thousands.
"Who else is capable of conquering him in battle except for Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira,
whose protector is always Hṛṣīkeśa, the treasury of dharma and glory?
Speaking thus, they were filled with great joy.
O King, as your troops were being broken, the Sṛñjayas pursued them from behind;
the heroic Dhanañjaya turned against the division of chariots,
as did the two sons of Mādrī and the great car-warrior Sātyaki against Śakuni.
Seeing them all fleeing, afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena,
Duryodhana then spoke to his charioteer as if smiling:
"Pārtha shall not bypass me while I stand here with bow in hand."
"Station my horses at the rear of the entire army;
for if Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, fights from the rear,
he will not dare to overtake me, just as the great ocean cannot overstep its shore."
"Behold, O Sūta, this great army being pursued by the Pāṇḍavas!
Behold this dust raised by the troops on all sides!
And hear the many terrible and fearsome lion-roars!"
"Therefore, O charioteer, proceed slowly and protect the rear. While I stand here in battle and the Pāṇḍavas are held in check,
my army will quickly return with vigor."
Having heard those words of your son, which were worthy of one among the foremost of heroes,
the charioteer slowly urged on the horses covered in gold.
The foot soldiers, deprived of elephants, horses, and chariot-warriors, had cast away all regard for their own lives.
Twenty-one thousand warriors,
born in various lands and clad in garments of diverse colors,
then stood ready for battle, seeking great glory.
As they rushed toward one another there, filled with mutual excitement,
a great, terrible, and fearsome crush occurred.
At that time, O King, [they fell upon] Bhīmasena and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.
With a fourfold army, those from various lands held him back; yet other foot-soldiers advanced against Bhīma in battle,
shouting and slapping their arms in joy, desiring to reach the world of heroes.
Having encountered Bhīmasena, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— furious and intoxicated by battle— shouted aloud; they spoke of nothing else but,
enraged, surrounded him from all sides in order to seize him.
Surrounding Bhīma in the battle, they struck him from all sides;
though being slaughtered in that conflict while hemmed in by throngs of foot soldiers,
he did not waver from his seat upon the chariot, remaining like Mount Maināka.

But they, O great king, being enraged, set about to seize the great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍava, while warding off his other warriors. Bhīma then became incensed in battle by those who stood surrounding him.
Quickly descending from his chariot, he stood on foot,
grasping his great mace adorned with gold;
like Death himself with staff in hand, he struck down your warriors.
But the powerful Bhīma, with his mace, [struck] those who were deprived of chariots, horses,
and elephants; that bull among men, Bhīmasena, mace in hand, [attacked] those men who were bereft of their chariots and horses with his thunderbolt-like mace.
He crushed twenty-one thousand foot soldiers; having slain that host of men, Bhīma, whose prowess is truth,
soon reappeared with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at his front.
The foot soldiers, slain upon the ground, lay drenched in blood like blossoming *karṇikāra* trees broken down by the wind;
they were adorned with garlands of various flowers and wore diverse earrings.
Slain there were men of various castes who had gathered from many lands; that great host of foot-soldiers, covered with banners and standards,
lay mangled there, appearing terrible and fearsome in form.
