Led by Yudhiṣṭhira, all those great car-warriors of the entire army rushed toward your high-souled son, Duryodhana. Seeing all those great archers of yours turning their backs in retreat, they [pursued them].

Displaying the appearance of victors, they rushed forward swiftly for battle; yet they could not overcome your son, just as the ocean cannot overstep its shore. We then beheld that wonderful prowess of your son.
That which the Pārthas, though united, were unable to overcome— Duryodhana spoke to his own severely wounded army as they had not retreated very far and were resolved upon flight.
"I do not see any place on earth, whether on the plains or among the mountains, where the Pāṇḍavas would not slay you once you have gone there; what is the use of your flight?
Their force is small, and both the Kṛṣṇas are severely wounded."
"If we all remain here, our victory will be certain; however, if you depart and are scattered, the sinful Pāṇḍavas will pursue and slay you. It is better for us to stand firm in battle."
Listen, all you kṣatriyas who have assembled here:
since Death always slays both the hero and the coward alike,
what man who calls himself a kṣatriya would not fight, unless he were a fool?
"It is better for us to stand before the enraged Bhīmasena;
for one who fights according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, death in battle is easy.
A mortal must inevitably die at some time, even within his own home."
For one who fights according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, this death is eternal. Having conquered here, he attains happiness; being slain, he obtains great fruit after passing away.
Indeed, O Kauravas, there is no path to heaven better than the duty of battle.
"Slain in battle, he shall before long enjoy the worlds he has conquered.
Having heard his words and honored him, the kings once again turned against the Pāṇḍavas as assailants.
As they were swiftly charging forward with their ranks arrayed,
the striking Pārthas, eager for victory, then advanced against them as strikers. The heroic Dhanañjaya turned his chariot toward the field of battle.
Wielding the bow Gāṇḍīva, renowned throughout the three worlds,
the two sons of Mādrī and the mighty Sātyaki rushed forward with joy and speed toward the army of your side where Śakuni stood.
Saṃjaya said:
When that flood of troops had retreated, Śālva, the lord of the Mleccha hosts,
turned with great fury toward the vast army of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having mounted that great elephant, which was in rut like a mountain,
as proud as Airāvata, the crusher of hosts of enemies,
and born of the Mahābhadra lineage;
O King, it was constantly well-honored by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
perfectly equipped by those learned in the determination of the treatises,
and always fit to be ridden in battles.
Seated upon Airāvata, that best of kings appeared like Śakra crushing the hosts of Daityas and instilling fear.
O King, like the sun rising at the end of the night,
he advanced against the sons of Pāṇḍu from all sides with that preeminent elephant.
He also tore [his opponent] apart with sharp arrows,
most terrible and resembling the thunderbolt of great Indra;
then, as he discharged those arrows in the great battle—
And as he led the warriors, O King, to Yama’s abode,
the monarch discharged his arrows and sent all the combatants to the realm of Death.

Neither among their own ranks nor among the enemy did they see any opening in him, just as the Daityas could find none in the wielder of the thunderbolt when he stood upon Airāvaṇa during the crushing of the army.
O King, just as the Daityas of old [beheld Indra],
those Pāṇḍavas, Somakas, and Sṛñjayas saw that very same elephant on every side.
He was indeed wandering alone like the elephant of Mahendra,
while the army of his enemies was being put to flight.
It appeared as if surrounded on all sides;
it did not stand its ground in the battle out of intense fear,
as they were then crushing one another.
Then that great Pandava army was suddenly shattered by that lord of men;
it fled in haste toward the four quarters.
Seeing her broken by that forceful one with the speed of a lordly elephant,
all your chief warriors in battle were unable to withstand him.
There they honored that lord of men and blew conchs as bright as the moon;
then, hearing the clamor of the Kauravas, [the Pāṇḍavas...]
The commander of the Pāṇḍavas and Sṛñjayas, the son of the Pañcāla king, could not endure with anger that [Arjuna] was released from his bonds amidst the sounds of conchs and shouts of joy.
Then that high-souled one, hastening for victory, indeed advanced against that elephant,
just as Jambha did in the encounter with Śakra.
Seeing that lord of serpents, Airāvaṇa, the mount of Indra, suddenly charging toward him in battle,
that lion among kings [beheld] the king of the Pañcālas.
O King, he swiftly dispatched that elephant for the slaughter of Drupada’s son;
it then rushed suddenly toward him as it charged.
He pierced him with three foremost iron arrows of fierce velocity— sharpened, blazing, cleansed by the smith, and resembling the sun.
Then the high-souled one discharged five other sharp, preeminent iron arrows (nārāca) at Kumbha;
pierced by them in battle, that supreme elephant—
Then, having turned back, he fled swiftly;
but Śālva seized that king of serpents as he was suddenly driven away and being put to flight.
He swiftly urged [the elephant] on with goads and hooks,
directing it toward the chariot of the Pāñcāla king;
seeing the elephant suddenly charging, he—
Dhrishtadyumna, the hero, having quickly seized a mace from his own chariot, swiftly descended to the ground with trembling limbs out of fear.
Then that great elephant, having suddenly crushed that chariot— its body adorned with gold, along with its horses and driver—
took it up in his trunk.
Having seen the son of the Pāñcāla king afflicted by that best of elephants, he then crushed him upon the surface of the earth.
Bhīma, Śikhaṇḍin, and the grandson of Śini rushed toward him with sudden speed;
and with their arrows, they suddenly checked his momentum.
As that elephant charged toward him from all sides,
it was indeed restrained by the chariot-warriors;
though being held back by them in the battle, it wavered.
Then the king showered forth arrows on all sides,
like the sun emitting its web of rays;
by those swift shafts, the multitudes of chariots were struck down.
Having witnessed that deed of Śālva, O King, all the Pāñcālas, Matsyas, and Sṛñjayas fled here and there from every side.
Making the air resound with cries of "Alas! Alas!", those foremost of men hemmed in the elephant from all sides in battle;
meanwhile, the heroic king of the Pañcālas acted with haste.
Grasping a mace that resembled the peak of a mountain,
O Bhārata, that hero, the slayer of enemies, pursued the elephant with speed and without agitation.
Then, brandishing his mace, he struck the elephant— which resembled the earth-supporting mountain and was as bright as a rain cloud— with great force as it was shedding rut.
The powerful son of the Pāñcāla king,
his frontal globes split open, suddenly roared and vomited a profusion of blood from his mouth.
The elephant,
resembling a mountain, fell down like a peak shaken by an earthquake as that lord of elephants was being struck down.
While your son’s army raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!",
that hero of the Śinis struck off the head of King Śālva with a sharp broad-headed arrow.
With his head severed in battle by the Sātvata,
he fell to the earth together with the king of elephants,
like a massive mountain peak struck down.
"By the thunderbolt impelled by the Lord of the Gods," Sañjaya said:
"But when that hero Śālva, the ornament of the assembly, had been slain..."
Your army was shattered by his force, like a great tree by a tempestuous wind. Seeing that army thus broken, the heroic and mighty mahāratha Kṛtavarman held back the enemy host in battle.
But those heroes, O King, having seen the Sātvata standing in battle like a mountain, being showered with arrows in the fray, turned back;
then the battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas commenced.
O Great King, having made death their only means of turning back,
those who had retreated engaged in a wondrous battle with the enemy; for the Sātvata alone held back the Pandava army, which was otherwise difficult to approach.
When those mutual friends had performed that difficult deed,
a great lion-roar arose from the delighted warriors, reaching up to the heavens.
O bull of the Bharatas, by that sound, the Pāñcālas were struck with terror.
The mighty-armed Sātyaki, the grandson of Śini,
encountered the exceedingly fierce Śatavarman, that great hero of immense strength.
Having approached King Kṣemadhūrti, who possessed great power...
With seven sharp arrows, he sent him to the abode of Yama.
As that mighty-armed one approached, scattering his keen shafts,
the wise son of Hṛdika swiftly rushed toward that bull among the Śinis.
Roaring like two lions, those two foremost of chariot-warriors,
wielding excellent weapons and armed with bows, rushed at one another.
The Pāṇḍavas, along with the Pañcālas and other warriors, as well as the best of kings, [stood by].
They became spectators of those two lions among men;
with iron shafts and calf-toothed arrows, the great car-warriors of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas struck each other like two elephants in rut.
As the son of Hṛdika and the bull among the Śinis traversed various paths,
they repeatedly concealed one another with showers of arrows;
the shafts of those two lions of the Vṛṣṇis were launched by the force and strength of their bows.
In the sky we beheld him moving with great speed like a bird;
having encountered that one whose deeds are true, the son of Hṛdika pierced his four horses with four sharpened arrows.
That long-armed one, enraged like an elephant struck by a goad,
pierced Kṛtavarman with eight excellent arrows. Then, with arrows sharpened on stone and released from a fully drawn bow, Kṛtavarman—
Having struck Sātyaki with three arrows, he cut his bow with one.
Discarding that excellent bow which had been severed, the bull of the Śini clan,
the descendant of Śini, swiftly took up another bow along with an arrow.
Taking that best of bows, the most excellent of all archers— having strung it, he who was of great heroism, great intelligence, and great strength,
could not endure the cutting of his bow by Kṛtavarman.
Enraged, the great car-warrior quickly advanced against Kṛtavarman;
then, with ten well-sharpened arrows,
that bull among the Śinis struck Kṛtavarman’s charioteer, his horses, and his standard.
Then, O King, the great archer Kṛtavarman, that mighty chariot-warrior,
beholding his gold-adorned chariot with its horses and driver slain,
was overcome by a great rage and raised his spear, O Sire.
Desiring to kill the bull among the Śinis, he hurled it with the strength of his arms.
But the Sātvata, in that battle, having pierced that spear with sharp arrows,
caused it to fall down pulverized, as if bewildering the descendant of Madhu.
Then, with another broad-headed arrow, he struck him in the heart.
With his horses slain and his charioteer killed by Yuyudhāna in that battle,
Kṛtavarman— though skilled in weapons— fell to the earth.
When that hero had been deprived of his chariot by Sātyaki in a single combat,
a very great fear arose among all the troops,
and an extreme despondency came upon your son.
When Kṛtavarman had been deprived of his chariot, his driver killed and his horses slain,
and seeing that subduer of foes with his driver and horses destroyed,
O King, Kṛpa rushed forward, desiring to slay the bull of the Śini clan.
Lifting him onto the seat of his chariot in the very sight of all the archers,
the mighty-armed one quickly bore him away from the field of battle, O King,
now that Kṛtavarman had been deprived of his chariot by the grandson of Śini.

The entire army of Duryodhana once again turned its back in retreat. Enveloped by the dust raised by the troops, the enemy could not perceive them; O King, your men fled in all directions, with the exception of King Duryodhana.
But Duryodhana, beholding his own army broken nearby,
rushed forward with great speed and alone held back all of them—
the enraged Pāṇḍavas and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata.

O noble one, that invincible warrior, with his sharp weapons, unflinchingly held back Śikhaṇḍin, the sons of Draupadī, the hosts of the Pañcālas, the Kekayas, the Somakas, and the Pañcālas themselves.
In that battle, your mighty son stood firm and vigilant,
illuminating every direction like the great fire purified by mantras at a sacrifice;
even so did King Duryodhana prevail throughout the conflict.
The enemies could not advance against him, just as mortals cannot advance against Death in battle.
Then, mounting another chariot, the son of Hṛdika returned to the fray.
Saṃjaya said:
But your son, O great king, that best of chariot-warriors standing upon his chariot—
O Bhārata, he was some indomitable man against the Pāṇḍavas,
appearing irresistible in battle like the majestic Rudra.
The earth was indeed covered by his thousands of arrows;
he drenched the enemies with shafts as clouds drench mountains with torrents of rain.
And there was not a single man among the Pāṇḍavas in that great battle who could withstand him.
Whether it was a horse, an elephant, or even a chariot, there was nothing that remained unpierced by his arrows.
O lord of the people, O Bhārata, whatever warrior I beheld in the battle, each and every one of them was indeed covered with your son’s shafts.
Just as an army is seen completely shrouded by the dust raised by its own troops, so too was [the enemy force] covered by the arrows of that high-souled one;
O lord of the earth, we beheld the earth itself turned into a mass of arrows.

Among those thousands of warriors, both yours and the enemy's, it was my conviction that Duryodhana alone was a true man— provided by Duryodhana himself, a swift-handed archer who had initiated the fray.
There we beheld the wonderful prowess of your son,
O Bhārata, in that the Pārthas, though united, could not overcome him alone.
O bull of the Bharatas, he pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with a hundred arrows in the battle.
He pierced Bhīmasena with seventy arrows, Sahadeva with seven,
Nakula with sixty-four, Dhṛṣṭadyumna with five,
the sons of Draupadī with seven each, and Sātyaki with three.
O noble one, he severed Sahadeva’s bow with a broad-headed arrow. Casting aside that broken bow, the powerful son of Mādrī seized another great bow and rushed toward the king.
Then he pierced Duryodhana in battle with ten arrows;
and then the heroic Nakula, that great archer, pierced the king with nine arrows of terrible form and uttered a roar.
Sātyaki also struck the king with a straight-knotted arrow;
the sons of Draupadī with seventy-three; Dharmarāja with seven;
and Bhīmasena with eighty arrows afflicted the king.
Though being showered from all sides by hosts of arrows from those great-souled warriors,
O great king, he did not waver while the entire army looked on;
such was the lightness, the grace, and the prowess of that high-souled one.
All men beheld him surpassing all beings.
But the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O king of kings, having traveled only a short distance and not seeing the king, turned back, still clad in their armor.
As they rushed forward, a terrible and tumultuous uproar arose,
like that of the agitated ocean at night during the rainy season. Having encountered the unconquered king in battle, they—
The great archers, acting as assailants, advanced against the Pāṇḍavas;
the son of Droṇa held back the enraged Bhīmasena in battle.
Then, O Great King, arrows were released in every direction.
In that battle, neither the heroes nor the cardinal and intermediate directions could be discerned. O Bhārata, those two performers of cruel deeds, both of whom were difficult to withstand,
fought with terrible forms, each seeking to counter the other's actions.
Terrifying the entire world, their skin lacerated by the snapping of bowstrings,
the heroic Śakuni oppressed Yudhiṣṭhira in battle;
the powerful son of Subala, having slain his four horses, [continued the assault].
Struck by the mechanical device, even the two wheels of the chariot were shattered; likewise, the sword-blade, the bow, the sharpened javelins,
the iron arrows, the half-arrows, and even the excellent mallets were destroyed.
Brandishing a gold-handled spear, slings, and battle-axes,
he who was firm in truth performed this terrible deed;
then the powerful one let out a roar, making all the armies tremble.
In that interval, the powerful Sahadeva carried away the heroic and unconquered king on his chariot from the field of battle;
then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Lord of Dharma, mounted another chariot.
Having pierced Śakuni with nine arrows, he struck him again with five;
then that foremost of all archers let out a great roar. That battle, O noble one, was wonderful and terrible in appearance.
Producing delight for the beholder and frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*,
the immeasurable-souled Ulūka rushed against the great archer Nakula, who was fierce in battle, from all sides with showers of arrows.

In that very same way, the heroic Nakula hemmed in the son of Subala on all sides in battle with a great shower of arrows. Those two heroes there in the conflict were both high-born sons and great chariot-warriors.
As they fought, each having committed offenses against the other, they beheld one another;
and likewise, O King, Kṛtavarman, while fighting the descendant of Śini, the scorcher of enemies,
shone like Śakra against Bala in battle.
In that battle, Duryodhana, having severed Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s bow,
pierced him with five sharp, whetted arrows while remaining unperturbed;
then he struck the one whose bow was broken with further sharpened shafts.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna also, seizing his supreme weapon in the battle,
fought the king while all the archers looked on.
O bull of the Bharatas, the combat between those two in that encounter was great.
Like two rutting, pre-eminent elephants locked in combat,
the enraged Gautama, a hero in battle, pierced the mighty sons of Draupadī with many straight-knotted arrows.
His battle with them was like that of an embodied being with the senses—
terrible in form, irresistible, and utterly beyond restraint;
and they oppressed him, as the senses oppress a fool.
And he, highly incensed, fought back against them in battle;
thus, O Bhārata, did that wonderful combat take place between him and them,
O Lord, like the struggle of embodied beings with their own senses as they repeatedly arise.
Men engaged with men, elephants with elephants, horses with horses, and chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors; thus,
O lord of the people, the melee became even more terrible in appearance.

"This is wonderful, this is terrible, this is fierce"— such were the many and horrific battles that took place, O Lord, O Great King. Having encountered one another in combat, those subduers of enemies...
In that great battle, having encountered one another, they pierced and struck each other down;
a thick cloud of dust arising from their weapons was seen,
O King, stirred up by the wind and by the galloping horses and riders.
The dust raised by the rims of chariot wheels and by the breaths of the elephants— tawny like the clouds of twilight— ascended the path of the sun; there,
the sky became as if of a single hue due to the archers.
When the sun was deprived of its luster by being covered with that dust,
the earth became shrouded, as did those heroic great-chariot warriors;
yet in a mere moment, it became free of dust on all sides.
O best of the Bharatas, on that ground drenched with the blood of heroes,
that fierce and terrible dust then subsided. Then, O great king, O Bhārata, I beheld duels between the combatants.
At that most terrible midday, O king of kings, the brilliant splendors of the armor were seen there according to their excellence and seniority; meanwhile,
a tumultuous roar arose from the falling arrows in the battle.
Like a great bamboo forest burning on all sides,
Sañjaya said:
"While that battle of terrible form and fearsome nature was thus proceeding..."
There, the army of your son was broken by the Pāṇḍavas;
however, having warded off those great car-warriors with great effort,
your son continued to fight the host of the Pāṇḍavas.
The warriors, desiring the welfare of your son, suddenly turned back;
when they had thus returned, there occurred a most terrible battle between your men and the enemies,
resembling the war between the gods and the asuras.
Among your enemies and in your own army, there was not a single one who turned his back. They fought by means of inference and by calling out names to one another;
as they fought with each other, their destruction was great.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with great rage and desiring to conquer the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their kings in battle,
pierced the son of Śaradvat with three gold-feathered arrows whetted on stone.
With four [arrows], he struck down Kṛtavarman’s excellent horses;
Aśvatthāman, however, bore away the illustrious son of Hṛdika.
Then the son of Śaradvat pierced Yudhiṣṭhira with eight [arrows].

Then King Duryodhana dispatched seven hundred chariots in battle to where that king Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was located. Those chariots, manned by warriors, possessed the speed of thought and the wind.
They rushed in battle toward the chariot of the son of Kuntī;
surrounding Yudhiṣṭhira on all sides, O great king,
they made him invisible with their arrows, just as clouds obscure the sun.
Seeing the King of Dharma treated in such a manner by the Kauravas,
those car-warriors led by Śikhaṇḍin, highly incensed, could not endure it;
they were mounted on chariots yoked with horses of supreme speed and covered with networks of small bells.
They arrived, protecting Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī.
Then there commenced a fierce battle, with blood for its water,
resembling the war between the gods and the asuras.
Likewise, there was another great battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus, which increased the population of Yama’s kingdom;
having slain seven hundred chariot-warriors among the attacking Kurus.
The Pāṇḍavas, together with the Pañcālas, once again checked [your son].
There, a great battle took place between your son and the Pāṇḍavas;
such a thing had never been seen by us, nor even heard of before.
While that battle was thus proceeding lawlessly on all sides,
as your warriors and those of the other side were being slain,
and while the combatants were shouting amidst the sounds of excellent conchs being blown;
With the twanging of bowstrings from the foremost warriors, with the sound of palms clapping on all sides,
with loud shouts of "Bravo! and the roaring of archers,
the battle grew exceedingly fierce as vital organs were being pierced.
O noble one, while the warriors ran about greedy for victory,
when a slaughter had arisen on all sides and grief was born upon the earth,
and while the hair-parting ceremonies (*sīmantonnayana*) of many excellent women were being performed;
While that most terrible battle, devoid of all restraint, was thus proceeding,
there then appeared most dreadful portents foreboding destruction;
the earth, together with its mountains and forests, trembled while emitting a great sound.

O King, meteors accompanied by clubs and flames fell from the sky to the earth, having struck the solar disc, as they shattered on all sides. Winds blew in every direction, raining down gravel from below.
The Nāgas shed tears and were violently seized by trembling;
yet, disregarding these terrible and most dreadful portents,
the Kṣatriyas consulted together once more for battle and stood firm, undaunted.
In the delightful and holy Kurukṣetra, those desiring to go to heaven,
Śakuni, the son of the king of Gāndhāra, then spoke;
with his utmost power, Śakuni rushed against the Pāṇḍava army.
"Fight in the front until I slay the Pāṇḍavas from behind!
While he was thus slaying the Pāṇḍavas, who are fierce in battle, from behind,
the swift Madra warriors then joined us as we advanced.
Others likewise, filled with joy, raised shouts of "kila-kilā.
But having once again encountered us, those unassailable warriors, who had found their mark, shook their bows and overwhelmed us with showers of arrows.

Then, seeing that the army of the King of Madra had been struck down there by the enemies, and observing Duryodhana’s force likewise, it turned its back once more. But then the powerful King of Gandhāra spoke these words again:
"Turn back, you who know not dharma! Fight! What is the use of your flight?
Otherwise, the pleasure of dalliance with celestial women and this very gateway to the glorious abode of the Thirty-three will be destroyed."

Having spoken thus, Śakuni departed swiftly again and again toward Lakṣadhvaja and Vasiṣṭha with that great army, O bull of the Bharatas, which possessed the speed of thought and wind and consisted of ten thousand horses.
While that slaughter of men was proceeding, the king of the Gāndhāras— by means of his force of warriors fighting with spotless lances—
displayed his prowess and struck the Pāṇḍava army from behind with sharpened arrows.
O great king, that vast army of the Pāṇḍavas was shattered on all sides like a cloud driven by the wind. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, seeing his own army broken nearby, [beheld the situation].
Undisturbed, he urged the mighty Sahadeva:
"Yonder son of Subala, clad in armor, is afflicting our rear;
behold this evil-minded one, O Pāṇḍava, as he slaughters the army!"
"Go, you and the sons of Draupadī, and slay Śakuni Saubala!
O sinless one, I, together with the Pāñcālas, will protect the chariot division.
Let all the elephants and horses go along with you."
"O high-minded one, slay Śakuni Saubala along with three thousand foot-soldiers who are scattering [arrows] at us; there,
by the power of my meditation, you will remain unharmed— of this there is no doubt."
"And there is no other founder of the teaching remaining besides you;
whatever you command," he said thus with a joyful mind.
Then seven hundred elephants arrived, mounted by those holding bows in their hands.
Five thousand horses, the valiant Sahadeva,
three thousand foot soldiers, and all the sons of Draupadī charged in battle against Śakuni, who was intoxicated with the pride of war.
Then, O King, the powerful son of Subala, greedy for victory, bypassed the Pāṇḍavas and struck at the rear of their army. The horse-riders of the swift Pāṇḍavas, however, were filled with fury.
Having bypassed those chariots, they entered the army of Saubala;
those heroic horsemen, stationed in the midst of the elephants, overwhelmed that great force of Saubala with showers of arrows.
O King, because of your evil counsel, that great battle ensued, frequented by men who were no cowards, where maces and spears were raised aloft;
the sounds of bowstrings ceased, and the chariot-warriors became mere spectators.

O bull of the Bharatas, no distinction could be seen between one's own side and the enemy's; the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas beheld the falling of spears hurled by the arms of heroes like the collision of celestial lights.
O lord of the people, the sky there was covered by many stainless spears falling here and there, and it shone brightly;
O King, the appearance of the javelins as they fell on all sides was magnificent.
O best of the Bharatas, then, like locusts in the sky,
horses with their limbs drenched in blood and their riders cast away fell by the hundreds and thousands.
Having encountered one another and crushed each other,
they were seen, though unhurt, vomiting blood from their mouths.
Then, as the army was enveloped by dust, a terrible darkness arose.
O King, while the dust was thick, I saw those subduers of enemies— the horses and the men— retreating from that place;
others had fallen upon the ground, vomiting much blood.
Locked together hair-to-hair, the men were unable to move;
dragging one another from the backs of their horses, those of great strength encountered each other like wrestlers and struck one another down.
Many there were dragged away by horses, their lives departed;
others, many seekers of victory, fell upon the ground—
men who considered themselves heroes were seen here and there.
The earth was seen strewn by the hundreds and thousands with severed arms smeared with blood and with disheveled hair; at that place,
it was not possible for anyone to travel far by horse.
The surface of the earth was covered with slain horses along with their riders,
and with warriors whose armor was drenched in blood, who had seized their weapons and raised them aloft,
bearing various terrible implements and seeking to slay one another.
O lord of the people, having fought for a moment against those who were very close by and whose troops were mostly slain in battle, Śakuni, the son of Subala,
then retreated from there with the six thousand horses that remained.
In the same way, the Pāṇḍava army, drenched in blood and with its mounts exhausted,
retreated with the six thousand horses that remained;
and the horsemen of the Pāṇḍavas, drenched in blood, spoke.
"Today we shall slay Śakuni along with his sons and kinsmen,
and thereafter the wicked Duryodhana, by the grace of the Pāṇḍavas;
for we are very close to him in battle and have largely renounced our lives."
"It is not possible to fight here with chariots, much less with great elephants.
Let chariots advance against chariots and elephants against elephants;
we shall follow behind together, having renounced our lives."
Having fled from that [battle] in great haste, they have resorted to various pretexts; for Śakuni has retreated and remains stationed within his own army,
and King Saubala will not come back to the fight again.
Then the sons of Draupadī and those intoxicated great elephants proceeded to where the Pāñcālya, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
was; and Sahadeva also, O Kauravya, as a cloud of dust arose.
Alone, he proceeded to where King Yudhiṣṭhira was. Then, after they had departed, Śakuni Saubala,
filled with rage, struck at the side of Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s army.
Then that tumultuous battle resumed, with both your men and the enemy casting away their lives, each desiring the slaughter of the other. For they gazed upon one another in that encounter of heroes.
O King, warriors fell by the hundreds and thousands;
as their heads were being severed by swords in that destruction of the world,
a great sound arose like that of falling palmyra fruits.
O lord of the people, as the bodies of those who had been liberated [from life] fell broken upon the earth, and as their arms and thighs— still clutching weapons—
fell, there arose a very great, hair-raising sound of crunching.
Striking down even their brothers, sons, and friends with sharpened weapons,
the warriors rushed about like birds competing for meat,
enraged as they encountered one another.
"Me first! Me first! they cried, as they struck down thousands [of foes]. With heaps of horsemen fallen from their seats and deprived of life, horses fell about by the hundreds and thousands.

O lord of the people, a tumultuous roar arose from the swift-moving horses as they galloped and were struck down, and from the shouting men clad in armor, along with the clashing sounds of spears, swords, and javelins.
O King, because of your evil counsel, they pierced the vital organs of one another;
for thus the warriors, enraged and striking at each other,
were overcome by exhaustion— furious, with weary mounts, and parched with thirst.
Wounded by sharp weapons, your men turned back;
many there, intoxicated by the scent of blood and deprived of their senses,
slew both enemies and their own kin as they encountered them one after another.
O King, on that tumultuous day of joy for wolves, vultures, and jackals, many kṣatriyas, greedy for victory, fell to the earth, overwhelmed by showers of arrows. Their lives had departed.
A terrible destruction of forces occurred while your son looked on;
O lord of the people, the earth was covered with the bodies of men and horses,
variegated with the water of blood, increasing the fear of the timid.
O Bhārata, hacking each other again and again with swords, spears, and spikes, your men and the Pāṇḍavas could not prevail,
striking with all their might as long as they retained their breath.
Warriors were falling about, vomiting blood from their wounds;
a headless trunk was seen, seizing a head by the hair and raising a sharp sword smeared with blood.
O lord of men, when many headless trunks had risen up,
the warriors were overcome by faintness from the stench of blood; then,
as the noise subsided, the great army of the Pāṇḍavas [remained].
With only a few horses remaining, the son of Subala turned back;
then the Pāṇḍavas, greedy for victory, rushed forward in haste— foot soldiers,
elephants, and cavalry with uplifted weapons.
Having hemmed him in and surrounded him on all sides,
they struck him with various kinds of weapons, desiring to reach the further shore of battle. Seeing the army being routed while your son looked on, [they attacked].
Seeing those [enemies] rushing from all sides, your men—
along with their horses, infantry, elephants, and chariots— rushed against the Pāṇḍavas.
Some foot soldiers [attacked] one another with their feet and fists.
The heroes struck one another in battle; then, their weapons exhausted, they fell.
Charioteers fell from their chariots and elephant-riders from their elephants, like Siddhas fallen from their celestial vehicles when their merit has been spent.
Thus, exerting themselves against one another in that great battle,
the warriors struck down fathers, brothers, friends, and even sons;
such was the lawless carnage, O best of the Bharatas.
While that most terrible battle, thick with spears and arrows, was raging,
Saṃjaya said:
"When that tumult had subsided and the army had been struck down by the Pāṇḍavas..."
With the remaining seven hundred horses, the son of Subala returned.
Having quickly approached the army, that subduer of enemies, urging them on in battle, spoke repeatedly with great joy: "Fight!"
There he asked the kṣatriyas, "Where indeed is the king, the great chariot-warrior?
But having heard Śakuni’s words, O bull of the Bharatas, they said:
"There stands the Kaurava, the great chariot-warrior, in the midst of the battle."
Where this very great umbrella stands, radiant like the full moon; where these chariots, equipped with quivers and armored, stand ready;
and where this tumultuous noise resounds, like the roar of rain clouds.
"Go there quickly, O King, and then you shall see the Kaurava.
Thus addressed by those heroes, Śakuni Saubala then set out for that place where your son was, O lord of men.
Surrounded on all sides by heroes who never retreat in battle,
Śakuni then, seeing Duryodhana stationed in the array of chariots,
gladdened all your warriors who were likewise with their chariots.
O lord of the people, appearing joyful and considering his own task already accomplished, he addressed these words to King Duryodhana:
"Slay the chariot division, O King; all the horses have been conquered by me."
"Yudhiṣṭhira cannot be conquered in battle without sacrificing one's own life.
Once that division of chariots protected by the Pāṇḍava has been destroyed,
we shall slay these elephants, as well as the infantry and the others."
Having heard his words, your warriors, greedy for victory,
joyfully rushed with speed toward the army of the Pāṇḍavas;
all of them had their quivers opened and their bows grasped.
Shaking their bows, they let out lion-like roars.
Then, O lord of the people, there arose once more the thunderous sound of bowstrings being struck,
and the most terrible whizzing of well-aimed arrows became manifest.
Seeing them approaching with speed and bows raised,
Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, spoke to the son of Devakī:
"Without agitation, urge on the horses and enter this ocean of an army."
Today I shall reach the end of my enemies with sharpened arrows,
O Janārdana; today marks the eighteenth day of this great battle that has been ongoing as we have encountered one another.

"O Mādhava, behold how the army of these great-souled ones—which was like an infinite ocean—has today met its destruction in battle; see how such is the course of destiny. Indeed, the force of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son was like the very sea."
"O Acyuta, having encountered us, [the Kuru host] has become like a mere puddle in a cow's footprint. O Mādhava, if Bhīṣma were slain, peace might be established here;
yet that fool, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, being utterly childish, did not do so."
O Mādhava, those words spoken by Bhīṣma, which were beneficial and wholesome,
Suyodhana— whose intellect was lost— did not act upon them.
When that Bhīṣma had fallen and descended to the surface of the earth, [the battle continued].
I do not know what the cause was by which this battle proceeded, now that Droṇa has been slain, as well as Karṇa and Bhūriśravas in the conflict, and Duḥśāsana, Śālva,
and Śalya along with their followers.
And while Bhagadatta, the lord of heroes, remained alive, that battle did not subside—
by which sinful man Bhīṣma, as well as Droṇa, Kṛpa, Vidura, and even his own father and mother, were rejected for the sake of peace.
I consider the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to be utterly deluded and extremely foolish,
since they entered into battle again even after the son of Śantanu had fallen;
and likewise immediately thereafter, when Droṇa, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, was slain.
The slaughter did not cease with Rādheya and Vikarṇa;
indeed, the carnage did not subside even when the Sūta’s son, Rādheya, was slain.
When only a small remnant of this army remained and the Sūta’s son had been struck down, [the slaughter continued].
When that tiger among men had been slain along with his son,
the slaughter did not cease; when the heroic Śrutāyus was killed, as well as Jalasaṃdha of the Puru lineage and King Śrutāyudha, the slaughter did not cease.
O Janārdana, while Bhūriśravas, Śalya, and Śālva were still present,
as well as among the heroic warriors of Avanti, that carnage did not cease;
nor did it cease when Jayadratha had been slain, nor even when the Rākṣasa Alāyudha was killed.
The slaughter did not cease even when Bāhlīka and Somadatta had been slain;
nor when the heroic Bhagadatta and Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja were killed,
nor when various kinds of troops raised from many different countries had been destroyed.
Even when Duḥśāsana was slain,
the slaughter did not cease; and seeing the brave kings, the various regional rulers,
and the powerful warriors slain in battle, O Kṛṣṇa, the slaughter did not cease at all.
Seeing the commanders of the *akṣauhiṇīs* struck down by Bhīmasena,
[Duryodhana] did not cease the carnage, whether out of delusion or greed;
and he beheld this army in battle, its heroes slain and utterly shattered.
Even when Alambuṣa was slain,
the slaughter did not cease; seeing his brothers, companions, and even his maternal uncles,
as well as his sons, all struck down in battle, the slaughter did not cease at all.
Who indeed, born in a royal family— especially one of the Kuru lineage—
other than Suyodhana, would engage in such great and futile enmity,
having seen these preeminent kings destroyed and this vast army laid waste?

Knowing him to be superior in virtue, strength, or even valor, what wise man, being undeluded and discerning between the beneficial and the harmful, would fight? For he did not take to heart the beneficial words spoken by you.
How could he listen to anyone else regarding peace with the Pāṇḍavas,
by whom Bhīṣma the son of Śantanu, Droṇa, and Vidura were rejected for the sake of peace? What indeed can be his remedy now?
O Janārdana, because of his folly, he rejected his aged father;
likewise, he rejected his mother who, seeking his welfare, spoke words that were beneficial. Having thus disregarded them, whose words would he find acceptable?
"O Janārdana, it is evident that this man has been born as the destroyer of our lineage;
for his conduct and policy are seen to be such, O lord of the people.
It is my conviction, O Acyuta, that he will not give us back our kingdom."
"O dear one, I have been told many times by the high-souled Vidura:
'The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will not, under any circumstances, give up his share while he still breathes, O giver of honor.'"
"Sin shall prevail against you, though you are sinless;
he cannot be conquered otherwise than through battle, O Mādhava. Thus indeed did Vidura, who perceives the truth, always speak to me.
Today I understand all that resolve of that evil-minded man,
which was spoken as words by the high-souled Vidura;
for he who, having heard the salutary words from the son of Jamadagni exactly as they were, [did not act upon them].
Standing surely at the mouth of destruction, that evil-minded one showed contempt [for others].
For it was said by many perfected beings (*siddhas*) as soon as Suyodhana was born:
"Upon encountering this wicked-souled one, the warrior class (*kṣatra*) shall go to its ruin."
O Janārdana, these words of theirs were indeed prophetic;
for the kings have indeed met their destruction on account of Duryodhana.
Therefore, O Mādhava, today I shall slay all the warriors in battle.
When the Kṣatriyas have been swiftly slain and the camp made empty,
he will seek battle with us for his own destruction;
for by this inference, O Mādhava, the enmity would surely come to an end.

Thus do I perceive, O Vārṣṇeya, reflecting with my own wisdom upon the words of Vidura and the conduct of that evil-minded one. Drive toward the Bharata host, O hero, so that I may strike them down with my sharp arrows.
"O Mādhava, today I shall bring security to the King of Dharma by slaying the evil-souled Duryodhana and his army in battle,
while this weak host of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son looks on."
09,023.049 Saṃjaya said:
09,023.049a Thus addressed by Savyasācin, the scion of the Daśārhas, with reins in hand,
fearlessly entered that flood of enemy forces in battle.

The highly illustrious one plunged into that formidable and excellent bow [of the enemy], which was bristling with spears as its thorns, where maces and iron clubs formed the paths, chariots and elephants were the great trees, and it was overgrown with the creepers of cavalry and infantry.
There Govinda moved about on his chariot adorned with many banners. O King, those white horses, urged on by the descendant of Daśārha, were seen in all directions as they bore Arjuna in the battle.
Then Savyasācin, the scorcher of foes, advanced in his chariot upon the battlefield,
scattering hundreds of sharp arrows like a cloud pouring down torrents of rain.
A great sound arose from those straight-knotted arrows.
As they were being covered by Savyasācin with arrows in that battle,
the floods of shafts fell to the earth without even sticking in their armor;
those arrows, dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva, possessed a touch equal to Indra’s thunderbolt.
O lord of the people, having struck down men, elephants, and horses as well,
the arrows fell in battle like noisy moths;
everything was completely covered by the shafts dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva.
Neither the cardinal nor the intermediate directions could be discerned in that battle;
the entire world was filled with arrows marked with the name of Pārtha—
arrows with golden shafts, cleansed with oil, and polished by smiths.
Being scorched by Pārtha like elephants by fire,
the Kauravas, being slaughtered by his sharp arrows, collapsed,
O Bhārata; Pārtha, bearing his bow and arrows, appeared as if blazing.
In battle, he consumed the warriors like a blazing fire consuming dry grass—
just as the black-trailed fire, released by forest-dwellers at the edge of a forest, burns the undergrowth with a roar.
Just as a blazing and powerful fire, exceedingly prosperous, [consumes] a forest of many trees covered with dry creepers,
so did he, possessing the prowess of a multitude of iron arrows;
With arrows as his flames and possessing fierce, diverse, and sharp energy, that impetuous warrior, unable to endure [the enemy], swiftly consumed your entire army.
His well-aimed arrows, gold-tufted and life-taking, did not merely stick in their armor;
indeed, he did not discharge a second arrow.
Whether on foot, on horseback,
or on an elephant, with arrows of many forms and shapes,
he indeed entered the host of great chariot-warriors.
That very same one, your son, alone slaughtered your army, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt [Indra] slew the Daityas,
or as Dhanañjaya did with his arrows in battle.
Saṃjaya said:
As those heroes, striving and never retreating,
were discharging their weapons, Dhanañjaya rendered their resolve futile with his Gāṇḍīva bow.

O best of the Bharatas, that army was seen being slaughtered by Kirīṭin as he discharged arrows of great power, whose touch was like Indra’s thunderbolt and which were unbearable, just as a cloud releases torrents of rain.
While your son looked on, he fled from the battle;
others abandoned their fathers, brothers, and even their companions. Some chariots had their draft animals killed, while others had their drivers slain.
O lord of the people, some had their axles, yokes, wheels, and poles shattered;
others had their arrows exhausted, while still others were afflicted by shafts. Some, though unhurt, fled all at once, oppressed by fear.
Some, having taken hold of their sons, cried out as most of their mounts had been slain;
others cried for their fathers, and still others for their companions. O tiger among men, they also called upon their kinsmen, brothers, and relatives.
O lord of the people, some fled, abandoning [their positions] here and there;
many great car-warriors there, severely pierced and losing consciousness, were seen groaning, O men, struck by the arrows of Pārtha.
Others, having placed them upon their chariots and comforted them for a moment,
returned to battle once they were rested and free from thirst.
Some, having abandoned them, departed, desiring once more to fight.
O best of the Bharatas, some, intoxicated by battle, were carrying out your son’s command; others, having drunk water and refreshed their mounts, were putting on their armor.
Some, having comforted their brothers and placed them in the camp,
and others their sons, and others their fathers, again set their hearts on battle. O lord of the people, some prepared their chariots according to the rank of their leaders.
Having plunged into the Pāṇḍava host, they again set their hearts on battle;
those heroes, covered with networks of small bells, shone like the Daityas and Dānavas intent upon conquering the three worlds.
Suddenly arriving on chariots adorned with gold,
some [warriors] fought against Dhṛṣṭadyumna within the ranks of the Pāṇḍavas;
so too did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the prince of the Pañcālas, and the great car-warrior Śikhaṇḍin.
And Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, fought against the division of chariots.
Then the Pāñcālya king, filled with rage and surrounded by a vast army,
rushed forward, highly incensed and intent on slaying your men.
Then, O lord of men, hundreds and thousands of your warriors rushed against him in battle; and as he was thus charging forward, O Bhārata, your son dispatched many volleys of arrows at him.
O bull of the Bharatas, he pierced each one with ten arrows. Then, O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna was quickly struck in the arms and chest with many iron shafts by your son, the archer.
With many swift-acting iron shafts (*nārāca*) and half-iron shafts (*ardhanārāca*),
with calf-toothed arrows (*vatsadanta*) polished by smiths,
he slew the four horses.
Deeply pierced like an elephant tormented by a goad,
that great archer dispatched his four horses to death with arrows and struck off the head of his charioteer from his body with a broad-headed shaft.
Then King Duryodhana, the subduer of enemies, having had his chariot destroyed, mounted the back of a horse and retreated not very far away;
for the mighty one beheld his own army with its prowess destroyed.
O great king, your son proceeded to where the son of Subala was. Then, when the chariots were broken, three thousand great elephants surrounded the five Pāṇḍava car-warriors on all sides.
O Bhārata, those five tigers among men, surrounded in battle by that elephant division, shone like planets enveloped by clouds. Then,
O great king, the mighty-armed Arjuna, having found his mark, [advanced].
He went forth on his chariot, drawn by white horses and with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer;
surrounded on all sides by those elephants resembling mountains,
he crushed the elephant army with bright, sharp iron arrows.
There we beheld great elephants struck down by a single arrow—
some already fallen, some being felled, and others mangled by Savyasācin.
But Bhīmasena, seeing those elephants, resembled a rutting elephant himself.
Seizing his great mace with his hand, the powerful one rushed forward,
swiftly leaping from his chariot like Death himself with staff in hand;
seeing that great car-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas with his mace raised, he charged.
Your soldiers were terrified; they discharged excrement and urine.
The entire army was agitated at the sight of Vṛkodara with mace in hand.
By Bhīmasena’s mace, the elephants had their temples split open and were covered in dust.
We beheld them being struck down, their frontal globes crushed and their wounds gushing with blood;
we saw those mountain-like elephants running away,
having been struck by Bhīmasena’s mace as they fled.
They fell down, uttering cries of distress like mountains whose wings have been severed.
Seeing those many elephants with shattered frontal globes fleeing here and there and falling down, your soldiers were struck with terror.
Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with rage, as did the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
struck the elephant-warriors with sharp arrows fletched with vulture feathers.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, however, having defeated the lord of men in battle—
When your son had departed, having mounted the back of a horse,
and seeing all the Pāṇḍavas surrounded by elephants,
O great king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, together with all the Prabhadrakas, [advanced].
The son of the Pāñcāla king, desiring to slay the elephants, advanced;
however, not seeing the subduer of enemies Duryodhana in the division of chariots,
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata [also moved forward].
Not seeing the king as that slaughter of men proceeded, those great car-warriors, believing your son to have been slain there, asked the kṣatriyas, "Where indeed has Duryodhana gone?"
With dejected faces, they questioned their son.
Some said, "When the charioteer was slain, he departed toward where the son of Subala is.
Others, however, who were kṣatriyas severely wounded there, spoke thus:
"What need have you for Duryodhana if he remains alive?
Fight all together; what will the king do for you?
Then all those kṣatriyas remained steadfast in their own duties.
Those kṣatriyas, their limbs wounded and most of their mounts slain,
being tormented by arrows, spoke as if their words were not quite distinct:
"Let us destroy this entire force by which we are surrounded."
Having slain all these elephants, the Pāṇḍavas were advancing. Upon hearing their words, the mighty Aśvatthāman abandoned that army of the Pāñcāla king, which was difficult to withstand.

Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, those heroes with firm bows, abandoned their division of chariots and proceeded to where the son of Subala was. Then, when they had departed, those led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna [advanced].
O King, the Pāṇḍavas advanced, slaughtering your men.
But seeing those great car-warriors rushing forward, exultant and displaying their prowess,
the heroes on your side then lost all hope for their lives.
Your army became mostly pale-faced;
seeing them with their weapons exhausted and themselves surrounded,
O King, I abandoned my own life along with two divisions of the force.
With myself as the fifth, we fought against the army of the Pāñcāla king;
having stationed ourselves in that place where the son of Śaradvat stood,
the five of us engaged in battle, though we were oppressed by the arrows of Kirīṭin.
Against Dhṛṣṭadyumna and his great army, a massive battle took place for us there.
We were all defeated by him and retreated from the field of combat. Then I beheld that great car-warrior Sātyaki approaching.
With four hundred chariots, that hero rushed at me in battle; though my horses were exhausted,
I somehow escaped from Dhṛṣṭadyumna and fell into the army of the Mādhavas,
like a sinner falling into hell.
There, a terrible battle took place for a moment, most cruel;
but the mighty-armed Sātyaki, having destroyed my equipment,
seized me alive as I lay fallen on the ground, unconscious.

"Everyone is rushing toward victory; today I have captured Saṃjaya!"—saying this, O King, the grandson of Śini (Sātyaki) then seized me. Then, in what seemed like a mere moment, that elephant division was slaughtered.
With Bhīmasena’s mace and Arjuna’s iron arrows,
the great elephants— resembling mountains— were crushed on all sides; thus,
the progress of the Pāṇḍavas became almost imperceptible.

He emerged on his very chariot, with white horses and Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer. Then the mighty Bhīmasena, O great king, cleared away the great elephants of the Pāṇḍavas, thereby creating paths for the chariots.
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata,
not seeing Duryodhana, the subduer of enemies, in the array of chariots,
searched for the king, your son, that great car-warrior.
Abandoning the Pāñcāla king, they departed for where the son of Subala was,
distressed at not seeing the king while that destruction of men was occurring.
Saṃjaya said:
O Bhārata, when that elephant division had been destroyed by the son of Pāṇḍu,
and while the army was being slaughtered in battle by Bhīmasena,
they beheld Bhīmasena, the subduer of enemies, moving about in that manner.
O King, having encountered in battle Antaka, the life-taking one, enraged with staff in hand, the remnants of your sons—
while your Kuru son Duryodhana remained unseen— were struck down.
United together, the uterine brothers rushed toward Bhīmasena:
Śrutavān, Saṃjaya, Jayatsena, Śrutāntaka, Durvimocana, and the powerful Durviṣaha.
Śrutavarmā and Śrutarvā, Sujāta and Durvimocana, O great king, Durmarṣaṇa, Jaitra, Bhūribala, Ravi,
Jayatsena, Sujāta, as well as Durviṣaha and Ariha.
Durvimocana by name, and likewise Duṣpradharṣa,
and the mighty-armed Śrutarvā— all of them experts in battle—
these sons of yours, having united together from all sides, [surrounded him].
Having rushed toward Bhīmasena, they hemmed him in from every direction.
Then, O great king, Bhīma once again mounted his own chariot and released sharpened arrows at the vital organs of your sons.
Being scattered by Bhīma in that great battle, your sons warded off Bhīmasena like an elephant from a slope;
yet they struck at Bhīma himself, remembering his former transgressions.
Then, enraged in battle, Bhīma swiftly struck off Durmarṣaṇa’s head with a razor-sharp arrow and caused it to fall to the ground. Then, with another broad-headed shaft capable of piercing all armor—
The great car-warrior Bhīma, the subduer of foes, slew Śrutānta, your son;
then, as if laughing, he pierced Jayatsena with an iron shaft and felled that Kuru prince from the seat of his chariot.
He fell from his chariot, O King, and quickly died upon the ground. Then, O Sire, Śrutarvan, filled with rage, pierced Bhīma with a hundred straight-knotted arrows feathered with vulture plumes.
Then, enraged in battle, Bhīma struck these three— Jaitra, Bhūribala, and Ravi— with three arrows resembling poison and fire.
Slain, those great car-warriors fell from their chariots to the ground.
In spring, they were like *kiṃśuka* trees variegated with blossoms that had been lopped off.
Then, with another sharp iron arrow,
that scorcher of foes struck Durvimocana and sent him to his death.
Slain, that best of chariot-warriors fell from his chariot to the earth,
like a tree growing on a mountain peak broken by the wind. Then, your two sons, Duṣpradharṣa and Sujāta, [were also slain].
He struck down each one by two at the front of the army in that battle;
those two best of chariot-warriors fell, their limbs pierced by stone-tipped arrows.
Then, beholding your other son still striving, [he attacked].
With a broad-headed arrow (bhallā), Bhīma pierced Durviṣaha in battle during that encounter;
struck down, he fell from his mount while all the archers looked on.
Having seen many of his brothers slain by a single man in the fray, [he was filled with rage].
Overcome by indignation, Śrutarvā rushed toward Bhīma,
brandishing his massive bow adorned with gold and discharging many arrows resembling poison and fire.
O King, having severed the Pāṇḍava’s bow in that great battle,
he then covered him, whose bow was broken, with twenty arrows.
Thereupon, the great car-warrior Bhīmasena took up another bow.
He showered your son with arrows and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
A great battle took place between them, wonderful in form and terrifying, just like that which occurred previously in combat between Jambha and Vāsava.
There, by those auspicious arrows released by the two of them, which resembled the staff of Yama,
the earth became completely covered;
indeed, the entire earth, the sky, and all the directions were thus shrouded.
Then, O King, Śrutarvā, filled with rage, drew his bow and struck Bhīmasena in the arms and chest with arrows in that battle. Thus deeply pierced, O great king, by your son, the archer, [Bhīmasena]—
Enraged, Bhīma was as agitated as the great ocean during the change of the moon;
then, O noble one, Bhīma, possessed by fury,
dispatched your son’s charioteer and four horses to the abode of Yama with his arrows.
Seeing him deprived of his chariot, the one of immeasurable soul covered him with feathered arrows, displaying his lightness of hand.
O King, being without a chariot, Śrutarvā took up a sword and a shield.
Then, as he was about to seize his sword and his radiant shield marked with a hundred moons,
the Pāṇḍava struck off his head from his body with a razor-sharp arrow.
Thereupon, the head of that great-souled one was severed by the razor-sharp shaft.
His body fell from the chariot to the earth, making it resound;
when that hero had fallen, your men, bewildered by fear yet desiring to fight,
rushed toward Bhīmasena in battle.
As they rushed forward swiftly from that ocean-like army which remained after the slaughter,
the powerful Bhīmasena, clad in armor, received them;
and having encountered him, they indeed surrounded him on all sides.
Then Bhīma, though hemmed in by your men with their sharpened arrows,
oppressed them all like the thousand-eyed Indra against the Asuras.
Thereafter, having slain five hundred great car-warriors along with their chariot-fenders, he [advanced].
In battle, he again struck down seven hundred elephants;
having slain ten thousand foot soldiers and eight hundred horses with his supreme arrows, the Pāṇḍava shone resplendent.
But Bhīmasena, the son of Kuntī, having slain your sons in battle,
O Lord, considered himself to have achieved his purpose and his birth to have been fruitful.
And as he was thus fighting and slaughtering your men, [the king spoke].
O Bhārata, your troops did not dare even to look at him.
Having routed all the Kurus and slain their followers,
he then produced a sound with his two arms, terrifying the great elephants.
"O lord of the people, with the majority of its warriors slain, your army,
O great king, was reduced to a mere remnant and fell into a miserable state.
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, Duryodhana and your son Sudarśana,
who remained as the survivors of that battle, were then stationed in the midst of the cavalry.
Then, seeing Duryodhana stationed in the midst of the cavalry—
The son of Devakī spoke to Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī:
"The enemies have been mostly slain and our kinsmen protected;
having taken Sañjaya with him, that bull among the Śinis has returned."
O Bhārata, Nakula and Sahadeva were exhausted after fighting the wicked followers of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in battle;
these three remained stationed there, having abandoned Suyodhana.
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the great car-warrior Aśvatthāman—
there stands that Pāñcālya prince, endowed with supreme glory,
having slain Duryodhana’s army along with all the Prabhadrakas.
O Pārtha, there stands Duryodhana in the midst of his cavalry,
with a parasol being held over him, looking about again and again;
having arrayed his entire army, he is stationed in the middle of the battlefield.
"Having slain him with sharp arrows, you will have accomplished your purpose.
O subduer of enemies, seeing the elephant division destroyed and you arrived,
slay Suyodhana before these troops flee."
"Let someone go to the Pāñcālya and say, 'Come quickly!
O dear one, this sinner shall not escape, for his army is exhausted;
having slain your entire force in battle, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [will prevail].'"
Thinking the sons of Pāṇḍu already conquered, he assumes this great form,
just as the mighty Śakra of old did after slaying the army of the Daityas;
for he has seen his own forces struck down and oppressed by the Pāṇḍavas.
"O King, that monarch will surely come to his own destruction in battle.
Thus addressed, Phalguna spoke these words to Kṛṣṇa:
"O giver of honor, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been slain by Bhīma."
O Kṛṣṇa, those two who have stood here until now shall no longer exist today.
Bhīṣma is slain, Droṇa is slain, and Karṇa Vaikartana is slain;
Śalya, the king of Madra, is slain, and Jayadratha is slain, O Kṛṣṇa.
Five hundred horses remained for Śakuni, the son of Subala;
O Janārdana, only two hundred chariots remained;
more than a hundred elephants remained; and three thousand foot soldiers remained.
"Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, the lord of the Trigartas,
Ulūka, Śakuni, and the Sātvata Kṛtavarman—
this, O Mādhava, was the remainder of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s army."
"Indeed, liberation from Time does not exist for anyone on this earth;
behold Duryodhana standing there even though his army has been slaughtered—
this very day the Great King shall have his enemies destroyed."
"I shall not let anyone among the enemies escape," I thought;
"O Kṛṣṇa, those who today do not flee from the battle, fierce as they are in combat—
all of them I shall slay, even if they should be non-human."
"Today in battle, highly enraged, I shall remove the king's long-standing sleeplessness by striking down the Gāndhāra with my sharp arrows. Indeed,
that evil-doing son of Subala has, through deceit, seized those jewels."

"I won those things back in the assembly hall during the game of dice; today, I shall win them back again. And all the women of Nāgapura shall learn of this today, upon hearing that their husbands and sons have been slain by the Pāṇḍavas in battle."
"O Kṛṣṇa, today indeed all our work will be completed;
today Duryodhana shall abandon his blazing prosperity and his very life. O Kṛṣṇa, if he does not flee from me in battle out of fear."

"Know him to be already slain, O Vārṣṇeya, that foolish son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. For this host of horses, O subduer of enemies, is indeed incapable of enduring the sound of my bowstring and palms; go on until I have killed him."
Thus addressed by the illustrious Pāṇḍava,
O King, the descendant of Daśārha urged the horses toward Duryodhana’s army. Beholding that host, three great car-warriors stood ready.

O sire, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, and Sahadeva set forth with lion-like roars, desiring to slay Duryodhana. Seeing them all together, moving with speed and with bows raised, [the enemy was struck with fear].
The son of Subala rushed in battle against the attacking Pāṇḍavas;
your son Sudarśana advanced against Bhīmasena,
while Suśarmā and Śakuni fought with Kirīṭin.
Your son, mounted upon the back of a horse, rushed toward Sahadeva;
then, O lord of men, your son effortlessly and swiftly struck Sahadeva’s head violently with a lance.
Struck by your son, he sat down upon the seat of the chariot,
his entire body drenched in blood, hissing like a venomous serpent. Then, O lord of the people, Sahadeva regained consciousness.
Enraged, he covered Duryodhana with sharp arrows;
and Pārtha Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, displaying his prowess in battle,
severed the heads of heroes from the backs of their horses.
Then Pārtha scattered that host with many arrows;
having struck down all the horses, he advanced toward the chariots of the Trigartas.
Thereupon, those great car-warriors of the Trigartas united together.
He showered Arjuna and Vāsudeva with volleys of arrows; then,
having struck Satyakarman with a razor-sharp shaft,
the highly illustrious son of Pāṇḍu cut the pole of his chariot.
And with a razor-sharp arrow whetted on stone, O Lord, the highly illustrious one, laughing, severed the head adorned with earrings of refined gold belonging to Suśarman.
Then, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when that hero was slain.
O King, due to your own ill-advised policy, [he] then took up the Satyeṣu [missile] while the surging hosts of your warriors looked on,
just as a hungry lion in the forest seizes a deer, O King.
Having slain him, Pārtha then pierced Suśarman with three arrows and destroyed all those chariots adorned with gold.
Then Pārtha, hastening forward, [attacked] that which had been well-prepared over a long period of time.
Discharging the sharp poison of his wrath toward the lord of Prasthala,
O bull of the Bharatas, Arjuna first covered him with a hundred arrows and then slew the horses of that archer.
Then, taking up a sharp arrow resembling the staff of Yama,
he quickly discharged it toward Suśarman as if laughing.
That arrow was launched by that archer, who blazed with rage.
Having encountered Suśarman in battle, he pierced his heart;
deprived of life, O great king, he fell upon the surface of the earth,
gladdening all the Pāṇḍavas and causing distress to your own troops.
Having slain Suśarman in battle, he brought his thirty-seven sons— mighty chariot-warriors— to their destruction with his arrows; then,
having killed all of his followers with sharpened shafts, [he proceeded].
The great car-warrior advanced against the remnants of the Bharata army. But Bhīma, enraged in battle, O lord of men, as if laughing, made your son Sudarśana invisible with his arrows.

Then, laughing though enraged, he severed his head from his body with an exceedingly sharp razor-headed arrow; slain, he fell to the earth. When that hero had been killed, his followers then [advanced].
Then Bhīmasena effortlessly consumed that vast forest of troops with the fire of his arrows; meanwhile,
[the enemy warriors] surrounded Bhīma in battle, scattering sharp shafts.
Then Vṛkodara, with sharp arrows whose touch was like Indra’s thunderbolt, completely overwhelmed that army from all sides;
and in an instant, O bull of the Bharatas, Bhīma slaughtered it.
While they were being destroyed, the mighty army commanders,
O Bhārata, approached Bhīmasena and then fought him;
but the Pāṇḍava covered them all with terrible arrows.
In the same way, O King, your men surrounded the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas on all sides with a massive shower of arrows;
everything became utterly chaotic for the Pāṇḍavas in their encounter with the enemy.
And as your men and the sons of Pāṇḍu desired to fight one another in battle,
the warriors there then fell, struck down by each other,
O King, while both armies lamented for their kinsmen.
Saṃjaya said:
When that battle, which caused the destruction of men, horses, and elephants, had commenced,
O King, Śakuni the son of Subala advanced against Sahadeva.
Then, as he was rushing forward swiftly, the powerful Sahadeva dispatched showers of arrows that moved as fast as locusts;
and Ulūka pierced Bhīma in the battle with ten shafts.
O great king, Śakuni, having pierced Bhīma with three arrows,
covered Sahadeva with ninety shafts.
Those heroes, O king, having encountered one another in battle, [assailed each other].
They pierced him with sharpened arrows fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks—
arrows with golden shafts, polished on stone, and released from their bows and arms up to the ear,
O lord of the people; and a rain of arrows was discharged by them.
He covered all the directions with his arrows, like a rain-cloud with its torrents.
Then, O Bhārata, the enraged Bhīma and Sahadeva,
both possessed of great strength, moved about in that battle, causing a great slaughter in the fray.
O Bhārata, covered by those two with hundreds of arrows,
that army of yours became like the sky shrouded in darkness here and there,
O lord of the people, as horses ran about, themselves veiled in shafts.
In various places, O noble one, paths were formed by those dragging away the many slain,
along with the fallen horses together with their riders,
as well as shattered armor and broken lances.
O scorcher of enemies, with double-edged spears, javelins,
and lances, the earth became covered as if strewn with variegated flowers;
there, O great king, the warriors, having encountered one another, [fell].
Enraged, they moved about in battle, striking one another;
with faces whose eyes were rolling in fury and whose lips were bitten in rage,
the earth was covered by [fallen heads] adorned with earrings and resembling the filaments of a lotus.
O great king, with severed arms resembling the trunks of serpent-kings— still adorned with armlets, armor, swords, spears,
and battle-axes— and with other headless trunks (kabandhas) that had risen up and were dancing in the fray;
O Lord, the earth became filled with throngs of flesh-eating creatures and turned terrible when only a small remnant of the Kuru army remained in that great battle;
then the Pandavas, becoming overjoyed, sent them to the abode of Yama.
In that interval, O great king, the powerful and heroic son of Subala struck Sahadeva violently on the head with a lance;
overwhelmed, he sat down upon the floor of his chariot.
O Bhārata, seeing Sahadeva in that state, the powerful Bhīmasena,
filled with rage, held back all the troops and pierced them by the hundreds and thousands with iron shafts.
Having pierced through him, the subduer of enemies let out a lion’s roar;
terrified by that sound, all the followers of Śakuni,
along with their horses and elephants, fled suddenly in fear.
Then, seeing them broken, King Duryodhana said:
"Turn back, you who are ignorant of righteousness! Fight! What is the use of your flight?
By establishing fame here, one enjoys the higher worlds after death."
The hero who gives up his life in battle without showing his back,
having transcended the realm of Śūliya and Pāśa, attains the world of Śakra.

Thus addressed by the king, those followers of Saubala turned back toward the Pāṇḍavas, making death their only means of retreat. O Indra among kings, as they rushed forward there, a most terrible noise was raised.
Resembling an agitated ocean, it became turbulent on all sides. O great king, seeing those followers of Saubala rushing toward them, the Pāṇḍavas, intent on victory, advanced against them.
O lord of the people, having recovered his breath, the invincible Sahadeva pierced Śakuni with ten arrows and his horses with three shafts;
then, as if laughing, he cut through the bow of Saubala with his arrows.
Then Śakuni, intoxicated by battle, took up another bow and showered Sahadeva with straight-knotted arrows; and then,
O King, Ulūka was filled with great wrath.
Ulūka, O great king, pierced Nakula with sixty arrows and Bhīmasena with seven;
he also struck Sahadeva with seventy arrows,
seeking to protect his father in battle.
In that battle, Bhīmasena pierced him with sharpened arrows;
he struck Śakuni with sixty-four, and those standing at his side with three each.
Being slaughtered by Bhīma with iron shafts tempered in oil, they were overcome.
O Great King, afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena, they fled;
then, O Sire, Ulūka, enraged, raised his bow, while they,
their enthusiasm gone and tormented by fear, fled away, O Great King.
Ulūka, however, pierced Sahadeva with sharp arrows;
enraged in battle, he covered Sahadeva with showers of shafts,
like clouds accompanied by lightning covering a mountain with torrents of rain.

Then, O Great King, as he was charging forward, the valiant and powerful Sahadeva struck off Ulūka’s head with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla). Struck down by Sahadeva, he fell from his chariot to the ground.
With all his limbs drenched in blood, he gladdened the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
But seeing his son slain there, O Bhārata, Śakuni,
with a throat choked with tears and sighing deeply, recalled the words of Kṣattṛ.
Having reflected for a moment, his eyes filled with tears and sighing deeply,
he approached Sahadeva and pierced him with three arrows.
The powerful warrior, having warded off those released shafts with his own volleys of arrows, [proceeded].
O great king, in that encounter, Sahadeva cut off Śakuni’s bow. When his bow was severed, O Indra among kings,
Śakuni Saubala then seized a massive sword and hurled it at Sahadeva.
O lord of the people, as that weapon of terrible form was suddenly rushing toward him,
he cut it in two in the encounter as if laughing;
seeing his sword thus severed in two, he seized a massive mace.
He hurled it at Sahadeva, but it fell fruitlessly to the earth. Then the King of Gandhāra, desiring to retaliate,
[discharged] a most terrible spear that rose up like the Night of Doom.
Enraged, the son of Subala dispatched it toward the Pāṇḍava. As it came rushing suddenly, Sahadeva, as if smiling, cut it into three pieces in the battle with arrows adorned with gold.
Cut into three pieces, that spear adorned with gold fell to the ground,
shattering like a blazing flash of lightning falling from the sky.
Seeing the spear destroyed and the son of Subala afflicted by fear, [he acted].
When fear arose, all your men, along with the son of Subala, fled;
then a great shout was raised by the Pāṇḍavas, who appeared victorious,
and consequently, almost all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra turned their backs in retreat.

Seeing them indeed despondent, the powerful son of Mādrī warded them off in battle with many thousands of arrows. Then he [advanced] against that force protected by the Gāndhāras and held firm for victory by the horses in the rear.
Then, O King, remembering that his own share remained, Sahadeva approached Śakuni, who was departing on the battlefield, with a chariot adorned with gold. Sahadeva pursued the son of Subala.
Having strung his mighty bow and drawing that great weapon, he rushed toward the son of Subala and,
filled with rage, struck him violently with stone-sharpened arrows feathered with vulture plumes, as if striking a great elephant with goads.
The wise one spoke to him, restraining him as if to remind him:
"Abiding by the duty of a Kṣatriya, fight and be a man!
O fool, why did you rejoice then while gambling with dice at the assembly hall?"

"O evil-minded one, since you defeated us by means of fraudulent dice in the midst of the assembly, receive today the fruit of that action! Those wicked-souled ones who formerly mocked us have been slain."
Duryodhana is a charcoal-brand of his lineage, and you are his surviving maternal uncle.
Today I shall strike off your head with a razor-sharp arrow,
plucking it from your body like fruit from a tree with a crushing club.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, the mighty Sahadeva,
that tiger among men, rushed forward with great speed, filled with rage.
Then the invincible Sahadeva, a lord of warriors, having approached—
Drawing his bow with great force, as if laughing in his wrath,
he pierced Śakuni with ten arrows and his horses with four;
then, having cut down his umbrella, standard, and bow, he roared like a lion.
With his standard, bow, and umbrella shattered by Sahadeva,
the son of Subala was then pierced in all his vital organs with many arrows.
Thereafter, O great king, the powerful Sahadeva once again—
He discharged an unassailable shower of arrows at Śakuni.
Then, enraged in that conflict, the son of Subala [attacked] Sahadeva, the son of Mādrī.
Desiring to kill him, the son of Mādrī alone swiftly rushed forward with a javelin adorned with gold as it was being raised against him.
At the front of the battle, he simultaneously severed the lance and his two well-rounded arms with three broad-headed arrows; then,
with great speed, he let out a loud roar in the midst of the fray.
With a swift-acting arrow made of firm iron and gold-feathered, he,
well-composed and wielding that most steadfast weapon, released it with great force.
With a broad-headed arrow that penetrates all armor,
he once more struck off the head from the body;
and [he severed] his head and his two well-rounded arms.
First his spear fell to the ground,
and afterwards his headless trunk, drenched in blood and quivering, fell down, terrible to behold.
From the excellent chariot of that king of kings,
which was adorned with the finest gold and jewels,
that high-souled one let out a lion’s roar.
Having slain the son of Subala,
that high-souled one, having struck down the falling [enemy] with gold-feathered arrows, proceeded toward the southern direction.
The high-souled one struck the lord of the earth with an arrow adorned with gold,
blazing like the sun and well-sharpened.
With his head severed in battle by the Pāṇḍava,
the son of Subala fell to the earth;
that head was struck down by a swift arrow.
Enraged, the son of Pāṇḍu struck down that very man who was the root of the Kurus' misconduct with an arrow whetted on stone and feathered with gold.
Beholding Śakuni with his head severed,
lying upon the ground with his limbs drenched in blood,
your warriors lost their courage out of fear.
Taking up their weapons, they fled in all directions;
those Gandhāra warriors, with weapons grasped, suddenly rushed toward the son of Mādrī.
Fleeing in haste with parched mouths and deprived of consciousness,
they were struck by the roar of Gāṇḍīva;
afflicted by fear, their chariots, horses, and elephants were shattered.
And the foot soldiers, together with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, were unable to fight with force in the midst of the battle.
Then, having caused Śakuni to fall from his chariot;
Filled with joy, O Bhārata, the sons of Pāṇḍu,
exultant in battle, blew their conchs together with Keśava, gladdening the soldiers.
And all of them, honoring him and speaking joyfully of Sahadeva in the battle, said:
"By good fortune, that deceitful and evil-souled one has been slain!"
"O hero, [he was slain] by you in battle along with his son.
Sañjaya said:
"Then, O great king, the followers of Subala's son became enraged."
Having abandoned their lives in that clamor, they surrounded the Pāṇḍavas;
Arjuna, intent on securing Sahadeva’s victory, received them,
as did the radiant Bhīmasena, who resembled an enraged venomous serpent.
With his Gāṇḍīva bow, Dhanañjaya rendered futile the resolve of those who, with spears, double-edged swords, and javelins in hand, sought to slay Sahadeva; he did so as they rushed forward,
their arms grasping their weapons.
With broad-headed arrows, Bībhatsu cut off both their heads and their horses;
struck down by Savyasācin, that hero of the world, they fell swiftly to the earth, deprived of life.
Then, O Lord, King Duryodhana, seeing the destruction of his own army,
summoned the hundreds of chariots remaining from the slaughter,
as well as elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, O scorcher of foes, and became enraged.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke these words to them all together:
"Having encountered all the Pāṇḍavas along with their hosts of friends in battle,
