and having quickly slain the King of Pañcāla together with his army, return."
Accepting those words with their heads bowed, those warriors,
intoxicated by battle, advanced against the Pārthas in the fray at the command of your son.
As they rushed swiftly toward them— those who had survived the great slaughter in the battle— [the Pārthas...]
O best of the Bharatas, in a mere moment, those high-souled Pāṇḍavas overwhelmed that army with arrows resembling venomous serpents;
having encountered the battle, it found no protector and was destroyed.
Though striving to maintain his position out of fear, the armored warrior could not hold his ground;
as the horses galloped about and the army was shrouded in dust,
neither the cardinal nor the intermediate directions could be discerned in that battle.
Then, O Bhārata, many men having emerged from the Pāṇḍava ranks struck down your troops in battle as if in a mere moment;
thereafter, O Bhārata, that army of yours was completely destroyed.
O Bhārata, those eleven *akṣauhiṇīs* that had assembled for your son were all slain in battle by the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas, O Lord—
among those thousands of high-souled kings on your side.
O King, Duryodhana alone was seen, severely wounded;
then, having looked in all directions and seeing the earth empty,
and being deprived of all his warriors, he beheld the Pāṇḍavas in the battle.
O great king, hearing those high-souled ones shouting on all sides, joyful because all their aims were accomplished, and hearing the sound of the whizzing arrows,
Duryodhana was overwhelmed by dejection.
With his strength and mounts depleted, he set his mind on retreat.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When my army had been slain and the camp made empty,"
"O Sūta, what portion of the Pāṇḍavas' army remained at that time?
Tell this to me as I ask you, for you are indeed skilled, Saṃjaya;
and tell me also what my dull-witted son Duryodhana did."
Seeing the destruction of his forces, that lord of the earth stood alone.
Sañjaya said:
"There were two thousand chariots and seven hundred elephants."
O King, five thousand horses and ten thousand foot soldiers—
this was the great remaining force of the Pāṇḍavas that Dhṛṣṭadyumna took up and stood firm in battle.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, King Duryodhana, that foremost of chariot-warriors, stood alone; he saw no ally whatsoever in the battle,
as his own forces were being destroyed and the enemies were roaring.
Having seen this, O Great King, that sole lord of the earth,
O tiger among the Bharatas, was overwhelmed by dejection;
abandoning his slain horse, he fled toward the east out of fear.
Your son Duryodhana, the commander of eleven armies,
the radiant one, having taken up his mace, set out on foot toward the lake.
Having gone not very far from there on foot, O lord of men—
He recalled the words of the wise Vidura, who was devoted to righteousness: "Surely the highly intelligent Vidura foresaw this long ago—
this great slaughter of ourselves and of the kṣatriyas in battle."
Reflecting thus, O King, as he was about to enter the lake with a heart tormented by grief upon seeing the destruction of his army—
even though he was Duryodhana, the lord of eleven akṣauhiṇīs— [he proceeded].
He encountered a severe calamity, for destiny is indeed most powerful.
And the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
rushed in great wrath against your army, O monarch.
With his *gāṇḍīva* bow, Dhanañjaya rendered futile the resolve of the shouting forces who held spears, double-edged swords,
and lances in their hands; having slain them with sharpened arrows, along with their ministers and kinsmen.
Standing upon his chariot drawn by white horses, Arjuna shone most brilliantly.
When Subala’s son had been slain along with his horses, chariot, and elephants,
your army became like a vast forest that has been cut down.
O King, in that army of Duryodhana consisting of many hundreds of thousands,
no other great car-warrior was seen alive,
except for the heroic son of Droṇa and likewise Kṛtavarman.
O King, out of compassion for Gautama and for your son, the king, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, upon seeing me, laughed and said to Sātyaki:
"What is the use of capturing this man? There is no purpose in him remaining alive."
Having heard the words of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the great chariot-warrior grandson of Śini then raised a sharpened sword and prepared to kill me. Approaching him, the highly wise Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana spoke.
"Let Saṃjaya be released alive; he must not be killed under any circumstances.
Having heard these words of Dvaipāyana, the grandson of Śini joined his palms in reverence and, releasing me, then said to me: "Farewell, Saṃjaya; go in peace."
Having been permitted by him, I set out for the city at evening, clad in blood, having cast off my armor and laid down my weapons; yet,
when I had retreated only a *krośa*, I found him standing there with mace in hand.
O King, I saw Duryodhana alone, severely wounded;
his eyes filled with tears, he was unable to look at me as he gazed upon me standing there in such a deplorable state.
And seeing him alone in the battle, grieving, I too was overwhelmed by sorrow for a moment and was unable to say anything;
he who [once led] a thousand consecrated kings wearing jeweled crowns.
Having brought all tribute under his own control,
the earth, adorned with jewels and bounded by the four oceans,
was in former times made to pay tribute solely for the sake of Karna.
His commands were spread abroad even in foreign kingdoms by his very ears;
for that king as he ruled, there was no weariness in his weapons.
Seated in Hastināpura, he possessed a kingdom that was secure and free from thorns.
Out of his sovereign power, he protected [the world] and did not even remember Kubera; O King, lord of the earth, as he traveled from palace to palace,
his path was made of gold whenever he entered a temple.

During the departure of the lord of the earth, the houses of the fortunate ones became beautiful with lofty archways that blocked out the rays of the sun with their banners. Ascending an elephant resembling Airāvata, the powerful king was like Indra himself.

O Lord of the Earth, seeing him— who used to travel with such immense splendor— now standing all alone on the ground, resembling Indra yet deeply wounded and traveling on foot, the greatest affliction has come upon me.
O King, for such a Lord of the World as he, today there occurred an incomparable calamity; indeed, destiny alone is most powerful. Therefore, I then related to him everything regarding that seizure.
And by the grace of Dvaipāyana, he obtained liberation from the battle while still alive;
then, having meditated for a moment as it were and regained his consciousness, he inquired after his brothers and all the troops. Then he asked about me.
To him, I, having seen everything with my own eyes, related all of that:
how all his brothers had been slain and his army struck down.
"O lord of men, it is said that only three chariot-warriors remain of your side."
"Thus did Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana speak to me at the time of my departure.
Sighing deeply as it were and looking at me again and again,
he touched me on the shoulder with his hand and addressed you, my son."
"O Saṃjaya, no one other than you survives here in this battle;
I see no second [survivor] here, for the Pāṇḍavas are accompanied by allies.
O Saṃjaya, speak to the lordly king whose wisdom is his eye."
"Your son Duryodhana has entered the lake," they said;
"deprived of such friends, sons, and brothers,
and with the kingdom seized by the Pāṇḍavas— who indeed would live, such as I am?"
"You must tell them all this, and that I have been released from the great battle,
lying here in this lake of water, alive though severely wounded.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, the monarch entered that lake.
And by his power of illusion, the lord of men solidified the waters. When he had entered that lake, I alone saw three chariots with exhausted horses arrive together at that place.
Seeing the heroic Kṛpa Śāradvata, the son of Droṇa— the best among chariot-warriors—
and Kṛtavarman the Bhoja, all wounded by arrows and gathered together,
they all looked toward me and quickly urged on their horses.
Having approached me, they said, "By good fortune you live, O Saṃjaya! And they all questioned me concerning your son, the lord of people:
"Is King Duryodhana still alive, O Saṃjaya?"
I then informed them that the king was safe,
and I related everything that Duryodhana had said to me;
I also told them of the lake into which the lord of men had entered.
But Aśvatthāman, O King, having heard those words of mine and beholding that vast lake, lamented piteously: "Alas! Shame! That lord of men does not know that we are still alive."
"For we are indeed capable of fighting the enemies along with him.
Having lamented there for a long time, those great car-warriors,
the best among chariot-fighters, fled upon seeing the sons of Pāṇḍu in the battle.
Having placed me upon Kṛpa’s well-adorned chariot,
those three remaining charioteers who had survived the slaughter returned to the encampment of the army;
there, the outposts were terrified as the sun had set.
Hearing of the destruction of your sons, everyone cried out in lamentation.
Then, O great king, the elderly men appointed to protect the women took the royal wives and set out toward the city.
There, as they all cried out and wept on every side, a great sound arose upon hearing of that destruction of the army. Then, O King, those women wailed again and again.
Making the earth resound with their cries like female ospreys,
they struck their heads with their nails and palms;
and wailing here and there, they then tore out their hair.

O lord of the people, making sounds of "Alas! Alas! and beating their breasts, they wailed and wept there, crying out in distress. Then the ministers of Duryodhana, with throats choked by tears, were deeply afflicted.
Taking the king’s wives with them, they set out toward the city;
and the gatekeepers, O lord of the people, holding rattan staffs in their hands,
[brought] bright beds provided with excellent coverlets.
Taking them with them, the guardians of the women departed quickly for the city; other people, mounting chariots yoked with mules,
set out toward the city, each taking his own wife.
O great king, the people beheld those women— who had never before been seen even by the sun within their homes— as they proceeded toward the city;
O best of the Bharatas, those women were endowed with such exquisite delicacy.
Having lost their own kinsmen and relatives, they fled swiftly toward the city;
even the cowherds and shepherds ran toward the city,
men fleeing in agitation, tormented by the fear of Bhīmasena.
Moreover, they were seized by a fierce and most terrible fear of the Pārthas;
looking at one another, they then fled toward the city.
While that extremely dreadful rout was thus taking place,
Yuyutsu, bewildered by grief, reflected on what the occasion required:
"Duryodhana has been defeated in battle by the Pāṇḍavas of terrible prowess;
he who was the commander of eleven armies, and his brothers have been slaughtered."
All the Kurus have been slain, led by Bhīṣma and Droṇa;
I alone have escaped by the turn of fate and through chance,
while all the camps have fled in every direction.
They flee here and there, their protectors slain and their vigor destroyed;
never before seen in such a state, they are afflicted by sorrow, their eyes agitated with fear,
like terrified deer looking toward the ten directions.
"O Lord, whatever ministers of Duryodhana remain alive have fled toward the city, taking the royal ladies with them;
I believe the time has come for us to enter along with them."
Having obtained the permission of Yudhiṣṭhira as well as Bhīmasena,
that mighty-armed one reported this matter to both of them;
the king, who was ever compassionate by nature, became pleased with him.

Embracing the son of the Vaiśya woman, the mighty-armed one bid him farewell. Then, mounting his chariot, he urged the horses forward swiftly; and he escorted the king’s wives back toward the city with great honor.
Accompanied by them, as the sun was quickly setting,
he entered Hastināpura with a throat choked with sobs and eyes full of tears;
there he beheld the highly wise Vidura, whose eyes were likewise filled with tears.
To him, whose mind was stricken with grief as he emerged from the presence of the king,
Satyadhṛti spoke while he stood bowed before him:
"By good fortune, my son, you live even though this destruction of the Kurus has occurred."
"Without the king's permission, why indeed have you come here?
Tell me the entire reason for this in detail.
Yuyutsu said:
O dear one, when Śakuni had been slain along with his kinsmen, sons, and relatives,
King Duryodhana— his retinue having been mostly killed—
then abandoned his own horse and fled in fear toward the east.
When the king had departed from the encampment,
everyone, agitated by fear, fled toward the city.
Then [they took] all the wives of the king and his brothers.

Having placed [the king] upon vehicles, the supervisors of the women fled in fear. Then, having taken leave of the king along with Keśava, I entered Hastināpura, protecting myself from public reproach.
Having heard these words spoken by the son of the Vaiśya woman,
Vidura, the knower of all dharma and of immeasurable soul, recognizing that the moment had arrived, honored Yuyutsu, who was skilled in speech.
All this has come to pass for you at the time appropriate for the destruction of the Bharatas. Out of compassion, you have remembered the duty of your lineage;
by good fortune, my son, you have returned from this battle that destroys heroes to the city.
We beheld him gathered together like the rays of the sun; he was the staff for the blind king, who was greedy and lacked foresight,
whose mind had been struck down by fate despite his repeated entreaties.
"O son, you alone have always remained by the side of one afflicted by calamity.
Today you shall rest here; tomorrow you will go to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having spoken these words, Vidura, the knower of all dharma, [departed].
He sent Yuyutsu, saying, "Go to your own home, my son.
Yuyutsu, too, having bowed to the Kṣattṛ, went to his own home;
and having given leave to Yuyutsu, [the king] entered the royal palace.

Seeing the city, which was being loudly wailed over in grief by the people of the capital and the provinces as "Alas! Alas!", joyless, stripped of its splendor, like a lake from which the serpents have been taken,
empty in appearance and desolate, he became even more deeply dejected.
Vidura, the knower of all dharma, with a distressed inner self,
entered the king’s presence, O King, and sighed slowly and repeatedly;
Yuyutsu also then spent that night in his own home.

Though being honored by his own people, he did not rejoice, being deeply distressed as he contemplated the intense mutual destruction of the Bharatas. Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men...
Then one should invoke the goddess Sarasvatī and thereafter proclaim victory.
Sañjaya said:
"O Indra among kings, in what seemed like a mere moment, everything appeared empty."
When the army had fled, the camp— once resounded by the cries of rutting elephants— was silent; there, where the great chariot-warriors could not even wake up to the great noise [of the battle],
we did not hear the sound of any human being whatsoever.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "O Sañjaya, when all the armies had been slain by the sons of Pāṇḍu on the field of battle,
what did those remnants of my army do?"
"What did Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, the heroic son of Droṇa, and the dull-witted King Duryodhana do then? Saṃjaya said:

While the wives of the high-souled Kṣatriyas were fleeing and the camp was deserted and empty, the three chariot-warriors became deeply distressed upon hearing the roar of the victorious sons of Pāṇḍu.
Seeing the camp in flight at evening, those who were devoted to the king did not approve of staying there; they then proceeded toward the lake.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous soul, was also there in the battle together with his brothers.
O King, filled with joy and desiring the slaughter of Duryodhana, he rushed about; yet those [Pāṇḍavas], enraged and seeking victory, though searching with great effort for your son,
did not find the lord of men.
Indeed, with mace in hand, he retreated with great speed;
when Duryodhana, abandoning the battle, fled on foot,
he entered that lake and solidified the waters by means of his own *māyā*.
When all the Pāṇḍavas, their mounts being utterly exhausted,
reached their own camp, they halted there along with their soldiers. Then Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata—
When the Pārthas had encamped, they proceeded slowly toward that lake. Having reached the lake where the lord of men lay,
they addressed the invincible king as he slept upon the waters.
"O King, arise and fight Yudhiṣṭhira along with us!
Either, having conquered, enjoy the earth; or, being slain, attain heaven.
O Duryodhana, the entire strength of those [Pāṇḍavas] has been destroyed by you."
O lord of the people, those soldiers who remain there have for the most part been overcome; they are not able to withstand your impetuosity when you are protected by us. Therefore, arise, O Bhārata!
Thus addressed, he replied there to those great chariot-warriors.
Duryodhana said:
"By good fortune, I see you all released from such a slaughter of men."

"Having rested and being free from fatigue, we shall all defeat those bulls among men who are still alive after the clash with the Pāṇḍus and Kauravas; for you are exhausted and we too are severely wounded."
Their strength has been aroused; therefore, I do not favor fighting them now.
O heroes, it is no wonder that you possess such great resolve, nor that you have supreme devotion toward us; yet, this is not the time for valorous action.
"Having rested for one night today, I shall fight back against the enemies in battle tomorrow along with you; of this I have no doubt. Saṃjaya said:
Thus addressed, the son of Droṇa spoke to the king, who was fierce in battle:
"Arise, O King—may it be well with you! We shall conquer our enemies in combat through the merit of sacrifices and public works, through charity, truthfulness, and the recitation of prayers."
"O King,
I swear that if I do not slay the Somakas in battle before this night has passed, may I never attain the joy of those who perform sacrifices, which is fit for the virtuous."
"O Lord, I shall not remove my armor until I have slain all the Pāñcālas;
I speak this truth, so hear it from me, O ruler of men.
While they were thus conversing, some hunters arrived at that place.

O Great King, those hunters were constantly exhausted by their loads of meat; O Lord, out of supreme devotion, they would regularly bring loads of meat to Bhīmasena whenever they happened to come there for water.

Stationed there, they all gathered together in secret and heard that entire conversation, as well as the words of Duryodhana, while the Kuru prince was intent on avoiding battle. All those great archers likewise [listened].
Then those who were longing for battle indeed exerted the utmost persistence. Beholding those great car-warriors of the Kauravas thus intent,
and seeing the king himself standing in the water with no mind for fighting, [the enemy prepared].

Having heard that conversation between them and the king who was in the water, O Indra among kings, the hunters recognized Suyodhana as he remained within the waters. For they had previously been questioned by the son of Pāṇḍu regarding your son.
Having arrived there by chance, they searched for the king; then, O King,
remembering those words spoken at that time by the son of Pāṇḍu,
those hunters spoke this softly to one another.
"Let us announce that Duryodhana is here; the Pāṇḍava will give us wealth.
It is well known to us that King Duryodhana is in this lake.
Therefore, let us all go where King Yudhiṣṭhira is."
To tell the wise Bhīmasena that the intolerant Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, was sleeping in the water;
let us all report to that wielder of the bow that he is lying in the water.
"He will give us abundant wealth, being well-pleased;
what need have we for this dried, withered, and emaciated meat?
Having spoken thus, the hunters, desiring wealth, were then filled with great joy.
Taking up loads of flesh, they set out toward the camp;
and the Pāṇḍavas, O great king, those strikers who had achieved their aim,
could not see Duryodhana stationed on the battlefield.
Desiring to reach the end of that wicked man's treachery,
they dispatched spies in all directions across that field of battle.
Having returned, however, they all reported that King Duryodhana was missing.
Together, the soldiers reported this to the King of Dharma.
Having heard those words of the spies, O bull of the Bharatas,
the king fell into deep anxiety and sighed heavily.
If there remains even a slight deficiency, victory will be uncertain;
for how could one obtain a kingdom that is honored by victory and other such qualities?
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the Pāṇḍavas stood there dejected.
O Lord, departing from that place in haste,
the hunters arrived at the camp joyful upon seeing King Duryodhana;
though they were being forbidden, they entered while Bhīmasena looked on.
Having approached the mighty Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena,
they related to him everything that had occurred and all that they had heard.
Then, O King, Vṛkodara gave them much wealth.
The scorcher of foes reported all of that to Dharmarāja:
"O King, that Duryodhana has been discovered by my hunters;
he lies there, having solidified the waters—for his sake you are consumed with grief."
O lord of the people, having heard those pleasing words of Bhīmasena,
Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī, became joyful along with his brothers;
and having heard that the great archer had entered the lake of water.
Then, placing Janārdana at their head, they departed with great speed;
O lord of the people, a tumultuous roar of joy then arose from all sides among the delighted Pāṇḍavas and the Pañcālas.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, they let out lion-roars and war-cries;
the kṣatriyas, O King, rushed swiftly toward the Dvaipāyana lake. "The wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra has been discovered! He has been seen!"—thus they cried repeatedly in the battle.
The Somakas there, appearing joyful, shouted out on all sides. O lord of the earth, as those swift chariots sped away with great velocity, a tumultuous sound arose that reached the very heavens.
Desiring to rescue Duryodhana, they followed King Yudhiṣṭhira here and there in haste, though their mounts were exhausted;
Arjuna, Bhīmasena, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī likewise pursued him.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna the Pāñcālya, the unconquered Śikhaṇḍin, Uttamaujas, Yudhāmanyu, the unconquered Sātyaki,
and those who remain of the Pāñcālas, as well as the sons of Draupadī, O Bhārata.
Then all the horses, elephants, and hundreds of foot-soldiers followed;
and then, O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
arrived at the famous lake of Dvaipāyana where Duryodhana was located.
It possessed cool, pure, and heart-pleasing water, like a second ocean; there,
O Bhārata, by means of a most wonderful rite and through the power of destiny, your son remained after you had solidified the water with your illusory power (*māyā*).
"O lord of men, O king, that ruler of people lies within the waters with mace in hand, invisible to any mortal man. Then King Duryodhana, dwelling within the depths of the water,"
A tumultuous sound, like the roar of clouds, was heard. Then,
O king of kings, Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, approached that lake,
O great monarch, for the sake of slaying your sons.
With the great blare of conchs and the sound of chariot wheels,
raising a vast cloud of dust and making the earth tremble,
the great car-warriors heard the noise of Yudhiṣṭhira’s army.
Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa said this to the king:
"For here come the Pāṇḍavas, exultant and appearing victorious;
we shall therefore withdraw, and may your majesty grant us leave."
But Duryodhana, having heard those words of those illustrious men,
said "So be it," O Lord, and by means of his illusory power (māyā) he solidified that lake.
They, however, taking leave of the king, were deeply overcome with grief.
O great king, Kṛpa and the other chariot-warriors traveled a long distance;
having gone a great way, O noble one, they beheld a banyan tree and,
being utterly exhausted, they halted there, reflecting upon the king.
The mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra lies asleep, having solidified the waters;
and the Pāṇḍavas have also arrived at that place, desiring battle.
How indeed will the battle take place? What will become of the king?
"O King, how indeed will the Pāṇḍavas respond to the Kaurava?"—
thinking thus, O King, those car-warriors headed by Kṛpa unyoked their horses from the chariots and took up positions there.
Saṃjaya said: Then,
when those three charioteers had departed, the Pāṇḍavas proceeded to that lake where Duryodhana was.
Having reached the lake of Dvaipāyana, O best of the Kurus,
and seeing that reservoir of water solidified by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the joy of the Kurus addressed these words to Vāsudeva.
Behold this illusion employed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
having solidified the waters, he lies within them, for he has no fear of anything human.
Having created this divine illusion, he has indeed entered into the depths of the water.

"O Mādhava, even if the wielder of the thunderbolt himself were to provide assistance to him in battle, this man, who is skilled in deceit, shall not escape from me alive by means of his own treachery;
rather, the world shall see him slain in combat."
Śrī Vāsudeva said:
"O Bhārata, O Yudhiṣṭhira, destroy this illusion of the illusionist with your own power of illusion; an illusionist is to be slain by means of illusion—this is the truth."
"O best of the Bharatas, employing illusion through many strategic means upon the waters, slay the evil-minded Suyodhana. By means of such strategic devices, Indra slew the Daityas and Dānavas."
By means of many ritual expedients, Bali was bound by that Great-Souled One; for indeed,
in former times, the great asura Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu were both destroyed through ritual action alone.
O King, Vṛtra was slain by action alone; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, O King, the Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, the son of Pulastya, was slain by Rāma along with his kinsmen and followers.
"O King, by resorting to the application of action, you too must likewise exert your prowess;
for in the past, the great Daitya Tāraka and the heroic Vipracitti were slain by me through the means of action."
O Lord, Vātāpi and Ilvala, as well as Triśiras,
and the two Asuras Sunda and Upasunda were destroyed by means of ritual action alone;
likewise, the great Daitya Tāraka and Andhaka were also slain.
"O Lord, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, the triple heaven is enjoyed by Indra through the means of action;
action is powerful, and there is nothing else at all. So too are the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and kings [conquered] through action."
"Since they have been struck down by the means of action, therefore perform your duty.
Sañjaya said:
"Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, the son of Pāṇḍu, firm in his vows,"
O great king, O descendant of Bharata, the son of Kuntī, as if laughing, addressed your mighty son who was standing in the water:
"Suyodhana, for what purpose have you made this effort in the waters?"

O lord of the people, having caused the destruction of the entire warrior class and his own kin, he has now entered a body of water desiring to preserve his own life. Arise, O King Suyodhana, and fight with us!
"O best of men, where has that pride and that arrogance of yours gone, you who,
O King, stand here terrified after having solidified the waters?
All people in the assembly speak of you as a hero."
I consider that valor of yours, as you lie within the waters, to be in vain.
Arise, O King, and fight; you are a Kṣatriya born of noble lineage. Especially as a descendant of the Kurus, remember your birth in that family.
How can you, praising your own birth in the Kuru lineage,
now take refuge in the water out of fear of battle?
To avoid combat and to lack steadfastness— this is not the eternal dharma.

O King, fleeing from battle is a practice favored by the ignoble and leads away from heaven. Having seen these sons, brothers, and fathers fallen here, how can you, desiring to live, fail to reach the further shore in this war?
"Having caused the death of your relatives, friends, maternal uncles, and kinsmen, how is it, dear one, that you now remain in this lake?
Thinking yourself a hero, you are no hero; you speak falsely, O Bhārata."
"O evil-minded one, while the whole world listens, you cry out, 'I am a hero.
For heroes never flee by any means upon seeing their enemies;
or rather, tell me with what resolve you, a so-called hero, abandon the battle."
Therefore, arise and fight, casting off your fear!
Having caused the destruction of the entire army and your brothers as well, O Suyodhana,
you should no longer set your mind on life out of a desire to fulfill your duty.
O Suyodhana, relying on the dharma of a kṣatriya, you who are like me—
by depending on Karṇa and Śakuni, the son of Subala— you did not realize your own [true] self due to delusion, as if you were an immortal.
Having committed that very great sin, O Bhārata, fight back!
For how could one such as you, out of delusion, find pleasure in flight?
Where has that manliness of yours gone, and where is your pride, O Suyodhana?
Where has your valor gone, and where has your great prowess vanished?
Where has your mastery of weapons gone, and why do you lie here in this pool of water? Arise, O Bhārata, and fight according to the duty of a Kṣatriya!
Either defeat us and rule this earth,
O Bhārata, or, slain by us, you shall sleep upon the ground.
This is your first duty, ordained by the Great-Souled Creator.
"Act upon that exactly as it is; become a king, O great chariot-warrior.
Sañjaya said:
"O great king, having been addressed thus by the wise son of Dharma..."
Standing in the water, your son spoke these words:
Duryodhana said,
"O Great King, it is no wonder that fear should enter a living being."
O Bhārata, it was not out of fear for my life that I retreated;
rather, being without a chariot, without quivers, and with my flank-guarding charioteer slain,
I— being alone and without a following in battle— sought a moment’s rest.

"O lord of the people, it was not for the sake of my life, nor out of fear, nor from despair that I entered this water; rather, this was undertaken by me simply out of exhaustion. You too, O son of Kuntī, along with those who follow you, must take rest."
"Having risen, I shall fight all of you in battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"We have all indeed been refreshed; we have sought you for a long time."
Therefore, rise now and fight here, O Suyodhana!
Either, having slain the sons of Pṛthā in battle, obtain a prosperous kingdom;
or, being slain by us in combat, you shall attain the world of heroes.
Duryodhana said:
"O joy of the Kurus, O lord of men, all these brothers of mine, for whose sake I desired the kingdom of the Kurus, have now been slain."
I do not venture to enjoy this earth, now that its jewels are exhausted and its preeminent kṣatriyas have been slain, any more than one would enjoy a widowed woman. Yet,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even now I still hope to conquer you in battle.
O bull of the Bharatas, having shattered the enthusiasm of the Pāñcālas and the Pāṇḍavas,
I do not think that war is appropriate at this time,
now that Droṇa and Karṇa have been silenced and the Grandfather has been slain.
"O King, let this entire earth now be yours alone;
for what king, indeed, would wish to rule a kingdom without allies—
having abandoned such friends, sons, brothers, and even fathers?"

"If the kingdom were seized by you, who indeed could live like me? I shall go to the forest, clothed in deerskins; for there is no pleasure in sovereignty for one whose party has been destroyed, O Bhārata."
"O King, this earth of yours is now filled mostly with those whose kinsmen have been slain, its horses killed and its elephants destroyed. Enjoy it, free from all anxiety.
As for me, I shall go to the forest, clad in the skins of wild animals."
"O Lord, now that I have been conquered, I have no desire for life. Go, O Indra among kings, and enjoy the earth whose lords have been slain—
its warriors killed, its jewels lost, and its defenses destroyed— just as you please."
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard those piteous words from Duryodhana, your son, who was staying within the waters, the highly illustrious Yudhiṣṭhira spoke as follows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O father, do not utter these lamentations of one in distress while standing in the water;
O King, this does not take root in my mind, like the cry of a bird."
"O Suyodhana, even if you were capable of giving [the earth],
I would not desire to rule over the earth given by you;
I would not accept this earth given by you through unrighteousness."
For the acceptance of gifts, O King, is not recorded as the duty of a Kṣatriya.
I would not desire even the entire earth given by you;
rather, having utterly defeated you in battle, I shall enjoy this land.
"And how can you wish to give away the earth when you have no power over it?
O King, why was this earth not given by you at that very time,
when we were rightfully entreating you for the sake of peace for our lineage?"
"O King, having first rejected the mighty Vārṣṇeya, what is it now that you give? For what indeed is this confusion of mind?
What king, when assailed by an enemy, would wish to give away his land?"

"O joy of the Kurus, you are not the master today to give away this earth, nor, O King, to seize it by force; how then can you wish to give it? Having defeated me in battle, you should protect this earth yourself."
O Bhārata, that which could be supported by the very tip of a needle from this earth— even such a small portion as that you did not give to me in the past;
how then, O lord of people, do you now offer this entire earth?
Previously you would not relinquish even the point of a needle; how then can you now abandon the earth?
Having attained such sovereignty and ruled this world, what fool indeed would resolve to give the land to an enemy?

But you, utterly deluded by sheer folly, do not perceive that even though you desire to give away the earth, today you shall be deprived of your life. Either defeat us and rule this earth, or else depart.
Or else, O King, slain by us, go to the unsurpassed worlds; for as long as both of us— myself and you— remain alive,
there will certainly be doubt among all beings regarding our victory.
"O man of evil intellect, your life now depends upon me. I could indeed grant you life at my will, but you are not worthy to live.
For you have made a special effort to burn us."
O King, they were tormented by you through venomous serpents, poisons, and even by being cast into the water; and by the seizure of their kingdom,
by your unpleasant words, and by the dragging of Draupadī.
"Because of your senseless prattle and because you have taken refuge in dwelling in the forest, come out from the lake and fight; then it will be better for you.
For this reason, O wicked one, your life shall not be preserved."
"Arise, arise, and fight! That will be for your welfare.
Sañjaya said:
"In this way, various words conducive to victory were spoken again and again."
Those heroes proclaimed [this] here and there, O lord of men.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Thus being threatened, my son, the lord of the earth..."
How was that hero, the scorcher of his enemies, who was wrathful by nature, ever before subjected to threats? For he had never heard a harsh rebuke,
and he was honored by all the world for his royal dignity.
How could he, whose own parasol-shade and even the radiance of the sun cause him distress due to his arrogance,
endure such words?
And this entire earth, including the barbarians and forest-dwellers, is [under his command].
O Sañjaya, he whose very life is sustained by your grace before your very eyes—
being thus threatened especially by the sons of Pāṇḍu,
deprived of his own servants, and utterly surrounded in that desolate place— [how will he endure?]"
"Having heard those bitter words, repeated again and again, what did he say to the sons of Pāṇḍu? Tell me that, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
O King, being thus threatened by Yudhiṣṭhira together with his brothers while standing in the water, your son,
that lord of men, heard those bitter words while situated in a precarious position.
Sighing long and hot breaths again and again while staying within the water,
the king, wringing his hands repeatedly from within the depths of the water,
set his mind on battle and addressed the king:
"You Pārthas, all together with your friends, are equipped with chariots and mounts;
I alone am despondent, deprived of my chariot and with my mounts slain,
surrounded by many who have taken up their weapons and are mounted on chariots."
"How can I, being alone, on foot, and unarmed, venture to fight?
O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should each fight me one by one;
for it is not right for one man to be fought by many heroes in battle."
Especially since you are without armor, exhausted, and resting by the water; with your limbs severely wounded and your mounts and soldiers fatigued—
O King, I have no fear of you, nor of Pārtha Vṛkodara.
Whether from Phalguna or Vasudeva, or again from the Panchalas,
or from the twins, or from Yuyudhana, or whoever else among your soldiers—
being alone and enraged, I do not venture to fight them all here.
"O lord of men, the fame of virtuous people is rooted in righteousness;
therefore, protecting both righteousness and fame in this world, I declare:
rising up, I shall fight all of you in battle."
Just as the year follows all the seasons that arrive in succession,
so today— even though I am without weapons and without a chariot— do you, along with your chariots and horses,
follow me like all the stars follow the sun at the end of the night.
"I shall destroy them with my splendor; stand firm, O Pāṇḍavas!
Today I shall attain freedom from debt to the illustrious Kṣatriyas—to Bāhlīka, Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and the high-souled Karṇa."
Of the heroic Jayadratha and Bhagadatta, both of them;
of Śalya, the king of the Madras, and of Bhūriśravas;
and of the sons of Śakuni Saubala, O best of the Bharatas.
"By slaying you along with your brothers today, I shall attain freedom from my debt to my friends, well-wishers, and kinsmen. Having spoken these words, the lord of men fell silent.
"Your illustrious son Duryodhana is within the waters.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By good fortune, O Suyodhana, you too recognize the duty of a Kṣatriya!"
"By good fortune, O mighty-armed one, your mind is set upon battle alone.
By good fortune you are a hero, O Kauravya; by good fortune you understand the nature of combat, since you alone desire to fight all of us in this encounter."
"O hero, having come together one-on-one, you shall fight with whatever weapon you deem appropriate; we stand here as your spectators. Furthermore, O hero, I grant you this desired wish."
"By slaying one [of us], you shall obtain the kingdom; or, being slain, you shall attain heaven.
At that moment, O King, as he finished speaking, the Siddhas cried out loudly.
Duryodhana said:
"If one of you is granted as my choice today to fight me in this arena,
and if this mace is selected from among these weapons with your consent—
then whichever one of you brothers deems himself capable may face me."
Let him fight with me on foot with a mace in this battle;
wonderful chariot-duels have occurred at every step,
so let this one great and marvelous mace-duel take place today.
Men desire even to change the course of food;
let there also be a change in battles, if it be your will.
O mighty-armed one, with my mace I shall defeat you along with your younger brother.
"The Pāñcālas, the Sṛñjayas, and whoever else are your soldiers—
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I have never felt any agitation even before Śakra himself in battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Arise, arise, O son of Gāndhārī! Fight me, O Suyodhana!
Meeting one-on-one in combat with mace, O mighty one, be a man, O son of Gāndhārī, and fight with full concentration!"
"Today your life is at an end, even if you possess the speed of thought.
Saṃjaya said:
That tiger among men, your son, could not endure these words.
Like a great elephant hissing within a hollow in the midst of water,
that wise man, being repeatedly prodded by the goad of her words, could not endure her speech, just as a noble horse cannot endure the whip.
Having violently agitated the waters, the heroic one took up his heavy mace—
made of the essence of stone and adorned with golden armlets—
and rose up from within the water like a great serpent hissing.
Having pierced through the solidified water and placed his iron mace upon his shoulder,
your son rose up like the sun blazing with its rays;
then he took up that heavy mace made of refined steel and adorned with gold.
The wise and mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra grasped his mace.
Seeing him with mace in hand, like a mountain with its peak,
he stood there like the enraged trident-wielder Śiva standing before all creatures.
Clad in armor, the descendant of Bharata shone like the scorching sun. As that mighty-armed subduer of foes emerged with mace in hand,
all living beings regarded him as Death himself with staff in hand.
O lord of men, all the Pāñcālas beheld your son like Śakra with the thunderbolt in his hand, or like Hara with the trident in his hand.
Seeing him having crossed over, they rejoiced on every side.
The Pāñcālas and the sons of Pāṇḍu slapped their palms against one another.
But regarding that as a mockery, your son Duryodhana,
his eyes rolling in rage, seemed as if he wished to consume the Pāṇḍavas.
Knitting his brows into a three-pronged frown and biting his lip,
he then replied to those Pāṇḍavas along with Keśava:
"O Pāṇḍavas, today I shall give a fitting answer to this mockery of yours."
"Slain this very day, you and the Pañcālas shall go to the abode of Yama.
But your son Duryodhana, having risen from that water,
stood there with mace in hand, drenched in blood.
His body, smeared with blood and drenched with water, then shone like a mountain with flowing streams. There,
the Pāṇḍavas regarded that hero as one with his mace raised.
Like the wrathful son of Vivasvat with his *kiṃkara* servants raising their hands, that heroic one,
roaring like a thundercloud and like a bull bellowing in joy,
then challenged the sons of Pṛthā to battle with his mace.
Duryodhana said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, you all must approach me one by one in battle;
for it is not right, O hero, for one man to be fought by many in combat."
Having cast off his armor, being especially exhausted, and drenched in water; with his limbs severely wounded and his mounts and soldiers slain;
deprived of all equipment and destitute of armor, weapons, and missiles.
"Let the gods in heaven behold me fighting all alone! I must certainly fight with all of you;
you yourself always know what is appropriate and what is inappropriate."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Suyodhana, how was it that this wisdom was not yours,
when many great car-warriors slew Abhimanyu in battle?"
The duty of the warrior (kṣatradharma) is exceedingly cruel, indifferent, and utterly merciless;
otherwise, how could they have slain Abhimanyu while he was in such a state?
For all of you are knowers of dharma, and all are heroes ready to lay down your lives.
For those who fight according to the rules of conduct, the supreme destination is said to be the world of Śakra; yet,
if it is the very dharma that one person must not be slain by many, then how was it, according to your view, that many slew Abhimanyu?
Every living being, when standing in distress, reflects upon the vision of Dharma;
one established in a high station beholds the gate ordained for the world beyond.
O hero, put on your armor and restrain your hair!
"O Bhārata, take also whatever else you do not possess;
whether it be an arrow, a spear, or even a mace—I grant you yet another boon.
And furthermore, O hero, I grant you this one wish."

"Whichever of the five Pāṇḍava sons you wish to fight here, slay him and become king; or, being slain, attain heaven. O hero, except for your life, what dear service can we perform for you in battle?"
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O King, your son took up his golden armor and his wonderful helmet adorned with refined gold.
With his helmet fastened and wearing armor of beautiful gold,
O King, your son shone like a golden king of mountains.
Girt for battle and armed with a mace, O King, he stood ready at the forefront of the fray.
Your son Duryodhana said to all the Pāṇḍavas:
"Let one among you brothers fight with me with the mace;
I shall fight either Sahadeva, or Bhīma, or Nakula."

Or rather, O bull of the Bharatas, today I shall fight with either Phalguna or you upon meeting in combat, and I shall be victorious on the field of battle. Today I shall reach the end of this enmity, which has been so difficult to overcome.
"O tiger among men, with this mace bound with bands of gold,
consider that there is no one equal to me in mace-fighting;
with this mace, I shall slay all of you who have gathered here."
Not one among all of you is capable of fighting me according to the rules of fair combat;
it is not proper for me to speak such words of arrogant pride. Nevertheless, I shall make these words of yours bear fruit right before your eyes.
"In this very moment, whether it be true or false,
let him who indeed fights with me today take up his mace.
Sañjaya said:
O King, while Duryodhana was thus roaring again and again,
Vāsudeva, filled with rage, said this to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"If indeed this man were to choose you in battle, O Yudhiṣṭhira..."
"Whether it be Arjuna, Nakula, or even Sahadeva—
O King, why have you uttered such a rash word as this:
'Slaying only one in battle, become the king of the Kurus'?"
For by this, you have become proficient through thirteen years spent here;
now, discharge the debt for those words previously spoken by you with the intent to kill Bhīmasena, as that matter has now come to fruition.
"O King, regarding this iron man [effigy] intended for the slaughter of Bhīmasena,
O bull of the Bharatas, how indeed might our purpose be accomplished? For you, O best of kings, have acted out of compassion rather than rashness."
"I see no other opponent for him in battle except Vṛkodara Pārtha, and he has not yet exerted himself to the full. Therefore,
this game of dice has begun once again just as before."
"O Lord of the People, there is indeed an inequality between Śakuni and yourself.
Bhīma is powerful and capable, while King Suyodhana is skilled;
between one who is merely strong and one who is skilled, O King, the skilled one is superior."
"O King, you have placed this enemy on even ground; you have cast yourself onto a most treacherous path and brought us to distress.
For who, having completely conquered all other enemies, would then be defeated by a single foe?"
Having staked everything with a single hand, he would thus find the challenge agreeable;
likewise, having fallen into distress, he might lose the kingdom he had obtained.
Indeed, I do not see anyone in this world, even with mace in hand, who could withstand that best of men.
Whoever today should fight Duryodhana in battle would,
by his skill, indeed distinguish himself; for even an immortal would be capable of conquering him when he stands with mace in hand.
Whether it be Phalguna, yourself, or the two sons of Mādrī—
neither you, nor Bhīma, nor Nakula, nor Sahadeva, nor even Phalguna—
I do not consider any of you capable [of withstanding me] in combat when I am armed with my mace.

"O Bhārata, King Suyodhana is indeed capable and skillful enough to conquer you by right means. Why then do you speak of him as an enemy, saying, 'Fight with a mace' and 'Become king after slaying us one by one in battle'?"
"Having encountered Vṛkodara, our victory is indeed in doubt;
for this one of great strength is skilled in combat, even when we fight according to the rules of fair conduct. Or rather, having slain us all alone, you may once again become king."
"Surely this offspring of Pāṇḍu and Kuntī does not belong to the portion of the kingdom;
rather, it was created for dwelling in the forest or for living on alms.
Bhīma said:
O Madhusūdana, O delight of the Yadus, do not yield to despondency;
today I shall reach the far shore of this enmity, which is so exceedingly difficult to cross.
I shall slay Suyodhana in battle; of this there is no doubt.
"O Kṛṣṇa, victory is indeed certain for Dharmarāja;
this mace of mine is one-and-a-half times heavier than that of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Do not feel distressed, O Mādhava."
"With this mace, O Janārdana, I am eager to fight in battle; let all of you be my spectators,
even against the three worlds including the gods, as they bear various weapons in combat."
"I would fight joyfully in battle—even Suyodhana himself—let alone today.
Sañjaya said:
"While he was speaking thus, his eyes wide with joy,"
Laughing, swelling with rage, and roaring repeatedly; panting again and again, he let out shouts of defiance incessantly,
manifesting many kinds of transformations that intensely incited fury.
While Vāyu was performing this for the sake of uprooting your son,
Vāsudeva, his mind at ease, then spoke these words to Bhīma:
"O mighty-armed one, it is no marvel that you would slay Suyodhana."

By whom Vaiśravaṇa and Maṇibhadra, the king of the yakṣas, were defeated in battle, and by whom many thousands of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas were overcome— who indeed could calculate his strength in battle, O son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?

You, who—without the use of weapons—slew Hiḍimba of terrible form, possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants; Baka, who was twice that strength; Kirmīra, four times that strength in combat; and Kīcaka, who was like an elephant.
"You are the slayer of the Kaurava; in this matter, who could have any doubt?
When Vāsudeva had spoken thus, Dharmarāja replied:
"O Kṛṣṇa, it is by your very splendor that he shall slay Suyodhana."
"This man has indeed fulfilled his vow and likewise brought an end to his enemies;
having done what was disagreeable to Bhīmasena, what man could be happy?
Thus spoke Sātyaki, whose soul is devoted to Kṛṣṇa, looking toward Keśava and Bhīma.
O Keśava, this Vṛkodara is no ordinary man in the art of mace-fighting;
he who, when enraged, could pulverize all the mountains in an instant—
what need is there to speak of that warrior who possesses a superhuman body?
With elephants he struck down elephants, with horses horses, and likewise with chariots chariots,
right before your eyes and solely for my pleasure;
thus did Phalguna honor the prowess of Bhīma.
Nakula and Sahadeva praised him again and again; likewise,
the Pāñcālas led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, along with the Somakas and the kings who remained after the slaughter, all extolled Vṛkodara.
And with various words, they honored him with great respect. Everyone praised those words of Bhīmasena.
Then Bhīma, possessed of terrible strength, [was addressed] by those led by Vāsudeva.

The Pāṇḍava, together with the Pañcālas, was thus celebrated for his deeds and honored as a great archer; at that very moment, he was intensely emboldened and grew in strength like the great ocean during the full moon.
With his hair standing on end from joy, he spoke with delight to all his friends,
to Keśava, Dharmarāja, and all his younger brothers:
"Today I shall release my anger, which has been suppressed for a long time."
"Today I shall extract the dart that has been embedded by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
As Vṛkodara was speaking thus, Vāsudeva,
being delighted, honored him and spoke these words.

Relying upon you, O mighty-armed one, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira has slain his enemies and attained his own radiant sovereignty; of this there is no doubt. All the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been struck down by you in battle.
Kings and princes, as well as elephants, have been struck down;
the Kalingas, Magadhas, Easterners, Gandharas, and Kurus likewise—
having encountered you in this great battle, O son of Pāṇḍu, they have been slain.
Having slain Duryodhana as well, O Kaunteya, bestow the earth together with its oceans upon Dharmarāja, just as Viṣṇu did for the Lord of Śacī;
and having encountered you in battle, that wicked son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall perish.
"Having broken his two thighs, you shall fulfill your vow.
However, O Pārtha, you must always fight the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra with great effort,
for he is skilled, powerful, and ever-experienced in battle."
Then, O King, Sātyaki honored the Pāṇḍava,
and Mādhava honored him with various words.
The Pāñcālas and the sons of Pāṇḍu, led by Dharmarāja, likewise paid him homage.
Everyone praised those words of Bhīmasena.
Then Bhīma, possessed of terrible strength, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira,
who was standing with the Sṛñjayas like the scorching sun.
"Having encountered him in battle, I am eager to fight;
for this lowest of men is not able to defeat me in combat.
Today, I shall release the intense anger that has long been stored within my heart."
Just as Arjuna [extinguished] the fire at Khāṇḍava against Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
O Pāṇḍava, today I shall extract the dart of grief lodged in your heart;
having slain that wicked man with my mace, O King, be happy today.
"O sinless one, today I shall place upon you a garland made of glory.
Today Suyodhana shall be deprived of his life, his fortune, and his kingdom.
And today King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard that his son has been slain by me—"
"He will remember that inauspicious deed which arose from his bird-like intellect.
Having said this, the heroic best of the Bharatas raised his mace and stood up for battle,
like Śakra summoning Vṛtra.
Unable to endure that challenge, your exceedingly powerful son immediately advanced against me, like one rutting elephant against another,
as your son stood ready for battle with mace in hand.
All the Pāṇḍavas beheld him, who was like the peaked Mount Kailāsa;
having encountered that mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra all alone,
like an elephant strayed from its herd, the Pāṇḍavas rejoiced.

Neither agitation, nor fear, nor exhaustion, nor pain came upon Duryodhana as he stood in battle like a lion. Seeing him with his mace raised, like the peaked Mount Kailāsa, [the enemy was struck with awe].
Then, O King, Bhīmasena said to Duryodhana:
"Remember that evil deed which was done toward us by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and by you, as it occurred at Vāraṇāvata."
And Draupadī was tormented in the midst of the assembly while in her courses;
and the king was defeated at dice through the deliberate resolve of Śakuni.
Furthermore, O evil-minded one, whatever other wicked deeds you have committed—
Behold the great fruit of his sinlessness toward the sons of Pṛthā:
on your account, that highly illustrious one, the son of Gaṅgā, the best of the Bharatas, and the grandfather of us all, lies slain upon a bed of arrows.
Droṇa has been slain, and Karṇa has been slain; the powerful Śalya has been slain. And that Śakuni, the original instigator of this enmity, has been killed in battle.
Your heroic brothers have been killed, as have your sons along with their armies.
Brave kings who never retreated in battle have been slain;
these and many other bulls among the Kṣatriyas have been killed. Likewise, the wicked Prātikāmī, the one who caused Draupadī such suffering, has been slain.
"You alone remain, the destroyer of your lineage, the lowest of men.
Even you I shall slay today with my mace; of this there is no doubt.
Today, O King, I shall destroy all your pride in battle."
"O King, [you have harbored] a vast hope for sovereignty over the Pāṇḍavas and committed a wicked deed.
Duryodhana said:
"What is the use of much boasting? Fight with me today!"
"Today, O Vṛkodara, I shall dispel your desire for battle.
Do you not see me, O wicked one, standing ready for a mace-duel,
grasping a great mace that resembles a peak of the Himavat mountains?"

"O sinful one, what enemy today dares to conquer me while I am armed with my mace and fighting according to the rules of fair combat— even Purandara among the gods? As for that wicked deed of mine which was previously mentioned,"
All of that was done so that I would not have even the slightest cause for suspicion; indeed,
I would have forcibly brought about my dwelling in the forest, service in another's house,
and likewise a transformation of my appearance.
Your kinsmen have been slain, and this destruction is equal for both of us;
yet if my own fall were to occur now in battle,
that would indeed be most praiseworthy, for time alone is the cause therein.
"Even today, there is no victor over me in the field of battle by means of righteousness (dharma). If you should conquer me through deceit, infamy will surely remain;
being unrighteous and disgraceful, you will certainly suffer remorse hereafter."
"Do not roar in vain, O son of Kuntī, like a waterless autumn cloud!
Display whatever strength you possess today in battle.
Having heard those words of his, the Pāñcālas along with the Sṛñjayas...
Desirous of victory, they all honored those words;
O King, the men further cheered King Duryodhana, who was like an elephant in rut being incited by the sound of clapping hands.
There the elephants trumpet and the horses neigh repeatedly;
the weapons of the Pāṇḍavas, who desire victory, blaze forth.
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, when that most terrible battle had commenced and all the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were seated,
Rāma, whose banner bears the palm tree, then appeared as those two were about to engage in combat.
O King, having heard that from his two disciples, Halāyudha arrived.
Seeing him, the lords of men were exceedingly delighted; having honored him and approached him, they greeted him and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites.
After they had paid their respects, they then spoke these words:
"O Rāma, behold the skill of your two disciples in battle," they said.
And then Rāma, having seen Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, spoke.
And seeing Duryodhana, the Kaurava, standing with mace in hand, [Bhīma said:
"Forty-two days have passed since I departed;
I set out under the constellation Puṣya and have now returned under Śravaṇa."
"O Mādhava, I am indeed desirous of witnessing the mace-duel between these two disciples.
Then, with maces in hand, those two heroes, Duryodhana and Vṛkodara,
shone brightly as they both stood upon the field of battle.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having embraced Halāyudha,
enquired after his welcome and welfare exactly as it was;
and the two great archers, the Kṛṣṇas, also saluted Halāyudha.

O King, the two illustrious and heroic sons of Mādrī, as well as the five sons of Draupadī, embraced one another with great affection; then, having offered their salutations, they stood before the mighty son of Rohiṇī.
Then, O lord of men, your powerful son Bhīmasena likewise honored Balarāma with his mace raised; having saluted him, the two of them then embraced the wielder of the plow.
Having honored him there again and again with a welcome,
they said to Rāma, "Behold the battle, O mighty-armed one!
Thus did the lords of men speak to the high-souled son of Rohiṇī.
Then Rāma, having embraced the Pāṇḍavas as well as the Sṛñjayas,
inquired after the welfare of all those Pāṇḍavas of immeasurable prowess;
and they likewise, having approached him, asked after his health.
Having honored all the Kṣatriyas in return, the high-minded wielder of the plow (Balarāma) engaged them in conversation concerning their welfare according to their respective ages;
then, out of affection, he embraced Janārdana and Sātyaki.
Having smelled the tops of their heads, he inquired after their welfare;
and they, O King, honored their guru according to the prescribed rites,
filled with joy like Indra and Upendra honoring Brahmā, the lord of the gods.
Then the son of Dharma said to the subduer of enemies, the son of Rohiṇī:
"O Rāma, behold this great battle between the two brothers," O Bhārata.
In their midst stood the mighty-armed and illustrious elder brother of Keśava.
Being honored by the great chariot-warriors, he sat down, supremely delighted.
Standing in the midst of the kings, dressed in blue garments yet possessing a white radiance,
he shone like the moon surrounded by hosts of stars in the sky.
Then, O King, there occurred between those two sons of yours a tumultuous and hair-raising encounter that brought about their end.
Janamejaya said:
Previously, when that war was imminent, the lord Rāma took his leave of Keśava and departed accompanied by the Vṛṣṇis, saying:
"O Keśava, I shall not provide assistance to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
"And I shall not return to the sons of Pāṇḍu as I came.
Having spoken thus, Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, then departed. O Brahmin, you ought to relate his return once more.
"Tell me in detail how Rāma arrived and how he witnessed the battle, for you are indeed skilled in this, O best of men.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When the high-souled Pāṇḍavas had settled at Upaplavya,
O mighty-armed one, Madhusūdana was dispatched to the presence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra for the sake of peace and for the welfare of all embodied beings.
Having gone to Hastinapura and met with Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
he spoke words that were true and especially beneficial;
yet the king did not act upon them, just as was previously described to you.
Failing to obtain peace there, O lord of men, the mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the best of men, returned to Upaplavya. Then Kṛṣṇa, having been dismissed by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, returned.
That tiger among men arrived at the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
O tiger among men, when they were inactive, he spoke this to the Pāṇḍavas;
having related what was said and how it had occurred, he addressed the Pāṇḍava.
"Driven by time, the Kurus do not heed my words.
O sons of Pāṇḍu, depart together with me under the asterism Puṣya. Then, as the armies were being divided, that best of the strong—
The high-minded son of Rohiṇī spoke to his brother Kṛṣṇa:
"O mighty-armed Madhusūdana, let assistance be given even to them. But at that time, Kṛṣṇa did not heed those words of his.
The wise Hari always performed everything for the destruction of his enemies;
at that time and in that place, he recalled this again and again. Then, his soul overcome with indignation, the joy of the Yadus departed.
The highly illustrious wielder of the plow, accompanied by all the Yādavas, undertook a pilgrimage to the Sarasvatī during the conjunction of the Maitra constellation; meanwhile,
the Bhoja subduer of foes took refuge with Duryodhana.
Accompanied by Yuyudhāna, Vāsudeva—
the slayer of Madhu— set out toward the Kurus, placing the Pāṇḍavas at his head, after the heroic son of Rohiṇī had departed under the asterism Puṣya.
While still on the road, Rāma spoke to his attendants:
"Bring the provisions for the pilgrimage and all necessary implements;
fetch the sacred fires from Dvārakā as well as the officiating priests."
"Let gold, silver, cows, garments,
horses, elephants, chariots, donkeys, camels,
and all other vehicles and equipment for the sake of the sacred ford be brought here immediately."
"Go swiftly up the Sarasvatī river against its current,
and bring hither hundreds of officiating priests and the best of the twice-born.
Having thus instructed his messengers, the mighty Baladeva—
O King, at that time during the slaughter of the Kurus,
Rāma— the best of the Yadus, glorious and illustrious— set out on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, traveling upstream along the Sarasvatī from the ocean as he recalled his previous journey.
O bull of the Bharatas, he was surrounded by officiating priests, friends, and other foremost among the twice-born, as well as by chariots, elephants, horses, servants,
and many vehicles drawn by cattle, mules, and camels.
O Bhārata, those vehicles awaited them in various places— those children of long life who were weary and exhausted in body;
and for the sake of those who were hungry, food was prepared on all sides.

O King, various kinds of gifts were to be distributed in every region for the sake of worship and for those who seek them; likewise, many such provisions were prepared so that whichever twice-born man desired to eat at any place, he might have his wish fulfilled at that time.
O King, at that time,
the men stationed there by the command of Rauhineya brought various things for him and, O monarch, they piled up heaps of food and drink all around him.
Costly garments, couches,
and coverlets were prepared there for the sake of honoring the brahmins who desired comfort;
and there, O Bhārata, whichever brahmin or kṣatriya lay down to sleep, [he found rest].
In every place, everything was seen to be prepared for him alone;
at that time, all the people remained or moved about according to their pleasure.
There were vehicles for one desiring to travel and drinks for one who was thirsty.
O bull of the Bharatas, men there brought delicious foods for the hungry, as well as garments and ornaments. O King, that path shone forth, bringing comfort to everyone.
At that time, O hero, for the men going there, it was like heaven itself—
constantly filled with joy, provided with delicious food, endowed with auspiciousness,
and crowded with hundreds of various people amidst markets, shops, and merchandise.
Abounding with various trees and creepers and adorned with diverse jewels,
the high-souled one, established in his vows,
bestowed wealth upon the holy pilgrimage sites, O King.
The renowned hero of the Yadus, the wielder of the plow, gave sacrificial fees to the twice-born,
as well as thousands of cows that yield milk.
He gave to the twice-born horses born in various lands, well-garbed and with horns bound in gold,
as well as vehicles and female slaves.
Jewels, pearls, gems, and coral;
horn-silver, gold, and bright silver; and vessels made of iron and copper.
Rāma gave thus abundant wealth to the most excellent among the twice-born at the best of tirthas on the Sarasvatī; so did that great-souled one bestow his riches.
He of incomparable power and noble conduct proceeded by stages from there to Kurukṣetra.
Janamejaya said:

O best of bipeds, tell me of the origin of the virtues of the sacred fords (tīrtha) of Sarasvatī, as well as their fruit and the accomplishment of ritual acts; O Blessed One, describe them in due order and succession.
"O Brahmin, best among the knowers of Brahman, my curiosity is indeed great.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, [I shall describe] the details of the sacred fords (tīrthas) and the origin of their virtues in their entirety."
"O Indra among kings, listen in its entirety to this meritorious account as it is being told by me,
O great king, O hero of the Yadus, concerning what occurred in the past together with the officiating priests, friends, and hosts of brahmins."
He arrived at the holy Prabhāsa, where the Moon,
the lord of the stars, while being afflicted by consumption,
was released from his curse and regained his splendor.
It illuminates the entire world, O lord of men;
because it thus shines upon this most excellent sacred site on earth,
it is therefore called Prabhāsa.
Janamejaya said:
For what reason was the blessed Soma seized by consumption,
and how did the Moon immerse himself in that most excellent of sacred fords?
"How did the moon, having plunged into it, become replenished once again?
Tell me all this in detail, O great sage.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O lord of the people, those daughters who were born of Dakṣa appeared; Dakṣa gave twenty-seven maidens to Soma,
O Bhārata, for the purpose of calculation and their association with the lunar mansions.
O Indra among kings, those wives of Soma were indeed endowed with auspicious marks;
they were all large-eyed and peerless in beauty upon the earth,
yet Rohiṇī excelled them all in the perfection of her form.
Then the Blessed One, the Maker of Night, took delight in her;
she became dear to his heart, and therefore he enjoyed her constantly.
For in former times, O Indra among kings, Soma dwelt with Rohiṇī for a long time.
Then the constellations became angry with that high-souled one.
Going to their father, Prajāpati, they spoke without hesitation:
"Soma does not dwell among us; he always favors Rohiṇī alone."
"O Lord of Creatures, we have all come together into your presence;
we have been humiliated. Be our refuge yourself, O Father!
We shall dwell here with restricted food, devoted to the practice of austerity."
Having heard their words, Dakṣa then spoke to Soma:
"Behave equally toward your wives, lest great unrighteousness touch you.
And Dakṣa said to them all: "Go into the presence of Soma."
"By my command, the Moon shall dwell equally among all of them. Released by him, they then departed for the abode of the cool-rayed one.
Nevertheless, O lord of the earth, the blessed Soma once again—
He dwells indeed with Rohiṇī, taking delight in her again and again. Then all those [Nakṣatras], united together, spoke once more to their father:
"We shall dwell in your hermitage, intent upon serving you."
"Soma does not dwell among us; he did not heed your words.
Having heard those words of theirs, Dakṣa then spoke to Soma:
"Behave equally toward your wives, O Virocana, lest I curse you."
But disregarding those words of Dakṣa, the blessed Moon continued to dwell with Rohiṇī; thereupon, they became angry once more,
and having gone to their father, they bowed their heads and spoke to him.
“Soma does not dwell among us; therefore, be our refuge.
O Blessed One, the Moon always dwells in Rohiṇī alone;
he does not heed your words, nor does he desire affection for us.”
"Therefore, protect us all so that Soma may indeed enter into us.
Having heard this, O lord of the earth, the Blessed One became enraged and, out of wrath, unleashed a wasting disease (*yakṣman*) upon Soma; and it entered the Lord of the Stars.
Overwhelmed by consumption, the Moon wasted away day after day;
yet, O King, he made every effort for the sake of being freed from that consumption,
performing various sacrifices, O Great King, as the maker of night.
He was not released from the curse, and he indeed went to his destruction.
As the Moon then waned, the medicinal herbs were no longer produced;
they all became tasteless, devoid of flavor, and entirely stripped of their potency.
When the destruction of plants occurred, there was also the destruction of living beings;
all creatures became emaciated as the moon waned.
Then, O lord of the earth, the gods assembled and spoke to Soma.
"Why does this form of yours not shine forth?
Tell us the entire cause by which this great fear has come upon you;
having heard your words, we shall then take the necessary action."
Thus addressed, the one marked with the hare (the Moon) replied to them all concerning the curse, its cause, and likewise his own consumption (yakṣman).
Having heard his words, the gods went to Dakṣa and spoke to him.
"Be gracious, O Blessed One; let this curse be withdrawn from Soma.
For that Moon has waned and only a small remnant is visible.
And because of his decline, O Lord of Gods, all creatures have likewise fallen into decay."
Climbing plants, medicinal herbs, and various seeds—when these perish, we also perish; and without us, what would the world be?
Therefore, O Teacher of the World, you ought to show us your favor.
Thus addressed, Prajāpati reflected and then spoke these words:
"It is not possible for my word to be turned back otherwise;
however, O highly fortunate ones, she shall desist because of some particular cause."

"May the moon always behave equally toward all his wives. By emerging from the excellent sacred ford of Sarasvatī, O gods, the one marked by the hare shall wax full again; that indeed is my true word."
Soma will always undergo waning for half a month and waxing for half a month; this word of mine is the truth. Having gone to the western ocean, the Sarasvatī meets with the sea.
"May he propitiate the Lord of Gods; through that, he shall obtain his beloved.
Then, by the command of the Ṛṣis, Soma went to Sarasvatī;
he indeed went to Prabhāsa, the supreme sacred ford of the Sarasvatī.
On the new moon day, that being of great splendor and immense radiance emerged there,
illuminating the worlds and attaining the state of the cool-rayed moon.
And all the gods, O king of kings, having reached Prabhāsa, attained abundant prosperity.
Having become united with Soma, they stood before Dakṣa.
Then Prajāpati dismissed all those deities;
and the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke these words once more to Soma:
"Do not despise women, my son, nor ever the Brahmins. Go forth with constant diligence and carry out my command. Having been thus dismissed, O great king, he then departed for his own abode.
And the subjects became joyful, and as before they partook of their food. All this has been related to you, how the maker of night was cursed,
and how Prabhāsa became the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O Great King, on the new moon day, the illustrious one marked with the hare always bathes at the supreme sacred ford of Prabhāsa and is thereby nourished;
for this reason, O protector of the earth, people know him as Prabhāsa.
Having emerged from that [lake], the moon attained supreme radiance;
it illuminated the worlds and likewise nourished its own form.
Having bathed there, Rāma, the wielder of the plow, being pleased, then gave sacrificial fees.
Then the powerful Acyuta went to Camasodbheda,
which people indeed call by that name;
there, the plow-wielder gave distinguished gifts.
Having stayed there for one night and bathed according to the prescribed rites,
the elder brother of Keśava then went to the well in haste;
having obtained there the great fruit of that primary rite for a safe journey, he proceeded.
"O Janamejaya, because of the moisture of the plants and the earth,
O Indra among kings, the Siddhas know the Sarasvatī even when she has disappeared.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Therefore, O great king, the plow-armed one [Balarāma] then went to the well situated in the river belonging to the illustrious Trita;
having given much wealth there and likewise honored the twice-born brahmins.
Having touched the water right there, the mace-armed one was filled with joy;
for it was there that the great ascetic Trita, devoted to dharma,
had lived, and while dwelling in that well, that high-souled one drank the Soma.
Having abandoned him there, the two brothers went home.
Then Trita, the best of Brahmins, cursed them both.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, how did that well come to be, and how did that great ascetic, the best of the twice-born, fall into it? Why was he abandoned by his two brothers,
and how did those two brothers leave him in the well and go home?"
"And how did he perform the sacrifice, and how indeed did he drink the Soma?
Tell me this, O Brahmin, if you consider it fit to be heard.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, in a former age there were three brothers who were sages:
Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, who resembled the suns.
They were all equal to Prajāpati and likewise possessed of progeny.

All were conquerors of the world of Brahmā through their asceticism and exponents of the Veda. Gautama, their father, who was always devoted to dharma, was constantly pleased with them by virtue of their austerity, self-restraint, and discipline.
Having gained their affection over a long period of time,
the Blessed One departed for a place that was as if suited to his own nature.
Those kings who had previously been the patrons (*yājya*) of that high-souled one [remained behind].
When he had ascended to heaven, they all honored his sons;
O King, by virtue of their deeds as well as their study,
Trita attained preeminence just as his father had.
All those highly fortunate sages, endowed with auspicious marks,
honored that illustrious man solely on account of his wisdom.
O King, it so happened at one time that the two brothers, Ekata and Dvita, [were there].

They set their minds upon performing sacrifices, and especially for the sake of wealth. O scorcher of foes, a thought arose in them: "Having taken Trita with us, and having gathered all those entitled to sacrifice, let us then receive the sacrificial animals."

"Having attained this sacrifice of great fruit, we shall drink Soma with joy," they said, O great king; and so the three brothers indeed made this agreement. Having thus established their pact, O monarch, they departed from their home.
Thus, having approached all those who were to be sacrificed for,
and having performed the sacrifices for them, they obtained from those sacrificers a great many animals;
and by means of that sacrificial rite, they accepted [the offerings] according to the prescribed rule.
Those high-souled great seers proceeded toward the eastern direction,
O Great King; Trita went at their head with joy,
while Ekata and Dvita followed behind, driving the cattle.
Seeing that great herd of cattle, a thought arose in both of them:
"How might these cows belong to us two, even without Trita? Then Ekata and Dvita spoke to one another.
O lord of men, learn what those two wicked ones said to one another:
"Trita is skilled in sacrifices; Trita is proficient in the Vedas;
Trita will obtain many other cows."
"Therefore, let us two go together, driving the cows before us;
as for Trita, let him go as he pleases, separated from us.
As they were traveling at night, a wolf appeared on the path.
Likewise, there was a great well not far away on the bank of the Sarasvatī.
Then Trita, seeing a wolf standing before him on the path,
fled out of fear of it and fell into that very well.
Then the highly fortunate Trita, that best of sages, staying within the well in that bottomless, most terrible place that struck fear into all beings,
let out a cry of distress; and those two sages heard it.
Knowing that he had fallen into the well, his two brothers, Ekata and Dvita,
abandoned him out of fear of the wolf and greed, and departed;
thus was that great ascetic forsaken by his two brothers who were greedy for the animal.
O Great King, at a waterless well covered with dust,
Trita perceived himself submerged in a pit overgrown with weeds and grass,
O best of the Bharatas, like a sinner fallen into hell.
For the wise one, fearing death and not yet having drunk the Soma, calculated with his intellect:
"How indeed might the Soma be drunk by me while remaining here?
Having reflected thus, that great ascetic [remained] at that well.
There, by chance, he saw a creeper hanging down. Then, having reflected upon water in that dust-filled well, the sage mentally prepared his sacrificial fires and offered himself as the priest.
Then, having conceived that creeper as Soma, the sage of great asceticism—
mentally contemplating the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman verses—
made pebbles into pressing-stones and performed the extraction, O King.

He made clarified butter and water the portions for the dwellers of heaven; having performed the pressing of Soma, he produced a tumultuous sound. And that sound of Trita, O King, which possessed the quality of Vedic phonetics (*śaikṣa*), indeed entered heaven.
And he completed that sacrifice exactly as prescribed by the exponents of the Veda.
While the sacrifice of the great-souled Trita was thus proceeding,
all of heaven became agitated, yet the cause was not understood.
Then Bṛhaspati heard a very tumultuous sound;
having heard it, the priest of the gods spoke to all the deities:
