"The sacrifice of Trita is proceeding; let us go there, O gods."
"For when enraged, that one of great ascetic power could create even other gods.
Having heard those words of his, all the deities together proceeded to the place where that sacrifice of Trita was being performed.
Having gone there to that well where Trita was, those gods beheld that high-souled one, consecrated for the sacrificial rites;
and having seen that high-souled one endowed with supreme splendor, they [approached him].
Then they said to the highly fortunate one, "We have arrived seeking our shares.
Thereupon the seer said to the gods, "O dwellers of heaven, behold me,
sunk in this terrifying well and deprived of my senses."

Then, O great king, Trita duly assigned their portions accompanied by sacred mantras, and they were then filled with joy. Thereupon, having received the portions obtained according to the prescribed rites, the denizens of heaven—
With joyful hearts, they granted him whatever boons he desired in his mind.
He, however, chose this boon from the gods: "May you rescue me from here;
and whoever shall touch the water in this well, let him obtain the state of one who has drunk the Soma."
Thereupon, O King, the wavy Sarasvatī rose up;
the delighted Sarasvatī quickly came to that well. Trita, lifted up by her, stood there worshipping the dwellers of heaven.
Having said, "So be it," O King, the gods departed as they had come;
Trita also, being pleased, then went to his own abode.
But he, having approached those two brothers who were the sages, was then filled with rage.
The one of great asceticism spoke harsh words and uttered a curse:
"Since you two, greedy for the sacrificial animal, have run away leaving me behind,
therefore you shall roam about in the form of those fanged creatures."
"By this sinful deed, you two shall be cursed by me;
your offspring shall indeed be golangulas, bears, and monkeys.
O lord of the people, as soon as he had spoken thus, in that very instant—
Thus did those two appear according to the word of the speaker of truth.
There too, the one of immeasurable prowess, Halāyudha, touched the water,
gave various gifts, and indeed honored the twice-born.
Having seen that well and praised it again and again,
the noble-minded one reached Vinaśana, situated on the river.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O King, the plow-wielder arrived at Vinaśana,
where the Sarasvatī disappeared out of hatred toward the Śūdras and Ābhīras; for it was there,
O best of the Bharatas, that the Sarasvatī vanished due to that animosity.
Therefore, the seers have always called that place Vinaśana. Having touched the waters there at the Sarasvatī, the mighty Bala then proceeded to Subhūmika on the excellent bank of the Sarasvatī.
And there, radiant Apsarases with stainless faces, ever untiring, sport with pure diversions; and there,
O lord of men, the gods together with the Gandharvas [assemble] month after month.
They approached that sacred ford, frequented by Brahmins;
there, O King, Gandharvas and hosts of Apsarases were seen gathered together, meeting as they pleased and according to their comfort.
There the gods, the ancestors, and all the plants rejoice,
being repeatedly strewn with divine, merit-bestowing flowers. O King, that auspicious place is the pleasure ground of those apsarases.

It is renowned as Subhūmikā, situated on the excellent bank of the Sarasvatī. Having bathed there and given wealth to the Brahmins, Mādhava heard that divine song and the sound of musical instruments.
Having seen the vast shadows of the gods, Gandharvas, and Rakshasas,
the son of Rohini then proceeded to the sacred ford of the Gandharvas;
there the Gandharvas, headed by Vishvavasu, were endowed with the power of asceticism.
They performed most delightful dances, instrumental music, and songs.
There, Haladhara gave various kinds of wealth to the Brahmins,
as well as goats, sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, gold, and silver.
Having fed the twice-born and gratified them with all their desires and great wealth,
Mādhava departed together with the brahmins while being praised by them. From that Gandharva-tīrtha, the mighty-armed subduer of enemies went forth.
Wearing a single earring, he came to the great sacred ford of Garga’s Stream,
where the aged Garga, whose soul was purified by asceticism,
had attained knowledge of the course of time and the movements of the celestial luminaries.
O Janamejaya, both terrible portents and auspicious signs were manifested at that auspicious ford of the Sarasvatī by the high-souled one;
and because of his name, that ford is known as Gargasrota.
There, O King, the sages of firm vows constantly waited upon the highly fortunate Garga for the sake of knowledge regarding time, O Lord.
Having gone there, O great king, Bala, anointed with white unguents, [approached him].
Having duly given wealth to the sages of purified souls,
and having likewise bestowed various kinds of foods upon the twice-born,
he, clothed in blue garments, then proceeded to Śaṅkhatīrtha, O one of great fame.
There, the powerful one whose banner is the palm tree beheld the great Śaṅkha mountain, towering like Mount Meru,
resembling a white peak, frequented by throngs of sages,
and situated on the bank of the Sarasvatī.
Yakṣas, vidyādharas, and rākṣasas of immeasurable splendor, as well as piśācas of boundless strength and siddhas by the thousands—
all of them, having abandoned all other food, [subsist] on the fruit of that lord of the forest.
By means of vows and observances, they ate only at specific times; and having undertaken various such rules,
O bull among men, they wandered about separately, remaining invisible to human beings.
Thus, O lord of men, is that lord of the forest renowned in this world;
there lies the purifying *tīrtha* of the Sarasvatī, famous throughout the world.
And in that *tīrtha*, the tiger among the Yadus gave [offerings] to those of illustrious fame.
Having honored the twice-born with vessels of copper and iron as well as various kinds of garments, and having himself been honored by those whose wealth is asceticism,
O King, Halāyudha returned to the holy Dvaitavana forest.
Having gone there and seen the sages wearing various garbs, Bala bathed in the water and indeed paid homage to the twice-born. Likewise, he gave the brahmins abundant articles of enjoyment.
Then, O King, Bala set out along the southern bank of the Sarasvatī;
having traveled not very far, the mighty-armed and highly illustrious Acyuta, whose nature is dharma, arrived at the sacred ford known as Nāgadhanvana.
O great king, there is the abode of Vāsuki,
the king of serpents, who possesses great luster and is surrounded by many snakes; there,
fourteen thousand *ṛṣis* and *siddhas* reside.
O Kaurava, in that place where the gods, having assembled, duly consecrated Vāsuki— the best of serpents and king of all snakes—
there exists no fear from serpents.
There too, having duly bestowed heaps of jewels upon the brahmins,
O King, he set out toward the eastern direction, blazing with his own splendor.
In that direction were various sacred fords and supreme holy sites.
Having bathed repeatedly in those sacred fords with joy, the wielder of the plow (Lāṅgalin) gave wealth to the twice-born and departed toward the great ascetics.
Having saluted those hosts of sages dwelling there, the one whose weapon is the plow (Halāyudha) proceeded on his way.
Then Rāma went to a great sacred ford frequented by sages,
where the Sarasvatī turns back again toward the east; likewise, he visited many other such holy sites.
Numbering in the hundreds and thousands, they are renowned at every step;
having bathed in those sacred fords (*tīrtha*) as prescribed there by the seers (*ṛṣi*),
and having observed the discipline of fasting and given abundant gifts, [he proceeded].
Having paid homage to those sages dwelling at that sacred ford,
he set out along the indicated path toward where the Sarasvatī flows again; however,
he turned back toward the east, like rain driven by the wind.

O King, seeing that best of rivers turned back there for the sake of visiting the high-souled sages of Naimiṣa, Bala, the wielder of the plow who was anointed with white unguents, was filled with wonder.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, O best of Adhvaryu priests, why did the Sarasvatī turn back from there to flow eastward? I wish for all of this to be explained."
"And for what reason was the joy of the Yadus astonished there?
O best of the twice-born, how is it that this most excellent of rivers has turned back?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O King, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, the ascetics of Naimiṣa,
firm in their vows, undertook a twelve-year sacrificial session (*sattra*).
Devoted to their observances, they were intent on their vows morning and evening, while others subsisted on food taken only at night.
In the summer, they practiced the penance of the five fires; in the rainy season, they slept under the open sky;
others likewise subsisted on grass and slept upon the path; and some lay upon the ground amidst fierce, thorny brambles.
While that very extensive twelve-year sacrificial session was underway,
O King, many ṛṣis gathered there;
and those highly blessed ones dwelt at that sacrifice according to the prescribed rites.
When the twelve-year sacrificial session at Naimiṣa had concluded, O lord of the people,
many sages arrived there for the sake of visiting sacred fords;
indeed, due to the great number of sages, [the banks of] the Sarasvatī were crowded, O lord of the people.
At that time,

O tiger among men, those best of the twice-born, out of a longing for sacred fords, took up residence along the bank of the river as far as Samantapañcaka on the southern shore, where the fords appeared like cities.
As those sages of purified souls were offering oblations there,
the quarters of the sky became filled with their great recitation of the Vedas; likewise,
they were filled by the *agnihotra* sacrifices being offered by those high-souled ones.
That best of rivers shone brilliantly on all sides with the Vālakhilyas,
O great king, and with ascetics who grind their food with stones,
others who use their teeth as a mortar, and still others who subsist by washing away food with water.
There were ascetics who subsisted on air, those who lived on water, and those who fed on leaves; others ate grain and smoke, while some fasted for a month,
and thousands of others likewise observed fasts on every lunar day.
Others were eaters from earthen vessels, and likewise some were eaters from the ground;

some were devoted to the domestic fire, and others were devoted to the three sacred fires. Some were intense practitioners who ate only the remains of offerings, while others were those who restricted their food intake.
Engaged in various disciplines and likewise sleeping on the bare ground,
there were indeed sages there near the Sarasvatī,
beautifying that best of rivers just as the gods beautify the Gaṅgā.
Thereafter, the sages who perform long sacrificial sessions arrived;
those observers of great vows found no space in Kurukṣetra.
Then, with their sacred threads, they indeed constructed that holy ford (tīrtha).

They offered the agnihotra oblations and performed various religious rites. Then, O king of kings, Sarasvatī appeared for their sake before that assembly of sages who were filled with anxiety and despair.
Then, O Janamejaya, having created many bower-groves out of compassion for the sages of holy asceticism, that best of rivers turned back;
thus, O king of kings, the Sarasvatī returned for their sake.
O King, that best of rivers then performed a great miracle: she flowed once more toward the west, saying, "Having made their journey not in vain, I shall now proceed further."
Right there in the middle of that bower, Sarasvatī, whose waters are meritorious, entered Kurukṣetra and departed just as she had come. O king of kings, thus that bower is remembered as Naimiṣeya.
"O best of the Kurus, perform great deeds at Kurukṣetra.
Having seen many groves there and that river having turned back,
the high-souled Rāma was then filled with wonder.
Having performed his ablutions there according to the prescribed rites, the joy of the Yadus gave gifts to the twice-born,
including various vessels and diverse kinds of food and drink, which he presented to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, O King, Bala set forth, being honored by the twice-born,
toward that excellent tirtha on the Sarasvatī,
which was filled with various flocks of birds and graced by swans, kāraṇḍavas, and cakravākas.
With *badara*, *iṅguda*, *kāśmarya*, *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, and *vibhītaka*;
with *panasa*, *palāśa*, *karīra*, and likewise *pīlu*;
and with *sāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, *kakubha*, and *ketaka*.
It was adorned with trees growing on the banks of the Sarasvatī, with *bandhana* and *syandana* trees,
as well as groves of *parūṣaka*, *bilva*, and *āmrātaka* trees,
and clusters of *atimuktaka* and *pārijāta* trees.

Abounding with groves of plantain trees, it was desirable, lovely, and enchanting; it was filled with many forest-dwelling sages who subsisted on air, water, fruits, and leaves, or who used their teeth as mortars, or who ground their food with stones.
Resounding with the sound of Vedic recitation, crowded with hundreds of herds of deer,
and frequented by men who were non-violent and devoted to dharma,
Halāyudha arrived at the sacred ford known as Saptasārasvata.
09,036.063c Where the great sage Maṅkaṇaka, having attained perfection, performed his austerities.
09,037.001 Janamejaya said:
09,037.001a Why is it called Saptasārasvata, and who was the sage Maṅkaṇaka?
"How did the Blessed One attain perfection, and what was his rule? In whose lineage was he born, and what did he study, O best of the twice-born?
I wish to hear this according to the rules, O most excellent of the twice-born."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, there are seven Sarasvatīs by which this world is pervaded;
for wherever they are summoned by the powerful, there the Sarasvatī appears."
Suprabhā, Kāñcanākṣī, Viśālā, Mānasa-hradā,
Sarasvatī, Oghavatī, Suveṇu, and Vimalodakā—
these rivers exist upon the great earth while the Grandfather [Brahmā] remains present.
In that sacrificial arena, which had been laid out and where the twice-born had assembled,
amidst the pure sounds of the proclamation of an auspicious day and the resonances of the Vedas,
the gods themselves were then busily engaged in that sacrificial rite.

And there, O great king, while his great-grandfather was consecrated and performing that sacrificial session (*sattra*) which fulfills all desires, whatever objects were conceived by the mind were then [attained] by those skilled in dharma and worldly prosperity.
O Indra among kings, they indeed waited upon the twice-born there at every turn; the Gandharvas sang there and the hosts of Apsarases danced,
while celestial musical instruments were played forth with ease.
The deities themselves were gratified by the perfection of that sacrifice;
they attained the utmost amazement—how much more so those of human origin?
While the Grandfather was thus seated upon a lotus during the performance of the sacrifice, [the gods were filled with wonder].
"O King," the ṛṣis said, "this sacrifice will not yield great fruit,
because the Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, is not seen here.
Hearing that, the Blessed One was pleased and then called the Sarasvatī to mind.
O king of kings, while the Grandfather was performing a sacrifice at Puṣkara, Sarasvatī appeared there by the name Suprabhā. Seeing that swift-flowing Sarasvatī, the sages were filled with joy.
Honoring the Grandfather (Pitāmaha), they held his sacrifice in high esteem.
Thus, this Sarasvatī, the best of rivers,
manifested at Puṣkara for the sake of the Grandfather and for the satisfaction of the wise.
O King, the sages gathered and sat together in Naimiṣa; there, O lord of men, were various discourses concerning the Veda. Those sages present there were masters of various branches of sacred study.
Having assembled, those sages called to mind Sarasvatī.
O great king, she, being meditated upon by the ṛṣis performing the sacrificial session,
appeared for the sake of assisting those high-souled ones who had gathered together, O Indra among kings.
The highly fortunate and holy Sarasvatī arrived there; O Bhārata, that best of rivers, Kāñcanākṣī, having been honored, came to Naimiṣa to the sages performing the sacrificial session.
When Gaya was performing a great sacrifice among the Gayas,
Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, was summoned to Gaya’s sacrifice.
Regarding the Gayas, sages of rigid vows say that she became the Viśālā.
That river, flowing swiftly, issued forth from the side of the Himavat;
and so it was, O Bhārata, at that sacrifice of Auddālaki,
when a vast assembly of sages had gathered there from all directions.
O King, in the northern region of Kosala, in that holy place,
the Sarasvatī was formerly meditated upon by the high-souled Auddālaka while he was performing a sacrifice;
then that best of rivers came to that region for the sake of the ṛṣi.

Honored by hosts of sages clad in bark and deerskins, she was indeed carried away by their minds; thus she became renowned as Manohradā. She dwelt on the auspicious Ṛṣabhadvīpa, frequented by royal seers, where the bamboos grow beautifully.
And while the high-souled Kuru was performing a sacrifice at Kurukṣetra,
O king of kings, the highly blessed Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, arrived there; so too did the Oghavatī, by the power of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Summoned to Kurukṣetra by Dakṣa while he was performing a sacrifice, the Sarasvatī of divine waters—
renowned as Suveṇu— flowed forth from Gaṅgādvāra as a swift-moving stream.
The divine Vimalodā, having been summoned again by Brahmā while he was performing a sacrifice,
went there to that holy mountain in the Himalayas.
Then, having gathered together, they all came to that sacred bathing place.
"Because of that, the sacred ford became renowned on earth as Saptasārasvata.
Thus, the seven Sarasvatīs have been proclaimed by name;
likewise, the sacred ford is remembered as Saptasārasvata."
O King, listen also to the great sport of Maṅkaṇaka, who had been a celibate student since his youth; O Bhārata, he saw a woman by chance there as he was immersed in the river.
O great king, as that faultless woman of beautiful eyes was bathing naked in the waters of the Sarasvatī, his seed fell into the water. That man of great asceticism then took up that semen in a jar.
Then that seer, whose soul was supremely righteous and who was the best among men,
underwent a sevenfold division while remaining within the jar. From that,
the seven seers were born, and from them the hosts of Maruts were produced.
Vāyuvega, Vāyubala, Vāyuhā, Vāyumaṇḍala,
Vāyujvāla, Vāyuretā, and the powerful Vāyucakra—
thus were these born as the progenitors of the Maruts.
O Indra among kings, hear this other even more wonderful account on earth—
the life of a great seer as it is renowned throughout the three worlds.
We have heard that in ancient times, the perfected sage Maṅkaṇaka was [pierced] by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
O King, when he was wounded in the hand, vegetable juice flowed from it;
seeing that vegetable juice, he was overcome with joy and began to dance.
Then, as he danced, everything both stationary and moving likewise began to dance.
O hero, O lord of men, both [the gods and the asuras] were dancing, utterly bewildered by his splendor;
then, O King, Mahādeva was entreated by the gods headed by Brahmā and by the sages whose wealth is asceticism for the sake of the ṛṣi.
"O God, you ought to act in such a way that he does not dance.
Then, seeing the sage who was exceedingly overcome with joy,
Mahādeva spoke for the sake of the welfare of the gods.
"O Brahmin, knower of dharma, for what reason do you indeed dance? O best of sages, for what reason is this cause for joy yours,
you who are an ascetic established on the path of dharma, O best of the twice-born?"
The sage said:
"O Brahmin, do you not see the vegetable juice flowing from my hand?
Seeing it, O Lord, I have indeed begun to dance with great joy."
Laughing, the God spoke to that sage who was deluded by passion:
"O Brahmin, I feel no astonishment; behold me!
Having spoken thus to the best of sages, the wise Mahādeva—
O Indra among kings, his own thumb was struck by the tip of his finger;
thereupon, O King, ashes as white as snow issued from the wound. Seeing that, O King, the sage was ashamed and fell at [the king's] feet.
He regarded him as the god Mahādeva and, filled with wonder, spoke these words;
he addressed the Lord of Pārvatī, who is adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
The sage said:
"I consider no other being to be greater than the god Rudra; O wielder of the trident, you are the refuge of the world of gods and asuras.
The wise here declare that this entire universe was created by you."
At the end of the eon, everything enters back into you alone;
even by the gods you cannot be fully known, so how could I? O sinless one, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are seen within you.
Whatever beings exist in the world worship you, the giver of boons;
you are indeed everything among the gods, both the creator and the one who causes all to act.
Through your grace, all the gods rejoice here, free from fear from any quarter.
O Śaṅkara, you are the Lord; by virtue of your supreme sovereignty, you shine forth most brilliantly.
Both Brahmā and Viṣṇu remain supporting the worlds while abiding in you.
O Maheśvara, the entire world has you as its root and ends with you;
for by you, O source of all, these seven worlds have been spread out.
In every way, O Lord of all beings, they worship you alone as the deity.
For this entire world, including all beings, both moving and stationary, is composed of you;
and you, O Supreme Lord, being well-pleased, bestow heaven— the highest station— upon those men who seek prosperity and are devoted to you.

O Great God, O Maheśvara, you grant the state of non-return to men who eternally seek the supreme good; by cultivating the karma of practitioners through the yoga of meditation, your grace, O Mahādeva, is never in vain.
"O lotus-eyed one, because I perform [this] with your assistance,
I take refuge in Śambhu, who is ever-present everywhere; indeed,
through action, mind, and speech, I have gone unto him alone."
Having thus praised Mahādeva, that ṛṣi bowed down and said:
"O Lord, whatever rashness has been committed here, such as this act of derision and the like—
by your grace, O Blessed One, may my ascetic merit not diminish."
Then the God, with a pleased mind, spoke again to that seer:
"O Brahmin, may your ascetic power increase a thousandfold through my grace;
and I shall always dwell here in this hermitage together with you."
And whatever man shall worship me here at this Saptasarasvata,
nothing whatsoever will be difficult for him to attain, both in this world and in the next;
they shall go to the world of Sarasvatī, of this there is no doubt.
O best of kings, this life-story of Maṅkaṇaka, who possessed great splendor, has been told to you; what more shall I relate to you? Furthermore, I have described how Saptasārasvata was born.
For he was born as a son to Sajanyā by Mātariśvan.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having stayed there and honored those dwelling in the hermitage, Rāma—
In that manner, Halāyudha felt auspicious joy toward Maṅkaṇaka;
having given gifts to the twice-born and fasted through that night,
the wielder of the plow rose in the morning, honored by the hosts of sages.
Having taken leave of all the sages and touched the water, O Bhārata,
the mighty Rāma proceeded swiftly for the sake of visiting sacred fords.
Then Halāyudha arrived at the Auśanasa Tīrtha.

O King, there is the place named Kapālamocana, where the great sage Mahodara was formerly liberated from the massive head of a Rākṣasa that had seized his shanks, after he had been hurled by Rāma. O Great King, [he was freed] there indeed.
There, in that place where all the wisdom of that great-souled one had manifested, the high-minded Kāvya had previously performed intense austerities;
staying there, he reflected upon the conflict between the Daityas and the Dānavas.
Having reached that most excellent and supreme sacred ford, O King,
Bala duly bestowed wealth upon the high-souled Brahmins.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, how did the great sage become liberated at Kapālamocana? How and for what reason did his head become attached [to him]?
Vaiśampāyana said:
O tiger among kings, in former times, while the high-souled Rāghava was dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, the rākṣasas there were indeed slain;
in Janasthāna, the head of an evil-minded rākṣasa was severed.
With its sharp edge, that [arrow] fell in the great forest;
by chance, O King, it struck Mahodara’s shank as he was wandering in the woods, and having pierced the bone, it quivered there.
At that time, because of that wound, the highly wise twice-born man was unable to visit sacred fords and shrines;
afflicted by pain from the festering discharge, the great sage [remained there].
"We have heard that he went to all the sacred fords on earth. Having traveled to all the rivers and oceans,
that man of great asceticism recounted everything to the sages of purified souls."
Although he had bathed in all the sacred fords, he did not attain liberation; however,
that lord of brahmins then heard the great words of the sages concerning the preeminent ford of the Sarasvatī known as Auśanasa.
It is the supreme field of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*) that pacifies all sins. Having gone there to that sacred ford (*tīrtha*) of Uśanas, O twice-born one,
as he was then performing ablutions at that ford of Uśanas, [the following occurred].
Then, leaving that head, it fell into the water;
freed from that head, he indeed attained supreme happiness.
And that head, O Lord, vanished within the water.
Then, O King, freed from disease, purified in soul, and cleansed of all taint,
Mahodara returned to his hermitage joyful, having accomplished his purpose.
Having reached that holy hermitage, the great ascetic was liberated.
He related all of that to the sages of purified souls. Having heard his words, O giver of honor,
they gathered together and gave that sacred ford the name Kapālamocana.
And that great sage, having gone once more to that preeminent sacred ford (tīrtha) and drunk the abundant water, then attained perfection as a muni. There,
Mādhava gave many gifts and honored the brahmins.
Then the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis went to the hermitage of Ruṣaṅgu,
O Bhārata, where the great sage Viśvāmitra had performed severe austerities and attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
And that great hermitage was fully endowed with all desired objects,
O Lord, and was always frequented by sages and brahmins.
Then the illustrious wielder of the plow (Balarāma), surrounded by brahmins, [proceeded].
O king of kings, he went to the place where Ruṣaṅgu had cast off his body.
O Bhārata, the aged Brahmin Ruṣaṅgu, who was constantly devoted to asceticism,
having reflected in many ways and at great length, had set his mind upon abandoning the body.
Then, taking all his sons with him, the great ascetic Ruṣaṅgu said there,
"Take me to Pṛthūdaka.
Recognizing that Ruṣaṅgu had reached an advanced age, those whose wealth was their asceticism [prepared to depart].
They led that man whose wealth was asceticism to a sacred ford on the Sarasvatī;
then that wise one was conducted by his sons to the holy Sarasvatī,
which is endowed with hundreds of fords and frequented by throngs of brahmins.
O King, having bathed there according to the prescribed rites, that best of sages, a man of great asceticism, recognized the virtues of the sacred ford and,
being well-pleased, spoke thus to all his sons who were attending upon him, O tiger among men.
The knower of the truth of action, delighted by the sight of that sacred ford, spoke:
"He who would cast off his body on the northern bank of the Sarasvatī at Pṛthūdaka, intent on silent recitation (*japa*), shall not be tormented by the thought of death tomorrow."
Having bathed there and sipped water, that righteous-souled Halāyudha,
who is devoted to brahmins, gave many gifts to the brahmins;
it was there that the Blessed One, the Grandfather of the worlds, created the worlds.
O King, it was there that Arṣṭiṣeṇa of the Kuru lineage— that best of sages, firm in his vows— attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa through great asceticism;
as did the royal sage Sindhudvīpa and Devāpi of great austerity.
Where the great sage Viśvāmitra, the venerable one of fierce splendor and great asceticism, attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa,
there the powerful and majestic Balabhadra arrived.
Janamejaya said:
"How did the venerable Ārṣṭiṣeṇa perform such intense austerity,
and how did Sindhudvīpa likewise attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa at that time?"
"O Brahmin, how did Devāpi and Viśvāmitra, O best of beings, [attain their states]?
Tell me that, O Blessed One, for my curiosity is great.
Vaiśampāyana said:

O King, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was an excellent brahmin named Ārṣṭiṣeṇa who lived constantly in his teacher’s household and was ever devoted to his studies. O King, while he was thus dwelling perpetually in the teacher’s household—
O lord of the people, his knowledge did not reach completion, nor did the Vedas;
thereupon, O King, that great ascetic became despondent and performed intense penance.
Then, indeed, by means of that austerity, he attained the unsurpassed Vedas.

O King, that best of sages, learned, endowed with Vedic knowledge, perfected, and possessed of great ascetic power, reached that sacred ford and performed intense penance. At that sacred ford, he granted three boons.
From this day forward, any person who bathes at this ford of the great river shall obtain the full fruit of a horse sacrifice.
From this day forward, there shall be no fear here from predatory beasts.
"Moreover, with but little effort, he shall obtain abundant fruit.
Having spoken thus, the sage of great splendor departed for the third heaven.
Thus was that blessed and powerful Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa perfected.

At that very sacred ford, O great king, the powerful Sindhudvīpa and Devāpi both attained the great status of Brahmins. Likewise, dear one, Kauśika, who was constant in austerity and had conquered his senses, [attained it there].
Through well-performed asceticism, he indeed attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
There was a great Kṣatriya named Gādhi, renowned on earth;
his son, O King, was the powerful Viśvāmitra.
O dear one, it is said that King Kauśika became a great yogin;
having then consecrated his son Viśvāmitra,
that man of great asceticism set his mind upon casting off his body, whereupon the subjects bowed down and spoke to him.
"O one of great wisdom, you must not go; save us from this great fear!
Thus addressed, Gādhi then replied to his subjects:
"My son shall become the protector of the entire world."
Having spoken thus, O King, Gādhi then settled Viśvāmitra and departed for the third heaven; Viśvāmitra became the king by the path of those who perform meritorious deeds.
Likewise, King Gādhi’s son was unable to protect the earth, despite his efforts;
then that king heard of a great danger from the *rākṣasas*.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, he departed from the city.
Having traveled a long distance, he arrived at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha. O King, there those soldiers of his committed many excesses.
Then the venerable brahmin Vasiṣṭha returned to his hermitage;
there he beheld the entire great forest being destroyed.
O great king, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was filled with rage.
"Create terrible Śabaras," he said to his own cow. Thus addressed, that milch-cow created men of fearsome appearance;
and they, having reached that army, shattered it in every direction.
Seeing that army in flight, Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi,
considering asceticism to be supreme, fixed his mind solely upon penance. O King, he remained concentrated at this excellent tīrtha of the Sarasvatī.
Emaciating his own body through restrictive observances and fasts,
he subsisted on water, fed on air, and lived on leaves; likewise, he slept upon the bare ground and observed various other distinct disciplines.
The gods repeatedly created obstacles to his vow,
yet the mind of that great-souled one did not waver from his discipline.
Then, having performed various kinds of austerities with supreme effort, he [proceeded].
By his splendor, the son of Gādhi became like the sun;
and seeing Viśvāmitra thus endowed with ascetic power, the Grandfather,
the giver of boons, of great majesty, considered that he had already granted him the boon.
"O King, he chose as his boon: 'May I become a Brāhmaṇa.
Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, replied, 'So be it.
Having attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa through his fierce asceticism, that highly illustrious one—"
Having accomplished his desires, he, like a god, wandered over the entire earth. At that excellent sacred ford (tīrtha), Rāma bestowed various kinds of wealth,
as well as milch cows, vehicles, and beds.
O King, having joyfully honored the best of the twice-born, he gave them garments, ornaments, and excellent food and drink; then,
O King, Rāma proceeded from there to the vicinity of Baka’s hermitage.
"Where, as tradition reports, Dālbhya Baka performed intense austerities.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"The joy of the Yadus went to that place which was crowded with those born from the womb of Brahmā."
O King, it was there that Baka Dālbhya, a man of great asceticism,
was honored by Dhṛtarāṣṭra while seeking cattle; he stayed for some time at a small water-shed on the path.
09.040.001e He offered up the kingdom of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Vicitravīrya;
09.040.002a emaciating his own body through asceticism of a terrible form,
that righteous and powerful soul was indeed possessed by great wrath.
Long ago, when the twelve-year sacrificial session of the Naimiṣeya sages had concluded with the Viśvajit rite, those wise seers went to the Pañcālas and begged the lord for sacrificial fees.
There, O King, those great seers received from the Pañcālas twenty-one healthy and vigorous young bulls. Then the king bestowed those bulls upon those brahmins.
The aged Baka said to them, "Divide these animals among yourselves.
"Having abandoned these animals, I shall beg from the best of kings.
Having spoken thus to all the seers, O King, the powerful one—
That best of Brahmins went to the palace of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Having approached King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men, Dālbhya requested cattle; however, he spoke to him in anger.
"O best of kings, having seen that those cows had died by chance, [the king said:
'O wretched Brahmin, take these animals away quickly if you so desire.
But then the rishi, who knew the dharma, having heard these words, began to reflect."
"Alas! Indeed, I have been addressed with cruel words in the assembly.
Having reflected for a moment, that best of the twice-born, overcome with rage, set his mind upon the destruction of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

Having cut out the flesh from the corpses, that best of the twice-born formerly offered it as an oblation into the kindled fire at the sacred ford of the Sarasvatī, within the kingdom of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O great king, Baka Dālbhya, having undertaken the supreme vow,
that man of great asceticism offered his kingdom as oblations with those very meats.
While that most dreadful sacrificial session was being duly performed, he remained steadfast.
O King, the kingdom of Dhṛtarāṣṭra then began to waste away. O Lord,
as that kingdom of the monarch was wasting away,
it was like an endless forest being cut down by an axe.
That [kingdom] became struck down, scattered, and senseless;
and seeing the kingdom thus scattered, O King, that lord of men,
the sovereign, became dejected and began to reflect.
In former times, he made an effort for the sake of liberation together with the Brahmins;
yet he did not attain any higher good, and the kingdom itself only wasted away.
Then, O King, that monarch and those Brahmins became despondent.
And when the king was unable to liberate the kingdom, O Janamejaya, he then questioned the diviners there. Thereupon the diviners said: "A sacrificial animal has been mistreated by you."

"Because you offer oblations with flesh, the sage Baka has taken your kingdom; by that act of yours, as your kingdom is thus being sacrificed, there is great destruction. This is the effect of his ascetic power, by which this great misfortune has come upon you."
"O mighty-armed lord of the earth, if you desire peace for the kingdom,
O King, propitiate him at the bower of waters by the Sarasvatī.
Then, having gone to the Sarasvatī, that king spoke to Baka.
Prostrating with his head upon the ground and joining his palms in reverence, O bull of the Bharatas, he said:
"I seek to propitiate you, O Blessed One; forgive my transgression. Forgive me, who am wretched, greedy, and whose mind has been destroyed by folly."
"You are my refuge and you are my protector; you ought to show me favor. Seeing him thus lamenting, his mind overwhelmed by grief, compassion arose within him, and he released that kingdom.
The seer became pacified and, abandoning his agitation,
offered another oblation for the sake of liberating that kingdom.
Having then liberated the kingdom and accepted many cattle, he departed.

With a joyful soul, he indeed returned once more to the Naimiṣa forest. Dhṛtarāṣṭra, too— the righteous-souled, high-minded king— having regained his composure, entered his own highly prosperous city.

At that sacred ford, O great king, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati performed a sacrifice with pieces of flesh for the destruction of the Asuras and the prosperity of the gods; thereupon, the Asuras began to perish.
Even by the gods, who appeared victorious in battle, he was shattered;
yet there too, the highly illustrious one, having bestowed horses, elephants, and chariots yoked with mules upon the Brahmins according to the prescribed rites, [departed].
O lord of the earth, taking highly precious jewels, abundant wealth, and plenty of grain,
the mighty-armed one went to the sacred ford of Yayāti,
where, O great king, the Sarasvatī [flowed] during the sacrifice of Yayāti.
Clarified butter and milk flowed forth for the high-souled son of Nahuṣa.
Having performed sacrifices there, Yayāti, that tiger among men and lord of the earth,
ascended joyfully and attained abundant worlds.
Furthermore, there, while the lord King Yayāti was performing sacrifice,
having displayed supreme magnanimity and eternal devotion toward him,
he granted to the Brahmins whatever desires each one wished for in his mind.
Whoever is present here at the sacrificial assembly when summoned,
for each of them that best of rivers provides houses, beds, and the like,
as well as communal meals and many kinds of abundant gifts.
Considering that to be the unsurpassed gift from the king, they,
being delighted, praised the monarch and bestowed auspicious blessings upon him. O King, this occurred at the sacrifice of Yayāti where the Sarasvatī was present.
Flowing forth, she bestowed the objects of desire upon the high-souled Brahmins; wherever any learned brahmin desired whatever objects he wished for,
there that best of rivers produced abundant essences.
There, the gods along with the gandharvas were delighted by the perfection of the sacrifice,
and human beings were filled with wonder upon seeing that excellence of the sacrificial rite.
Then there was Tālakeśu, a great bridge of dharma;
The high-souled one, perfected in self, constant in great giving,
firm in soul and self-controlled, approached the Vasiṣṭhāpavāha river of most terrible current.
Janamejaya said:
"How indeed did that Vasiṣṭha come to have the 'Apavāha' (the carrying-away) of such terrible velocity? And for what reason did that best of rivers carry the ṛṣi away?"
"O Lord, with whom did he have enmity, and what was the cause of it?
Tell me, O one of great wisdom, for I am not satiated by what is being told.
Vaiśampāyana said:

O descendant of Bharata, O King, a great and intense enmity arose between the young Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha, born of their rivalry in ascetic power. The great hermitage of Vasiṣṭha was located at Sthāṇutīrtha.
To the east and to the west was the domain of the wise Viśvāmitra,
O great king, where Sthāṇu performed most intense ascetic penance;
there, the wise proclaim that his formidable deed took place.
O Lord, having performed a sacrifice there and having worshipped Sarasvatī, the Blessed One Sthāṇu established that sacred ford as Sthāṇutīrtha. There,
O ruler of men, all the gods consecrated Skanda.

At that sacred ford on the Sarasvatī, where the great destruction of the enemies of the gods was achieved by means of a vast army, the great sage Viśvāmitra caused Vasiṣṭha to be moved by his fierce ascetic power; hear that now.
O Bhārata, day after day, those two great sages Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha,
whose wealth was their asceticism, engaged in a fierce rivalry regarding their penance. Among them, the great sage Viśvāmitra felt even greater distress.
Beholding the splendor of Vasiṣṭha, he fell into deep reflection;
for this thought arose in him, O Bhārata, who was ever devoted to righteousness:
"May this Sarasvatī quickly come to me, whose wealth is asceticism."
"He will bring Vasiṣṭha, the best of those who recite prayers, here with speed;
once that foremost of the twice-born has arrived here, I shall kill him, there is no doubt.
Having thus resolved, the venerable and great sage Viśvāmitra—

With eyes bloodshot with rage, he called to mind the best of rivers. When she was meditated upon by that sage, she became agitated; and that beautiful woman perceived him to be possessed of great heroism and intense wrath.
Then Sarasvatī, trembling and pale, approached the best of sages, Viśvāmitra, with her palms joined in reverence;
she was as deeply distressed as a woman whose husband has been slain.
"Tell me, what shall I do? she said to the best of sages.
Enraged, the sage said to her, "Bring Vasiṣṭha here quickly so that I may slay him this very day. Upon hearing this, the river was deeply distressed.

Then, with her hands joined in reverence, the lotus-eyed woman trembled like a well-rooted creeper shaken by the wind; and seeing her thus trembling with her palms pressed together, [the Blessed One spoke].
The enraged Viśvāmitra said, "Bring Vasiṣṭha here quickly! Then, O Bhārata, that best of rivers, being terrified and fearing the curses of both, reflected: "How shall this come to pass?"
She trembled violently, terrified like a creeper struck by the wind.
Seeing her in such a state, the sage spoke to the great river:
"Bring Vasiṣṭha to my presence without hesitation."
Having heard his words and knowing the evil he intended to do, she—
being aware of Vasiṣṭha’s incomparable power on earth—
approached Vasiṣṭha and urged him regarding this matter.
When she was addressed by the wise Viśvāmitra, that best of rivers,
trembling again and again out of fear of both curses,
reflected upon the great curse and was deeply terrified by the rishi.
Seeing her emaciated, pale, and filled with anxiety, O King, the righteous Vasiṣṭha, the best of men, said:
"Save yourself, O best of rivers; carry me away swiftly."
"Viśvāmitra will surely curse you; do not entertain such hesitation.
Having heard those words of that compassionate one, O Kauravya, that river reflected upon what might be done as a virtuous deed.
The thought arose in her: "Vasiṣṭha has indeed always shown me great compassion; therefore, I must act for his benefit. Then, O King, [she saw] that best of sages muttering prayers on his own bank.
Seeing Kauśika performing the oblation, Sarasvatī thought,
"This is the opportunity. Then that best of rivers,
by her own force, caused the erosion of the bank.
Carried away by that erosion of the bank,
the son of Mitrāvaruṇa then praised Sarasvatī, O King:
"O Sarasvatī, you have issued forth from the lake of the Grandfather."
This entire world is pervaded by your own supreme waters;
you alone, O Goddess who traverse the sky, pour forth rain from the clouds. We learn from you that you are indeed all the waters.
Nourishment, splendor, fame, accomplishment, growth, and Umā—you alone are Vāṇī and Svāhā; this entire world is dependent upon you.
You alone dwell here within all beings in fourfold forms.
Thus, O King, while being praised by the great seer,
Sarasvatī swiftly bore that brahmin toward the hermitage of Viśvāmitra;
and she repeatedly announced that sage to Viśvāmitra.
Seeing him brought by Sarasvatī, Viśvāmitra, filled with rage, rose up against the sage with his weapon raised; seeing that sage who had taken up arms and was intent on ending Vasiṣṭha’s life.
Kauśika was exceedingly enraged, like another Kāla or Death;
then he searched for a weapon that would bring about the end of Vasiṣṭha.
But seeing him so furious, the river, out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin, [fled].
But the tireless river carried Vasiṣṭha toward the eastern direction,
fulfilling the word of both while deceiving the son of Gādhi;
then, seeing that Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, had been carried away, [Viśvāmitra was filled with rage].
Then the indignant Viśvāmitra, filled with rage, said:
"O best of rivers, since you have deceived me and gone back again,
flow with blood, O auspicious one, that is pleasing to the leaders of the Rākṣasas!"
Then Sarasvatī, having been cursed by the wise Viśvāmitra, carried water mixed with blood for that entire year. Thereafter,
the ṛṣis, the gods, the gandharvas, and the apsarases likewise [lamented].
Seeing Sarasvatī in that state, they became deeply distressed.
Thus, O lord of men, the overflow from Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage became famous in the world as the Vasiṣṭhāpavāha;
and then that best of rivers returned once more to her own course.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been cursed by that wise and enraged Viśvāmitra,
she discharged blood at that auspicious and excellent sacred ford.
Then, O King, descendant of Bharata, the Rākṣasas arrived there;
they all sat there at their ease, drinking the blood.
Satiated by it, they were exceedingly happy, free from distress, and relieved of their feverish agitation.

Dancing and laughing, they were just like those who have conquered heaven. Then, after some time had passed, O lord of the earth, sages whose wealth was their asceticism arrived at the Sarasvatī on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Having bathed in all those sacred fords (tīrthas), those bulls among sages, who were wise and eager for ascetic merit, attained supreme joy; and then,
O King, they proceeded toward that particular sacred ford.
Then, O best of kings, those highly fortunate ones arrived at that dreadful sacred ford and saw the water of the Sarasvatī flooded with blood and being drunk by many rākṣasas.

O King, seeing those Rākṣasas, the sages of rigid vows exerted the utmost effort for the protection of the Sarasvatī. All those highly fortunate ones, observers of great vows, having assembled together—
Having summoned the best of rivers, they spoke these words:
"O auspicious one, tell us the reason why this lake of yours has fallen into such a state of agitation;
having heard it, we shall drink from it."
Then, trembling, she related everything exactly as it had happened.
Seeing her thus distressed, those whose wealth is asceticism said to her:
"O sinless one, we have heard the cause, and we have also heard of the curse."
"All those whose wealth is austerity shall do whatever is appropriate.
Having thus addressed the best of rivers, they then said to one another,
"We shall all liberate this Sarasvatī from the curse."
O King, all those brahmins, having propitiated Mahādeva, the Lord of Creatures and Master of the World, through austerities, observances, various fasts, restraints, and difficult vows;
They liberated that goddess Sarasvatī, the best of rivers;
by their very word, Sarasvatī returned to her natural state,
and her waters became clear just as they were before.
Having spoken thus, the sages liberated her from her suffering;
and once released, that best of rivers shone forth as she had before. Seeing the waters of the Sarasvatī thus treated by those sages, [the people were amazed].
Then those hungry rākṣasas likewise went to them for refuge; O King, with palms joined in reverence, the rākṣasas, afflicted by hunger,
spoke again and again to all those sages who were filled with compassion.
For we are indeed hungry and deprived of the eternal Dharma;
it is not by our own will that we have become doers of evil,
but through your lack of favor and our own wicked deeds.
This faction of ours increases because of these *brahmarākṣasas*. For indeed, those among the Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise the Kṣatriyas who hate the Brāhmaṇas become *rākṣasas* in this world.
Those living beings who show contempt for their teacher, the officiating priest, their preceptor, and likewise for their elders, become Rākṣasas in this world;
and among women, this condition increases through the defect of their birth.
"O best of sages, this is our position: whatever is appropriate hereafter, please do that for us here, O most excellent of the twice-born;
you are capable of delivering even all the worlds."
Having heard this from them, those sages praised that great river;
with disciplined minds, they spoke for the sake of the liberation of those rākṣasas:
"Whatever has been defiled by hunger or insects, and whatever may have been eaten as leavings—"

Food from which hair has fallen, that which has been shaken off, and even that which has been broken; food that has been blown upon, that which is unknown, and that which is excessively cold; food that has fallen, food from a woman who has recently given birth, and food from an unchaste woman.
Food touched by dogs is the portion of the *rākṣasas* here;
therefore, knowing this, a wise man should always avoid these kinds of food. For he who eats such food eats the food of the *rākṣasas*.
Then, having purified that sacred ford, those seers whose wealth was their asceticism urged that river toward the liberation of the Rākṣasas.
Having understood the intention of the great seers, that best of rivers [acted accordingly].
O bull among men, he brought forth the Aruṇā river from his own body.
Having bathed in it, those Rākṣasas cast off their bodies and went to heaven;
for, O great king, that Aruṇā is indeed the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having understood this matter, Śatakratu, the king of the gods,
bathed in that best of tirthas and was indeed liberated from evil.
Janamejaya said:
"For what reason did the blessed Śakra incur the sin of killing a Brahmin,
and how indeed, by bathing in this sacred ford, did he become free from stain?
Vaiśampāyana said:
Listen, O lord of men, to this narrative exactly as it occurred,
concerning how Vāsava formerly broke his agreement with Namuci. Fearing Vāsava, Namuci entered a ray of the sun.

Then Indra formed a friendship with him and spoke this agreement: "O best of Asuras, friend, I swear to you by truth that I shall not slay you with anything wet nor with anything dry, neither by night nor by day."
Having thus made this agreement and created a mist,
O King, the Lord Vāsava severed his head with the foam of the waters.
That severed head of Namuci followed Śakra from behind.
To Śakra, who was speaking from nearby, "O slayer of a friend, you are wicked," he,
being thus urged repeatedly by him with his head bowed,
reported this matter in great distress to the Grandfather (Brahmā).

The Teacher of the World said to him: "O Indra, Lord of the Gods, perform your ablutions in the Aruṇā according to the prescribed rite after sacrificing; for she is the remover of the sin of killing a Brahmin. O Śakra, this river of meritorious waters was indeed created by the sages."
Her movement here had previously been hidden;
then, having approached, the goddess flooded the Aruṇā with her waters. This great confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Aruṇā is sacred.
"O Indra of the gods, perform sacrifices here and give gifts manifold;
by bathing here, you shall be liberated from that most terrible sin. Thus addressed by Sarasvatī in the bower of the forest, O Janamejaya.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the rules, the slayer of Bala (Indra) sipped water at the Aruṇā river.
Released from that sin caused by the killing of a Brahmin,
Śakra performed numerous sacrifices at the word of Brahmā.
Having bestowed many gifts and bathed at the sacred ford, Śatakratu— purified of sin, free from passion, and endowed with splendor— shook off the murder of a Brahmin and,
with a joyful mind, the lord of the thirty gods ascended to the third heaven.

O Bhārata, O best of kings, that head of Namuci also, having been immersed right there, attained imperishable worlds that yield all desires. Having likewise touched the waters there, the high-souled Bala—
Having bestowed various kinds of gifts and having attained the supreme Dharma through noble deeds,
he went to that great sacred ford of Soma.
Where in the past Soma himself, O lord of kings, duly performed the Rājasūya sacrifice,
there the wise Atri was the chief of the brahmins.
In that sacrifice presided over by the Hotṛ priest, the Great-Souled One was the chief of the ritual,
at the conclusion of which there occurred a great slaughter of the Dānavas,
Daityas, and Rākṣasas by the gods.
That extremely fierce battle known as Tāraka,
wherein Skanda slew the one named Tāraka and obtained the generalship of the gods;
Where Mahāsena, the destroyer of the Daityas,
dwells in person as Kārttikeya, there that king of Plakṣa trees always stands, where the Youth (Kumāra) resides.
Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, you have described this power of the Sarasvatī;
now, O Brahmin, you ought to explain the consecration of Kumāra."
O best among speakers, at what time and in what place,
and by what ritual procedure, was the blessed Lord, the Master, consecrated;
and how did Skanda carry out that great slaughter of the Daityas?
"Tell me all this accordingly, for my curiosity is great.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"This curiosity of yours is worthy of the Kuru lineage."
O Janamejaya, these words of mine produce great joy;
indeed, O lord of men, listen as I relate to you the consecration and the power of that high-souled prince.
In ancient times, the fiery energy of Maheśvara was spilled and fell into the fire;
the Lord Agni, though a consumer of all things, was unable to burn that inexhaustible substance. Because of that, the carrier of oblations became exceedingly radiant and full of splendor.
At that time, he did not retain the embryo composed of splendor; rather,
by the command of Brahmā, the Lord approached Gaṅgā and deposited the divine embryo, which possessed a brilliance equal to the sun.
Then Gaṅgā, unable to sustain that embryo,
released it upon the delightful mountain Himavat, which is worshipped by the immortals.
There, the son of Fire grew, pervading the worlds.
Then the Kṛttikās beheld that high-souled lord, the son of Fire, in the form of a blazing flame within a clump of reeds; desiring a son, they all vied with one another, each exclaiming, "He is mine!"
Having perceived that disposition of the mothers, the Blessed Lord,
the Master, then drank from their flowing milk with his six mouths. Having observed that power of the infant, the Kṛttikās—
The goddesses, possessing celestial forms, were filled with supreme wonder,
O best of the Kurus, at that place on the mountain peak where the Blessed One was cast down by Gaṅgā; there, the entire mountain shone forth as gold.
As the fetus grew, the earth was gladdened by him;
consequently, all the mountains became mines of gold.
And the boy, possessed of great heroism, is known as Kārttikeya.
The son of Gaṅgā was previously endowed with the power of great yoga;
that god, possessed of both ascetic merit and heroism,
grew exceedingly, O king of kings, lovely to behold like the moon.
Enveloped in splendor, he lay upon that divine golden bed of reeds, being praised at that time by Gandharvas and sages;
likewise, thousands of celestial maidens danced before him.
Skilled in divine music and dance, those of lovely appearance offered hymns of praise;
and the river Gaṅgā, the best among streams, waited upon the god,
while the Earth herself, assuming her most excellent form, bore him.
Bṛhaspati performed for him the birth rites and other ceremonies;
and the Veda, appearing in four forms, waited upon him with palms joined in reverence.
The science of archery, with its four divisions, its collection of weapons, and its compendiums, [also attended him].
There, the absolute Word (Vāṇī) herself appeared before him in person.
He beheld the Lord of Devas, the husband of Umā, of great prowess,
seated together with the Daughter of the Mountain and surrounded by hundreds of hosts of spirits.
The classes of the hosts of spirits were most wonderful to behold;
they were deformed, with distorted shapes and strange ornaments and banners;
they had the faces of tigers, lions, and bears, as well as the faces of cats and sea-monsters.
Others had the faces of wild cats, as well as the faces of elephants and camels; some had the faces of owls, while others appeared like vultures and jackals,
with faces resembling curlews, pigeons, and even those of deer.
Others there assumed forms resembling those of porcupines, hedgehogs, iguanas, as well as donkeys, rams, and oxen.
Some, resembling mountains or clouds, were armed with discuses, firebrands, and maces.
Some had the luster of a heap of collyrium, and some the radiance of white mountains;
O lord of the people, the hosts of the Seven Mothers also arrived,
as did the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Vasus, and the Pitṛs.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Siddhas, serpents, Dānavas, and birds,
as well as the self-born Lord Brahmā together with his sons and Viṣṇu,
and Śakra likewise, approached to behold the supreme and infallible Kumāra.
And also the most excellent gods and Gandharvas headed by Nārada,
the celestial rishis and Siddhas led by Bṛhaspati, and those named the Ṛbhus— the boon-granting deities even of the gods— [all came].
The Yāmas and the Dhāmas also gathered there from all sides;
yet that Blessed One, though but a child, endowed with the power of great yoga,
approached the Lord of the Gods, the wielder of the trident and the Pināka bow.
Beholding him approaching, there arose simultaneously in the minds of Śiva, the Daughter of the Mountain, Gaṅgā, and Agni the thought:
"To whom will this boy first go out of respect?"
"May he even protect me"— this was the thought in the minds of them all.
Perceiving this intention of those four,
he simultaneously resorted to his yogic power and manifested various bodies.
Then, in an instant, the blessed Lord became fourfold in form:
Skanda, Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameṣa at his back.
Having thus divided himself into four, the blessed Lord remained so.
From where Rudra was, Skanda of wondrous appearance departed;
Viśākha went where the goddess, daughter of the mountain king, was;
and the blessed Śākha, whose form is wind, went toward Vibhāvasu (Fire).
Naigameṣa, the Kumāra who shines with the brilliance of fire, went to the Gaṅgā;
all four of them, possessing radiant bodies and identical forms, approached him calmly, and it was like a marvel.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas upon seeing that great wonder, marvelous and hair-raising. Then Rudra, the Goddess, and Pāvaka [approached] the Grandfather.
Together with Gaṅgā, they all prostrated before the Lord of the World.
Having thus prostrated according to the prescribed rites, O bull among kings,
they spoke these words, O King, desiring to do what was pleasing to Kārttikeya.

"O Blessed One, O Lord of Gods, for the sake of our pleasure, you ought to grant this boy a sovereignty according to his desire and as is fitting. Then that wise Blessed One, the Grandfather of all the worlds, [spoke].
He reflected in his mind, "What might he receive?"—
for indeed, all the sovereign powers of the gods, gandharvas,
and rākṣasas, as well as those of the bhūtas, yakṣas, birds, and serpents in their entirety.
Long ago, he had already appointed him among the classes of great-souled beings;
and the Great-minded One considered him capable of sovereign power.
Then, remaining intent on the welfare of the gods, he meditated for a moment.
O Bhārata, the Grandfather of all beings granted him the generalship over all creatures;
he appointed for him all those who are renowned as kings among the various hosts of gods.
Then the gods, led by Brahmā, took the prince and together went to the lord of mountains for the sake of his consecration;
[they went] to the holy Sarasvatī, the daughter of Himavat, the best of rivers.
At Samantapañcaka, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
all the gods and gandharvas sat upon the bank of the Sarasvatī— a sacred site endowed with every excellence— their hearts completely fulfilled.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having gathered all the materials for the consecration according to the scriptures,
Bṛhaspati offered clarified butter into the kindled fire in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Then, having sat upon a divine, supreme throne given by Himavān— which was adorned with the finest jewels, strewn with celestial gems,
and consecrated with a collection of all auspicious things accompanied by rites and mantras— [he performed the ceremony].
Taking the materials for the consecration, the hosts of deities—
Indra and Viṣṇu of great prowess, as well as the Sun and the Moon,
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and likewise Vāyu and Agni— [approached].
Accompanied by Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aryaman, Aṃśa, and Vivasvat; together with the wise Rudra, as well as Mitra and Varuṇa;
the Lord was surrounded by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, and the two Aśvins.
Together with the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the Pitṛs;
with the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas;
and with innumerable divine ṛṣis as well as the most excellent Brahman-ṛṣis.

He was surrounded by Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, those who subsist on air, those who drink the rays of the sun, and by the high-souled Bhṛgus, Aṅgirases, and ascetics; as well as by all the meritorious Vidyādharas and those perfected in yoga.
Pitāmaha, Pulastya, and Pulaha of great asceticism; Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Atri, Marīci, and Bhṛgu;
as well as Kratu, Hara, Pracetas, Manu, and Dakṣa.
O Lord of the People, the seasons, the planets, and the luminaries; the personified rivers and the eternal Vedas;
the oceans, the lakes, and various sacred fords (tīrthas).
O lord of men, the earth, the sky, the quarters, and the trees;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, Hrī, Śrī, Svāhā, Sarasvatī;
Umā, Śacī, Sinīvālī, as well as Anumati and Kuhū.
Rākā and Dhiṣaṇā, as well as the other wives of the dwellers of heaven;
Himavat, Vindhya, and Meru with its many peaks;
Airāvata with his followers, as well as the Kalās and the Kāṣṭhās.
O King, [he is] the months and half-months, as well as the seasons, night and day;
Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses, and Vāmana, the king of serpents;
Aruṇa and Garuḍa, and the trees together with the medicinal herbs.
The Blessed Lord Dharma, Kāla, Yama, Mṛtyu, and those who are the followers of Yama— all these gathered together in assembly. Furthermore,
because of their great number, the various hosts of deities have not been mentioned individually.

Then, from here and there, they all assembled for the sake of the prince’s consecration; O King, at that time, all those dwellers of heaven took up the vessels for the consecration and every kind of auspicious object.
O King, the celestial dwellers, filled with great joy, consecrated the prince with golden jars endowed with divine materials, and with the holy waters of the Sarasvatī and other divine streams.

O great king, the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, consecrated that high-souled general of the Asuras, who brings fear to them, just as in former times he consecrated Varuṇa as the lord of the waters.
And Kaśyapa of great splendor, as well as others who have not been mentioned—
pleased with them, the Lord Brahmā granted those powerful attendants, swift as the wind, endowed with the power to assume any form at will, perfected beings, and great companions.
Nandīṣeṇa, Lohitākṣa, and the esteemed Ghaṇṭākarṇa;
the fourth follower of his is known as Kumudamālin. Then there are Sthāṇu, Mahāvega, and the great attendant Kratu.
O Indra among kings, he gave to Skanda that which possesses a hundred illusions at will, endowed with the power of the vigor of desire, and capable of destroying the enemies of the gods—
the terrible-acting Daityas in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Enraged, he struck fourteen million [demons] with his two arms.
Then the gods gave him an army teeming with Nairṛtas—
an invincible force of universal form that brings about the destruction of the enemies of the gods.
Then all the gods, including Indra, as well as the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, sages, and the ancestors, raised a shout of victory.
Yama gave him two attendants, both resembling Yama and Kāla.
The powerful and highly effulgent Unmātha and Pramātha,
as well as Subhrāja and Bhāskara— those two who are the followers of the Sun—
the majestic Sūrya, being pleased, gave them to Kārttikeya.
Soma also gave two attendants, Maṇi and Sumaṇi, who resembled the peaks of Kailāsa and were adorned with white garlands and unguents. Likewise,
Hutāśana gave Jvālājihva and Jyotis to his son.
He gave him two heroic followers who crush the enemy armies—
Parigha and Vaṭa, both fearsome and possessed of great strength—
as well as Dahati and Dahana, who were fierce and esteemed for their valor.
Aṃśa also gave five attendants to the wise Skanda:
Utkrośa, Paṅkaja, and both Vajra and Daṇḍadhara;
and Vāsava, the slayer of enemy heroes, gave these to the son of Anala.
For those two had slain many enemies of Mahendra in battle; the highly illustrious Viṣṇu gave three attendants— Cakra, Vikramaka, and the mighty Saṃkrama— to Skanda.
O bull of the Bharata race, the two Aśvins, experts in all branches of knowledge, joyfully gave to Skanda the Vardhana and the Nandana;
and the one of great fame [gave] the Kundana, the Kusuma, and the Kumuda.

The Creator gave to that great-souled one [Skanda] the two attendants Ḍambara and Aḍambara; and Tvaṣṭṛ gave to Skanda two excellent followers of great illusion, Vakrānuvaktra, who were powerful, ram-faced, fierce in strength, and possessed of great magical powers.
The Lord Mitra gave to that high-souled prince two noble youths who were observers of excellent vows, true to their word, masters of asceticism and learning,
beautiful to behold, bestowers of boons, and renowned throughout the three worlds.

The Creator bestowed upon Kārttikeya those two world-renowned beings, Suprabha and Mahātman, both of whom were performers of auspicious deeds; as well as Pālitaka and Kālika, both of whom were masters of great illusion.
O Bhārata, Pūṣan gave two attendants to Kārttikeya—
Bala and Atibala— who had large mouths and great strength;
and Vāyu, O best of the Bharatas, likewise gave them to Kārttikeya.
Varuṇa, true to his promise, gave to Kārttikeya two exceedingly powerful beings with the faces of whales: Ghasa and Atighasa;
as well as the high-souled Suvarcas and likewise Ativarcas.
O King, Himavat gave [the sons] to the son of Hutāśana;
O Bhārata, Meru gave two attendants to the son of Agni— the high-souled Kāñcana and Meghamālin.
Meru himself gave two others— Sthira and Atisthira—
to the high-souled son of Agni, who possessed great strength and prowess;
[and he gave] Ucchrita and Atiśṛṅga, who fought with great boulders.
Vindhya gave both Saṃgraha and Vigraha as his attendants to the son of Agni;
and the Ocean also gave both Mahāpāriṣada and Gadādhara as attendants to the son of Agni.
Pārvatī, of auspicious appearance, gave Unmāda, Puṣpadanta, and likewise Śaṅkukarṇa to the son of Agni;
she also gave the two nāgas Jaya and Mahājaya to the son of Jvalana.
Vāsuki, the lord of the *pannagas* and tiger among men, bestowed [the gift].
In this manner, the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Vasus, and likewise the Pitṛs,
as well as the oceans, the rivers, and the mountains of great strength [bestowed their gifts].
They gave him commanders of the army divisions who carried spears and battle-axes,
equipped with divine weapons and adorned in various garbs.
Now hear the names of the others who were the soldiers of Skanda.
Equipped with various weapons and adorned with colorful ornaments and armor,
there were Śaṅkukarṇa, Nikumbha, Padma, and Kumuda;
as well as Ananta with twelve arms, and Kṛṣṇa and Upakṛṣṇaka.
Droṇaśravas, Kapiskandha, Kāñcanākṣa, Jalandhama, Akṣasaṃtarjana, O King, Kunadīka, Tamobhrakṛt,
Ekākṣa, Dvādaśākṣa, and likewise the lord Ekajaṭa.
Sahasrabāhu, Vikaṭa, Vyāghrākṣa, Kṣitikampana,
Puṇyanāman, Sunāman, Suvaktra, Priyadarśana,
Pariśruta, Kokanada, and Priyamālyānulepana.
Ajodarā, Gajaśiras, Skandhākṣa, Śatalocana,
Jvālājihva, Karāla, Sitakeśa, Jaṭin, Hari,
Pariśruta, Kokanada, Kṛṣṇakeśa, and Jaṭādhara.
Caturdaṃṣṭra, Aṣṭajihva, Meghanāda, Pṛthuśravas, Vidyudakṣa, Dhanurvaktra, Jaṭhara, Mārutāśana,
Udarākṣa, Jhaṣākṣa, Vajranābha, and Vasuprabha.
O Indra among kings, [the Nāgas] Samudravega and likewise Śailakampin;
Eṣa and Pravāha, as well as Nanda and Upanandaka;
Dhūmra, Śveta, Kaliṅga, Siddhārtha, and Varada.
Priyaka, Nanda, the powerful Gonanda, Ānanda, Pramoda, Svastika, Dhruvaka,
Kṣemavāpa, Sujāta, and Siddhayātra, O Bhārata.
Govraja, Kanakāpīḍa, Mahāpāriṣadeśvara,
Gāyana, Hasana, the heroic Bāṇa, Khaḍga,
Vaitālī, Atitālī, as well as Katika and Vātika.
Haṃsaja, Paṅkadigdhāṅga, Samudronmādana, Raṇotkaṭa, Prahāsa, Śvetaśīrṣa, Nandaka,
Kālakaṇṭha, Prabhāsa, and another, Kumbhāṇḍaka.
Kālakākṣa and Sita, Bhūtalonmathana as well,
Samudronmadana, Mahānādin, and Raṇotkaṭa; Kālaka and Prahāsa, and likewise Aṅgāraka and Vahnika.
These and many others, O Bhārata, were great śālīs, fierce in battle: Yajñavāha, Pravāha, Devayājī, Somapa, the highly effulgent Sajāla, and Kratha and Krātha.
Tuhana and Tuhāna, the heroic Citradeva,
Madhura, Suprasāda, and the mighty Kirīṭin;
Vasana, Madhuvarṇa, and Kalaśodara as well.
Dhamanta, Manmathakara, the valiant Sūcīvaktra,
Śvetavaktra, Suvaktra, Cāruvaktra, Pāṇḍura,
Daṇḍabāhu, Subāhu, as well as Raja and Kokilaka.
Acala, Kanakākṣa, Bālānām-ayika, Prabhu, Saṃcāraka, Kokanada, Gṛdhravaktra, Jambuka,
Lohāśavaktra, Jaṭhara, Kumbhavaktra, and Kuṇḍaka.
Madgugrīva, Kṛṣṇaujā, Haṃsavaktra, Candrabhā,
Candramas, Pāṇikarman, and the mighty Uḍuka; Pāṇikūrma, Śambūka, Pañcavaktra, and Śikṣaka.
Cāṣavaktra, Jambūka, Śākavaktra, and Kuṇḍaka—
these high-souled ones were joined in yoga, ever devoted to the Brāhmaṇas,
and were indeed the great attendants of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
O Janamejaya, youths, children, and the elderly—
attendants by the thousands— waited upon Kumāra.
Listen now, O Janamejaya, to those who possessed various kinds of faces.
Some had faces like tortoises and cocks, others had faces like hares and owls;
some had long faces, O Bhārata,
and others had faces like dogs and jackals.
Some had faces like those of donkeys and camels, as well as faces like those of boars;
some had faces like humans and sheep, as well as faces like those of jackals;
others were terrifying with faces like makaras and mouths like those of porpoises.
O Bhārata, some had the faces of cats and rabbits, others had long faces;
some had the faces of mongooses and owls, others likewise had the faces of dogs; some had the faces of mice and baboons, and others had the faces of peacocks.
Others had the faces of fish and sheep; some had the faces of goats, sheep, and buffaloes; others had the faces of bears and tigers, as well as the faces of leopards and lions;
there were terrifying ones with the faces of elephants, and others with the mouths of crocodiles.
O Bhārata, some had the faces of Garuḍas, others the faces of rhinoceroses, wolves, or crows;
some had the faces of cows, donkeys, or camels, while others had the faces of cats;
their bellies, feet, and limbs were enormous, and their eyes were like stars.
Some had faces like pigeons, while others had faces like bulls; some had faces like cuckoos, others had faces like hawks and partridges,
and still others had faces like lizards, all wearing garments free from dust.
With mouths like those of serpents, faces like spears, fierce countenances, and hundreds of faces;
wearing venomous snakes as garments and likewise using them as coverings;
with massive bellies and emaciated limbs, or with massive limbs and emaciated bellies.
With short necks and large ears, adorned with various serpents,
they wore the skins of lordly elephants as garments, as well as black antelope skins; O great king, some had mouths on their shoulders, while others had mouths on their bellies.
Some had faces on their backs, some on their jaws, and others even on their shanks; many had faces on their sides, as well as faces turned toward various directions.
Likewise, there were lords of the hosts with faces resembling those of insects and winged insects.
Others had the faces of various beasts of prey, with many arms and necks;
some had various trees for arms, while others had heads at their hips; they had mouths like the coils of serpents and dwelt in various thickets.

Some had their bodies covered with rags, while others were dressed in garments made of bark; some wore various types of attire, and others were clad in skins; they were adorned with diverse garlands and unguents.
Wearing various garments,
they were turbaned and crowned, with necks like conch shells and great splendor;
some wore diadems, others had five topknots, and likewise some had thick, matted hair.
Some had three crests, some two, and others had seven;
some wore topknots, some wore crowns, some were shaven-headed, and others had matted hair. Some wore variegated garlands, while others had hair upon their faces.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, they are always fond of combat;
with battle as their sole delight, they are eternally invincible even by the best of the gods.
They are dark-complexioned, with fleshless faces, long backs, and no bellies.
Some had thick backs and short backs; some had pendulous bellies and genitals;
some had long arms, some short arms, and some were dwarfs with short limbs.
Some were hunchbacked, some had long shanks, and some had ears and necks like those of elephants.
Some had noses like those of elephants, others like tortoises, and still others like wolves;
some had long lips and long tongues, while others were truly hideous with faces turned downward; some had large fangs, some short fangs, and others yet had four fangs.
O King, there were thousands of others, as formidable as lordly elephants,
with well-proportioned bodies, radiant, and finely adorned;
they had tawny eyes, spike-like ears, and crooked noses, O Bhārata.
They had broad fangs and large tusks, thick lips, and tawny hair;
they possessed various feet, lips, and fangs, as well as diverse hands and necks.
Covered in various types of armor, O Bhārata, they spoke in many different tongues.
The great attendants likewise rushed about, joyful and powerful, conversing with one another in the various regional dialects;
they had long necks, long nails, and long feet, heads, and arms.
O Bhārata, some had tawny eyes, blue throats, and long ears;
some were like the belly of a wolf, while others resembled collyrium.
Others still had white bodies, red necks, and tawny eyes.
O King, O Bhārata, there were many dappled horses of variegated colors;
some resembled chowrie-crests, others had white and red stripes;
they were of various hues and uniform tints, with a luster like that of peacocks.
Those who indeed possess various weapons and are skilled in diverse missiles and arms—
listen now as I describe their weapons once more;
the remaining attendants have taken up their respective armaments.
Some had nooses raised in their hands, with gaping mouths and donkey-like faces; others had wide eyes and blue throats, with arms like iron bars.
Some held *śataghnīs* and discs in their hands, while others carried maces in their palms.
With tridents and swords in their hands, they were likewise massive in body and possessed of great strength;
with maces and *bhuśuṇḍi* weapons in their hands, as well as *tomara* lances in their grasp; and with swords and clubs in their hands, and staffs in their hands, O Bhārata.
With various terrible weapons, those high-souled ones of great speed, great strength, and great impetuosity— likewise the great attendants who delight in battle—
were filled with joy upon seeing the consecration of Kumāra.
With their limbs adorned with networks of bells, those beings of great prowess danced;
these and many other great attendants, O King,
waited upon the high-souled and illustrious Kārttikeya.

Divine beings, those of the atmosphere, and those of the earth— heroes swift as the wind and commanded by the gods— became the followers of Skanda. There were thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of such as these.
They stood surrounding the high-souled one who had been consecrated.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, hear now of these groups of mothers who followed the Kumāras."
O hero, O Bhārata, listen as I proclaim the names of those illustrious mothers, the slayers of hosts of enemies,
by whom the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, are pervaded.
Prabhāvatī, Viśālākṣī, Palitā, Gonasī, as well as Śrīmatī, Bahulā, and likewise Bahuputrikā; Apsujātā, Gopālī, and Bṛhadambālikā.
Jayāvatī, Mālatikā, Dhruvaratnā, Bhayaṅkarī,
Vasudāmā, Sudāmā, Viśokā, Nandinī,
Ekacūḍā, Mahācūḍā, and Cakranemi, O Bhārata.
Uttejanī, Jayatsenā, Kamalākṣī, Śobhanā, Śatruñjayā, Krodhanā, Śalabhī, Kharī,
Mādhavī, Śubhavaktrā, and Tīrthanemi, O Bhārata.
Gītapriyā, Kalyāṇī, Kadrulā, Amitāśanā, Meghasvanā, Bhogavatī, Subhrū, Kanakāvatī,
Alātākṣī, Vīryavatī, and Vidyujjihvā, O Bhārata.
Padmāvatī, Sunakṣatrā, Kandarā, Bahuyojanā,
Saṃtānikā, O Kauravya, Kamalā, Mahābalā,
Sudāmā, Bahudāmā, Suprabhā, and Yaśasvinī.
O Indra among kings, she is fond of dancing and wears a girdle of a hundred mortars;
she possesses a hundred bells, is the joy of hundreds, the delight of Bhaga, and the beautiful woman;
she is embodied, cool as the moon, and Bhadrakālī, O Bhārata.
Saṃkārikā, Niṣkuṭikā, Bhramā, Catvaravāsinī,
Sumaṅgalā, Svastimatī, Vṛddhikāmā, Jayapriyā,
Dhanadā, Suprasādā, Bhavadā, and Jaleśvarī.
Eḍī, Bheḍī, and Sameḍī, as well as Vetālajananī;
Kaṇḍūti, Kālikā, and Devamitrā, O Bhārata; Lambasī, Ketakī, Citrasenā, and Balā.
O King, [the daughters were] Kukkuṭikā, Śaṅkhanikā, and likewise Jarjarikā;
Kuṇḍārikā, Kokalikā, Kaṇḍarā, and Śatodarī; Utkrāthinī, Jareṇā, Mahāvegā, and Kaṅkaṇā.
Manojavā, Kaṇṭakinī, Praghasā, and likewise Pūtanā;
Vegā, Pāṣi, Viṭapāvāsā, Kānanākrīḍanaprabhā, Khaśayā,
Curvyuṭi, Vāmā, Krośanā, and Taḍitprabhā.
Maṇḍodarī, Tuṇḍā, Koṭarā, Meghavāsinī,
Subhagā, Lambinī, Lambā, Vasucūḍā, Vikatthanī,
Ūrdhvaveṇīdharā, Piṅgākṣī, and Lohamekhalā.
Pṛthuvaktrā, Madhurikā, and likewise Madhukumbhā;
Pakṣālikā, Manthanikā, Jarāyu, and Jarjarānanā;
she who is known as Dahadahā and likewise Dhamadhamā, O King.
O Indra among kings, Khaṇḍakhaṇḍā, Maṇikuṇḍalā,
Amocā, and Lambapayodharā were there, O Kauravya,
as well as Veṇuvīṇādharā, Piṅgākṣī, and Lohamekhalā.
She with the face of a hare and an owl, black-complexioned, with shanks like those of a donkey and great speed;
she with the face of a porpoise, white, with red eyes and terrifying;
she with matted hair, moving at will, long-tongued, and fierce in her strength.
