Kāleḍikā, Vāmanikā, and Mukuṭā, O Bhārata;
Lohitākṣī, Mahākāyā, and Haripiṇḍī, O lord of the earth; Ekākṣarā, Sukusumā, and Kṛṣṇakarṇī, O Bhārata.
Kṣurakarṇī, Catuṣkarṇī, Karṇaprāvaraṇā,
Catuṣpathaniketā, Gokarṇī, Mahiṣānanā,
Kharakarṇī, Mahākarṇī, Bherīsvanā, and Mahāsvanā.
Śaṅkhakumbhasvanā, Bhaṅgadā, Mahābalā,
Gaṇā, Sugaṇā, as well as Abhīti and Kāmadā; Catuṣpatharatā, Bhūtitīrthā, and Nyagocarā.

O Bhārata, she is the giver of cattle, the giver of wealth, and the giver of happiness; she is of great fame, the giver of milk, the giver of cows and buffaloes, and possesses beautiful horns. She is the foundation, the well-established one, the radiant one, and the most resplendent.
Gokarṇī, Sukarṇī, Sasirā, and likewise Stherikā; Ekacakrā, Megharavā, Meghamālā, and Virocanā—
these and many other Mothers, O bull of the Bharatas.
O Bhārata, there were thousands of followers of Kārttikeya of various forms— long-nailed, long-toothed,
and long-snouted women, who were upright, sweet-voiced, in the prime of youth, and well-adorned.
Endowed with majesty and capable of assuming any form at will, their limbs were sometimes fleshless and white, and at other times resembling gold;
some resembled black clouds, O bull of the Bharatas, while others were smoke-colored.
They were of ruddy luster, highly fortunate, with long hair and white garments;
they bore their braids tied upward, had tawny eyes, and wore long girdles;
likewise, they had protruding bellies, long ears, and large breasts.
Some had copper-colored eyes, some were copper-hued, and others had tawny eyes;
they were granters of boons, moving at will, and ever-joyful.
They were of the south, the fierce ones, those of the moon, and the mighty ones of the north.
O scorcher of foes, O bull of the Bharatas, there are those belonging to Varuṇa, Mahendra, and Agni; likewise those of Vāyu, Kumāra, and Brahmā;
as well as those of Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and the mighty Vārāhī.
There were others belonging to Viṣṇu, exceedingly terrifying, cruel in form, and fearsome; they were equal to Apsarases in beauty, like the wind in speed,
like cuckoos in their speech, and like Kubera in their supernatural power.
They are like Śakra in prowess and like fire in their brilliance;
they are ever a source of fear to enemies in combat. They can assume any form at will and are equal to the wind in speed.
Possessing inconceivable power and vigor, and likewise inconceivable prowess,
they dwell in trees and crossroads, making their homes at the junctions of four paths; they reside in caves and cremation grounds, and have their abodes in mountains and waterfalls.
Wearing various ornaments, likewise adorned with diverse garlands and garments, they possessed various and wonderful costumes as well as various languages;
they were distinguished by many excellent qualities and by variegated weapons and decorations of every kind.
These and many other hosts, terrifying to their enemies,
followed that Great-souled One with the approval of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
And he bestowed upon him divine [garments] inlaid with various jewels.
Then, O tiger among kings, the blessed Indra, the subduer of Pāka, gave a spear-weapon to Guha for the destruction of the enemies of the gods—
a weapon of great sound, with a massive bell, radiant and white-hued.
O bull of the Bharatas, Paśupati gave him a banner with the color of the rising sun, as well as a great army of all beings—
terrible, equipped with various weapons, and endowed with the power of asceticism and heroism.
That army named Dhanañjayā, which was invincible due to its own qualities,
protected by thirty thousand warriors whose strength equaled that of Rudra,
never knew how to retreat from battle.
Viṣṇu gave him the Vaijayantī garland, which increases strength;
Umā gave him two dustless garments with the brilliance of the sun;
and Gaṅgā gave him a divine, supreme water-pot born of nectar.
Bṛhaspati affectionately gave a staff to the prince;
Garuḍa gave his beloved son, a peacock with variegated plumage;
and Aruṇa gave a cock, whose feet serve as weapons.

King Varuṇa gave him a noose endowed with strength and heroism; likewise, the Lord Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, gave the black antelope skin to that devotee of Brahman and granted him victory in battles.
Having obtained the generalship of the host of gods,
Skanda shone like a second blazing, radiant fire;
he was then accompanied by his attendants and the Mothers.

That formidable army of the Nairṛtas— equipped with bells and raised banners, accompanied by kettledrums, conchs, and drums, and provided with weapons and flags— set forth for the destruction of the Daityas, gladdening the preeminent gods.
Like the autumnal sky, it shone, adorned with celestial lights.
Then those hosts of gods and the multitudes of ghostly armies,
remaining unperturbed, sounded their drums and abundant conchs.
They sounded kettledrums, jharjharas, kṛkacas, cow-horns,
āḍambaras, gomukhas, and loud-sounding ḍiṇḍimas;
and all the gods, together with Indra, offered praise to the Kumāra.
The celestial Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Then Mahāsena, being pleased, granted a boon to the thirty gods:
"I shall slay in battle those enemies who seek to kill you."
Having received that boon from that best of the gods,
the high-souled deities, their hearts filled with joy, considered their enemies already slain;
a roar of exultation arose from all the hosts of living beings.

When the boon was granted by the Great-Souled One, he filled the three worlds. Surrounded by a vast army, Mahāsena set forth for the sake of slaying the Daityas in battle and for the protection of the dwellers of heaven.
Resolve, victory, righteousness, success, fortune, fortitude, and mindfulness—
these, O lord of men, marched at the head of Mahāsena’s armies.
With that terrifying goddess, who held a trident and a mallet in her hands, the god [proceeded].
Holding a flaming brand, adorned with variegated ornaments and armor,
and bearing maces, clubs, iron arrows, spears, and lances in his hands,
Guha advanced, roaring with the sound of a proud lion.
Seeing him, all the Daityas, Rākṣasas, and Dānavas fled in all directions, agitated by fear on every side; meanwhile,
the gods, with various weapons in their hands, rushed toward them.
Seeing this, the lord Skanda, endowed with energy and strength, became enraged;
he repeatedly discharged his terrible *śakti* weapon,
augmenting his own splendor like a fire fed with oblations.
O great king, while the Śakti weapon was being discharged by Skanda of immeasurable splendor, a flame like a meteor fell upon the surface of the earth,
and likewise, thunderous crashes and portents fell upon the ground.
O King, just as at the time of universal destruction there are most terrible [omens],
so too was a single spear hurled by the son of Fire;
from that, O bull of the Bharatas, millions of spears flew forth.
In that battle, the blessed Lord slew with his spear-weapon the lord of the Daityas named Tāraka,
who possessed great strength and prowess and was surrounded by ten thousand powerful and heroic Daityas, O King.
In the battle, the Lord slew Mahiṣa, who was surrounded by eight padmas [of followers],
and he killed Tripāda, who was surrounded by ten ayutas;
and Hradodara, who was surrounded by ten nikharvas.
Together with his followers, whose hands were grasping various weapons, he struck them down;
there, O King, the princes and their attendants raised a great roar as they slaughtered the enemies, filling the ten directions.
Filled with joy, they danced, leaped, and laughed;
O Indra among kings, then, by the flames of the *śakti* weapon spreading in every direction as if yawning,
the entire three worlds were struck with terror.
Thousands of Daityas were consumed by fire, while others perished from the roars of Skanda;
some enemies of the gods were struck down by his banner,
and others, terrified by the sound of his bells, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Some, mangled by weapons, fell down deprived of life;
thus did the heroic and mighty Kārttikeya slay many powerful assailants, the enemies of the gods, in battle.
Then there was a Daitya named Bāṇa, the son of Bali, who possessed great strength;
having reached Mount Krauñca, he oppressed the hosts of gods.
The noble-minded Mahāsena marched against that enemy of the gods.

Out of fear of Kārttikeya, he sought refuge in the Krauñca mountain. Then the blessed Kārttikeya, filled with great wrath, pierced the Krauñca mountain— which resounded with the cries of cranes— with the spear given to him by Agni.
With its *sāla* trunks and *sarala* trees, its monkeys and elephants in flight,
its birds startled from the sandbanks,
and its serpents darting out; it resounded with the cries of swarms of langurs and bears as they fled.
With the gait and roar of deer, filled with startled sṛmara antelopes,
and with śarabhas and lions suddenly rushing forth,
that mountain shone brilliantly even though it had reached a pitiable state.
The Vidyādharas dwelling on its peaks flew up,
and the Kiṃnaras were greatly agitated, startled by the sound of the falling spear.
Then, the Daityas rushed forth by the hundreds and thousands.
From that blazing, preeminent mountain, adorned with various ornaments and garlands,
the attendants of Kumāra overcame and struck them down in battle.
And then the Blessed One, filled with wrath, [assailed] the son of the lord of the Daityas.
He swiftly struck down his younger brother, just as the Lord of the Gods slew Vṛtra;
and the son of Agni, the slayer of enemy heroes, pierced Krauñca with his spear,
having made himself manifold and then single again by means of his great soul.
The spear hurled at him in battle returned again and again to his hand; such is the power of the blessed son of Agni, and even greater than this,
through his heroism, his twofold application, and his splendor, fame, and glory.

By him the Krauñca mountain was split asunder and hundreds of Daityas were slain. Then that blessed Lord, having destroyed the enemies of the gods and being honored by the deities, attained supreme joy.
When the excellent mountain Krauñca was split asunder and the son of Caṇḍa was struck down,
then, O King, O Bhārata, kettledrums resounded and conchs blared;
and the celestial women released an unsurpassed rain of flowers.
A holy breeze blew, carrying divine fragrances;
the Gandharvas and the great ṛṣis who were performers of sacrifice offered praise to him. Some resolved that he was the Lord, the son of the Grandfather.
Some call Sanatkumāra— the first-born of all, the source of Brahman—
the son of Maheśvara; others call him the son of Vibhāvasu, and they also say he is the son of Umā, the Kṛttikās, and Gaṅgā.

In one form, in two forms, and indeed in four forms, the Lord of Yogins, the God of great power, appeared by the hundreds and thousands. This, O King, has been narrated to you: the consecration of Kārttikeya.

And hear now of the sanctity of the lineage of tirthas along the Sarasvatī. O great king, when the enemies of the gods had been slain, there was a preeminent tirtha created by Kumāra, like a second heaven.
Then the Lord, the son of Agni, standing there at that sacred ford, bestowed various sovereign powers upon the leaders of the Nairṛtas throughout the three worlds.
Thus did the Blessed One, the destroyer of the Daitya race, act at that tīrtha.
O great king,
that sacred ford where the Lord of Waters, Varuṇa, was formerly consecrated by the hosts of gods is named Oujasa; there, O bull of the Bharatas, Deva-senāpati was consecrated by the deities.
Having bathed in that excellent sacred ford and having worshipped Skanda,
the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) gave gold, garments, and ornaments to the brahmins.
Having stayed there for one night, Mādhava, the slayer of enemy heroes, departed.
Having worshipped that most excellent sacred ford and touched its waters, the wielder of the plow—
the best of the Mādhavas— became joyful and his mind was filled with delight.
All this that you asked of me has now been related to you.
Just as the Blessed Skanda, though but a child yet possessed of great strength, was consecrated by the assembled gods and made their commander-in-chief, O King. Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, I have heard in truth this most wonderful account of the prince’s consecration in full detail and according to the prescribed rites;
having heard it, O one rich in asceticism, I consider myself purified."

My hair stands on end with joy and my mind is serene. Having heard of the consecration of the prince as well as the slaughter of the Daityas, supreme delight has arisen within me; indeed, my curiosity is redoubled.
"O one of great wisdom, O best of beings, you are indeed skilled; tell me how the Lord of Waters was consecrated in this office by the gods and the asuras.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Listen, O King, to this wondrous account exactly as it occurred in a former kalpa.
At the beginning, while that Kṛta Yuga was proceeding according to its established order,
all the deities assembled and spoke thus to Varuṇa."
"Just as Śakra, the king of the gods, always protects us from fears,
so may you also become the lord of all rivers. And let your dwelling always be, O god, in the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters."
"This ocean, the lord of rivers, shall come under your control, and its waning and waxing shall occur in conjunction with the moon. To those gods, Varuṇa spoke these words: "So be it."

Then, having all assembled, they consecrated Varuṇa, the dweller of the ocean and lord of the waters, according to the rites prescribed by sacred law. Having thus anointed Varuṇa as the lord of aquatic creatures, the gods departed.
Having honored the Lord of Waters, they returned to their own respective places. Then the highly illustrious Varuṇa was consecrated by the gods over the rivers,
the oceans, the streams, and the lakes.
He protected [the earth] according to the law, just as Śatakratu protects the gods.
Then, having performed ablutions there and given various kinds of wealth,
that highly wise slayer of Pralamba proceeded to Agnitīrtha.
When the fire within the womb of the *śamī* tree was no longer seen because it had been extinguished,
and when the destruction of the worlds and the world-system had occurred, O sinless one,
[the gods] approached the high-souled Grandfather of all the worlds.
"The venerable Agni has vanished, and we do not know the cause.
Let there be no destruction of all the worlds; let him restore his fire for us.
Janamejaya said:
"For what reason did the Blessed Agni, the creator of the world, disappear? And how was he discovered by the gods? Tell me that in truth.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Terrified by Bhrigu’s curse, the powerful and illustrious Jātavedas, having reached the womb of the Śamī tree, then vanished. When the Fire-god had thus disappeared, all the gods, including Indra, were filled with anxiety.
Then, deeply distressed, they searched for the lost fire.
Thereupon, having reached Agnitīrtha, they beheld the fire dwelling there according to the prescribed rite, situated indeed within the heart of a śamī tree.
O tiger among men, all the gods, led by Bṛhaspati and accompanied by Indra,
were filled with joy upon reaching that blazing fire;
they then returned as they had come, and he became a consumer of all things.
O protector of the earth, having bathed there as well— where it had been declared by the expounder of Brahman due to the curse of Bhṛgu— the wise one went to the source of Brahman,
where the Blessed One, the Grandfather of all the worlds, created [the universe].
There, in ancient times, the Lord Brahmā bathed together with the gods and created foods for the deities according to the prescribed rites;
having bathed there and given various kinds of wealth, he departed.

O King, the lord Ailavila went to the Kaubera tīrtha; having performed great austerities there, he attained the sovereignty over wealth. O King, while he remained right there, riches and treasures likewise [attended him].
O best of men, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) then approached that sacred ford;
having gone there and bathed according to the prescribed rites, he gave wealth to the brahmins.
There, in that most excellent forest belonging to Kubera, he beheld that place.
Where in the past great asceticism was performed by that high-souled one,
and where King Kubera obtained abundant boons—
the lordship over wealth and friendship with Rudra of immeasurable splendor.

O mighty-armed one, it was there that the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) swiftly attained his status as a *sura*, his position as a world-guardian (*lokapāla*), and his son Nalakūbara; and it was right there, having assembled with the hosts of Maruts, that he was consecrated.

And that delightful vehicle of his was given— a divine aerial chariot (*vimāna*) yoked with swans called Puṣpaka— as well as the sovereignty over the Nairṛtas. Having bathed there, O King, Bala gave away abundant gifts.
Anointed with white unguents, Rāma proceeded swiftly to the sacred ford known as Badarapācana, frequented by all living beings;
it was auspicious, endowed with forests that bloom out of season, and always possessed of flowers and fruit.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Rāma went to the excellent tīrtha called Badarapācana,
where ascetics and siddhas dwell, and where a maiden of firm vows [performed her penance].
O Lord, Bharadvāja’s daughter, named Sruvāvatī, was peerless on earth in beauty; a maiden living as a celibate student,
O King, she performed most intense austerities with many observances.
"May the King of the Gods be my husband"— having thus resolved,
O descendant of the Kuru lineage, many years passed for that beautiful woman as she practiced those various severe vows, so difficult for women to perform.
O lord of the people, by that conduct, by her asceticism,
and by her supreme devotion, the blessed Lord Pākaśāsana was pleased;
the powerful sovereign of the thirty gods came to her hermitage.
Assuming the form of the high-souled brahmin-seer Vasiṣṭha,
she beheld him— Vasiṣṭha, the best of those who practice austerities— and,
O Bhārata, she honored him with the rites observed by sages.
The auspicious and sweet-spoken lady, who was well-versed in the rules of conduct, said:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, O Lord, what do you command?
O you of noble vows, today I shall give you everything according to my ability."
"O ascetic rich in penance, because of my devotion to Śakra, I will not give you my hand under any circumstances. Through vows, observances, and austerities,
I must indeed satisfy Śakra, the lord of the three worlds."
Having been addressed thus, O Bhārata, the Blessed Lord, looking at her as if with a smile, spoke to her who was well-versed in religious observances, consoling her as it were:
"O lady of excellent vows, you are indeed performing severe penance; I know you."
"O auspicious one, O lady of lovely countenance, whatever purpose this undertaking of yours has in your heart shall all come to pass exactly as it is;
for everything is obtained through austerity, and everything rests upon austerity."

O fair-faced one, those divine abodes belonging to the gods are to be attained through austerity; great happiness has austerity as its root. Having performed severe austerity here and casting off the body, human beings [attain them].
"O auspicious one, they attain divinity; listen to these words of mine:
'Cook these jujubes, O blessed lady of virtuous vows. Having said, 'Cook them,' the Blessed One, the slayer of Bala, departed."
Having addressed that auspicious lady, he then performed his silent recitation (*japya*). Not far from that hermitage, at an excellent sacred ford (*tīrtha*),
O Great King— at that very ford where he performed his recitation— [he remained].
O great king, at Indratīrtha, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
the blessed Lord Pākaśāsana, the sovereign of the gods, performed the cooking of jujube fruits for the purpose of testing that [tīrtha].
Then, O King, purified, restrained in speech, free from fatigue, devoted to that task, and clad in clean garments, she placed [the vessel] upon the fire;
O tiger among kings, she of the great vow cooked the jujube fruits.
O bull among men, as she continued to cook, a very great length of time passed;
yet those [grains] did not cook, and the day reached its end. Furthermore, the entire store of wood belonging to her was consumed by the fire.
Seeing that fire was without wood, she then set her own body ablaze.
First casting her two feet into the fire, that woman of lovely appearance, being free from sin, would replace her burnt feet once they were consumed.
Though her feet were burning, the blameless one, whose eyes were like lotus petals, paid no heed to the pain out of a desire to please the great seer; neither did she feel despondency,
nor did her countenance change.
Having set her body ablaze with fire, she was filled with joy even in the midst of the water. And those words of hers remained constantly in her heart, O Bhārata:
"In every way, the jujube fruits alone must be cooked," so the maiden thought.
Keeping those words of the great seer in mind, that auspicious woman began to cook the jujube fruits, O Bhārata, yet they did not cook. Then the blessed Fire-god himself consumed her feet.
At that time, not even the slightest mental distress arose in her.
Then, having witnessed this deed of hers, the Lord of the Three Worlds was pleased and revealed his own form to the maiden.
And the best of the gods spoke to that maiden of steadfast vows:
"I am pleased with you, O auspicious one, because of your devotion, your asceticism, and your self-restraint.
Therefore, whatever desire you hold dear, O auspicious one, it shall be fulfilled for you."
"O highly fortunate one, having cast off this body, you shall dwell with me in the third heaven.
And this excellent sacred ford of yours shall remain permanent in the world, O fair-browed one; it shall remove all sins and be known by the name Badarapācana."
Famous throughout the three worlds and frequented by the Brahman-sages,
it was indeed at this most blessed and auspicious of sacred fords in ancient times that the Seven Sages, having left Arundhatī behind, departed for the Himavat mountains.
Then those highly fortunate ones, having gone there with firm resolve,
set out indeed to gather fruits and roots for the sake of their sustenance. While they were dwelling there in the forest of the Himalayas, seeking a livelihood, [the following occurred].
Then a twelve-year drought occurred;
having established a hermitage there, those ascetics dwelt within it,
and the auspicious Arundhatī also became constantly devoted to austerity.
Then, seeing Arundhatī established in severe ascetic discipline, the three-eyed Lord, the granter of boons, became well-pleased. Thereupon,
the highly illustrious Mahādeva assumed the form of Brahmā.
Approaching her, the god said, "O auspicious one, I desire alms.
Thereupon, that woman of beautiful appearance replied to the brahmin:
"O sage, my store of food is exhausted; eat these jujube fruits here."

Then Mahādeva said, "Cook these, O lady of excellent vows. Thus addressed, that illustrious woman, desiring to do what was pleasing to the Brāhmaṇa, placed the jujube fruits upon the kindled fire and cooked them.
Then she listened to divine, delightful, and meritorious stories; indeed,
that terrible twelve-year drought had passed while she was fasting,
cooking, and listening to these auspicious tales.
That most dreadful time passed for her as if it were but a single day.
Then those sages returned from the mountain, bringing fruits with them;
thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke then to Arundhatī.
"Approach these sages as before, O knower of dharma;
I am pleased with you, O knower of dharma, because of your austerity and self-restraint.
Then the blessed Lord Hara revealed his true form.
Then he spoke to them regarding her great conduct:
"O Brahmins, the austerity that you have accumulated on the slopes of the Himalayas and the austerity of this woman— these, in my opinion, are not equal."
"For by this ascetic woman, most difficult penance has been performed;
twelve years were completed by her while fasting and cooking. Then the Blessed One spoke again to that very Arundhatī.
"Choose a boon, O blessed lady, whatever is desired in your heart.
She, whose eyes were large and copper-hued, spoke to the god in the assembly of the seven seers:
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased with me, let this place become a supreme sacred ford (tīrtha)."
09.047.044e Beloved by the Siddhas and the divine seers, it is known by the name Badarapācana.
09.047.045a Thus, O Lord of the gods, one who dwells there for three nights, pure and fasting, shall obtain the fruit of twelve years.
Having said "So be it" to her, Hara then departed for heaven;
the god, praised by the Seven Sages, replied to the ascetic woman.
The ṛṣis were filled with wonder upon seeing Arundhatī—
unwearied, unaltered in complexion, and enduring hunger and thirst—
and thus did the pure Arundhatī attain supreme perfection.

O highly fortunate lady of firm vows, since you have indeed bestowed such excellence upon this vow for my sake, O blessed one, I grant this to you today, being well-pleased by your disciplined observance.

"O auspicious one, O excellent lady, I shall grant you a boon that is superior even to the boon which was given to Arundhatī by that high-souled one; and through his grace and by your own splendor, O auspicious one, [I shall bestow it]."
I shall further proclaim another boon here according to the prescribed rule:
he who, being well-composed, shall dwell for a single night at this sacred ford (tīrtha),
having bathed there, shall attain worlds that are difficult to reach even after casting off the body.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious and powerful thousand-eyed god then departed from Srucāvatī,
the holy city, and returned once more to heaven.
O King, when the wielder of the thunderbolt had gone, a rain fell there.
O best of the Bharatas, drums of great sound resounded on all sides amidst divine flowers of celestial fragrance;
and a wind of holy scent blew with gentle propriety, O lord of the people.
Having cast off her beautiful body, she attained the status of Indra’s wife;
having obtained him through fierce asceticism, O Acyuta, she took delight with him.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, who was her mother, and where did that beautiful woman grow up?
O Brahmin, I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is great.
Vaiśampāyana said:
The seed of the high-souled Bhāradvāja, the brahmin seer,
was spilled when he beheld the large-eyed Apsaras Ghṛtācī approaching; that best among those who recite prayers took up that seed with his hand.
Then she cast it into a leaf-cup, and there that auspicious girl was born. Having performed all the birth rites for her, the great sage Bhāradvāja, whose wealth is asceticism, gave her a name.
"O you who possess the sacrificial ladle," said the righteous-souled one in that assembly of the hosts of sages.
And having left her in the hermitage, he departed for the forest of the Himalayas.
There too, the high-souled one performed his ablutions;
Having bestowed wealth upon the great brahmins,
that foremost of the Vṛṣṇis, with a perfectly composed mind, then proceeded to the sacred ford of Śakra.
Vaiśampāyana said: Then,
having gone to Indratīrtha, the powerful and preeminent among the Yadus bathed according to the prescribed rites and bestowed wealth and jewels upon the brahmins.
For there, that king of the immortals performed a hundred sacrifices;
and the lord of the gods bestowed vast wealth upon Bṛhaspati,
including all the unrestricted *jārūthya* rites accompanied by various sacrificial fees.
There, he performed the sacrifices as prescribed by those who had mastered the Vedas;
for at that place, the lord of the gods had previously performed a hundred such sacrifices.
O best of the Bharatas, that immensely radiant one performed those sacrifices a hundred times over.

Then, having filled it according to the prescribed rites, he became renowned as Śatakratu. And because of his name, that auspicious, meritorious, and eternal sacred ford became known as Indratīrtha, which liberates one from all sins.
Having performed his ablutions there according to the prescribed rites, the mace-armed hero honored the brahmins with drinks, clothing, and food,
and then proceeded from that excellent and auspicious tirtha to Rāmatīrtha.
There, the highly fortunate Bhārgava Rāma, a performer of great austerities,
having repeatedly cleared the entire earth of the foremost of the Kṣatriyas,
placed Kaśyapa, the best of sages, at the head as his preceptor.
He performed the Vājapeya sacrifice and a hundred Aśvamedhas;
he gave away the earth together with its oceans as sacrificial fees,
having bestowed various gifts endowed with many kinds of jewels.

O Janamejaya, having given wealth there to the twice-born at that sacred and excellent *tīrtha*, frequented by gods and celestial sages, Rāma went to the forest together with his cows, elephants, female slaves, and goats.
Having sipped water according to the rule and honored the twice-born,
the fair-faced one gave wealth at a holy ford in an auspicious place;
then, having saluted the sages, he proceeded to the Yamunā-tīrtha.
O lord of the earth, it was there that the highly fortunate Varuṇa, the son of Aditi and possessor of white radiance, performed the Rājasūya sacrifice;
having conquered both humans and gods in battle there.

Varuṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, undertook an excellent sacrifice. When that excellent sacrifice was completed, a battle broke out between the gods and the Dānavas, bringing destruction to the three worlds.
O Janamejaya, when the Rājasūya, the best of sacrifices, had concluded,
there arose a most terrible battle involving the Kṣatriyas. At that time, Rāma, whose weapon was the plough, was at that excellent tīrtha.
Having bathed there and given wealth to the twice-born, Mādhava—
the Lord who grants all desires— honored and worshipped the sages with reverence, and the omnipresent one also bestowed gifts upon other seekers there.
Then, wearing a garland of forest flowers and being praised by the twice-born, the lotus-eyed one, filled with joy, proceeded from there to Ādityatīrtha,
O best of kings, where the blessed Lord Bhāskara, the maker of light, performed sacrifice.
He attained sovereignty over the luminaries as well as their power.
On the banks of that river, indeed, all the gods together with Vāsava,
the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Gandharvas, and the Apsarases were present.
Dvaipāyana, Śuka, and Kṛṣṇa Madhusūdana,
as well as Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas, O lord of the people—
these and many others, thousands in number, are perfected in Yoga.
O scorcher of foes, at that auspicious and holy ford of the Sarasvatī,
Viṣṇu, having slain the two Asuras Madhu and Kaiṭabha in ancient times, bathed there,
O best of the Bharatas, at that most excellent and supreme of tīrthas.
And the righteous-souled Dvaipāyana, O Bhārata, having bathed at that very spot,
attained supreme yoga and reached the highest perfection; likewise, Asita Devala, a man of great asceticism, did so at that same place.
Having resorted to the supreme yoga, the seer attained yoga.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"In that very place, the righteous one, whose wealth is asceticism, continued to dwell."
In ancient times, Asita Devala, having established himself in the dharma of the householder,
was constant in righteousness, pure, self-controlled, having laid aside the rod of punishment, and possessed of great austerity;
he was equal toward all living beings in deed, thought, and speech.
O Great King, he was free from anger, regarding blame and praise as equal; he maintained an even disposition toward the pleasant and unpleasant, possessing a vision of equanimity like that of Yama.
That one of great asceticism viewed gold and a clod of earth with the same eye.
Constantly worshipping the deities and guests together with the twice-born,
always devoted to celibacy and ever dedicated to dharma,
he then approached, O great king, and having established himself in yoga, became a mendicant.

O King, the wise sage Jaigīṣavya, possessed of great luster and constant in yoga, dwelt with a concentrated mind at that sacred ford in the hermitage of Devala; O great king, that man of great asceticism attained perfection.
While the great sage Jaigīṣavya was dwelling there, Devala, even as he looked upon him, did not engage him in accordance with dharma;
nor was he recognized by that high-souled sage, Devala.
In this manner, O Great King, a long period of time passed for them;
yet Devala did not see the sage Jaigīṣavya.
At one point, however, Jaigīṣavya revealed himself to Devala.
O Janamejaya, at the time for food, that wise wandering ascetic,
a knower of dharma, approached Devala when it was time for alms.
Seeing the great sage arrived there in the form of a beggar, he [Devala]—

He showed the highest respect and likewise felt immense joy; O Bhārata, Devala, with a concentrated mind, honored him for many years according to his ability and according to the rites prescribed by the Ṛṣis.
Once, O King, a very great anxiety arose in that high-souled Devala upon seeing the immensely radiant sage:
"Many years have passed while I have been engaged in his worship."
And this indolent monk did not say anything at all;
reflecting thus, the illustrious Devala, traveling through the air and holding his water-pot, proceeded toward the great ocean.
O descendant of Bharata, as that righteous-souled one was proceeding toward the ocean, the lord of rivers, he then beheld Jaigīṣavya already arrived there before him. Thereupon,
the lord Asita was filled with wonder and fell into reflection.
"How has this monk arrived, and how indeed has he bathed in the ocean?"—
thus did the great seer Asita reflect at that time.
Having bathed in the ocean according to the prescribed rites, he, being pure, recited his prayers.
Having performed his prayers and daily rites, the illustrious one returned to his hermitage;
O Janamejaya, taking a jar filled with water,
that sage then entered his own hermitage grounds.
There he saw Jaigīṣavya seated in that hermitage;
yet Jaigīṣavya did not speak to him at all,
for that great ascetic lived in the hermitage like a piece of wood.
Having seen him, who was like the ocean itself, immersed in the waters of the sea,
the wise Asita Devala, O King, first beheld him having entered the hermitage and began to reflect.
O Indra among kings, having witnessed the power of Jaigīṣavya’s asceticism born of yoga,
that best of sages then reflected:
"How is it that he has been seen by me both in the ocean and in the hermitage?"
Reflecting thus, O lord of the people, that sage Devala, who had mastered the mantras, rose from that hermitage into the sky for the purpose of testing the mendicant Jaigīṣavya.
He beheld the Siddhas moving through the intermediate space, absorbed in meditation,
and he saw Jaigīṣavya being honored by those Siddhas. Then Asita, highly incensed, resolute, and firm in his vows, [proceeded].
That Devala indeed beheld Jaigīṣavya going to heaven;
he then saw him proceeding from there to the world of the ancestors,
and from the world of the ancestors, he saw him going to the realm of Yama.
From there he beheld him proceeding toward the world of the Sun;
rising up from that as well, he beheld the great sage Jaigīṣavya proceeding toward the highly praised world of the Moon.
He rose up toward the worlds of those who perform sacrifices with single-minded devotion, auspicious realms that ascend upward;
from there, he flew up further toward the worlds of those who maintain the *agnihotra* fire,
and even beyond those, toward the worlds of those ascetics rich in austerity who perform the *darśa* and *paurṇamāsa* sacrifices.

To them that wise one appeared; from those worlds of the animal-sacrificers, he beheld the stainless world being honored by the gods. He saw those whose wealth is austerity performing the various *cāturmāsya* sacrifices.
Devala beheld that place being reached by those who perform the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, as well as those rich in asceticism who worship with the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, proceeding in that very manner.
He saw in those worlds the highly wise ones performing the Vājapeya, the best of sacrifices, as well as the Bahusuvarṇaka;
and he saw those who were sacrificing with the Puṇḍarīka and the Rājasūya.
In those worlds, Devala beheld Jaigīṣavya;
he saw them, the best of men, performing the Aśvamedha, the foremost of sacrifices, as well as the Naramedha, in those very worlds.
And those who perform the Sarvamedha, which is difficult to attain, as well as the Sautrāmaṇi—
among their worlds, that Devala beheld Jaigīṣavya,
O King, as well as those who sacrifice with various twelve-day sacrificial sessions (dvādaśāha-satra).
In those worlds, Devala saw Jaigīṣavya;
then Asita beheld him who had attained co-residence (salokatā) with the worlds of Mitra and Varuṇa, as well as those of the Ādityas.
Then Asita beheld all those places— the abode of the Rudras, the Vasus, and that of Bṛhaspati— and he saw him having passed beyond them all,
ascending to the world of the cows as he proceeded toward the sacrificial assembly of Brahmā.
Then Asita beheld Jaigīṣavya passing through the worlds;
he saw the brahmin leaping up by his own splendor into three other worlds,
and he followed him as he proceeded to the worlds of women devoted to their husbands.
Then Asita, the subduer of enemies, could no longer see the excellent sage Jaigīṣavya, who had vanished while established in yoga. The highly fortunate Devala reflected upon Jaigīṣavya.

Then Asita, being disciplined, composed, and with palms joined in reverence, questioned those foremost of beings in the worlds— the perfected ones who perform the sacrifice of Brahman— regarding their power, their excellence in vows, and the incomparable perfection of yoga.
"I do not see Jaigīṣavya; tell me of that one of great splendor. I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is indeed great. When he asked this, the Siddhas then spoke to him as he questioned them.
Having seen the power of that treasury of asceticism exactly as it is,
the Siddhas said:
"Listen, O Devala of firm vows, as we declare the truth of the matter."
Jaigīṣavya has gone to the eternal, imperishable world of Brahmā.
Having heard these words of those perfected ones performing the sacrifice of Brahman,
Asita Devala quickly leaped up and then fell down.
Then those Siddhas spoke again to Devala:
"O Devala, O ascetic, there is no path for you to go to that abode of Brahmā which Jaigīṣavya has attained."
Having heard those words of the Siddhas, Devala again descended through all those worlds in due order and returned to his own holy hermitage like a bird.
As he was entering, Devala beheld Jaigīṣavya; then,
having witnessed the power of Jaigīṣavya’s yoga-born asceticism, Devala reflected with a mind disciplined by dharma.
Then, O King, Devala, approaching the great sage Jaigīṣavya with humility and bowing low, said to that high-souled one:
"O Blessed One, I wish to abide in the dharma of liberation."
Having heard those words of his, he gave him instruction on the supreme method of yoga and what ought and ought not to be done according to the scriptures.
Then, seeing that his mind was set upon renunciation, the great ascetic [proceeded].
They performed all his funeral rites according to the prescribed ritual. Then,
seeing that he had set his mind on renunciation, all living beings together with the ancestors wept aloud, saying, "Who will now provide for us?"
Having heard those piteous words of the beings as they cried out in the ten directions for liberation, Devala set his mind upon abandoning [his life].
Then, O Bhārata, he [prepared] sacred fruits and roots.
The flowers and the medicinal herbs are crying out in distress by the thousands: "Surely that petty and evil-minded Devala will cut us down again— he who,
having granted safety to all beings, does not remain mindful of his promise."

Then, O best of kings, that most excellent sage Devala further reflected with his own intellect upon whether liberation or the duty of a householder would be more conducive to one's welfare; having thus resolved in his mind, he remained steadfast.
Having abandoned the duties of a householder, he took delight in the dharma of liberation.
Having reflected upon these and other matters, O Bhārata, Devala then attained supreme perfection and the highest yoga through his firm resolve.
Then the gods, led by Bṛhaspati, having assembled together,
praised Jaigīṣavya and the asceticism of that practitioner of penance.
Thereupon, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke to the gods at that time.
"Jaigīṣavya possesses no ascetic power, for he causes Asita to marvel. To that wise man who spoke thus, those denizens of heaven replied to the great sage Jaigīṣavya, declaring, "It is not so!"
There is nothing superior to this, nor anything equal in power,
splendor, austerity, and yoga of that great-souled one.
Such was the power of the righteous Jaigīṣavya, as was that of Asita.
This excellent place and sacred ford belongs to those two great-souled ones.
Having touched the water there and having given wealth to the twice-born, the high-souled wielder of the plow [departed].
Having attained supreme merit through his noble deeds,
he went to that great tīrtha of Soma.
Vaiśampāyana said:

O Bhārata, when the Lord of the Stars had performed the Rājasūya sacrifice there, a great battle known as the Tārakāmaya occurred. Having bathed there as well and having given gifts, the self-possessed Bala [departed].
The righteous-souled one went to the sacred ford of the sage Sārasvata,
where in former times, during a twelve-year drought, the sage Sārasvata taught the Vedas to the best of the twice-born.
Janamejaya said:
How did the sage Sārasvata, rich in asceticism, teach the Vedas in former times during a twelve-year drought?
09,050.005 Vaiśampāyana said: O great king, in former times there was a wise sage of great asceticism,
renowned as Dadhīca, who was a celibate student with his senses fully subdued.
O Lord, Śakra was constantly afraid of that one of extreme asceticism;
he could not be enticed even by various kinds of rewards. Therefore, for the sake of tempting him, the subduer of Pāka dispatched [a messenger].
O great king, while that high-souled one was gratifying the gods at the Sarasvatī, the beautiful and auspicious celestial nymph Alambuṣā appeared near him.
Seeing that divine form,
the seed of that seer of purified soul was discharged into the Sarasvatī; the river took it up,
and having seen that seed, O bull among men, she held it within her womb.
That great river conceived that embryo for the sake of a son,
and at the proper time, that best of rivers gave birth to a son;
O Lord, she then went toward the ṛṣi, taking that son with her.
O Indra among kings, seeing that best of sages in the assembly of seers, the river then spoke while offering him her son:
"O Brahman-sage, this is your son; he was carried by me out of devotion to you."
"O Brahmarṣi, when I saw that semen of yours which had been discharged before Alambusā, I indeed held it within my womb out of devotion to you,
with the firm resolve: 'May this vital energy of yours not go to ruin.'"
"Accept your own blameless son, given by me.
Thus addressed, he accepted him and attained the highest joy;
and like one reciting a mantra, that best of the twice-born affectionately smelled his head.
Having embraced her for a long time, O best of the Bharatas,
the great sage, being well-pleased, then granted a boon to the Sarasvatī:
"The Viśvedevas, along with the Pitṛs, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases..."
"O fortunate one, they shall attain satisfaction when they are satiated by your waters.
Having spoken thus, he, pleased and with a supremely joyful soul, praised the great river with these words; listen to them duly, O King.

"O highly fortunate one, you issued forth from the lake of Brahmā in ancient times; O best of rivers, the sages of rigid vows know you well. And you, O lady of lovely appearance, have always been a source of pleasure to me."
"Therefore, O woman of excellent complexion, your son shall be great; renowned by your very name, he shall be a creator of the world. Known as Sārasvata, he will be a man of great asceticism."

"O highly fortunate one, during a twelve-year drought, this Sārasvata will teach the Vedas to the bulls among the twice-born. And you, O auspicious one, shall always be the most meritorious of all sacred rivers."
"O highly fortunate Sarasvatī, by my grace you shall become [thus]," he said. Having been thus praised by him and having obtained the boon, that great river,
O bull of the Bharatas, departed joyfully taking her son with her.
At that very time, during the conflict with the gods and the dānavas,
Śakra wandered through the three worlds seeking a weapon;
yet the blessed Śakra did not find a weapon at that time.
"Whatever might be suitable for the slaughter of those enemies of the gods," Śakra then said to the deities, "the great asuras cannot be slain by me without the bones of Dadhīca."
"Therefore, O best of gods, go and request that foremost of sages, saying:
'Give us the bones of Dadhīca; with them we shall slay our enemies.
Then, being thus entreated by the gods, that best of sages [consented] with effort to give his bones."
"Renounce your life," he said, and without hesitation, he did so;
thus, that doer of what is pleasing to the gods attained imperishable worlds. Then Śakra, with a heart full of joy, [took] his bones.
He caused various divine weapons to be fashioned—
thunderbolts, discuses, maces, and abundant heavy clubs—
for he had been empowered by that supreme ṛṣi through his intense asceticism.
Then, by Bhṛgu, the son of Prajāpati,
there was born that world-creator Atikāya— radiant, fashioned from the very essence of the worlds, as massive as a mountain, tall, and a lord renowned for his greatness.

And Indra, the subduer of Pāka, was constantly trembling with fear at his splendor. O Bhārata, by means of that thunderbolt, empowered by mantras and born of Brahmanic energy, which had been released in great wrath, the Blessed One [struck him].
He slew ninety-nine heroes among the Daityas and Dānavas. Then,
after a great and most terrifying period of time had passed,
O King, a twelve-year drought occurred.
During that twelve-year drought, O King, the great seers, afflicted by hunger, fled in all directions in search of sustenance. Seeing them thus scattered from every quarter, the sage Sārasvata then—
He set his mind on departing, but Sarasvatī said to him:
"O son, you must not go from here. I shall always provide you with food—the finest of fish. Stay here, O Bhārata."
Having been addressed thus, he offered libations to the ancestors and likewise to the deities;
he took his food daily, sustaining both his life-breaths and the Vedas.
Then, when that drought had passed, the great seers—
They questioned one another once more for the sake of their Vedic recitation;
yet, O king of kings, as they all ran about overcome by hunger, the Vedas were lost to them, and not a single one among them possessed any inspired insight.
Then a certain rishi, having approached them, spoke to those [ascetics] about Sarasvata,
that most excellent of rishis who was self-restrained and engaged in his private Vedic recitation;
having gone there, he described to them the exceedingly radiant Sarasvata.

While he was performing his Vedic recitation, which resembled that of the immortals, in a secluded place, O King, all the great seers gathered there and, having assembled, spoke these words to Sārasvata, the best of sages: 09,050.042c He was performing his Vedic recitation, which resembled that of the immortals, in a secluded place among people.

09,050.043a Then, O King, all the great seers gathered there; having assembled, they spoke this to Sārasvata, the best of sages: 09,050.043c [They spoke] to Sārasvata, the best of sages, having come together.
Then the sage said to them, "Teach us! and further added, "O sirs, enter into discipleship with me according to the prescribed rite.
Thereupon the host of seers replied, "You are but a child, my son."
He said to those sages, "May my dharma not perish":
"For he who should speak unrighteously or should accept [a gift] through unrighteousness—
let both of them die quickly, or let both become enemies."

"Not by years, nor by gray hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) is great among us. Having heard these words of his, those sages acted according to the rule.
Therefore, having obtained the Vedas, they once again established the Dharma.
Sixty thousand sages became disciples of the brahmin seer Sārasvata for the purpose of studying the Vedas.
Then, remaining under the control of that boy, all those brahmin-sages brought handful after handful of darbha grass for his seat.
Having given wealth there as well, the son of Rohiṇī—
Then the mighty elder brother of Keśava,
being joyful, proceeded in due order to that great and famous sacred ford where the old maiden resided.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, how did the maiden formerly become devoted to asceticism? For what purpose did she perform penance, and what was her religious observance?"
"O Brahman, this which I have heard from you is most difficult to achieve and unsurpassed.
Tell me the entire truth as to how she remained established in her ascetic penance.
Vaiśampāyana said:
There was a ṛṣi of great heroism, Kuṇi Gārgya, who was highly renowned. Having performed extensive austerities, O King, that powerful one, the best among those who practice penance,
begot a daughter of his own mind, who possessed beautiful eyebrows.
And seeing her, the highly illustrious Kuṇi Gārgya was exceedingly delighted;
O King, he abandoned his body here and went to the third heaven.
Then that auspicious woman of beautiful brows, whose eyes resembled lotuses, [remained].
Having established a hermitage through great and fierce austerity, that blameless woman formerly worshipped the ancestors and the gods with fasts;
O King, a long time passed for her as she practiced such severe penance.

Although she was being offered by her father to a husband, that blameless woman did not desire him; for she could find no husband who was a worthy match for herself. Thereupon, she emaciated her own body through fierce asceticism.
Devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, she dwelt in the lonely forest; though she felt her life's purpose was fulfilled, she grew weary and,
having observed the vow of celibacy since her youth, she reached old age.
O Indra among kings, emaciated by old age and by her ascetic penance,
she was unable to move even a single step by herself; at that time,
she indeed set her mind upon departing for the next world.
Seeing her desirous of liberation, Nārada said to her:
"O sinless one of great vows, how can there be worlds for you who are an uninitiated maiden? For thus have we heard in the world of the gods."
"Supreme ascetic merit has been attained by you, but the worlds have not yet been conquered.
Having heard those words of Nārada in the assembly of sages, she said:
"O most excellent ones, I shall give half of my ascetic merit to my husband."
When this had been said, the sage born of Gālava, formerly named Śṛṅgavān, took her hand and spoke this agreement:
"O beautiful one, I shall touch your hand today only according to an agreement."
"If you must dwell with me for one night," he said,
"so be it," she replied, and then she gave him her hand. Having offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite and the established rules, she performed the ceremony.
And Gālava performed the grasping of her hand and her marriage ceremony.
O King, that night she became a young woman of celestial beauty,
adorned with divine ornaments and garments, and wearing divine garlands and unguents.
Seeing her, who seemed to illuminate the surroundings with her own radiance, Gālava was filled with joy;
he stayed for one night, and at dawn she said to him:
"O Brahmin, O best among those who practice austerities, the agreement that was made by you with me—"
"I have stayed here; may you be blessed, may it be well with you, I am now departing.
Having been granted leave, she spoke further: "Whoever, being composed, shall dwell for one night at this sacred ford after having offered libations to the gods,"
"Whoever correctly practices for fifty-six years,
he shall obtain the fruit of that *brahmacarya*.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous woman then cast off her body and went to heaven."
The ṛṣi too became dejected, brooding over her beauty; with great difficulty, he accepted half of his ascetic merit as the price of their agreement.
Having thus prepared himself, he followed her path.
"O best of the Bharatas, he was afflicted with grief, having been overcome by her beauty.
This great life-story of the old maiden has been explained to you,
as well as her practice of celibacy and her auspicious departure to heaven."
While staying there, Halāyudha heard that Śalya had been slain.
Having also given gifts to the twice-born there, O scorcher of foes,
he then grieved for Śalya, who had been killed in battle by the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, having emerged from the gate of Samantapañcaka,
Mādhava Rāma questioned the hosts of sages regarding the fruit of Kurukṣetra.
O Lord, being thus questioned by that lion of the Yadus, they [described] the fruit of Kurukṣetra.
Those high-souled ones related everything to him exactly as it had happened.
The sages said:
"The northern altar of Prajāpati is so called."
O Rāma, the eternal gods of heaven, who bestow great boons, once gathered at Samantapañcaka for a sacrificial session with an excellent offering.
And formerly, by that wise and best of royal seers,
the high-souled Kuru, who possessed immeasurable splendor, this was practiced for many years.
Thenceforth, it became renowned here as Kurukṣetra.
Rāma said:
"For what purpose was this field ploughed by the high-souled Kuru?"
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, I desire to hear this as it is being told.
The sages said:
"O Rāma, it is said that in ancient times, Kuru was constantly engaged in plowing."
Having approached from the triple heaven, Śakra asked him the reason:
"O King, what is this that is occurring with such great effort?
O royal sage, what is your intention for which this earth is being ploughed?"
Kuru said:
"O Śatakratu, those men who shall die here in this field will go to the worlds of the righteous, free from all evil."

Then, having laughed at him, the lord Śakra departed for the third heaven; meanwhile, the royal seer, undaunted, continued to till the earth. And Śakra, coming again and again, laughed at him repeatedly.
Śatakratu, having repeatedly questioned him who was undaunted, departed.
But when the king, by means of fierce asceticism, began to tear up the earth,
Śakra then spoke to the gods concerning what the royal seer intended to do.
Having heard that, the gods spoke these words to the thousand-eyed one:
"O Śakra, let the royal seer be invited to choose a boon, if it is possible;
for if men who have died here indeed go to heaven..."
"Without having sacrificed to us with these rites, our share shall not be granted.
Then, having arrived there, Śakra spoke to the royal seer:
"Enough of your distress; let my word be done."
"O King, O great-minded one, let those humans who, being free from sloth, cast off their bodies while fasting,
or those who are slain in battle— even if they have been born as animals—
become partakers of heaven, O Indra among kings."
"So be it," King Kuru then said to Śakra;
having taken his leave of him with a joyful heart,
the slayer of Bala quickly returned once more to the third heaven.
"O best of the Yadus, it is even so; this was ploughed of old by the royal seer,
and it was authorized by Śakra for those who cast off their lives—
by the foremost of gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as by meritorious royal seers."
There shall be no place on earth more meritorious than this. Whatever men perform supreme austerity here,
they shall all, upon casting off the body, go to the abode of Brahmā.
Furthermore, those fortunate men who shall indeed bestow gifts,
their [merit] will truly become multiplied a thousandfold before long;
and those humans here who, seeking what is auspicious, shall dwell constantly.
They shall never behold the realm of Yama;
and those lords of men who perform sacrifices with great rituals,
their residence shall be in Triviṣṭapa as long as the earth endures.
Moreover, Śakra himself, the lord of the gods, sang a verse here that was composed at Kurukṣetra; listen to it, O Halāyudha:
"Even the dust particles from Kurukṣetra, when raised by the wind,"
Even one who has performed evil deeds is led to the supreme goal. By becoming resolute in this way—thinking, "I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I shall dwell in Kurukṣetra"—one will thereby attain heaven.
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I dwell in Kurukṣetra. Thus, even while prattling and reflecting again and again, he attends to the practice of standing, silence, and the hero's posture (vīrāsana).
Whether standing at a distance or nearby, one will certainly attain heaven— just as the preeminent gods, the best of Brahmins,
and foremost among royal sages such as Nṛga and others.
O lion among men, having performed sacrifices with costly rites and cast off their bodies, they have attained a happy rebirth;
[those who dwell] between Tarantuka and Arantuka.
Including the lakes of Rama and Macakruka,
this Samantapañcaka of Kurukṣetra is called the northern altar of Prajāpati.
This great and auspicious merit of the denizens of heaven is highly esteemed and endowed with the qualities of the celestial realm;
therefore, all the lords of the earth [also seek it].
"The slain shall go to the destination of the great-souled ones," thus spoke Śakra himself, together with Brahmā and the others;
and all that was approved by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O Janamejaya, having then beheld Kurukṣetra and distributed gifts, the Sātvata went to a vast and divine hermitage.
Adorned with groves of madhūka and mango trees, crowded with *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees, filled with *ciribilva*, holy, and thick with *panasa* and *arjuna* trees—
seeing that preeminent place of auspicious characteristics, the best of the Yādavas [was moved].
He asked all those sages, "To whom does this excellent hermitage belong?
They all replied to the high-souled Halāyudha, O King:
"Listen in detail, Rāma, as to whose hermitage this was in the past."
In this place, the god Viṣṇu formerly performed supreme austerity;
here all his eternal sacrifices were performed according to the prescribed rites. It was right here that the Brāhmaṇī, who had practiced celibacy since her youth, attained perfection.

Engaged in yoga, she went to heaven; perfected through austerity, that ascetic woman became illustrious, O King. She was the daughter of the high-souled Śāṇḍilya, firm in her vows, virtuous, self-controlled, and a lifelong celibate.
Having performed severe penance, which is indeed difficult for women to practice,
she attained supreme *yoga* and went to the unsurpassed heaven; having enjoyed the fruit of the horse-sacrifice in that hermitage, that auspicious woman became one among the successful.
The highly fortunate one, honored by those of self-restraint, has gone to heaven.
Having approached that holy hermitage and seen it, the bull among the Yadus,
having heard the words of the sages, proceeded to that hermitage.
Having heard the words of the sages, he went to that supreme hermitage.
In that hermitage, a man obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Then, having paid homage to those sages on the slopes of the Himavat, Acyuta departed.
Having withdrawn all his military camps,
the powerful Tāladhvaja ascended the mountain; having gone not very far from there and beholding that holy and excellent sacred site, he was filled with supreme wonder.
And Balarāma reached the source of the Sarasvatī, Plakṣaprasravaṇa,
and arrived at Kārapacana, the most excellent and supreme of tīrthas;
there, the mighty Halāyudha also gave gifts.
Having bathed in the cool water, he departed from there and went with great joy to the hermitage of Mitra and Varuṇa;
having bathed in the holy, very cool, pure, and clear water.
Raṇadurmada gratified the ancestors and the gods;
having stayed there for one night with ascetics and Brahmins,
Acyuta went to the holy hermitage of Mitra and Varuṇa.
To that place on the Yamunā where Indra, Agni, and Aryaman had formerly attained delight, he went from Kārapacana. Having bathed there as well, the righteous-souled one attained supreme satisfaction.
Accompanied by the ṛṣis and the siddhas, that one of great strength, the bull among the Yadus,
sat down and listened to auspicious discourses. While they were thus seated, the venerable sage Nārada arrived.
Then he arrived at that place where Rāma was staying.
While Rāma, whose splendor was incomparable, remained there,
the venerable seer Nārada, possessed of great majesty, arrived.
Enveloped in a circle of matted locks, wearing a golden garment, and performing great austerities,
O King, he carried a golden staff and likewise bore a water-pot;
taking up that beautiful lute, the kacchapī, which produced pleasant sounds.
Skilled in dance and song, honored by gods and brahmins,
a maker of quarrels and ever fond of strife,
he went to that place where the illustrious Rāma was stationed.
Having risen and honored that sage of firm vows, they all questioned the celestial rishi regarding everything that had occurred concerning the Kurus. Then,
O King, Nārada, who knows all dharmas, related it to him.
Having related everything exactly as it had happened regarding the past destruction of the Kurus,
the son of Rohiṇī then spoke to Nārada in a piteous voice:
"In what state is that kṣatriya class, and what has become of those kings who were there?"
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, I have previously heard all of this;
yet, a great curiosity has arisen in me to hear it in detail.
Nārada said:
Bhīṣma has already been slain, as have Droṇa and the Lord of Sindhu;
Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, and his sons, those great chariot-warriors, have also been killed,
along with Bhūriśravas, O son of Rohiṇī, and the heroic King of Madra.
These and many other mighty ones,
kings and princes who never retreated in battle, have indeed sacrificed their dear lives for the sake of the beloved Kaurava.
"O Mādhava, all have been slain by the Pāṇḍavas and have gone toward the path of heaven;
but hear from me, O mighty-armed one, regarding those who remain unslain in the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son— the survivors are Kṛpa and the heroic Bhoja."
And the valiant Aśvatthāman, while the shattered armies fled in all directions—
these three were the crushers of assemblies:
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the heroic son of Droṇa.
O Rāma, they too then fled in fear in the ten directions.
When the army had been slain and Kṛpa and the others had fled, Duryodhana,
deeply afflicted by grief, entered the lake named Dvaipāyana.
While the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra lay there upon the solidified waters,
the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, tormented him with fierce words.
Thus being pierced on all sides by those words, O Rāma, the powerful man—
Having risen from the lake, the hero, grasping his great mace,
has now approached to fight with Bhīma; and that encounter between the two,
O Rāma, will immediately become most terrible.
"O Mādhava, if you have curiosity, go there without delay;
behold this most terrible battle between your two disciples, if you so desire,
in today's combat of Rāma."
O hero, [regarding] Bhīma and the Kaurava;
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Nārada and having honored those bulls among the twice-born, [he spoke].
He dismissed all those who had come with him, and he commanded his followers, saying, "Go back to Dvārakā. Having descended from that auspicious Plakṣaprasravaṇa, the best of mountains, he departed.
Then, his mind filled with joy upon hearing of the great fruit of the sacred fords,
the infallible Rāma sang this verse in the presence of the brahmins:
"Where could there be a delight equal to dwelling by the Sarasvatī?"
Whence could there be virtues equal to those who dwell by the Sarasvatī?
Having reached the Sarasvatī, people have gone to heaven;
they will always remember the river Sarasvatī.
Sarasvatī is the most meritorious among all rivers;
Sarasvatī always brings happiness to the world. Having reached the Sarasvatī, even people of very wicked deeds [are purified].
They never grieve, neither in the next world nor in this one.
Then, looking repeatedly at the Sarasvatī with affection,
that scorcher of enemies ascended his bright chariot yoked with horses.
On that swiftly moving chariot, that bull among the Yadus arrived,
desiring to witness the impending combat between his two disciples.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus, O Janamejaya, did that tumultuous battle take place,
at which King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, overcome with grief,
spoke these words upon seeing Rāma present as the mace-duel was about to begin.
"O Sañjaya, how did my son fight against Bhīma?
Sañjaya said:
"Having obtained the presence of Rāma, your son Duryodhana..."
Desirous of battle, the mighty-armed and valiant king rejoiced; and upon seeing the wielder of the plow, O Bhārata, he rose up and,
filled with supreme affection, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having honored him according to the prescribed rites,
he offered him a seat and inquired after his well-being;
then Rāma spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira.
O best of kings, I have heard from the sages as they spoke words that were sweet, consistent with the Dharma, and truly beneficial for heroes:
that Kurukṣetra is supremely meritorious, purifying, and leads to heaven.
It is frequented by gods, sages, and high-souled brahmins. O noble one, those men who cast off their bodies there while fighting shall have a certain residence in heaven together with Śakra.
"O lord of the people, let us go quickly from here to Samantapañcaka;
it is renowned as the northern sacrificial altar (*uttaravedī*) of Prajāpati in the world of the gods. It is the most meritorious and eternal site in the three worlds."
"Having met his death in battle, heaven will certainly be his. Having said, "So be it," O Great King, the heroic and powerful Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, set out toward Samantapañcaka.
Then King Duryodhana, seizing his great mace,
the radiant one, went on foot in indignation toward the Pāṇḍavas. As he proceeded thus, mace in hand and clad in armor, [the Pāṇḍavas beheld him].
The gods dwelling in the intermediate space honored him, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!
And the men there who were skilled in speech attained great joy upon seeing him.
Surrounded by the Pāṇḍavas, that son of yours, the king of the Kurus, [shone forth].
Adopting the gait of a lordly elephant in rut, he proceeded;
then, by the blare of conchs, the great sounds of kettledrums,
and the lion-roars of the heroes, all the quarters were filled.
Then those best of men reached Kurukṣetra,
proceeding toward the western region as directed by their son;
and having arrived, they encircled it on all sides in every direction.
To the south of the Sarasvatī is the supreme bathing-place of Svayaṃnāma;
in that region, on ground free from barrenness, they chose to engage in battle.
Then Bhīma, clad in armor, took up his mace, which was as massive as a mountain peak.
O great king, assuming a form truly like that of Garuḍa,
your son shone in battle— wearing a bound head-protector and clad in golden armor— like a golden king of mountains, O monarch.
Both heroes, Bhīma and Duryodhana, were covered in armor;
in that encounter, they appeared like two enraged elephants.
Standing in the midst of the circle of battle, those two brothers were bulls among men.
O Great King, they shone like the risen sun and moon;
they glared at one another like two enraged great elephants,
O King, burning each other with their eyes and desiring to slay one another.
O King, with a heart full of joy, the Kaurava took up his mace;
licking the corners of his mouth, O King, his eyes bloodshot with rage and panting,
the valiant King Duryodhana then seized his mace.
Glaring at Bhīmasena, he challenged him like one elephant challenging another.
Likewise, the valiant Bhīma, taking up a club made of the essence of stone,
challenged the king as a lion challenges a lion in the forest.
With maces raised in their hands, Duryodhana and Vṛkodara shone in that encounter like two mountains with their peaks;
both were intensely enraged, and both possessed terrible prowess.
Both were disciples in the art of mace-fighting of the wise son of Rohiṇī;
both were equal in their deeds, like Yama and Vāsava,
and likewise equal in their deeds, possessing great strength like Varuṇa.
O great king, those two were like Vāsudeva and Rāma, as well as Vaiśravaṇa; in battle they resembled Madhu and Kaiṭabha,
and both were equal in their deeds to Sunda and Upasunda in combat.
Rāma and Rāvaṇa, as well as Vālin and Sugrīva—
those two scorchers of foes were equal to Time and Death themselves,
charging at one another like two elephants in rut.
Arrogant in their union with their consorts like two rutting elephants in autumn, those two bulls of the Bharata race were like two intoxicated elephants eager for victory;
both were like serpents vomiting forth the blazing venom of their wrath.
Glaring at one another, those two subduers of enemies,
both tigers among the Bharatas, were endowed with great prowess;
like two unassailable lions, they were scorchers of foes in a mace-duel.
Those two heroes, armed with claws and fangs, were as difficult to withstand as tigers;
agitated for the destruction of creatures, they were as hard to cross as the oceans;
and like two enraged red-bodied planets (Mars), those great chariot-warriors scorched everything in their path.
Like two clouds born in the east and west, agitated by the wind,
roaring most violently and pouring down rain as if in the monsoon;
so too were those two great-souled ones, radiant, effulgent, and possessed of great strength.
The two best of the Kurus appeared like two suns risen at the end of time;
like two highly enraged tigers, or like two roaring clouds,
those mighty-armed ones rejoiced like two maned lions.
Like two elephants in a great fury, like two blazing fires,
those two high-souled ones appeared like two peaked mountains;
their lips quivering with rage, they glared at one another.
Those two high-souled ones, the best of men, met together with maces in hand;
both were exceedingly joyful and both were highly esteemed, neighing like noble steeds and trumpeting like elephants.
Roaring like two bulls, Duryodhana and Vṛkodara shone like two Daityas intoxicated with strength— those two best of men. Then,
O King, Duryodhana said this to Yudhiṣṭhira:
Together with his brothers, the high-souled Kṛṣṇa,
and Rāma of immeasurable prowess,
he stood amidst the Sṛñjayas like the scorching sun, uttering words esteemed for their heroic valor.
"Protected by the Kekayas, the Sṛñjayas, and the high-souled Pāñcālas,
this battle has been resolved between both myself and Bhīma.
Sit down, O best of kings, and witness the clash."
Having heard the words of Duryodhana, they agreed to it accordingly. Then that vast circle of kings, seated together,
appeared resplendent like the orb of the sun in the sky.
In their midst, O great king, sat the glorious and mighty-armed elder brother of Keśava; being honored on all sides,
he shone resplendent in the center of the kings, clad in blue garments and possessing a white radiance.
Like the moon surrounded by the constellations at night,
O great king, those two, maces in hand and difficult to approach,
stood facing each other, lacerating one another with fierce words.
Then, having spoken unpleasant words to one another, those two bulls of the Kuru race stood gazing at each other like Vṛtra and Śakra in battle.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O Janamejaya, there occurred a tumultuous battle of words—
tumultuous and hair-raising— which increased their fury and reached its ultimate intensity.
Where King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, overcome by grief, spoke these words:
"Fie upon human existence, whose end is such as this!
For my son, the lord of eleven armies, has been overpowered."
Having commanded all the kings and enjoyed this earth,
he took up his mace and set out for battle on foot with great speed;
for though he was the lord of the world, my son now appears as if he were helpless.
"Raising his mace, he goes forth; what else can this be but fate?
Alas, O Sañjaya, a great sorrow has been encountered by my son!
Having spoken thus, the lord of men, afflicted by grief, fell silent.
09,055.006 Sañjaya said: 09,055.006a Then that valiant hero, roaring with joy like a bull bellowing like a cloud, challenged Pārtha to battle in the fray.
When the high-souled Kuru king was challenging Bhīma,
Bhīma then challenged Suyodhana to battle.
While the high-souled Bhīmasena was thus challenging him, [the encounter began].
Most terrible forms of various kinds appeared;
winds blew with thunderous crashes, a rain of dust fell,
and all the directions became shrouded in darkness.
Great sounds accompanied by thunderclaps, tumultuous and hair-raising, arose;
likewise, meteors fell by the hundreds, bursting through the surface of the sky. And Rāhu swallowed the sun out of season, O lord of the people.
The earth, along with its forests and trees, trembled with a great trembling; harsh winds blew from below, raining down gravel,
and the very peaks of the mountains fell upon the surface of the ground.
Deer of many forms rushed from the ten directions; jackals, blazing and of terrible aspect, howled most dreadfully;
and there were most horrific thunderclaps that made one's hair stand on end.
O Indra among kings, in a direction ablaze with ill omen, beasts uttered inauspicious cries;
the waters in the wells swelled up on all sides,
and then, O monarch, great disembodied sounds were heard.
Having observed these and other such omens, Vṛkodara then spoke to his eldest brother, the King of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira:
"This dull-witted Suyodhana is not capable of defeating me in battle."
Today I shall release the anger that has long been hidden within my heart, like the fire at Khāṇḍava against Suyodhana, the lord of the Kauravas; today,
O Pāṇḍava, I shall extract the thorn that dwells in your heart.
Having slain this wicked one, the lowest of the Kuru lineage,
with my mace today, I shall place upon you a garland composed of glory,
having struck down this evildoer with my mace at the forefront of the battle.
"Today I shall split his body into a hundred pieces with this mace;
he shall not enter the city named after the elephant again. For the release of serpents upon his bed and the administration of poison in his food—"
O sinless one, [you shall experience] the fall from the pinnacle of authority, the burning in the house of lac, the mockery in the assembly hall, the seizure of all your possessions,
a year of living in concealment, and dwelling in the forest.

"O best of the Bharatas, today you shall reach the end of these sufferings— the infliction of pain upon Draupadī and the stripping away of her garments. By slaying him in a single day, I shall be free from my debt to myself."
O best of the Bharatas, today the life of the evil-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son has come to an end, as has his sight of his mother and father.
O Indra among kings, today the happiness of that wicked-minded Kuru king has likewise perished.
O Great King, the sight of women is now finished once and for all. Today, this defiler of the lineage of Śantanu, the king of the Kurus,
shall lie upon the earth, having abandoned his life-breaths, his fortune, and his kingdom.
"And today, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard that his son has been slain by me,
will remember that evil deed which was born of Śakuni’s counsel.
Having spoken thus, O tiger among kings, the valiant one took up his mace.
Like Śakra challenging Vṛtra, he stood ready for battle.
Seeing him with his mace raised, resembling the peaked Mount Kailāsa,
Bhīmasena, filled once more with rage, spoke to Duryodhana.
For the sake of you, O evil-minded one, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra has suffered, as have you yourself,
and all of us have likewise fallen into misery, O wicked-souled one.
Remember that evil deed which was committed at Vāraṇāvata,
and how Draupadī was tormented in the assembly hall while she was in her courses,
and how the king was cheated at dice by you and the son of Subala.
The great suffering we endured in the forest on your account, and that which we suffered in the city of Virāṭa as if we had entered another womb—
all of that I shall now exact upon you, O evil-minded one, for by good fortune you have been seen!
On your account, that powerful son of Gaṅgā, the best of chariot-warriors, lies slain upon a bed of arrows, killed by the son of Yajñasena;
and Droṇa has been killed, as well as Karṇa and the powerful Śalya.

Śakuni, the son of Subala and the original instigator of the fire of enmity, has been slain; likewise, the wicked Prātikāmī, who caused Draupadī such suffering, has been killed. All your brothers have been slain—heroes who were valiant warriors.
"These and many other kings have been slain on your account;
today I shall slay you with my mace—of this there is no doubt.
Thus spoke Vṛkodara loudly, O Indra among kings.
"O King, your son, whose prowess is truth, spoke thus, free from fear:
'What is the use of this much boasting? Fight, O Vṛkodara!
Today, O lowest of your lineage, I shall destroy your desire for battle.'"
Thus addressed by Duryodhana, Vṛkodara replied:
"O base Duryodhana, no one like you can truly terrify me with words, as one might terrify an ordinary man."

"By good fortune, this battle with maces, long desired by me and cherished in my heart, has been brought about by the gods through you. O evil-minded one, what is the use of speaking at length or boasting?"
"Let this word be fulfilled through action; do not delay.
Having heard those words of his, all the kings and the Somakas who were assembled there offered him their praise.
Then, honored by all and with his hair standing on end from joy,
that delighter of the Kurus again made his mind firm for battle. The lords of men [applauded] him, like an elephant in rut, with the clapping of their hands.
They further incited the impatient Duryodhana;
then the high-souled Vṛkodara, the son of Pāṇḍu, raising his mace, rushed with speed toward that high-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
There the elephants trumpeted and the horses neighed repeatedly;
even the weapons of the Pāṇḍavas, who were desirous of victory, blazed forth.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Duryodhana, seeing Bhīmasena in such a state,
advanced against him with great speed and a loud roar, his spirit undaunted. They rushed at one another, bellowing like two horned bulls.
A great roar of crashing thunder arose from their clash,
and between them there occurred a tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end,
like the combat between Indra and Prahlāda as they sought to conquer one another in war.
Roaring like two bulls, Duryodhana and Vṛkodara moved in circular maneuvers with their maces held ready in their hands,
both in the paths of circling turns and in the striking with the maces.
