The battle between those two lions among men was without distinction; that mace of Bhīma, as it whirled about, appeared like blazing tongues of fire, terrifying and radiant with its bright, molten-golden surface.
Struck by the mace of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, O Great King, Bhīma’s mace emitted flames of fire during that mace-duel;
it released a shower of glowing coals, which was like a marvel.
Like two great elephants with their tusks or two mighty bulls with their horns,
those two shone as they struck one another with their maces, remaining unhurt; yet when their limbs were struck by the mace, they were instantly drenched in blood.

Struck violently on his left side with the mace by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena did not waver, like an immovable mountain; he appeared most beautiful to behold, like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
Then, being struck again and again by the force of Bhīma’s mace,
he writhed and freed himself, like a rogue elephant throwing off its mahout;
and the sound of those two lions among men was heard in all directions.
The crashing sound of the falling maces was like the roar of two thunderbolts.
Having struck each other with those great maces and then withdrawn, the two of great heroism stood once more upon the excellent path and moved in circular maneuvers.
Then, having rushed at one another, the two heroes stood with their great maces raised;
indeed, being struck by those iron rods, they both fell down. Springing up again with speed, they moved in circles.
Then those two heroes, powerful in their specific skills of action, displayed themselves with maces raised like two mountains with peaks;
they struck one another like two mountains during an earthquake.
Severely struck by each other’s maces due to their mutual agitation, those two heroes fell down simultaneously; yet, having recovered their senses, they rose up together.
Though both were deeply struck in their vital organs, they remained utterly overwhelmed.

Those two of great strength, their entire bodies drenched in blood, maces in hand and high-minded, were seen by the onlookers as they vied with one another— those two great-souled ones appearing like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom.
While that most terrible great battle was thus proceeding,
the sky shone forth beautifully as if filled with swarms of fireflies;
so it appeared while that tumultuous and exceedingly chaotic conflict continued.

"O dear one, in that terrible battle, both of those subduers of enemies, filled with intense fury, became utterly exhausted while fighting. After resting for a moment, those two scorchers of foes once again [prepared for combat]."
There, having firmly grasped their beautiful maces, they both attacked one another; seeing those two bulls among men, possessed of great heroism and fully composed,
they were like two powerful elephants intoxicated with rut for the sake of a female elephant.
Beholding both of them, possessed of boundless prowess and grasping their maces,
the gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas were struck with the utmost wonder. Seeing Duryodhana and Vṛkodara with their maces raised, they were filled with amazement.
Doubt arose among all living beings regarding victory. Then,
having come together once more, those two brothers, the best among the strong,
sought each other's weaknesses and moved against one another's vulnerabilities.
O King, the spectators beheld that heavy, fierce, and murderous mace of Bhīmasena as he whirled it in battle— a weapon resembling the staff of Yama and raised like the thunderbolt of Indra.
A very loud and terrible noise arose for a moment. Then,
beholding the son of Pāṇḍu brandishing that mace of no small velocity, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was struck with amazement.
Moving through various paths and circles, O Bhārata,
the hero Vṛkodara then shone forth even more brilliantly.
Having encountered one another, as they both exerted themselves in protecting each other, [the battle raged on].
Like two cats for the sake of prey, they struck at each other again and again;
Bhīmasena, however, moved through various paths,
as well as diverse circular maneuvers and manifold positions.
The *gomūtrikā* (cow’s urine) patterns, various maneuvers, and the *gatapratyāgata* (going and returning); the evasion of blows,
dodging, charging forward, the throw, and the firm stand.
Expert in mace-fighting, they performed maneuvers of turning away and turning toward, leaping down and leaping up,
advancing and retreating; as they moved in this manner, they struck one another.
Deceiving one another once more, those two best of the Kurus moved about; sporting with great strength, they circled in various mandalas.
Then, mace in hand, those two powerful warriors stood poised in their respective mandalas.
O King, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra moved in a rightward circle,
while Bhīmasena moved in a leftward circle there at the head of the battle; as Bhīma was thus maneuvering, [the enemy]—
O great king, Duryodhana struck him on the side. Struck then by your son, O Bhārata, Bhīma disregarded that blow and whirled his heavy mace.
O great king, they beheld that terrible mace of Bhīmasena, which was like Indra’s thunderbolt and raised like the staff of Yama. Seeing Bhīmasena brandishing his mace, your son—
Raising his terrible mace,
O King, that subduer of enemies struck back at his foe; it was as fearsome as the staff of Yama,
O Bhārata, by the force of the wind generated by the mace of your son.
A very tumultuous sound arose and a fiery energy was produced;
there was a great sound there, tumultuous and hair-raising.
Moving through various paths and circular maneuvers in their respective divisions, he [advanced].
The radiant Suyodhana shone even more intensely than Bhīma. That great mace, hurled with all his might by Bhīma,
fierce and loud-sounding, released fire accompanied by smoke and flames.
Seeing the mace being brandished by Bhīmasena, which emitted flames and sparks of fire on all sides, Suyodhana shone greatly as he whirled his own heavy mace made of the essence of stone.
Indeed, upon seeing the force of the mace-wind of that high-souled one,
fear entered all the Pāṇḍavas along with the Somakas.
Displaying their martial play in every direction throughout the battle, those two [continued their combat].
Those two subduers of enemies suddenly struck each other with their maces;
having encountered one another like two elephants with their tusks,
O great king, they both shone, drenched in blood.
Thus did that battle of terrible form unfold,
unrestrained and cruel, like the encounter between Vṛtra and Vāsava when the day had turned;
and seeing Bhīma standing firm, your mighty son [advanced].
Moving along most wonderful paths, he rushed toward the son of Kuntī;
then Bhīma, enraged, struck that gold-adorned mace of his as the other was likewise furious and possessed of great speed.

O great king, from the collision of those two [clubs], a sound accompanied by sparks arose, like that produced when two thunderbolts are hurled. By that forceful [club] released there by Bhīmasena, [the earth was shaken].
O Great King, as it fell, the earth trembled;
the Kuru prince could not endure that mace being parried in battle,
like an enraged elephant at the sight of a rival elephant.
O King, having whirled his left [leg] in a circle and being firm in his resolve,
he struck the son of Kuntī on the head with a mace of terrible velocity. Struck by that [mace] by your son, Bhīma, the Pāṇḍava—

O great king, he did not tremble; it was like a marvel. And that wonder, O king, all the troops honored, seeing that though struck by the mace, Bhīma did not waver even a single step from his position.
Then Bhīma of terrible prowess hurled at Duryodhana a heavy, blazing mace adorned with gold. The mighty one,
remaining unperturbed, met that blow with great agility.
Duryodhana’s effort was in vain, and there arose a great wonder. But that mace, O King, hurled by Bhīma as it fell,
made the earth tremble with a sound like a mighty thunderclap.
Leaping again and again along the paths of the *kauśika* birds,
your son rendered the descent of Bhīma’s mace futile through his skillful action;
seeing Bhīmasena deprived of his mace, he rushed toward him.
O King, having set out, that son of Kuntī advanced toward the space between three chariots;
perceiving the impending fall of the mace, he eluded Bhīmasena.
Having thus deceived Bhīma with his mace, that best of the Kurus—
Enraged, the mighty one struck him in the region of the chest with his mace.
Struck by the mace and fainting in that great battle, Bhīma—
being struck by your son— did not know what ought to be done.
While that was occurring, O King, the Somakas and the Pāṇḍavas became deeply discouraged in their resolve and were dejected in spirit;
but he, enraged by that blow like an elephant, [rushed forward].
Like an elephant rushing toward another elephant,
he charged at your son; then the impetuous Bhīma, with his mace, rushed with speed against your son, like a lion against a wild elephant.
Approaching the king,
O monarch, he who was skilled in the discharge of the mace whirled his mace, aiming it at your son;
then Bhīmasena struck Duryodhana in the side.
Overwhelmed by that blow, he fell to the earth upon his knees.
O Lord of the World, when that best of the Bharatas had thus fallen to the ground on his knees,
a great roar then arose from the Sṛñjayas.
Hearing that roar of the Sṛñjayas, O bull among men,
your son, the best of the Bharatas, was filled with indignation and grew furious.
Rising up, the mighty-armed one hissed like an enraged serpent.
As if wishing to consume him with his eyes, he glared at Bhīmasena;
then that best of the Bharatas, mace in hand,
rushed forward as if intending to crush Bhīmasena’s head in the encounter.
That great-souled one of terrible prowess struck the great-souled Bhīma on the temple; though struck, he who resembled a mountain did not waver.
Struck by the mace in battle, that son of Pṛthā shone even more brilliantly.
O King, with blood gushing forth like an elephant in rut,
Bhīma of terrible prowess became enraged, O great monarch,
and then [hurled] his iron mace, the slayer of heroes.
Seizing [his mace], which resounded like a thunderbolt,
the elder brother of Dhanañjaya, the crusher of enemies, exerted his strength and prowess and struck his foe.
Struck by Bhīmasena, your son fell down, his bodily frame trembling violently,
like a tree in full bloom struck down by the force of the wind.
Like a *sāla* tree shaken in a great forest, he fell;
then the Pāṇḍavas roared and rejoiced upon seeing your son fallen upon the earth.
Then your son, having regained consciousness,
leapt up like an elephant from a lake;
that king was then constantly filled with indignation.
The great car-warrior, maneuvering with practiced skill,
struck the Pāṇḍava who stood before him;
with his limbs overwhelmed, he touched the earth.
Having struck Bhīma down upon the earth by his might in battle, that Kaurava let out a lion’s roar;
and with a splendor equal to a thunderbolt, he pierced him as well.
By the falling of the mace, his body was protected;
then a great roar arose in the sky from the gods and the Apsarases who were shouting.
And a magnificent rain of various flowers, cast down from on high by the immortals, fell; then,
a supreme fear entered the enemies.
Having observed that best of men fallen upon the ground,
yet seeing that the Kaurava had not lost his strength and noting the penetration of his firm armor;
Then, after a moment, having regained consciousness and wiped his own blood-stained face,
he steadied himself with fortitude, his eyes rolling.
Vṛkodara stood there, having steadied himself with great strength;
then followed the two twins, who were like Yama in prowess,
along with the son of Pṛṣata and the heroic son of Śini.
Calling out "I am here! I am here! and hastening forward, they rushed toward your son, seeking his death;
but the mighty Pāṇḍava seized them once again.
Approaching your son himself like Time,
the Lord of the Gods moved about, free from fatigue and trembling, as he did against Namuci in the supreme battle.
09,057.001 Saṃjaya said:
09,057.001a Then, having seen the battle between the two leaders of the Kurus thus fully roused,
Arjuna spoke to the illustrious Vāsudeva.
"Between these two heroes in battle, who do you consider the superior?
Or which one possesses the greater qualities? Tell me this, O Janārdana.
Vāsudeva said:
The instruction for these two was equal, yet Bhīma is more powerful;
however, this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra has exerted greater effort than Vṛkodara.
But Bhīmasena, fighting according to the rules of dharma, will not be victorious.
"Indeed, by fighting unfairly, he shall slay Suyodhana.
We have heard that the Asuras were conquered by the gods through illusion,
and that Virocana, O friend, was defeated by Śakra through illusion."
The slayer of Bala withdrew Vṛtra’s splendor by means of his illusory power (*māyā*).
Therefore, let Bhīma employ his formidable prowess consisting of *māyā*;
let the heroic Bhīma, relying upon his strength, fulfill his pledge.
"O Dhanañjaya, at the time of the gambling match, Bhīma vowed:
'In battle, I shall break Suyodhana's thighs with my mace. Having fulfilled that vow, this crusher of enemies—"
And let him destroy the deceitful king by means of deceit itself. If he relies on his strength and strikes according to the rules of fair combat,
then King Yudhiṣṭhira will find himself in a precarious position.
I shall speak further; listen to me, O Pāṇḍava.
Due to the transgression of Dharmarāja, fear has come upon us once again, for we have performed a most great deed by slaying the Kurus headed by Bhīṣma.
Victory has been won, supreme fame attained, and enmity avenged. Yet, in this way, that very victory which was achieved has once again been rendered doubtful.
O Pāṇḍava, this is a great lack of foresight on the part of Dharmarāja.

Since such a battle was staked upon the victory of a single man—Suyodhana being a skilled hero who has likewise reached this final pass—it is heard that this ancient verse was sung by Uśanas: [The verse follows: "Even if one hundred years have passed, a wise man should not abandon hope; for even a small root, when watered, eventually grows into a great tree."
Listen as I recite these nine thousand five hundred and seven verses, which contain the true meaning of reality. Regarding this matter, there is indeed an ancient verse that has been fixed;
it was heard by Uśanas and is celebrated by the virtuous who are experts in the science of ethics.
One must fear the remnants of the enemy who are retreating, broken, and seeking to live, for they have reached a single path; likewise,
one must fear those who have suddenly fled in desperation, having lost all hope for their lives.
"Even Śakra himself, O Dhanañjaya, would not be able to stand before this Suyodhana, who is broken, whose army is slain, who has entered the lake,
who is defeated, who seeks the forest, and who is hopeless of regaining the kingdom."
Who indeed, being wise, would again challenge him to a duel in combat? Might not Suyodhana seize back even your conquered kingdom—
he who has practiced diligently with the mace for thirteen years?
He moves both upwards and across, desiring to slay Bhīmasena. If the mighty-armed one does not kill him by unrighteous means,
this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall become your Kuru king.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Keśava, Dhanañjaya,
while Bhīmasena was looking on, struck him on the thigh with his hand. Then, regaining his composure, Bhīma moved about the battlefield with his mace.
O King, the son of Pāṇḍu moved through various wonderful circular maneuvers— both *yamaka* and others—
as well as the rightward circle, the leftward circle, and the "cow's urine" pattern,
as if utterly bewildering his enemy.
In the same way, your son also, skilled in the maneuvers of the mace,
moved with agility and grace, desiring to slay Bhīmasena; both of them brandished their terrible maces, which were smeared with sandalwood and aloe-wood paste.
Seeking to reach the end of their enmity, like two enraged Deaths in battle,
those two preeminent heroes, bulls among men, desiring to slay one another,
fought like two Garuḍas seeking the flesh of a serpent.
As the two kings, Bhīma and Nṛpa, moved in various wonderful circles,
sparks of fire were produced there from the impact of their clubs. As those two powerful heroes struck each other simultaneously in that battle, flames burst forth.
O King, as they struck each other equally like two rutting elephants, the sound of their blows arose like the roar of two oceans agitated by the wind.
In that fierce and extremely tumultuous battle at that time,
both of those subduers of enemies became utterly exhausted from fighting. Having rested for a moment, those two scorchers of foes once again [prepared themselves].
Enraged, they seized their great maces and struck at one another;
between them there occurred a battle of terrible form, unrestrained,
O king of kings, as they lacerated each other with the blows of their maces.
Exerting themselves with great speed, those two powerful heroes with eyes like bulls struck one another like two buffaloes stuck in the mud;
their entire bodies were mangled and they were drenched in blood.
They appeared like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom upon the Himalayas;
but when Duryodhana had revealed a vulnerability, Pārtha,
smiling slightly, suddenly rushed forward.
Seeing him come close in battle, the wise and mighty Vṛkodara hurled his mace at him with great force. O lord of the people, seeing that discharge of the weapon, your son—
Then, recoiling from that spot, the [mace] fell fruitlessly to the ground;
having thus evaded that blow, your son,
that best of the Kurus, struck Bhīmasena with his mace in great agitation.
As Bhīma, of immeasurable prowess, was drenched by his own flowing blood, and as his eyes were bloodshot with rage,
a state like fainting came over him due to the heavy impact of the blow.
Duryodhana knew that the Pāṇḍava was afflicted in battle;
yet Bhīma, though his body was extremely tormented, sustained himself,
for he considered him still standing and about to strike in the fray.
Therefore, your son did not strike him again.
Then, O King, having rested for a moment while Duryodhana stood there,
the powerful Bhīmasena rushed at him with great speed.
O bull of the Bharata race, beholding him rushing forward in fury with immeasurable energy, your high-minded son, desiring to render that blow futile, resolved to hold his ground.
O King, wishing to deceive Vṛkodara, he desired to leap up;
Bhīmasena perceived that intention of the king,
and then, having rushed toward him and leaped over him like a lion, [he seized him].
O King, as he was attempting to evade by his movement and was about to spring up once more, the son of Pāṇḍu hurled the mace with great force at his thighs. That mace,
equal in impact to a thunderbolt, was launched by him of terrible deeds.
Then he broke the two beautiful thighs of Duryodhana;
that tiger among men fell, making the earth resound,
his thighs shattered by Bhīmasena, O lord of the earth, your son.
Winds accompanied by thunderclaps blew, and a rain of dust fell;
the earth, along with its trees, shrubs, and mountains, trembled as well,
when that hero, the lord of all kings, had fallen.
Then, O descendant of Bharata, a great meteor— loud-sounding, blazing, accompanied by a thunderclap, and terrifying—
fell as the lord of the earth fell;
likewise, there was a rain of blood and a rain of dust.
When your son had been struck down, Maghavan poured down rain there;
and a great roar of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and likewise Piśācas was heard in the sky, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then, from that terrible sound of the beasts and birds,
a most horrific clamor arose from the many creatures in every direction;
and those horses, elephants, and men who remained there [were struck with fear].
When your son was struck down, they let out a great roar;
there arose a mighty sound of kettledrums, conchs, and clay drums,
and even from within the earth, when your son had fallen.
O King, the quarters there were filled with headless trunks (kabandhas) of terrifying appearance, possessing many feet and many arms, dancing and inspiring fear;
they were likewise equipped with banners, missiles, and weapons.
Then, O King, when your son was struck down, the earth trembled;
O best of monarchs, the lakes and wells vomited forth blood,
and the rivers of great velocity began to flow backward.
O King, when your son Duryodhana had fallen, women appeared like men and men took on the forms of women;
seeing those miraculous portents, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas were struck with wonder.
O great king, all the Sṛñjayas were indeed great chariot-warriors;
O bull of the Bharatas, they all became agitated in mind,
while the Pāṇḍavas, together with the Sṛñjayas, were joyful in heart.
The gods, as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases, departed according to their desire,
O Bhārata, recounting that wonderful battle between your two sons. Likewise, O Indra among kings, did the Siddhas, Vātikas, and Cāraṇas depart.
Praising those two lions among men, they departed as they had come.
Sañjaya said:
Having then seen him fallen like a great, towering śāla tree...
All the Pāṇḍavas there became joyful in their hearts;
with their hair standing on end, they all gazed upon him like a maddened elephant struck down by a lion— all those Somakas as well.

Then, having slain Duryodhana, the powerful Bhīmasena approached that fallen lord of the Kauravas and spoke these words, O great king— Vṛkodara uttered a barb of speech that was exceedingly difficult to endure.
O dull-witted one, O evil-minded one, you who formerly mocked us in the assembly hall while Draupadī wore but a single garment, saying, "The cow! The cow!",
receive today the fruit of that derision.
Having spoken thus, he touched the crown with his left foot and trampled the head of that lion among kings with his foot.
In the same manner, Bhīma, the crusher of enemy forces, was inflamed with rage.
O lord of men, listen to these words he spoke once more:
"Those who previously danced before us, crying out again and again, 'A cow!
A cow!', we shall now dance back at them, crying out again and again, 'A cow! A cow!'"
Neither deceit, nor fire, nor gambling with dice, nor fraud, nor guile, nor even illusion belongs to us, as it does to this most evil-minded one;
relying on the strength of our own arms, we shall subdue our enemies.
Having reached the further shore of his supreme enmity,
Vṛkodara spoke slowly with a smile to Yudhiṣṭhira, Keśava, and the Sṛñjayas.
Those who brought Draupadī, while she was in her menses, before Dhanañjaya and the two sons of Mādravatī,
and those who made her naked in the assembly hall;
Behold those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas through the ascetic power of Yājñasenī—
those who formerly called us "sesame seeds without kernels."
The cruel sons of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been slain by us, along with their hosts and followers;
we shall go at our pleasure to heaven or to hell.
And again, as the king had fallen to the ground,
he beheld that mace resting upon his shoulder and crushed the king's head with his left foot.
"O King, Duryodhana was addressed as 'deceitful' by the delighted Bhīmasena, who, being of a base nature, kicked the foot of the Kuru monarch."
Seeing this done upon his head, the righteous leaders of the Somakas did not rejoice; nor did they approve when Vṛkodara, having thus slain your son, began to boast.
As he danced many times, Dharmarāja said this:
"You have discharged your debt of enmity; your vow has been fulfilled by you. Whether by auspicious or inauspicious action, cease now."

Do not crush his head with your foot; let not the great Law (*dharma*) pass you by. He who is the lord of eleven armies and the protector of even five [others]—his nature is not that of a mere mortal.
"O sinless one, this king, who was both a kinsman and a ruler, has been slain; this is not right for you.

O mighty-armed one, [if he were alive] he would have come to you, and that which is joined with unrighteousness should have been spoken. Do not crush the head of this lord of eleven armies with your foot."
Through the abandonment of dharma, both fame and great renown shall perish;
O sinless one, it is not right for you to strike one who has been struck down by a footstep—
such as the lord of the Kurus, the commander of eleven armies.
"O Bhīma, do not touch with your foot the king, who is indeed your kinsman.
His kinsmen have been slain, his ministers killed, his army destroyed, and he himself struck down in battle;
in every respect, this lord is to be pitied, not to be mocked."
"Ravaged, with his ministers slain, his brothers slain, and his progeny slain— his funeral offerings cut off and he himself a brother destroyed— this which you have done is not right.
Formerly, people used to say of you, 'That Bhīmasena is righteous.'"
"O Bhīmasena, why do you stand over the king?
Having seen King Duryodhana in such a state, the son of Kuntī,
with eyes filled with tears, spoke these words.
Having spoken thus to Bhīmasena, Yudhiṣṭhira, his throat choked with tears,
approached Duryodhana, the subduer of enemies, and spoke dejectedly:
"O dear one, you should not harbor anger, nor should you grieve for yourself in such a manner."
Surely we are experiencing the fruit of a most terrible deed committed in the past; surely this has been ordained by a powerful and high-souled Creator,
since we seek to kill you and you [seek to kill] us, O best of the Kurus.
O Bhārata, it is indeed through your own transgression— due to greed, pride, and folly— that you have encountered such great calamity,
having caused the slaughter of your friends, brothers, and likewise your fathers.
"Having slain your sons, grandsons, and teachers, you have now met your end.
Because of your transgression, we have killed those brothers of yours who were great chariot-warriors.
You should not grieve for yourself, O sinless one; your death is praiseworthy."
O Kaurava, we alone are now to be pitied in every circumstance; deprived of those beloved kinsmen, we shall live in misery,
overwhelmed with grief for our brothers and sons.

"How shall I see my widowed daughters-in-law overwhelmed by grief? O King, you alone remain well-established; your dwelling in heaven is certain, while we, indeed known as those destined for hell, shall endure terrible suffering."

Our kinsmen and others have been slain; I consider destiny to be insurmountable. Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law, overwhelmed and emaciated by grief as widows, will surely reproach us.
Having spoken thus, that king, afflicted by intense sorrow, sighed deeply;
and Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, lamented for a long time—
he who was great and naturally devoted to compassion.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sūta, having seen the king slain through unrighteousness, what did the mighty Baladeva, the best of the Mādhavas, say at that time?"
"O Sañjaya, tell me what the son of Rohiṇī, who was an expert in the special techniques of mace-fighting and skilled in mace-combat, did. Sañjaya said:
Seeing your son struck on the head by Bhīmasena,
Rāma, the strongest of the strong and the best among strikers, became violently enraged.
Then, in the midst of the lords of men, Halāyudha raised his arms.
Uttering a terrible cry of distress, he said, "Fie! Fie! Bhīma!
"Alas, fie! That a blow was struck below the navel upon one of pure prowess—this is something never seen before in a mace-duel, which Vṛkodara has now committed."
"It is the settled conclusion of the scriptures that one must not strike below the navel;
yet this fool, ignorant of the scriptures, acts according to his own will. As he spoke these words, a great rage arose within him.
Then, O Great King, beholding the king with eyes bloodshot with rage, Baladeva spoke these words:
"O Kṛṣṇa, this man has not merely fallen; he is simply my equal, the peerless one."
But because of the weakness of that which is supported, the supporter is reviled.
Then the powerful one, raising his formidable plow, rushed forward;
the form of that high-souled one with upraised arms was magnificent.
Like a great white mountain variegated with many minerals,
Madhusūdana, perceiving him rising up in a rage,
was accompanied by his brothers— Bhīma and Arjuna— who were experts in weaponry.
O Great King, the powerful one did not waver upon seeing the wielder of the plow; Keśava, bowing with humility, seized him as he was leaping up,
using his two firm, rounded arms with great effort and strength.
O Indra among kings, those two best of the Yadus— one fair and one dark— shone even more brilliantly together, like Mount Kailāsa and Mount Añjana joined,
or like the sun and moon in the sky at the end of the day, O King.
And Keśava spoke to him who was thus agitated, as if to pacify him:
"One's own advancement, the advancement of a friend, and likewise the rise of a friend's friend—this is the sixfold advancement for oneself; the opposite of this occurs among enemies."

When that which is contrary occurs even toward oneself or toward friends, one should know that it is a wasting of the mind; one should quickly perform rites for pacification. The Pāṇḍavas, whose prowess is pure, are our natural friends.
Your own sons, the sons of your paternal aunt, have been greatly humiliated by their enemies. You know well that fulfilling one's vow is the duty of a Kṣatriya;
therefore, in a great battle, I shall break the thighs of Suyodhana with my mace.
For this was previously vowed by Bhīma on the floor of the assembly hall;
moreover, O scorcher of foes, he had already been cursed long ago by the great seer Maitreya, who said:
"Bhīma shall break your thighs with his mace."
Therefore, I see no fault; do not be angry with me as I speak.
Those who are kinsmen by blood are indeed superior to those who are kinsmen by marriage;
likewise, the Pāṇḍavas became superior through their affection and their kinship.
"We are here bound to the Pāṇḍavas by ties of kinship and affection;
our prosperity increases through theirs. Do not be angry, O bull among men.
Having heard these words of Vāsudeva, the plow-wielder, who knows the dharma, spoke.
Rāma said:
Dharma, when well-practiced by the virtuous, restrains both [the other two goals]. But wealth belongs to one who is excessively greedy for it, and pleasure to one who is overly attached to it.
One who pursues virtue, wealth, and pleasure without oppressing either virtue and wealth,
or wealth and pleasure, enjoys ultimate happiness.
But all this has now been thrown into confusion by the oppression of virtue.
"O Govinda, Bhīmasena has spoken as you have told me.
Vāsudeva said:
"For he is free from anger, righteous in soul, and always devoted to dharma."
"You are renowned throughout the world; therefore, be appeased and do not be angry. Know that the Kali Yuga has arrived, and consider the vow of the Pāṇḍava.
Let the Pāṇḍava attain freedom from his debt to his enmity and his vow."
Therefore, that tiger among men, having slain the deceitful one in battle—
since he who would slay an enemy in battle by means of deceit against one skilled in deceit finds no unrighteousness therein— Bhīma has committed no wrong in killing his foe.
While that hero, who brings glory to the Kurus and Vṛṣṇis, was fighting in battle,
Karṇa, having been thus instructed by him, confidently severed his bow.
Then, with his bow shattered and deprived of his chariot, he remained steadfast in his manliness.
Having turned his weapons against him, he slew the son of Subhadrā, who did not flee;
from birth this evil-minded one has been greedy and sinful,
a wicked soul and a disgrace to his lineage, now struck down by Bhīmasena.
Why does he not recognize Bhīmasena’s vow, earned through thirteen years, while fighting? For Vṛkodara, leaping upward with speed, was intent on slaying him.
With his mace, he shattered Bhīma’s thighs, neither in a fixed spot nor in a circular maneuver. "Let the highly wise and mighty Bhīmasena go today!
Saṃjaya said:
O lord of the people, even after hearing this deception of dharma from Keśava,
Rāma was not at all pleased in mind and spoke these words in the assembly:
"Having slain the righteous King Suyodhana by unrighteous means..."
"In this world, the Pāṇḍava will attain fame as one who fights with crookedness;
yet even Duryodhana, that righteous soul, the king and lord of men, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having been slain while fighting fairly, shall attain the eternal goal."
Having entered the initiation for battle and spread out the sacrifice of war on the field, he offered himself as an oblation into the fire of his enemies and attained the purificatory bath of glory;
that great king, together with his friends, kinsmen, and relatives, shall go to heaven.
Having spoken thus, the powerful son of Rohiṇī, whose form resembled the peak of a white cloud, mounted his chariot and set out toward Dvārakā;
and so too did the Pāñcālas, along with the Vārṣṇeyas and the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of the people.
When Rāma had departed for Dvāravatī, they were not at all cheerful.
Then Vāsudeva spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, who was dejected, lost in thought with his face cast down, and whose resolve was stricken by grief.
"O Dharmarāja, for what reason do you permit this unrighteousness—
that the head of Duryodhana, whose kinsmen have been slain, who is fallen and unconscious, is being trampled with his foot by Bhīma?"
"O Knower of Dharma, O Lord of Men, why do you look on with indifference?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, it is not pleasing to me that Vṛkodara [should have acted thus] toward the king."

In his rage, he touched my head with his foot; yet I do not rejoice at the destruction of my kin. We have been constantly humiliated by deceit by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and after they spoke many harsh words, we were sent away to the forest.
"O Vārṣṇeya, reflecting that Bhīmasena’s grief dwells excessively within his heart, I overlooked this matter. Therefore, having slain that foolish, greedy man who was subject to the power of desire,"
"Let the son of Pāṇḍu obtain his desire, whether he has acted righteously or unrighteously.
Sañjaya said:
When the King of Dharma had spoken thus, Vāsudeva replied as follows.
When Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and King of Dharma, had spoken thus,
the mighty-armed Vāsudeva addressed Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Let it be so," said the scion of the Yadu clan, with great difficulty.
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, who desired the welfare and pleasure of Bhīma,
Arjuna approved of everything that had been done by Bhīma in battle,
even though his inner soul was displeased.
He did not say a single word to his brother, whether good or bad.
Bhīmasena, however, having slain your son in battle, being impatient with rage,
stood before him with joined palms, bowing and filled with joy.
O lord of the people, the one of great splendor, appearing victorious with eyes wide open in joy, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma: "O King,
today the earth is yours— secure and with its thorns removed."
"O Great King, rule over her while observing your own dharma.
But he who was the author of this enmity through deceit— he who delighted in treachery— lies here slain upon the earth, O Lord of the Earth."
Duḥśāsana and all those others who spoke so harshly,
as well as the son of Rādhā and Śakuni— all your enemies have been slain.
This earth, filled with jewels and its forests and mountains, [is now yours].
"O Great King, she has returned today to you whose enemies have been slain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The destruction of our enmity has come; King Suyodhana has been killed."
"By following the counsel of Kṛṣṇa, this earth has been conquered.
By good fortune, you have discharged both your debt to your mother and your own wrath. By good fortune you are victorious, O invincible one; by good fortune the enemy has been struck down."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Saṃjaya, having seen Duryodhana slain by Bhīmasena in battle,
what did the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas do?"
Seeing that Duryodhana had been slain, O Sañjaya, Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata took their respective positions. Sañjaya said:
O great king, seeing Duryodhana slain by Bhīmasena in battle—
like a lion slaying a rutting wild elephant in the forest—
the Pāṇḍavas, together with Kṛṣṇa, were there with joyful hearts.
When the joy of the Kurus had been slain, the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas brandished their upper garments and let out lion-like roars;
this earth could not endure them as they were thus possessed by joy.
Some brandished their bows, while others likewise twanged their bowstrings;
some blew great conch shells, and others struck upon kettledrums.
And in that same way, your enemies sported and laughed.
And those heroes repeatedly spoke these words to Bhīmasena:
"A most difficult and exceedingly great deed has been performed by you today in battle,
having slain the lord of the Kauravas with your mace after he had exerted himself greatly in the fight."
For people considered this slaughter of the enemy by you to be like the slaying of Vṛtra by Indra in the supreme battle;
as you moved through various paths and in all directions, describing circular maneuvers.
Who else but Vṛkodara could have slain this hero Duryodhana? You have reached the further shore of this enmity, which is so difficult for others to traverse;
such a feat as this could not have been accomplished by anyone else.
O hero, by good fortune, you have crushed the head of Duryodhana with your foot at the front of the battle, like an intoxicated elephant;
having waged a wondrous struggle, you are like a lion against a buffalo.
O sinless one, by good fortune you have drunk the blood of Duḥśāsana!
By your own deed, you have placed your foot upon the heads of those who wronged the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira. By good fortune this has been accomplished through your own action.
"O Bhīma, by the destruction of your enemies and by the slaying of Duryodhana,
by good fortune your very great fame has been spread throughout the earth.
Thus, surely, when Vṛtra was slain, the bards rejoiced in Śakra."
O Bhārata, even so we rejoice that you have slain our enemies;
know this, O Bhārata, that those hairs of ours which bristled at the slaying of Duryodhana do not yet cease to thrill even today.
Thus spoke the assembled bards there to Bhīmasena. To those joyful tigers among men, the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas,
as they were speaking what was fitting there, Madhusūdana addressed them.
"O lords of men, it is not right to kill again one who has already been struck down.
For this dull-witted man has been struck many times by fierce words;
he was slain at that very moment when he became devoid of shame."
Greedy, associating with the wicked, and transgressing the instructions of his friends— though he has been told many times by Vidura, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Gaṅgā, and the Sṛñjayas,
"Give half the kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas," [he still refuses].
Although it was being proclaimed to the Pāṇḍus, he did not give them their paternal share. He has no concern for what is seen or even heard, even in stories;
such people, having transgressed the bounds of propriety, meet with such a fate in this world.
Having heard those words of his, which were spoken with such malice,
the king— blazing as it were with rage and trembling with fury—
thought: "This lowest of men is neither a friend nor an enemy fit for me today."
"What is the use of addressing one who is so utterly shattered by words, who is like a mere log?
O lords of the earth, mount your chariots quickly; let us depart.
By good fortune, this evil-souled man has been slain along with his ministers, kinsmen, and relatives."
O lord of the people, having heard this insult from Kṛṣṇa, King Duryodhana, overcome by indignation, rose up;
he sat upon his haunches, supporting himself on the earth with both arms.
Casting a fierce, frown-browed glance at Vāsudeva,
the king assumed a form with his body half-raised,
O Bhārata, like an enraged venomous serpent whose tail has been severed.
Disregarding the terrible, life-ending agony,
Duryodhana assailed Vāsudeva with fierce words:
"O heir of Kaṃsa’s slave, you have no shame indeed for this!"
Since I was struck down unrighteously in this mace-duel by you,
who falsely invoked Bhīma’s memory, saying, “Break his thighs,” was it not known to me that you had spoken thus to Arjuna?
Having caused thousands of kings who fought fairly to be slain by many crooked means, you feel neither shame nor compassion,
even as you daily inflict great slaughter upon those heroes.
Having placed Śikhaṇḍin at the forefront, your grandfather was slain;
and having killed an elephant named after Aśvatthāman, O evil-minded one,
the Teacher laid down his weapons— was that not known to you?
And that heroic one was seen by you being struck down by this cruel Dhṛṣṭadyumna, yet you did not restrain him;
nor did you prevent the spear that had been requested for the sake of slaying the son of Pāṇḍu.

You deceived Ghaṭotkaca; who is more wicked than you? Even the mighty Bhūriśravas, with his arm severed and having resolved upon fasting unto death, was slain by the evil-minded descendant of Śini (Sātyaki), acting under your instigation.
While performing his supreme duty with the desire to conquer the son of Pṛthā, Karṇa was indeed distressed by the calamity of Aśvasena, the son of the lord of serpents;
and when his wheel had sunk again, he was defeated and afflicted by misfortune.
If you had fought fairly in battle against me, Karna, Bhīṣma, and Droṇa— the foremost of men— while Karna was occupied with his wheel and thus struck down,
your victory would certainly not have been certain.
But by you, ignoble one, through a crooked path, we and other kings who were fulfilling our own duty have been slain. By you,
O Kṛṣṇa, a master of illusion, was employed that illusion which steals away the light of the sun.
"Having done so, the Lord of Sindhu was slain; is that not known to me?
Vāsudeva said:
"O Gāndhārī, you are as good as dead, along with your brothers, sons, and kinsmen."
Together with his followers and friends, he has followed the path of evil;
by your own misdeeds, the two heroes Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been struck down,
and Karṇa too has been slain in battle— he who always conformed to your character.
"O fool, though entreated by me, you did not wish to give the paternal share—
the half of your own kingdom— to the Pāṇḍavas out of greed and the counsel of Śakuni.
Poison was given by you to Bhīmasena, and [it was prepared] for all the Pāṇḍavas."
The evil-minded one, together with his mother, set fire to the house of lac;
and formerly at Vāraṇāvata, the Pāṇḍavas were indeed filled with sorrow.
And at the gambling match, Yājñasenī was dragged into the assembly hall while she was in her courses.
At that very moment, O evil-souled and shameless one, you deserved to be slain;
for you defeated with deceit the son of Subala— who was ignorant of dice yet conversant with dharma and skilled in the game— therefore you are killed in battle.

Because Kṛṣṇā was tormented in the forest by the wicked Jayadratha while you were away on a hunt, that cruel man has now been slain at the hermitage of Tṛṇabindu— both through his own fault and because of yours.

"O sinful one, because Abhimanyu, though but a boy, was slain alone by many in battle through your own transgressions, you have therefore been killed in this war. You speak thus, claiming that those improper acts were committed by us."
Because of your deficiency, all that was performed by you was done excessively wrongly;
you did not hear the instructions of Bṛhaspati or Uśanas,
nor did you serve the elders, and you did not listen to beneficial words.

Overpowered by exceedingly intense greed and by craving, you committed these improper deeds; now experience their ripening. While performing your actions in battle, you were intent on the interests of the Pāṇḍavas.
That Śikhaṇḍin slew Bhīṣma for the sake of a friend was no transgression; nor was it a violation when the Preceptor, having set aside his own duty out of a desire for your welfare,
was slain in battle by the son of Pṛṣata while he himself was treading the path of the unrighteous.
O King, desiring to make his own vow true in battle,
the wise Sātvata Arjuna slew the great car-warrior, the son of Somadatta,
while he was fighting in the fray at some point.

O evil-minded one, do not speak thus: that tiger among men did not slay Karṇa in battle because he remembered the conduct of heroes, even though he had found many openings and was censured in every way.
Having understood the intention of the gods and desiring their welfare,
I did not discharge the *Astra* weapon at Arjuna’s elephant by his own will.
You, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa likewise—
In the city of Virāṭa, they were saved by his compassion;
remember then the prowess displayed by Pārtha among the Gandharvas. O son of Gāndhārī, there was no unrighteousness on the part of the Pāṇḍavas toward you in that matter.
Relying on the strength of their own arms and acting according to their own duty, those heroes, the scorchers of the foe, have conquered in battle; you, being sinful, have met your destruction.
Duryodhana said:

I have studied according to the rules, I have given gifts, and I have ruled the earth together with its oceans; my enemies stand at my feet— who indeed is more fortunate than I, who has performed that which is desired by those of the kṣatriya lineage who observe their own duty?
This very end has now been reached; who indeed is more fortunate than I? Human enjoyments worthy of the gods, difficult for kings to obtain, have been attained by me;
supreme sovereignty has been attained—what indeed could be more fortunate than this?
"O Acyuta, I shall go to heaven together with my friends and my kinsmen;
you, however, with your purposes frustrated, shall live on in grief.
I have no cause for despair, even though my head was struck by Bhīma’s foot."
"A crow, or a heron, or a vulture will leave its mark upon it in an instant.
Sañjaya said:
"O Bhārata, at the conclusion of these words of the Kuru king..."
A great rain of flowers, fragrant with merit, fell;
the Gandharvas played their instruments and the hosts of Apsarases sang most enchanting music.
The Apsarases sang praises connected with the king’s glory, and the Siddhas uttered words of "Excellent! Excellent!", O Bhārata. And a fragrant wind blew, auspiciously scented, gentle, and pleasant.
The sky shone forth, stainless and resembling lapis lazuli.
Having seen those most wonderful sights, the Pāñcālas, together with the Somakas, headed by Vāsudeva, were struck with supreme amazement.
Seeing the honor paid to Duryodhana, they were overcome with shame; hearing that those who had been slain were killed unrighteously, they grieved, afflicted by sorrow,
having heard that the Kaurava lords of the earth had been slain contrary to dharma.
O bull of the Bharatas, all the Pāṇḍavas, afflicted with grief,
lamented for Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and Bhūriśravas as well.
Seeing those Pāṇḍavas dejected in spirit and lost in thought, [the people were moved].
Kṛṣṇa, whose voice resounded like a cloud or a drum, spoke these words:
"This man cannot be slain by you in battle through straightforward combat, for he possesses exceedingly swift weapons, as do all those valiant great chariot-warriors."
This king cannot ever be slain through righteous means,
nor can all those great archers and mighty chariot-warriors headed by Bhīṣma;
yet I shall repeatedly employ numerous stratagems and the application of *māyā*.
All of them have been slain in battle by me, who desires your welfare; for if I had never committed such a deceitful act in combat,
how could you have further victory, how a kingdom, and how wealth?
Indeed, these means were ordained by me for that reason, O lords of men;
otherwise, victory would never have belonged to the sons of Pāṇḍu.
For all those four high-souled ones are the greatest chariot-warriors (*atiratha*) on earth.
He cannot be slain according to the law even by the world-protectors themselves;
likewise, this son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, mace in hand and free from fatigue,
cannot be slain according to the law even by Time himself bearing his staff.

And you should not harbor in your hearts the thought that this king has been slain; for by various means, many superior enemies have been unjustly put to death. This is the path followed by the gods of old when they destroyed the asuras.
The path followed by the virtuous is followed by all;
such was the destruction ordained for these great-souled ones by the Creator. Fate cannot be overcome by human effort.
"He who shall destroy the past, the present, and the future in a mere twinkling of an eye—
he is this Dhanañjaya, who would not wish to act otherwise than the decree of Fate. Having accomplished our purpose, we find it agreeable to take up residence for the evening."
"O lords of men, let us all, along with our horses, elephants, and chariots,
take rest. Having heard these words of Vāsudeva, the Pāñcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, were then greatly delighted and roared like a pride of lions.
Then Mādhava blew his conch, Pāñcajanya;
Arjuna, with a joyful soul, blew Devadatta, that most excellent of conchs;
and King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, blew Anantavijaya.
Vṛkodara, the performer of terrible deeds, blew his great conch Pauṇḍra;
Nakula and Sahadeva blew Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka;
likewise, Dhṛṣṭadyumna blew Jaitra, and Sātyaki blew Nandivardhana.
O bull of the Bharata race, by the great sound of those conchs,
the entire sky was filled and the earth trembled.
Then there arose the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums, and horns.
In the Pāṇḍu armies, musical instruments were sounded, and that sound became tumultuous;
others praised the Pāṇḍavas with words of hymns and auspicious blessings,
while the panegyrists and reciters of praise offered their eulogies with verses endowed with auspiciousness.
Delighted to see Duryodhana slain, those bulls among men [departed].
Sañjaya said:
Then all those lords of the earth proceeded toward their quarters for rest.
Blowing their conchs and filled with joy, those whose arms were like iron clubs—
O lord of the people— the great archer Yuyutsu and likewise Sātyaki followed behind the Pāṇḍavas as they proceeded toward our camp.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, all the sons of Draupadī,
and all the other great archers likewise went to their own tents. Then those Pārthas entered [the camp], which was shorn of its splendor and whose lord had been slain.
Duryodhana’s camp, now that the people had dispersed like an audience leaving a theater,
resembled a city whose festivities have ended, or a lake from which the elephants have been taken;
it was filled mostly with women and eunuchs, and presided over by elderly ministers.
Then, O King, having reached the camp of the Kuru king, those Pāṇḍavas— led by Duryodhana, wearing soiled saffron-colored garments, and with palms joined in reverence— waited upon them.

O great king, those best of chariot-warriors descended from their chariots. Then Keśava, who always stands devoted to the welfare of his beloved friend, addressed the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, O bull of the Bharatas.
"String the Gāṇḍīva and take up the two inexhaustible quivers;
then, O best of the Bharatas, I shall descend after you.
You yourself should descend first, for this is for your own welfare, O sinless one."
And the heroic Dhanañjaya, son of Pāṇḍu, did exactly as he had been told. Then Kṛṣṇa, the wise one, letting go of the horses' reins, descended from the chariot of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Then, when the great-souled Lord of Beings had descended,
the divine monkey, the banner of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, vanished.
That great chariot-warrior had been consumed by Droṇa and Karṇa with their celestial weapons.
Then,
O lord of the earth, that chariot of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow— complete with its quiver, reins, horses, yoke, and frame— suddenly blazed up with fire and fell to the ground reduced to ashes.
O Lord, seeing him thus reduced to ashes, the sons of Pāṇḍu were struck with wonder, O King;
and Arjuna,
having prostrated himself and saluted him with affection and joined palms, spoke as follows.
"O Govinda, O Blessed One, why was this chariot burnt by fire?
What was this great marvel that occurred, O joy of the Yadus?
Tell me that, O mighty-armed one, if you think it is something I may hear."
Having heard Arjuna’s words, Janārdana spoke again.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Arjuna, this one has already been scorched by many kinds of weapons."
"O scorcher of foes, because it was presided over by me, it did not shatter in battle;
but now, having been released by me today when you had accomplished your task, O son of Kuntī, it has shattered and been consumed by the splendor of the Brahmā-weapon."
Saṃjaya said:
Smiling slightly, the Blessed Lord Keśava, the slayer of enemies,
embraced King Yudhiṣṭhira and spoke to him.
"By good fortune you are victorious, O Kaunteya; by good fortune your enemies have been conquered.
By good fortune the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava are well, as are you yourself, O King, and the two sons of Mādrī."

"O Bhārata, having been released from this battle in which heroes have perished and enemies have been slain, quickly perform the duties that lie before you. We have arrived at Upaplavya together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow."
"O Lord, when you previously brought me the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), you said:
'O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, this Dhanañjaya is both your brother and your friend; he must be protected by you in all calamities.'"
When you spoke thus, I replied, "So be it.
O lord of men, that Savyasācin is protected by you;
he is victorious, O king of kings, a hero of true prowess who dwells together with his brothers.
"Released from this hair-raising battle that has destroyed so many heroes,"—
having been addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, O great king, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
with his hair standing on end, replied to Janārdana.

O crusher of enemies, who other than you could withstand the Brahmāstra discharged by Droṇa and Karṇa— even the wielder of the thunderbolt, Purandara himself— against the chariot-warriors headed by Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, and Śalya?
But by your grace, many have been conquered in battle;
and that Pārtha, though engaged in a great conflict, did not turn his back [in retreat]. Likewise, O mighty-armed one, through many successive turns by me—
O giver of honor,
through your grace many have been slain in battle by Bhīmasena, by me, and by the two sons of Yama; in deed, thought, and speech, you are our supreme refuge.
"The continuity of actions and the auspicious course of energy—this the great seer Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana told me at Upaplavya:
'Where there is Dharma, there is Kṛṣṇa; where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is victory.'"
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa then replied to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O Bhārata, you have eighteen akṣauhiṇīs, and they [the Pāṇḍavas] have as many;
yet, O joy of the Kurus, Arjuna here is not equal to them in strength."

Having obtained all those divine weapons from Śaṅkara, O Pāṇḍava, he was granted permission [by him], saying, "In battle you shall be equal to me or even superior to me. Thus authorized, the son of Pāṇḍu returned once more to the earth.
"O Lord, if you grant permission for what has been, what is, and what is yet to come,
it is my conviction that this tiger among men could, in half a moment,
slay Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Jayadratha."
In his anger, Dhanañjaya could destroy in half a moment all the gods,
asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and kiṃnaras;
indeed, he is capable of conquering even the three worlds— how much more so these mere mortals here?
Although he was ordained by fate and even urged by me,
Kṛtānta, being exceedingly powerful, did not set his mind on killing him.
O Lord of the Earth, in this regard, I have sung these true words well.
Everything was shown to me by him, and thus he conquered his enemies;
O lord of the earth, even the mighty-armed Arjuna is my equal. What could that powerful one not accomplish, having obtained the weapons from Maheśvara?
When this had been said, O Bhārata, those heroes entered your camp and took possession of the stores of treasure,
gems, and wealth; they seized silver, gold, jewels, and pearls.
Then there were excellent ornaments, woolen blankets, and skins;
elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as large couches;
countless male and female slaves, and all the requisites for a kingdom.
O bull of the Bharatas, having obtained that inexhaustible wealth of yours,
those great archers, who had conquered their enemies, raised a loud shout, O lord of men.
Then those heroes, having rested and unyoked their mounts, [proceeded].
All the Pāṇḍavas, as well as Sātyaki, stood still for a moment.
Then, O Great King, the highly illustrious Vāsudeva said:
"For the sake of our welfare, we must dwell outside the camp."
"Go without delay to where the goddess Jayantī resides;
this vow has been made by me as a preparation for the commencement of battle. Having said, "So be it," all those Pāṇḍavas and Sātyaki likewise departed.

Accompanied by Vāsudeva, they went outside for the sake of auspiciousness. Having reached the sacred river Oghavatī, O King, the Pāṇḍavas, whose enemies had been slain, then dwelt there for that night.

Then King Yudhiṣṭhira reflected upon what was appropriate for the occasion. Thereupon, they dispatched the Yādava to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura). And the powerful Vāsudeva departed with great speed.

Having placed Dāruka upon the chariot, they spoke to him as he was about to depart for where King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, was— whose army and Sūta Sugrīva were his mounts: "Console the illustrious Gāndhārī, whose sons have been slain."
Thus addressed by the Pāṇḍavas, that best of the Sātvatas set out for that city,
desiring to quickly reach Gāndhārī, whose sons had been slain.
Janamejaya said:

For what purpose did Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of dharma and tiger among kings, send Vāsudeva, the scorcher of foes, to Gāndhārī? For when Kṛṣṇa had previously gone to the Kauravas for the sake of peace...
He did not obtain that desire, and therefore this battle took place;
for when the warriors had been slain and Duryodhana likewise killed,
the earth was made free of rivals for the son of Pāṇḍu in the fight.
When the camp was deserted and fled, and supreme glory had been attained,
what indeed was the cause, O Brahmin, by which Kṛṣṇa departed again?
And this cause, O Brahmin, does not appear to me to be a small matter.
O best of Adhvaryu priests, explain in truth everything regarding that place where Janārdana, whose self is immeasurable, came of his own accord; and tell me,
O Brahmin, what was the cause for the certain conclusion of this undertaking.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, this follow-up question which you ask me is worthy of you;
I shall explain it to you correctly, O bull of the Bharatas."

O King, having seen Duryodhana— the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— slain by Bhīmasena in battle, O Bhārata, having seen that great warrior killed unrighteously through a mace-duel after he had transgressed the rules of combat;
Then, O great king, a great fear entered Yudhiṣṭhira as he reflected upon the highly fortunate Gāndhārī, who was endowed with ascetic power; for she,
possessed of such terrible austerity, could consume even the three worlds.
As he was reflecting thus, the thought occurred to him then:
"The first thing to be done is the pacification of Gāndhārī, who is blazing with anger;
for she, having heard that her sons have been slain by us in such a manner,"
Enraged by the fire of her mind, she will reduce us to ashes. How will Gāndhārī endure this intense suffering upon hearing that her son— though he fought fairly— has been slain through deceit?
Having reflected thus in many ways, filled with fear and grief,
Dharmarāja addressed these words to Vāsudeva:
"O Govinda, by your grace, the kingdom has been cleared of its thorns."
"O Acyuta, that which was unattainable even by the mind has been attained by us here;
O mighty-armed one, O delighter of the Yādavas, I witnessed with my own eyes this immense slaughter you suffered in that hair-raising battle."

O mighty-armed Acyuta, just as you formerly rendered assistance in the war between the gods and the asuras for the sake of slaying the enemies of the immortals, and how those enemies of the wise were slain, so too have you rendered us assistance.
And because we were protected by you acting as charioteer, O Vārṣṇeya—
if you had not been the protector of Phalguna in this great battle,
how could this ocean of an army have been conquered in combat?
O Acyuta, you have encountered enemies drawn up in battle array and already vanquished them;
you have endured massive blows from maces and even the striking of iron clubs,
as well as attacks with spears, javelins, lances, and battle-axes.
Indeed, harsh words were received by you who desire our welfare;
O Kṛṣṇa, for our sake you have heard very harsh words, and all those words of yours, O Acyuta, have now borne fruit since Duryodhana has been slain.
In battle, the falling of weapons will indeed be like the touch of a thunderbolt;
O Kṛṣṇa, act in such a way that all of this may not be lost again.
O Kṛṣṇa, our minds have reached the swing of doubt regarding victory.
O mighty-armed Mādhava, understand Gāndhārī’s anger;
for that highly blessed lady has always been emaciated by fierce asceticism,
and upon hearing of the slaughter of her sons and grandsons, she will surely consume us.

O hero, it is my opinion that the time has come to appease her. For what man other than you, O best of men, would be able to look upon her whose eyes blaze with anger and who is emaciated by the calamity that has befallen her son?
"O Mādhava, O subduer of enemies, it pleases me that my going there should take place for the sake of pacifying Gāndhārī, who blazes with anger;
for you are the creator and the transformer, the source and the dissolution of the worlds."
"O one of great wisdom, by means of words endowed with logic and reason, uttered at the proper time, you shall quickly pacify Gāndhārī;
and the venerable Grandfather Kṛṣṇa will also be present there."
"O mighty-armed one, best of the Sātvatas, you who desire the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas must by all means act to quell the wrath of Gāndhārī.
Having heard these words of Dharmarāja, the scion of the Yadu lineage [responded].
Addressing Dāruka, he said, "Let the chariot be made ready. Hearing Keśava’s words, Dāruka then hurriedly reported to the high-souled Keśava that the chariot was prepared.

Having mounted that chariot, Keśava, the best of the Yādavas, the scorcher of foes, the all-pervading lord, proceeded swiftly toward Hastināpura. Then, O great king, the blessed Lord Mādhava set forth on his chariot.
Having reached the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura), the valiant one entered it;
having entered the city, the hero made it resound with the noise of his chariot,
and being recognized by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he descended from his excellent chariot.
Undaunted in spirit, he approached the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
there he saw that best of sages who had arrived earlier. Janārdana then pressed the feet of both Kṛṣṇa and the king.
Keśava, remaining composed, offered his salutations to Gāndhārī as well.
Then Adhokṣaja, the best of the Yādavas, taking the hand of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, wept aloud.
Having shed tears born of grief for a moment,
and having washed his eyes with water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to rule,
that tamer of foes spoke these humble words to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O Bhārata, there is nothing concerning the past or the future that is unknown to you;
O Lord, how time has unfolded is well known to you.
All this was done by the Pāṇḍavas, who act in accordance with your will.
O Bhārata, how might the destruction of the lineage and the kṣatriya order be avoided?
Out of love for dharma, he made an agreement with his brothers and remained patient; though capable, he accepted exile in the forest after being defeated by the fraud of the dice game.
And the practice of living in concealment, disguised in various guises,
as well as many other hardships, were endured by me constantly as if I were powerless;
and when the time for battle arrived, I myself came forth.
In the presence of the entire world, you were asked for five villages;
yet, impelled by Time and driven by greed, you did not grant them.
O King, through your transgression, the entire warrior class has gone to its destruction.
You were constantly entreated for peace by Bhīṣma, Somadatta, Bāhlīka, Kṛpa,
Droṇa along with his son, and the wise Vidura;
yet you did not act accordingly.

O Bhārata, everyone whose mind is struck down by Time becomes deluded, just as you were previously when this matter was undertaken. For what else can it be but the conjunction of Time? Indeed, destiny alone is the ultimate resort.
And do not, O Great King, harbor ill-will toward the Pāṇḍavas;
there is not even the slightest transgression on the part of the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
whether in accordance with dharma, justice, or affection, O scorcher of the foe.
Having understood all this to be the fruit produced by your own faults,
you ought not to harbor malice toward the sons of Pāṇḍu;
for it is they who preserve the family, the lineage, the ancestral offerings, and whatever fruits are derived from having sons.
Today, the sovereignty over the Pāṇḍavas has been established for both you and Gāndhārī.
You yourself, O tiger among men, and the illustrious Gāndhārī—
do not, O tiger among men, grieve over any offense committed against the Pāṇḍavas.
Reflecting upon all this and your own transgression, regard the Pāṇḍavas with benevolence; homage to you, O bull of the Bharatas!
And you know, O mighty-armed one, what the King of Dharma’s affection for you is.
O tiger among the Bharatas, his devotion and affection were natural;
yet, having wrought this slaughter of his malevolent enemies,
he burned with grief day and night and found no peace.
O tiger among men, O best of the Bharatas, grieving for both you and the illustrious Gāndhārī, he finds no peace;
overcome by profound shame, he does not come to see you.

Having thus spoken to the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra— who was tormented by grief for his sons and whose senses were bewildered by his intellect— the best of the Yadus addressed these supreme words to Gāndhārī, who was emaciated by sorrow.
"O daughter of Subala, listen to what I shall say to you, O lady of excellent vows.
There is no woman in this world today who is your equal, O auspicious one.
And I know, O Queen, how [you behaved] in the assembly hall in my presence."
O auspicious lady, you have spoken words consistent with dharma and artha, beneficial to both sides, yet they were not heard by your sons;
and Duryodhana, seeking victory, was addressed by you with harsh words.

"Listen, O fool, to my words: where there is dharma, there is victory. That very principle has now come to pass in your case, O princess. Knowing this, O auspicious lady, do not set your mind on grief."
"O highly blessed lady, may your mind never at any time be inclined toward the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas;
for by the power of your asceticism, you are capable of consuming with your eyes, blazing with anger, the entire earth with all its mobile and immobile beings."
Having heard the words of Vāsudeva, Gāndhārī spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed Keśava, it is exactly as you say. My mind has become unsteady, for I am being consumed by mental agonies."
O Janārdana, having heard your words,
she has resolved upon this course; O Keśava, best among men, you, together with those heroic Pāṇḍavas, are the refuge for the blind, aged king whose sons have been slain.
Having spoken these words, Gāndhārī, consumed by grief for her sons, covered her face with her garment and wept aloud.
Then the mighty-armed Keśava [approached] her, who was emaciated by sorrow.
With words joined by logical reasons and causes, the Lord consoled them;
and having comforted Gāndhārī and Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Mādhava,
Keśava, perceived the intention formed by the son of Droṇa.
Then, rising quickly and bowing his head at the feet of Dvaipāyana, O king of kings, he spoke to the Kaurava:
"I take my leave of you, O best of the Kurus; do not set your mind on grief."
"The son of Droṇa harbors an evil intention; for that reason, I have suddenly risen up.
His mind has been set upon the slaughter of the Pāṇḍavas during the night.
Having heard these words, he spoke together with Gāndhārī.
The mighty-armed Dhṛtarāṣṭra said to Keśava, the slayer of Keśin:
"Go quickly, O mighty-armed one, and protect the Pāṇḍavas.
I shall soon meet with you again, O Janārdana."
Then Acyuta departed in haste with Dāruka;
O King, when Vāsudeva had gone, Vyāsa, whose soul is immeasurable and who is adored by the world, comforted Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men.
The righteous Vāsudeva, having accomplished his purpose,
departed from Hastināpura for his camp, O King, desiring to see the Pāṇḍavas.
Having reached the camp at night, he approached the Pāṇḍavas.
Having related that to them, he entered [the city] together with them.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"He was struck on the head with a foot, his thigh broken, and cast down to the earth."
"O Sañjaya, what did my son, who is proud and full of self-importance, say? The king is exceedingly wrathful and has long harbored enmity toward the Pāṇḍavas;
having fallen into the utmost calamity, what did he say in that great battle?"
Saṃjaya said:
"Listen, O King, lord of men, I shall relate to you exactly what occurred,
as it was spoken by the king when he was broken and fallen into that calamity."
O King, with his thigh broken and covered in dust,
the monarch gathered his hair and gazed toward the ten directions;
having restrained his locks with effort, he sighed like a serpent.
Gazing at me with eyes overwhelmed by tears of fury,
he thrashed his arms upon the ground like an elephant in rut,
shaking his disheveled hair and gnashing his teeth against one another.
Reproaching the eldest Pāṇḍava, he sighed and then said this:
"While Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu is our protector, and Karṇa the best among wielders of weapons,
and Gautama Śakuni as well, and Droṇa, the foremost of those who bear arms..."
Upon Aśvatthāman, as well as upon Śalya, the heroic Kṛtavarman,
and other great-souled heroes who have laid down their burdens,
I have reached this state; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
"O mighty-armed one, I, who was once the commander of eleven armies, have reached this state; when Time arrives, no one can transcend it.
You must tell my kinsmen who survive in this battle [of what has happened]."
"Just as I was slain by Bhīmasena through a violation of the rules of combat,
so indeed have many cruel deeds been committed by the Pāṇḍavas against Bhūriśravas,
Karṇa, Bhīṣma, and the illustrious Droṇa."

And this deed, born of infamy, has been committed by the cruel Pāṇḍavas, by which they will incur contempt among the virtuous; such is my opinion. What joy can there be for one endowed with integrity after achieving victory through deceit?
What wise man would approve one who breaks an agreement? What learned person would rejoice after gaining victory through unrighteousness,
as the sinful Vṛkodara, son of Pāṇḍu, now rejoices?
What indeed is more wonderful than this: that today, while I am with my thigh broken,
my head has been crushed by the foot of the enraged Bhīmasena— my head which was once blazing with splendor, endowed with fortune, and surrounded by kinsmen?
O Saṃjaya, that man who acts in this way is indeed honored.
My mother and my father are both well-versed in the dharma of the kṣatriyas;
therefore, O Saṃjaya, they, being afflicted by grief, should be informed of these words of mine.
O Sañjaya, the dependents have been properly maintained, and the earth, including the oceans, has been well-governed. Even while his enemies were still alive, he stood at their very head;
gifts have been given according to his ability, and what was pleasing to his friends has been done.
All my enemies have been subdued; who indeed has fared better than I?
Foreign kingdoms have been traversed and kings have been enjoyed like slaves. My subjects have been treated with kindness; who indeed has fared better than I?
All my kinsmen have been honored, and people worthy of respect have been fully worshipped; I have served this entire triad. Who indeed has fared better than I?
I have issued commands to the foremost of kings, and honor so difficult to attain has been obtained.
Having traveled with such well-bred steeds, who indeed could have a more auspicious end than I?
I have studied according to rule, given gifts, attained a life free from disease, and won the worlds through my own duty; who indeed could have a more auspicious end than I?
"By good fortune, I have not been defeated in battle and reduced to the state of a servant dependent on others;
by good fortune, O Lord, my vast fortune has gone to another upon my death.
This is what is desired by those of the kṣatriya caste who abide by their own duty."
This end has been attained by me; who indeed is more fortunate than I?
By good fortune, I have not turned back from the enmity like an ordinary man defeated; by good fortune, I have not been vanquished by resorting to any kind of dishonest intent.
Just as one might kill with poison a man who is asleep or even heedless,
so has the illustrious Aśvatthāman and the Sātvata Kṛtavarman been struck down by one who has transgressed dharma and violated his pledge.
Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, should also be told these words of mine:
"You ought not to place your trust in the Pāṇḍavas, who have repeatedly acted unrighteously and who violate their agreements."

The king spoke to the Vātikas: "Your son, whose prowess was truth, has been slain by Bhīmasena through unrighteousness in battle. Thus, I [have followed] Droṇa who has gone to heaven, as well as both Śalya and Karṇa."
Vṛṣasena of great heroism, Śakuni the son of Subala,
Jalasaṃdha of great heroism, King Bhagadatta,
the great archer Saumadatti, and Jayadratha the ruler of the Sindhus.
And [he saw] his brothers, who were like himself, led by Duḥśāsana,
as well as the valiant son of Duḥśāsana and both his sons, Lakṣmaṇa;
these and many others of my own kin, by the thousands.
I shall follow behind like a traveler who has lost his caravan.
How will my sister Duḥśalā fare, hearing that her brothers and her husband have been slain— wailing aloud, afflicted by grief?

"Accompanied by his daughters-in-law and granddaughters-in-law, my aged father, the king, together with Gāndhārī, will cry out; what destiny will he meet? Surely Lakṣmaṇa’s mother too, her sons slain and her husband killed,"
The beautiful, large-eyed lady will soon meet her destruction,
if the illustrious Cārvāka, that wandering mendicant eloquent in speech, learns of it; for he will certainly take revenge upon me.
"In the holy Samantapañcaka, renowned throughout the three worlds,
I shall meet my end and attain the eternal worlds.
Then, O noble one, thousands of people were filled with tears.
Having heard the lamentation of the king, the ten directions fled;
the terrible earth, together with its oceans and forests, and all things moving and unmoving,
then trembled with a roar, and the quarters of space became turbid.
Having approached the son of Droṇa, they reported everything as it had occurred—
the conduct during the mace-duel and the slaying of the king—
and having related all that to the son of Droṇa, O Bhārata, they all [stood there].
Distressed by suffering and their minds struck by grief, the disputants meditated for a very long time and then departed as they had come, afflicted with pain. Sañjaya said:
O King, having heard from the Vātikas that Duryodhana had been slain,
the remaining great car-warriors of the Kauravas—
pierced by sharp arrows, maces, *tomaras*, and spears— fled in all directions.
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman the Sātvata,
hurrying on swift horses, arrived at the battlefield;
there they beheld the high-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra struck down.
Like a great *śāla* tree in the forest broken by the force of the wind,
he lay writhing on the ground, drenched in blood,
like a mighty elephant in the wild brought down by a hunter.
Tumbling repeatedly and drenched in a flood of blood,
the discus belonging to the domain of the Sun fell by chance,
like an ocean dried up by a mighty wind.
Like the full moon in the sky with its orb shrouded in frost,
he— long-armed and possessing the prowess of an elephant—
was covered in dust and surrounded on all sides by terrible hosts of spirits and flesh-eating demons.
Just as servants desiring wealth [behave] toward the best of kings— [toward] that tiger among men who,
out of anger, has a frown upon his face and eyes rolling in rage,
like a tiger that has pounced in fury.
But seeing the king fallen upon the earth, all those great archers—
the car-warriors headed by Kṛpa—
were overcome with fainting; descending from their chariots, they rushed to the presence of the king.
And having gazed upon Duryodhana, they all sat down upon the ground.
Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa, his eyes filled with tears and sighing heavily,
spoke to the best of the Bharatas, the lord of the lords of all the worlds.
"Surely there is nothing at all in the human world that cannot be endured, since you,
O tiger among men, lie here covered in dust. For having previously been a king and having commanded the entire earth,"
"O Indra among kings, why do you stand alone today in this desolate forest?
I do not see Duḥśāsana, nor the great car-warrior Karṇa, nor all those friends of yours; what is this, O bull of the Bharatas?"
"Surely it is impossible for anyone to know the course of Destiny, since you,
who once lay at the head of all consecrated kings, now lie here covered in dust, O scorcher of foes."
He swallows the dust along with the grass; behold the reversal of time!
Where is that stainless parasol of yours, O King, and where is the fan?
And where has that great army of yours gone, O best of kings?
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
and joined by neighboring kings—
O Great King, those brothers of yours are equal to Śakra in prowess in battle.

Where have those slayers of enemies, possessed of great strength and prowess— your sons, O illustrious lord of kings, such as Lakṣmaṇa and the other great chariot-warriors— who were once devoted to brotherly affection, gone today?
O tiger among kings, you have created heroes who resemble the full moon through their tranquility, beauty, and splendor, and who possess prowess equal to Jayanta; indeed,
the course of actions is truly difficult to discern when various causes are involved.
Since you, having been the teacher of the world, have come to this state,
it is evident that fortune among all mortals is unstable;
yet, it appears everywhere as if fixed, eternally deluding men.
Constantly contemplated, especially by men who live in seclusion,
it should never be trusted, for by its very nature it is indeed unstable;
this is seen even in you, who were once a fierce rival of Śakra, when you fell into calamity.
"Indeed, today I have reflected upon this world as being impermanent.
Having heard those words of his who was especially distressed,
O King, your son spoke these timely words:
Wiping his eyes with both hands and shedding tears born of grief,
