the lord of men then addressed all those heroes, Kṛpa and the others:
"Such is this law of mortals, ordained by the Creator, so it is said."

The destruction of all beings is brought about by the turning of time; this very destruction has now come upon me, which you yourselves have witnessed directly. Having protected this earth, I have reached this final end.
"By good fortune, I have not turned back in battle in any calamity;
by good fortune, I have never been defeated by kings;
by good fortune, those kings have been repeatedly conquered by me in combat."
"By good fortune I have been slain by those wicked sons of Pāṇḍu, who, being evil-minded, have especially struck me down through deceit and unrighteously in this mace-duel."
"By good fortune, I have constantly exerted my energy while desiring to fight;
by good fortune, many elephants along with their riders have been slain in battle; and by good fortune, all the horses—well-bred, skilled, and swift—are [still] present."
By good fortune, those chariots adorned with gold have been struck down in battle by skilled warriors,
along with their riders, shattered by arrows at the forefront of the fray.
"By good fortune, all these archers, skilled in combat,
have fallen in battle with their limbs pierced by arrows;
by good fortune, my weapons indeed perish instantly in a moment."
"By good fortune I have been slain in battle, my kinsmen and relatives having been killed;
by good fortune I behold you all delivered from this slaughter of men. Alas, I am indeed slain in battle, my kinsmen and relatives having been killed."
"May you be endowed with well-being and prosperity; that is my supreme pleasure.
May you not grieve out of affection for my death, for if the Vedas are authoritative for you, eternal worlds have been won by me."
Considering the power of Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor,
I have not been led away from the well-performed duty of a warrior by him;
since he has been encountered by me, I am not to be pitied in any way whatsoever.
"O Indra among kings, having seen this, my victory proceeds;
you have performed what is worthy and consistent with yourselves. You have constantly striven for victory, yet destiny is difficult to overcome."
Having spoken these words, his eyes clouded with tears,
O Indra among kings, he became silent, utterly overwhelmed by the intensity of his pain. And seeing the king thus possessed by tears and grief, [he remained there].
The son of Droṇa blazed with wrath like the fire at the end of the world. Overcome by anger and wringing his hands together,
he spoke these words to the king in a voice faltering with tears.
"My father was slain by the base through a most cruel deed;
O King, I do not suffer so much because of that as I do today because of you.
Listen, O Lord, to these words of mine as I speak them in truth."
"O best of kings, today I shall be free from my debt to you;
I will do what is pleasing to you by accomplishing this unsurpassed task. O King, tell me whatever you desire in your heart, exactly as you wish."
"O tiger among kings, by my sacrifices, my works of public utility, my gifts, my righteousness,
and my good deeds, I swear by the feet of my father that today I shall [slay] all the Pāñcālas while Vāsudeva looks on."
And all the Sṛñjayas in their entirety,
O King, as well as all the monarchs led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
together with their armies, who remained after the battle.
"O Great King, by every possible means I shall lead [them] to the abode of the King of the Dead;
tonight, O Great King, I will slay the Pāṇḍavas.
Therefore, Your Majesty, you ought to grant me your permission."
Having heard these words of the son of Droṇa, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, your son, the Kaurava,
hearing that speech of the son of Droṇa which produced joy in his mind, spoke these words to Kṛpa.
"O Teacher, quickly bring a jar filled with water.
Having understood those words of the king, that best of Brahmins took a full jar and approached the presence of the king.

O great king, lord of the people, your son said to him: "O best of the twice-born, at my command let the son of Droṇa be consecrated as commander-in-chief; may you have prosperity, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me."

"A Brahmin, especially one who conducts himself according to the duty of a Kshatriya, must fight at the command of the king; thus do those who know the dharma understand. Having heard these words of the king, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, then [acted accordingly]."
By the king’s command, he consecrated the son of Droṇa in the generalship.
Having been consecrated, O great king, he embraced that best of monarchs and departed,
making all the quarters resound with a lion-like roar.
O Indra among kings, Duryodhana too, drenched in a flood of blood,
then entered that night which brought terror to all living beings;
and having quickly withdrawn from that battlefield, O King, they departed.
With minds agitated by grief and devoted to anxious reflection, while Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa were departing, King Aśvatthāman remained there, brooding upon their arrival.
O Indra among kings, when the Gadāparvan— which is desired by men— has been completed,
one should subsequently feed the Brahmins and honor the reciter well.
